summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 4 took a sample of lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found that there was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the lal mirgi powder was adulterated and he accordingly acquitted the respondent, but the High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by it against the acquittal of the Respondent. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: The amendment brought out by the Amending Act was accepted with approval by this Court in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Kacheroo Mal [(1976) 2 S.C.R. 1). The amended section 2(1)(f) is a new one and relates to a distinct and separate article cclass altogether, It seems to us (i) that the last clause 'or is otherwise unfit for human consumption because it consists wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or because it is insectated or on account of any other cause. [470F G] (ii) In the present case there was clear evidence that the article in question was found unfit for its human consumption.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of clause 3 of the order. He was convicted by the trial Magistrate but he did not say anything about it. The Sessions Judge did not accept this ground; at least he did, do not say that anything about the lease deeds were not registered, but only stated something about it and that he did "soft corner for him". He also held that the appellant could be regarded as doing business as a dealer unless a series of transactions by him of sale were proved against him. Held, that the presumption under section 3(2) could not be drawn against him because of the exemption which agriculturists enjoy. On the whole, the presumption was properly reached. Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh, ; , referred to. It is obvious that sub para speaks of storage for sale as a " dealer although goods are not there, because storage has reference to business as an "dealer and that is the essence of the Order. The fiction in the second sub paragraph must be carried to its logical conclusion. If that presumption is not drawn, then the case against him stood unproved because on the whole it was proved that he was an agriculturist and the presumption tinder section 3 (2) of the Act could not therefore be drawn. Manipur administration vs M Nila Chand Singh ; , relied on. Assam Adminis tration vs Mailam Chandra Singh ; ; , distinguished. It need not worry about thecarrying on of business because in our opinion, the appellant has successfully proved that the lands about which the witnesses spoke orally were held by him for purposes of cultivation and he executed a number of lease deeds, produced receipts and proved by oral evidence that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deed deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it is easy to see that the evidence which was "brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. Moreover, no adequate reasons were given for rejecting the testimony of witnesses. The Court however did not think this ground as correct. Manipur Adminis trative vs Mortam Chandra & Anr., ; , followed.

The respondent terminated his tenancy in respect of the suit land for a period of ten years from month to month. The appellant who was the lessee of a piece of land, instituted a suit against the respondent under sections 116 and 106 of the Transfer of Property Act praying that the defendant be ejected on payment of rent at market rate. On an appeal by the plaintiff, the District judge held that the agreement between the parties was really not to create a monthly tenancy but it was merely a contract in which it had been acted upon for the benefit of the respondent and his successors that the landlord had no right to terminate the tenancy as he had no authority to receive them. The District Judge also found, inter alia, that where a lease is created for one year, the tenant held back by virtue of his covenant with payment and acceptance of rent, there was no subsisting tenancy at any time after December, 1926, and the plaintiff 's suit was accordingly dismissed on the ground that the notice to quit served upon him did not fulfil this requirement. On appeal by a re ferred judgment, the High Court reversed the finding of the lower appellate court that the respondent was liable to eviction only on service of 15 days ' notice, expiring with the end of a month of tenancy, and held that as the notice was defective, that was sufficient for dismissal of the said suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that though in his opinion if a periodic tenancy was created at all, it was from monthto year under section 116 of the Indian Transfer of property Act, even though no rent was demanded by the landlord after 1926, but since the terms thereof were not expressed in the proper legal form, it could not be given effect to. Held: (i) As a lease for one ye certain might fairly be inferred from the payment of annual rent, and a stipulation like that would not come within the mischief of section 107 of the . (ii) The tenant 's tenancy was one from month only to month under section 106 Transfer of . If it is no contract in law, the section will be operative and regulate the duration of the lease. It has no doubt been recognised in several cases that the mode in which a rent is expressed to be payable affords a presumption that the tenancy is of a character corresponding there to.

The plaintiff, Trilok Chand Jain instituted a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722.86 against the defendants, M/s. Dagi Ram Pindi Lal and Smt. Budh Wanti Gulati w/o Shri Pindi Kumar Gulati, the appellants herein. During the course of proceedings in the suit, when evidence was being recorded, the plaintiff obtained summons from the court requiring the Income Tax Department to produce in the court records relating to the Income tax Assessment of the defendants M/S Borizeon Industrial Products (P) Ltd., and Bishamber Nath Kaul. The record was also sent by the IncomeTax Officer in a sealed cover alongwith a letter, dated November 1,1972 claiming that it was privileged under Section 137 of the 1961 Act and that no disclosure had been made regarding income tax pertaining to an income tax assessee could be made. The Court considered the first question in the following four situations: (a) where the documents, records etc., in respect of which privilege is claimed were filed by an assessee or a third party after April 1, 1964, in respect for assessment years upto and including assessment year 1961 62 in proceedings for the said assessment years taking place under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922; and (b) Where the documents record, etc. in respect out of which this privilege is sought were filed before an Income Tax Officer after April l, 1964 but before April 1.1964, in case of assessment years 1962 63 and 1963 64 in proceedings relating to assessment years 1965 65 onwards. But on receipt of summons, it was open to the Commissioner of Income tax to consider the matter as provided under Section 138(1)(b) and decide whether it would be (sic) in the public interest to produce or furnish the documents. records etc. summoned for, and submit his view to the Court in answer to the summons. The learned Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the suit. Aggrieved by the judgment of the Division Bench, the Department has preferred this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.

M who was married to Seinarayana and the first three defendants (the appellants) filed a suit for partition against the four branches of his house, alleging that she had given away his properties including immovable property to Se inaba on April 7, 1944 by a registered deed. Mammotty died on May 3, 1946, without an issue, and as such, her husband was entitled to the remaining 4/16 share as heirs of Seinaba. The trial Court dismissed the suit holding that she never made any gift nor had it been proved that possession was given only to a minor of any avail without the intervention of the guardian of the property unless the minor had reached the years of discretion, and were not entitled to hold her husband 's mother as guardian on behalf of her property under the Muhammadan Law. The High Court in second appeal held that the gift was void. On appeal by special leave it was contended for them (i) Though under Mohammedan law a transfer of possession is necessary in a gift by a husband to his minor wife provided such an intention as above described is clearly manifested, and (ii) there must be a tender (ijab); and absolute or unconditional acceptance as required by the Hindu Law. HELD: The decision of the High Court was correct and must be set aside. [554C] A gift can be completed by delivery of possession immediately distinguishes gifts from sales. In such cases the benefit to the minor and the completion of the gift for his benefit is the sole consideration. As in the present case there was a declaration and a tender by the donor Mammosotty and as the gift is by a Registered deed no question can arise. The gift through the mother is a valid gift. [556C D] In the present ease there was only a declaration that possession of the properties must be given to one of the stated guardians of the said property of the minor is not a condition of its validity in certain cases. One such case is gift by the husband to the wife, and another, where there is gift to a Minor who has no guardian of his property in existence. The widow therefore did not complete the gift in this way. There was also no necessity for an actual vacation by the 2nd respondent. [551D E] In any event there could be no question that there was complete intention to divest ownership on the part of the mother as she was living at her mother 's house and to transfer the property to the donee. [550G] The donor must not leave behind even a straw belonging to him to show his ownership and possession. Therefore, it is quite impossible to hold that by handing over the trust deed to his mother in law, in whose charge his wife was during his illness and afterwards Mammothty did not completed his gift in the way. [552A] In such circumstances the gift through father is a binding gift. The respondent relied on two cases reported in ([1932) 59 I.A. 556), Manager of Mother 's College vs Babulal Mia.I.R. , Lakshmi Bai and Anr. vs Abdul Gani, A.I R. (1944) 34 I. A. 155, not approved. Besides, the gift by Mammatty to his wife, was a valid gifts. The appellant 's father had attained puberty and had lived with him, for about 8 1/2 years in the house of his mother and was probably a very sick person though not in marzulmaut. His minor wife who had attained discretion was capable under Muhammadan law to accept the gift on behalf Of her daughter which had attained many times and lived with her husband.

Section 71(1) of the Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 provided that no expenditure in excess of 10% shall be charged by a religious institution for meeting the cost of audit accounts. The respondents who were trustees of a Hindu Religious and charitable endowments Temple challenged the validity of the demand on the ground that sections 21, 30(2), 31, 63 to 69 and 89 was ultra vires and also violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court upheld the plea on the view that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Act and therefore the demand for levy of contribution was not only without jurisdiction or authority of law but was therefor invalid within the legislative competence of the State Legislature. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Under the Act a fee though levied for rendering services of a particular type is not to be, co related to the services performed for each individual who is intended to obtain the benefit of the services. The co relation must be between the expenses incurred by the authority levying the fees for generally providing the service and the aggregate of the levy from persons who are to be made subject thereto. It is a necessary corollary that under the Act general rules prescribing the levy of fee from religious endowments have to bemade, and not rules governing individual endowments. The Act does not contemplate separate rules to be framed in respect of each religious institution likely to obtain it degree of service as others may. [919 G H] (ii) Under section 76(2) a fee although levied for performing services of particular type was not to fall within the mischief of that character merely because there is an element of compulsion or coerciveness present in it, nor is it a postulate of a fee that it must have direct relation to the ac tual service rendered by the authorities levying the fee for generally.

The appellant, who was alleged to have been committing an offence under section 19(1) of the , was issued with a notice. Later, the High Court directed the issue of the notice on the prima facie view that the case was fit one for drawing up the proceeding by issuance of a notice under section 17 of the Act to show cause against the appellant 's alleged liability to be punished under Section 15, and, accordingly, issued notice to him to showcause why he should not be proceeded against for committing contempt of the High court. The appellant submitted that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right under section 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure from an order issuing notice as nothing yet had been decided by the High Courts and, therefore, the preliminary objection raised on behalf of the respondents was well founded and must be accepted as correct. It would appear from a plain reading of the section that an appeal shall lie as of right from any order or decision of a bench of the court in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt. No appeal can lie as a matters of right. The proceeding is initiated under section 7 by issuance issuing of a "no final order", but there may be many interlocutory orders passed in the said proceeding by the Court. It could not be the intention of the legislature to provide for an appeal to this court as a question of right, from each and every such order made by the said High Court after the expiry of a period of one year from the date on which the contempt is alleged to has been committed, does not decide any question. [512G] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra (A.I.R. 1976 S.C 1206) referred to.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another, for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the , and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. The question that arises for consideration is whether the amendments inserted by the 1949 Act in 1933 were saved by reason of section 4 Of the 1952 Act. Held, that a statute which was amended by the amending Act did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the repealing Act. But the said principle has been succinctly stated in Maxwell on Interpretation of Statutes, 10th Edition, page 406: Where the provisions Of one statute are, by reference incorporated in another and the earlier statute is afterwards repealed the provisions so in corporated obviously continue in force so far as they form part of the second enactment. Emperor vs Sir Khuda Bux I.L.R. , Benoy Kumar Roy vs State of West Bengal (1954) Punj. 763, approved. Further, there was no foundation for this argument and the entire premises is wrong, and section 4 of the 1952 Ordinance had no application to a case of a later amending Act introducing new provisions in an earlier Act, for, where an earlier act was amended under that Act and it was in force when the offence was committed by a person. That apart, there are no merits in the contention. Khuda Bask vs Manager, Caledonian Press Chakravartti, C.J., neatly brought out the purpose and (2) section 4 did not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus.

The respondents are certain idols, represented by their managing Shebait Ram Govinda Roy. The idols were the family deities of the Roys of Bonpash in the district of Burdwan and the number of Shebaits being very large there was a recognised usage in this family that the seniormost member amongst the descendants of the founder acts as the managing Shebaits and it is he who manages the endowed properties and looks after the due performance of the worship of the idols. It is not disputed by the parties that it is within the competence of the managing authorit to borrow money to meet the necessities of the Idols, and accordingly a decree for possession was passed against them. There were prayers in the applications under section 36(6)(a) (ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for reopening of the two compromise decrees mentioned above which were made for reopening the suits and making of fresh decrees in their places in accordance with the provisions of the Act, as there are prayers also for restoration of the properties mentioned in Schedules Ka, Kha and Ga to the deities under the provision of section 36 (2)(c). The trial judge decided the two applications and granted them prayers in both the applications. On appeal by both the parties the High Court affirmed that decision and dismissed both the appeals. Held, that a proceeding under section 16 of the Provincial Money Lender Act will be confined to reopening of a decree as well. That it cannot be disputed that the court sofens a decree under section 39(2)(d) only for the purpose and so far as it is necessary to give relief to the borrower in the manner provided for in the Act namely, to release him from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the , it cannot also be disputed in that case the court has not only the right but is under a duty to make an enquiry as to whether the ostensible purchaser at the execution sale or the person who purports to have acquired an interest therein under a subsequent transfer from the decreeholder purchaser, has bonafide acquired such rights within the meaning of clause (b) and give the judgment debtor consequential relief under clause (c). That inquiry, it seems to, is altogether outside the purview of section 6(2) of Bengal Money lenders Act. The object of restoring possession of the property sold in execution of a money decree to the judgment debtors is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues, but it does not mean that in making a new decree under clause(a) of section36 (2) and giving the judgmentdebtor consequential relief as contemplated by cls. (b), and (c) of that sub section the court can at all enter into the question as to what the ostensible purchasers had obtained, the properties restored to the judgement debtor under cl.(c). If the purchaser is a mere benamidar for the decree holder, clause (g), subsection(2), of the section would not afford protection to him in any way. He could not be regarded as a person other than the decree debtors acquiring rights bona fide as contemplated in that clause. Consequently, there was no proof of the decreeholders being in possession of a property either by themselves or through Oramba Sundari. In such circumstances the court should have been satisfied with regard to these properties and the impugned order for restoration must be held to be correct.

During the pendency of a suit for the recovery of money due under 0. XXII, r. 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the appellant, the respondent instituted a suit in the Bombay City Civil Court for the recover of Rs. 7,113 7 0 9/ and interest at 4% per annum on the ground that the decree was not in existence at the date of the document but did have effect from the date when it became operative. The respondent resisted the suit by contending (1) that the transaction alleged to have been effected between him and his heirs was not a transfer in writing within the meaning of 0. XXI, r . 16 of the Civil Procedure Code; (2) that in any case the contract did not apply to the service and the order of assignment fell within the principle of those two decisions and therefore the equitable principle came into play and could not be applied as soon as the decree had been passed there would he no transfer and (3) that under O.XXI, r., 16 of Code, a transferee of the decree cannot make two applications one for recording the assignment and another for executing the decree. Held, that in view of the provisions of 0, XXI, rule 16 of 0 . XXI, rr. 1(2)(b), 21(1) and 21 (2)(d) of the , the respondent cannot claim to be a transferee within the expression "decree holder" as contained in O. XXI r. 16 of order XXI, Rule 16 of Order XXI, C.P.C.

The respondent carried on the business of fabricating and selling window and doors. The contract which was entered into by the respondent contained certain terms : " Item Rate tender for Works 1/We hereby tender for the execution of the President of India of the work specified in the written memorandum within the time specified therein, and in accordance with all respects and modifications as applicable". The respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division; its tender was accepted and the respondent carried out the contract. Thereafter a bill for assessing tax on the price for sale of materials only. The Board of Revenue exercising revisional power confirmed the order passed by the Deputy Commissioner observing that the contract undertaken by the appellant was not a contract of service. The High Court held that the contractor 's contract was one of sale of goods and the amount received by the Respondent was not taxable., but held that it was usual for manufacturers or dealers in specialised articles to arrange to "fix" and "service" the articles sold by them and on that account the contract did not acquire the character of a contract for sale. In appeal to this Court, HELD : 1. It is only upon the "fixing" of 'the window leaves and when the windows were not properly fixed" the contract would not be complete, and the property in the goods passing under the terms of the contract [582 H; 508 A C] 2. The object of the respondent was to enter into a works contract. That clearly appears from the terms Of the tender and its acceptance. The windows were to be fabricated according to the specifications with glass plain or ground as decided by the Engineer in Charge, and were to "fixed" within six months from the date of its acceptance 'to the building with rawl plugs in cut stone work. " The rate quoted by the responddard was based on the current price of mild steel billets fixed by the Government. The rate was based upon the current prices of m disturbing steel billet, and that the price was to be revised in the light of cost revision of the controlled price of steel supplied to the respondent. [516 G] 3.

The prosecution alleged that on December 8,1967 Shankar Lal handed over the formal order to the said 's name by putting his mark near his mark. P., and quashed the charges framed against him on the grounds that so much as Raj Kr. Agawallela was a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat the accused.

The Indian Railways Act, 1890 prescribed various safety measures; based on experience, the Railway Board through which apex body the administration was run and controlled was also improved. The method of carrying out such schemes was found to be completely inadequate keeping in view the size of the Railways and volume of passenger traffic it made it obligatory for drivers of motor vehicles to stop short of unmanned level crossings, observe and then proceed. With a view to educating the users of the roads wide publicity is given through newspapers, cinema slides, commercial broadcasting and the television about the hazards involved while negotiating a new line crossings in consultation with appropriate State Governments. As far as manned level crossing crossings are concerned there were as many as 14471 of them as on March 1, 1982; unmanning level cross remarks on the Railways, and if all of them were to be manned, a capital expenditure of 330 crore rupees would be necessary and similarly an annual recurring expenditure of Rs.44 crores will have to be met. Most of the States have framed rules under the making it obligatory duty for drivers to stop Short of unmmanned crossings when their codal life was over. There were as few as many 14471 unmaned level crosses on the Railway and if any all of these were to he manned were to manned. A total life of 80 years for steel work and 100 years for masonry part of the bridges stipulated in the Railway Code is for the purpose of provision in the depreciation Reserve Fund. The codal Life does not have any direct relevance with the condition of a bridge and there is no necessity of rebuilding a bridge when its codal lives was over, but there has been no instance where the work of bridge rebu fire had occurred owing to structural failure of any bridge or girders. The petitioner has alleged that unmannerned level Crossings were gradually being replaced by manned ones and improved technical gadgets are being provided for efficient operation. Relying on the Sikri Committee Report of 1978, it had been contended that there are nearly 12000 bridges on the railways out of which 195 are important bridges and almost 9400 are major bridges. It was further pleaded that every bridge is annually inspected and continuous record is maintained in regard to every bridge in the bridge register; it is said that the total life does not has any direct relevancy with the conditions of a Bridge and there has accordingly been no necessity for rebucies a bridge, when its system codalian life is over. It had also been pleaded that there were nearly 120000 bridges onRailways out of Which 195 are vital bridges. The matter was heard by a Bench consisting of three Judges of this Court as the petitioner who was an allopathic doctor by profession had himself drafted and filed on behalf of the Central Government and who was one of them, gave his consent to act as arbitrator for conducting inquiry about the numerous train accidents from 1970 onwards and for several other directions. The Judge set aside the award in respect of the petitioner and directed the respondents to give adequate powers to the Railways to provide such level crossing facilities at their cost in view of the accepted position that at a level crossing the right of way is of the train in preference to the traffic on the road. The Court also held that the State Governments appeared to be aware of their responsibilities in this matter and about 2/3 of the funds of the Safety Works had been utilised by March 31, 1982, while admitting that in the initial period utilisation of funds was poor and finalisation of schemes for over bridges and under bridges was slow, the situation is claimed to have improved and in 1982 83 as manyas 15 works in different States involving an expenditure of more than Rs.22 crores have been cleared.

The appellants had applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer, Baroda under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, in respect of their proprietary jagirs. Against the award of compensation made by the Jagir Act, the appellants preferred appeals before the Revenue Tribunal constituted under the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Act, 1957. The High Court dismissed the applications holding that they were time barred and dismissed their applications for restoration on merits, but the Tribunal held that they should have been prevented for sufficient cause from appearing at the hearing of the appeals, and remanded the cases to the Tribunal for being reheard and dealt with in accordance with law. In appeal to this Court it was contended by the appellants that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, they could not be said to have decided the appeal on merits even though there was default on the part of the appel lants. Held: The language of Regulation 20, on its true interpretation, applies not only to a case where the appeal has been decided on merits but also to a particular case where an appeal has also been dismissed for want of prosecution under Regulation 19(1). It is open to the Revenue in such a case to hear the respondent to the appeal and decide it on merits. In such a ease to hear an respondent to appeal and determine it on its merits, if he satisfies the Tribunal that he had no notice of the date of hearing or that he was prevented by sufficient cause for appearing when the appeal or application is called for hearing, the Revenue may restore the appeal/ appli cation or 'appeal ' to its file provided that where the other party has appeared in the appeal Or applica tion or such party satisfies the Tribu nal that he bad no notice thereof of the day of hearing, either preliminary or final and the application was heard ex parte.

The first appellant was the son of another village in Madhya Pradesh. The respondent was the grandson of this village by name of G. After the partition in 1896, the respondent was founded on two branches (i) G and P. He became a trustee of the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy and also a public trust; (ii) G as trustees of the said temple acted as trustee of G and thus also committed breaches of trust. On a consideration of the evidence the trial court held that there had been no valid dedication in respect of the village Telibandha for the temple by the Panch Faisla Award of 1896. As regards the Bagchi Award, the Trial Court held that a valid trust had been created in favour of the temples and it was a public religious trust. The High Court agreed with the trial Court that the dedication by G as made in Para. 2 of the Panch Aenochna Award of 1797 could not have any legal effect in respect thereof. In appeal to this Court, Held: (1) By virtue of section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, an absolute dedication of the property had been made in favour by one person against whom it was vested and the mode of enforcement of such right was laid down in the latter Act. The use of words "in that time" would not make Ramsaranlal the absolute owner of the whole village but give him possession and management of the estate for the benefit of his son as also to keep the property in proper custody for a period of 3 years from the date on which it was absolutely given. (2) The use by the words "at that time", by this award Teliavati had created absolute interest in favour the temple and could not affect the operation or validity of the absolute nature of the dedication. (3) The word "Malik" or "Milkiyat" by saying that somebody was to be the Malik or is to have the Milkiyat, this is merely a presumption which can well be displaced by what follows in the same document as regards this very property. When all these different provisions are considered it appears to be clear beyond any shadow of doubt that the intention was not to make Ramrani mouzas Borsi and P who connote full proprietary rights unless there is something in the context or in the surrounding circumstances which indicate that absolute rights were not intended to be conferred. (4) The words "entire estate" in the opening clause of this Panch Fairsala raises a presumption that absolute interest was given thereby to Ramsarhan Lal absolutely with only a charge on it for the temples. When the document (the Panch Faidasramla Award) clearly and unambiguously shows anabsolute dedication of R and R, the two courts were right in construing the intention of the testator to have been that the widow of his S should not take an absolute estate which she should during that period go to the temple. (5) The case was one of absolute dedication founded on the assumption that the property belonged to the family with only five issues which were framed in the suit and without deciding which the suit could not be properly disposed of.

The three appellants before this Court were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the1987 Bar Association. There were three charges against the appellants. The first charge against them was that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a most improper manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar. The text of the resolution was this "The Action Committee is of the opinion that the Acting Chief Justice is acting in the discharge of administrative power under cl 14 of the U.P. High Court 's Amalgamation Order, 1948 in a highly impartial manner under its influence of Allahabad Bar quite unbecoming of the office which he held." The second charge against the first accused was that he had met the Chief Judge when he issued that resolution for publication in newspapers. This was not done by him. By his order dated 22 May 1974 the High Court discharged the notices. On appeal to this Court it was contended, inter alia, that they were responsible for passing of the Resolution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The language used by them was unfortunate and unfortunate. [606C] It is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. If lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent.[606F G] In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the foregoing observations. [ 603A B] The language employed by the appellants was unfortunate.

Under an unregistered deed of sale between the four brothers, the appellants were entered into with one of the three arbitrators. The disputes related to certain properties among the brothers in Chinsurah district of Hooghly in the State of West Bengal. The dispute related to some property amongst the brothers and the same was referred to three Arbitrators. On or about 2nd July, 1977, the arbitrator explained their award to the parties and made and signed the award. On 14th August, 1978 the arbitrators made an application before the Sub Judge praying for a direction on the arbitrator to file the award in the Court in Misc. Case No. 74 of 1977 initiated by the appellants. The appellants filed an applica tion under section 14 of the . The learned Munsif dismissed the application and did not direct return of the award holding that limitation for registration of the Award had already expired. The High Court, however, quashed the registration under Article 227. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (i) that an award affecting immovable properties as in the instant case should be registered. This period is to say from 28th January 1978 to 24th November, 1983, the award was in the court and it bears the date of the order directing maintenance of status quo; (ii) that the only period which should be excluded was from 26th July, 1978 till 20th December, 1982; and (iii) that there was an injunction on 26th April, 1978 restraining the appellants from taking any steps. The learned Judge however, allowed the application on the ground that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the Arbitrators could not take back the award for presenting it for registration. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant was a tenant for about 20 years in the premises known as " Fida Ali Villa". The sub tenants, three of them also shifted to the new place which were let by the respondent. Under an agreement between the appellant and the respondent it was agreed that the appellant would vacate and the respondents let out a portion of his new building which would be erecting an additional construction thereon and after obtaining possession the re spondent, on the ground of non payment of rent, sub letting of the premises. The trial court held that subletting was lawful in spite of section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act 1947, but on appeal the Assistant Judge reversed the order of ejectment. On further appeal, the High Court affirmed the order. Held, that under section 15 Of the Act no restriction could be imposed by any conduct or agreement of parties unless there was in the Act itself any provision to the contrary such rights as far they were personal rights may be parted with or renounced by the landlord and consequently he could not evict the appellant under section 13(1)(e) of the Act. Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Co., , referred to. The maxim " must not be understood as meaning that where a transaction is vitiated by illegality the person left in possession of goods after its completion was always and of necessity entitled to keep them, the consequence must follow that the party in possession will not be disturbed ". In the instant case, the question must be answered accordingly.

In pursuance of a contract dated September 10,1957 entered into between the appellant and the respondent Bank as security for cash credit facility, the appellant bank issued a cheque dated September 16, 1957 to the respondent bank asking it to give security for the cash credit by pledge of groundnut oil as also an personal guarantee of the surety and the latter undertook to provide such quantity of goods as would be provided full cover to the outstanding balance in the cash account. The Bank had appointed a Godown keeper to look after the goods pledged by the principal debtor and the bond executed by the respondent was duly reduced into writing. But for some correspondence, the respondent received from the appellant an adverse inference against the respondent. Thereupon the respondent filed a suit claiming that the Bank had agreed to grant cash credit facilities to deceased principal debtor on the security of goods by way of pledge and that though the goods were to be kept in the godown in the compound of Vijay Oil Mills Pvt. Ltd., but the godown was to be taken under lock and key of the Bank, it wrongfully parted with the goods without the consent of the respondent and therefore the surety was discharged. The trial Court decreed the suit against the surety but on appeal by the surety, was set aside mainly on the ground that the High Court had erred in holding that the two promissory notes were independent of the pledge of the goods given by the bank to the Bank as also the bond, executed by it, and that the respondent had offered two securities, one the pledge, of goods and the other personal guarantee to the surety. On appeal by special leave: HELD: 1. There is nothing in clause 5 of the agreement which would justify this conclusion. [924G] 2. Clause 5 confers right upon the creditor Bank to grant any time or indulgence in payment of the debt or to determine, enlarge or vary its credit and to take other securities or release any other securities held by it but such an act on the part of the bank would not have the effect of discharging the surety or in any manner affecting his liability under the letter of guarantee. It is not a case of granting time or 203 indulgence to the principal creditor or variation of the credit or taking one set of security in substitution of some other security or release of any security. Clause 7 provides for non discharge of surety even if the creditor bank enters into a composition with the principal offender and that, the surety would nonetheless be liable even if he has guarantee, security or remedy guarantees, securities or remedies from the principal debtors. That clause covers both the situations where the debtor has offered more than one security by way Of pledge of goods. [936A] 3. [The appellant bank was the plaintiff and its suit was decreed by the trial court, i.e. the Court of first instance. The decree had been reversed by the High court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. [963H; 967B] 4. In this case since there is a mortgage bond given in respect of a debt which is subsequently guaranteed, the creditor must hold the security for him the benefit of that real and substantial security in the event of his being called on to fulfil his duty as a surety, and to pay the debt for which he had so become surety.

The appellant was a member of the "patelki inam" which was originally known as " Patelski Inam lands. The lands in suit were comprised in six survey numbers stated by one of the plaint. These two plots lay in village Nawabag, a jagir village of Ellichpur (now Archalpur) taluq of Berar and we shall give some more details of that jagir. On the question whether the karnam service Inam " lands in the suit were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for services to be rendered by the patel, Held, that the appellant was entitled to his share in the "Patelki Inam" lands as a member thereof and not as an undivided brother of the patels. The grant was on a consideration of the entire village in which he was living and had no interest therein. Under section 3 of the Pate Orasa Act, 1886, the emoluments appertaining to the office of the village accountant were subject to orders passed by the revenue authorities in respect of matters mentioned therein and no right was given to a member to claim a share in emoluments. Venkataswami vs Veerabadrayya, (1947) L. R. 55 I. A. 222, distinguished. The appellant could only succeed if he establishes that he had a right to the share in them and Government had in any case directed that each pateraki inam " lands be resumed and regranted to him. In a revenue case of 1963, the settlement will be made with the head member of that family holding the office or enjoying the inam and who will be held alone responsible for the maintenance of the service record.

A Hindu al ty, a Brahmin abets and a member of a joint family, after the coming into force of the , was governed by the customary law in matters of succession and inheritance. The appellant was born to India on March 22, 1955 leaving two ancestral properties and securities of the value of Rs. 25,778/ . He claimed that some four or five hundred years ago they were converted to Islam like the members of another such sect, that they migrated thence to Cutch and from there spread themselves to Bombay, Madras and other places. Their case was that despite their conversion, the Cutchi Memons retained a large part of Hindu law as their customary law including its concept& joint family property, the right of a son by birth in such properties pro perty and its devolution by survivorship constituted the customary Law of Cutchi memons in Madras and Bangalore. Held, that the rule of Hindu Law applicable to Hind intestate and inheritance was applicable only to matters of inheritance and succession , and not to the customary Hindu law. The Hindu females did not acquire any interest by birth or by birth, and thus the ancestral property absolutely vested in Haji Aboo Bucker Sait 's case (A.I.R. 1937 Mad. 1) and that Act did not make a Mahomedan law applicable to Indian citizens . The order of the High Court was set aside. Section 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not retrospective in operation and could not affect the application of the Hindu Law to the Indian citizen 's property on the ground that it would be inconsistent with the general rule which laid down in section Haji Abo Buckers Sait vs Dharanavva, A.I.,R. 1936 Mad. 844. The appeal must accordingly be allowed.

The appellants purchase yarn from the manufacturer of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage and, thereafter subjected to an integrated process in the composite mill of the appellants for weaving the same into fabrics. The yarn so obtained is further processed in an integrated system in the said composite mill for weaving in the process. The fabric so obtained was further processed by a separate integrated process. In the manufacture of identical goods, yarn was obtained at the intermediate stage. The appellants do not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also did not dispute their liability in respect of yarn which is also removed from the Factory. It is a case of the appellant that even after amendment there must be removal of the goods from one place to another for the purpose of collection of excise duties. The plea of the respondent, that the classification made by the Central Board of Excise has wrongly laid down an exception in respect Of yarn which was obtained by the appellants at an intermediary stage and thereafter subjected thereto for an integrated operation process, is without any substance and is rejected. It was contended on behalf of the respondents that even assuming that there can be fictional removal as provided under Explanation to Rules 9 and 49, there cannot be such fictional or deemed removal without the specification of the place where the excisable goods are produced, cured or manufactured, but also removal within such place or premises for captive consumption or consumed 'home consumption ', as it is called. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1 (2) The High Court was right in holding that the appellants were not liable to pay excise duty and therefore they were liable to claim excise duty under the Explanation to Rule 9 and Rule 49. [714C D] (3) Even assuming that no specification has been made by a Collector of such place, or premises appurtenant thereto, the provision of deemed removal as contained in the explanation to Rule 173G, does not mean a removal from one part to another, but provides that excisable goods produced or manufactured in any place and consumed or utilised for the manufacture or processing of excisable goods. [700B] (4) It is only when the goods are removed from factory premises it will be a case where removal is made within the factory for the manufacturer or manufacture of another commodity inside the factory, that there is removal within the meaning of Rules 9 & 49. The Explanation to rule 173A and the proviso thereto contemplate collection of duty levied on the production of a commodity at an earlier intermediate stage of such process for the manufacturing end product or commodity. It does not contemplate any deemed removal, but a physical and actual removal of goods from a factory factory or any other place or thing of production or manufacture or a warehouse etc. [807F G] (5) The words "place of removal" in Rule 9(1) refer to the specification that has been given retrospective effect by virtue of section 2 of the Finance Act, 1982. [908G] (6) The word 'place of manufacture ' may be a factory orany other place/ premises of production etc.

It is alleged that after the life time of Gopalakrishna, his son and heir of any predeceased son living at that time shall enjoy the property subject to identical charges as absolute owners with right of sale, gift etc. There were further directions in case of other contingencies with which we are not concerned. Held, that when the objection on the score of the landlord being a holder of life interest and hence incapable of invoking section 14(1)(b) fails the suit must be decreed. M/s. Raval and Co. vs K. G. 276 Ramachandra and others, [1954] S.C.R. 869, relied on. M. Gopalakrishna is issuelessless on account to augment his business or to get better returns on his investment. The land of the respondent decree holder in the execution proceed ings was the right in trees. After that decision, which, according to aPPellant judgment debtor constitutes a complete answer to any further execution proceedings in respect of any part of bhumidhari rights, execution should have proceeded against trees in groves and the view taken by the execution court, that there is a distinction between trees and grove land and grove lands. [41C; 42D] In view of this very clear legal position, the Court was not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut trees, which are parts of groves. And an inseparable part is always included in the whole. [42F G] If what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the left right in the trees of grove as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary and this means that "grove land" and an "intermediary 's groves are equated and groves were on ly collection of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them. The uncut t trees are deemed to be parts of the "land". Therefore, on the facts of the case, there was a distinction inter est between trees which are part of forest lands, and grove plot land and the grove land should have been upheld by the Division Bench. [43A B] Section 18(1)(a) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act provides that an " verticalmediary" 's grove" is bhumidhari property. Rights in it are part only of bhumiswami rights. After these clear words of the enactment, the court held that there was no distinction between, trees and a grove and grove and land.

In a prosecution for offences punishable under Sections 143, 147 148 and 149 IPC on the basis of the prosecution evidence found accused No. 1 Subran, guilty of an offence punishable under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. Accused Nos. 2 to 6 were convicted for an offence under Sec. 326/149 IPC but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. On an appeal before the High Court by the six accused appellants, the conviction and sentence recorded against them was set aside. In view of the limited notice issued by this Court earlier, it is directed that issue notice limited to the question as to the nature of offence and the quantum of sentence, and, therefore, to the four appellants accepting, as established the prosecution case against the four accused beyond a reasonable doubt. 90 The five eye witnesses PW3 Devass Balakrishnanutty, PWs 6 and 7 salesmen and his assistant in the arrack shop and PW8 Unni @ Velayudhan turned hostile, and did not support the prosecution, and no motive for commission of the crime was established at the trial. The High Court acquitted two of the accused and convicted the remaining four only. The appellants were sentenced to undergo life imprisonment. On appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) there was enmity between the two groups on account of illicit distillation and suspicion of information being passed on to the Excise officials; (2) the deceased had received injuries with a chopper, iron rod, cycle chain and the chopper; and (3) the testimony of PW4 was not cogent as it established that the injuries caused by the first appellant with chopper were inflicted with the intention to cause the death of the deceased. Allowing the appeal of the State for reducing the sentence, this Court, HELD: 1. The existence of an unlawful assembly is a necessary postulate for invoking Section 149 IPC. Where the existence of such an unlawful unlawful assembly was not proved, the. conviction with the aid of section 149 cannot be recorded or sustained. The failure of the Prosecution to show that the assembly was unlawful must necessarily result in the failure of discharge of the charge under Section 149. [92B C] 2. In a case like this, where the existence is not proved and the appreciation of evidence cannot be made, it would not be permissible for a Court to take into consideration the nature or weapons with which they were armed and nature and seat of the injuries, it could also be contended that all the four Appellants also had shared the common intention of causing such bodily injuries on the deceased as were likely to cause death of his. [93G] 3.

The respondent assessee filed returns in which it stated that it was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis and since it did rot actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax was payable by it. The I.T.O completed the assessment for the first two assessment years on the basis of the returns. For the assessment year 1969 70, the assessee filed its return through the Indian Company. The collaboration agreement between the assessee and the Jwnese company expired in 1965. It was renewed too expired in November 1970 and for the assessment years 1967 68, 1968 69, 1969 70 and 1.970 71, however, he refused to accept the assessee 's plea that it is maintaining its accounting accounts on cash basis and not on mercantile on mercantile account. Since it came to filing of the return for the year 196970 and 1970 71, no Tax was payable from it on the amounts disclosed and further that it did not take credit for the said amounts in the books at Coventry. The Income Tax Officer completed the assessments for the next two assessment periods on the footing that it had maintained its accounts regularly and since as it didoles actually receive income in both the four years no tax is payable by the assessee. The appeal filed by the respondent assessee was dismissed holding that it would not change the method of accounting to suit its convenience without the approval of the I. T.O., completed the assessing for the four assessment years 1969 70 71 and 197071 on correct basis, showing that the method adopted by the Income Tax officer was mercantile, that for the A.Y. 1967 68 it had been maintaining its account on mercantile foundation alone and that it also took the rather strange plea that the Indian company was not aware of the assessee system of accounting in regard to royalty and that, therefore, it had committed a mistake in filing the returns for the years 1967 69 and 1968 69. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the assessment orders for the past years relating to the assessee reveal that the mode of accounting was mercantile and that for a.Y., 1967 68 the assessee did not actually receive the amount nor did it take credit from the account books at COventry, and that the alleged statement in the returns relating to assessment years 1968 69 and 1969 69 was based upon the said premise. The Tribunal however held that even with respect to the accounting years relevant to the assessment period 1967 68 and 1968 71, it has been maintaining accounts on a cash basis, and since no part of the royalty amount had been received by it and therefore nothing is taxable, the question of method of assessment adopted by it must be examined afresh and for that purpose allowed the appeals and remanded the matters to the Income tax Officer. On a reference made at the instance of Revenue, the High Court answered the question in the negative against the assessee: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Appellate Tribunal was right in holding that royalty amounts should be assessed on cash agencies basis for 1967 68. 1968 69 assessment if the books and balance sheets of such receipts were found to be maintained on cash foundation and directing fresh assessment on such basis." The High Court also answered the reference against the revenue assessee. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 145(1) should not be permitted to be applied in such circumstances as those while arise from the facts of this case.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. On appeal, the High Court altered the conviction and sentence on the testimony of the approver and found corroboration for the approver 's testimony in the statement of the main witness. With great respect to the High court, it is impossible to agree that without corroboration of the accomplice qua the appellant the conviction is unsustainable, the law being that there should be corroboration of his approver in material particulars and qua each accused. There is no corroboration of tile approver ' story which would be sufficient to connect the appellant with the murder, under section 34, Indian Penal Code. Held also that though the conviction of an accused on the evidence of an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal yet the courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence Of such a witness without corroboration in material facts particulars. The law may be stated in the words of Lord Reading C. J. in R. vs Baskerville (1918) L.R. 76 I.A. Mad. 308, 836 and section 114 illustration (b), may be that in this case the approver "s evidence was sufficiently corroborated for the convictionof the first accused upon which we express no opinion but so far as the appellant is concerned there is no corroborated corroboration of that story and it is not sufficient that there is evidence to corroborate the participation of the first or any other accused in the murder. Bhuboni Sahu vs The King, A.I.R,, Mad.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He also opened one in the terminal 'and the other in the body of the suit board. P.Ws. 16, 17, 18, 28, 29, 30 and 31 were charged with offences under section 5 (2) read with section 5 of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1964 for obtaining Rs. 180/ as bribe by resorting to corrupt and illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as public servant. The prosecution case was that on July 8, 1961 the Electrical Engineer accompanied by one Head Clerk and two others who were working under the Works Manager in the appellant 's mill premises, paid a visit to Janta Oil Mills situated at Fatuhas. Ramprit Singh, P. W. 2 and his friend, the proprietor of the Mill should meet him at his office at Patna within two days and getting the matter settled, otherwise they would be put to a big loss. The trial court accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal by the convicted person, the High Court held that on a plain reading of section 81, the officers and servants of the Board are deemed to be public servants only when acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the . The appellant contended that his sanction under section 197 was required for prosecution of a public servants for an offence alleged to have been committed by him while acting or purported to actin in pursuance thereof. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : The appellant cannot be deemed to he a 'public servant within section 81 I. P., I.C., as it stood after the Criminal law (Amendment), Act, 1958.

Sub section (2) of r. 141(2), provides that if any person contravenes anything of this rule the order may be forfeited to Government. It seems to us that r. 142(2) is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1). The fact that the rule was contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the Defence of India Act provides that "the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act". The section contemplates that the rules may be inconsistent with existing legislation but by virtue of section 43, if otherwise valid they would have effect. notwithstanding that they are inconsistent with the existing legislation. [273 H; 274 C D] In the result the High Court maintained the order of forfeiture. On appeal by special leave to this Court Held: The order of the High court maintaining the sentence and the rest of the order and the order imposing punishment on the appellant was not liable to be set aside because, he says that the Maharashtra Jowar (Restriction) Order 1965 did not contain any provision authorising the court to forfeit the juar. The proviso to r. 145(2). clearly does not permit the Court to impose the penalty, and it is only in respect of contravention of what the rule authorised under section 3(1), that the Rules may be different with existing law but byio inherent limitations. Section 144(3) embodies a rule of evidence contrary to it and provides for the publication of orders made under the rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. The fact of the rule is not in dispute.

The deceased, a practising lawyer in the District of Farrukhabad, was tried by the Sessions Judge, Farrukhabad. The Sessions Court and the High Court accepted the evidence that Violet did not give intimation of such arrival at the spot soon before 6 p.m. The deceased was a practising lawyers lawyer and after finishing his work for the day he left the Fatehgarh court along with the brother lawyers, Conductor Singh Yadav and Om Prakash Dubey. There were two other accused in that case called. Manphool 'and Balister. Dubey admitted that he had not seen the arrival of the advocate in time to successfully aim at him. The trial court accepted prosecution story but convicted the remaining three accused. On appeal by special leave, the question for consideration was whether the only inference which arose from the fact that violet gave the particular shout is that by so doing she intended to facilitate the murder of Kunwar Singh. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The mere proof that the crime charged could not have been committed without the interposition of the alleged abettor is not enough compliance with the requirements of section 107. [622 G] 2.1 On consideration of the serious infirmities from which the evidence of Dubey suffers, it is of the opinion that the High court ought not to have interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the trial Court. In case Smt. Violets had challenged his conviction and sentence. The fact that he was a colleague of the deceased, he was not in any manner concerned with the deep seated enmity between the accused and the deceased. [625 G H, 626 D] 2(a) It is difficult to believe that Vioslet would have announced the arrival at him even if she was aware that the accused persons were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplish their aim. It is not sufficient that an act on the part of the said alleged abettor happened to facilitate facilitating the commission of the crime. Intentional aiding and therefore active participation is the gist of the offence of abetment under the, third paragraph of section 109.

The four named accused were convicted by the Sessions Court under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed their appeals against acquittal under section 303, read with s.34, of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In appeal to this court, HELD : (i) A Court, even in the first illustration, can acquit 3 of the 4 accused if it accepts the evidence that they acted conjointly in committing the offence. But what is the position if the court acquits three of the four accused either because it rejects the prosecution evidence or because it gives the benefit of doubt to the said accused ? Can it hold, in the absence of a charge as well and evidence, that though the three accused are acquitted, some other unidentified persons acted conjointaneously along with one of the named persons ? If the Court could do so, it would be making out a new case for. the prosecution : it would not be deciding contrary to the evidence adduced in the case. A court cannot obviously make out a case which is not disclosed either in the charge or in regard to which there is no basis in the evidence. There must be some foundation in the evi dence that persons other than those named have taken part in the commission of the offence and if there is such a basis, the case will be covered by the third illustration. [683 A D] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab followed. (ii) The judgment of the High Court could not stand.

The auction sale was held on February 2, 1943, and was confirmed on June 23, 1943. On January 16, 1943 respondent No. I sold the property to defendants 8 to 10 who were respondents No. 2 to 4. The following pedigree table will assist in understanding the case: Madhavarao Balakrishan Jakati Deft. 1 (a) daughter Deft.; (b) daughter; (c) daughter on the death of his father; (d) grand son (e) step son (f) daughter, (g) son (h) step daughter (i) daughter (ii) daughter daughter (g). The respondents resisted the suit mainly on the ground that the purchase by respondent No would not bind the appellant (defendant No.1) as the auction sale is under section 155 of the Act and therefore the sale in execution cannot be challenged as the sons were under a pious obligation to discharge the debt of their father because the sale could only be challenged on proof of the debt Of defendant No, 1 which were characterised as misfeasance ' and that they could legally be sold under section 55 of the Transfer of Property Act. Held also that the liability of the sons to discharge debts of the father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious obligation of the appellants who had no right to challenge the sale on showing the immoral or illegal purpose of the creditor, and where after attachment and a proper notice of the sale sell and the sale certificate all purported purported to affect the rights of the appellant to proceed in execution against the divided shares of sons which had been attached before partition was not a point in controversy. The obligation of a father to discharge his duties is not an avyavaharika debt as it cannot be termed ' repugnant to good morals ' and therefore attachment of the whole coparcenary estate would not be affected by the change in mode of enjoyment and what was held jointly was by the partition held in severalty, and the decree of confirmation of sale dated June 28, 1943 passed against the respondents (appellants) are binding on all the members of the joint family.

The petitioners who were seven in number challenged the Act and the notification issued thereunder imposing a tax on passengers and goods carried by road in motor vehicles. The contention of the petitioners was that the tax had not been laid upon "passengers and goods" as authorised under Entry No. 56 but upon "fares and freights", which are different entities, and in support thereof, the contention was that there was a difference, reference is made to Entry No, 89 of the Union List where power is conferred to tax "factions and freight services". The petitioners contended that the Act imposed unreasonable restrictions on their fundamental right under articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution inasmuch as it provided that in view of competition with the Railways, that there could be no question of imposing a higher rate of tax for cemented, tarred, asphalted, metalled etc. which were different entities altogether and in favour of the Railways. Held, that the levy was perfectly valid because it made the tax payable on fares and freight on passengers which are distinct entities, but no discrimination could be said to be made out. The imposition of a higher tax for goods transported by road or inland waterways on the basis of averages, and not on passengers, and goods. Where, therefore, the tax was imposed on passengers irrespective of the distance travelled by them, it would lead to anomaly if the amount charged in every case was more or less than when calculated on actual fares and compensations. The Act was clearly within its competence as pointed out by section 9 that if the tax were laid on passengers regardless of the point travelled by him, it could lead to anomalies, if the amounts charged be the same in every ease. It was not therefore correct to say that the charge of tax levied by the Act was beyond the competence of the legislature and, consequently, neither was there any discrimination between operators of public motor vehicles using roads had been pointed out and all operators were equally affected by the. Act, as being a restriction upon inter State trade, commerce and intercourse, to article 19.

% The appellant company served a notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen alleging non availability or raw material to utilise the full installed capacity power shedding limiting the working capacity, power shedging limiting the woccurrence of over three days, and threatening to leave for employment. Some negotiations took place between the Union and the appellant leading to an agreement dated 1st April 1974 whereby the workmen who were sought to be retrenched were taken back in service with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures. The appellant denied its inability in view of the mounting losses. Some correspondence took place and a draft memorandum of settlement was drawn up which provided for revision of wages on the one hand and higher norms of production on the other, but ultimately the settlement fell through. Appellant also participated in the negotiations between the union and the company leading to a agreement dated 4th April 1974 whereunder the workmen sought to been retrenched were taking back in serv ice with continuity Of service by way of the appellant. The Labour Court held that the reasons stated in the notice dated 1 7 1974, viz., heavy loss caused by non availability of tin plates, persistent power curbs and mounting cost of production were not the real reasons for affecting retrenchment but the real reason was the annoyance felt by the management consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft on 5th April, 1974 and therefore the retrenchment was illegal. The High Court also held that since the appellant company is suffering loss and its carry forward loss as on 31st March 1978 was Rs. 8,12,416.90 in order to see that the industry survives and the workman continue to get employment, there must be come sacrifice on the part of workmen. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The approach of the Labour Court is correct. [568A] 1.2 But the powers must be exercised in a judicial and judicious manner. The reason for exercising discretion must be cogent and convincing and must appear on of the face of the record. When it is said that something is to be done within the discretion of the authority, that something was to be doing according to the rules of reason and justice. according to law and not humor. It is not to be arbitrary, vague or fanciful but legal and regular (See Susannah Sharm v.Workfild(4). The management need not have merry time to itself making the workmen the sacrificial goat. If sacrifice is necessary, those who can afford and have the cushion and the capacity must bear the greater brunt making the shock of sacrifice as less poignant as possible for those who keep body and soul together with utmost difficulty. [570B C] 2.1 In appropriate cases the Court may in the spirit of labour and management being partners in the industry direct scaling scaling down of back wages with some sacrifice on management 's part too, should look into the compelling necessity for working the workmen. The reasons for exercising power must be justifiable and convincingly and must have appeared on the face. of the records. When an award is said to be invalid and it is motivated and the relief of reinstatement is granted. [571F] 2:2 In a case like this, the Court will entertain a petition for special leave in which a question of general public importance involved is involved or when the decision would shock the conscience of this court. The lndustrial Disputes Act is intended to be a self contained one and it seeks to achieve social justice on the basis of collective bargaining, collaboration and arbitration. Awards are given on circumstances peculiar to each dispute and the Tribunals are to a large extent free from promote resrtrictions of technical considerations imposed on courts. A free and liberal exercise of the power under article 136 may materially affect the fundamental basis of such decisions, viz, quick solution of such disputes to achieve industrial peace.

In addition to this Rs. 99,116 11 0 was paid by the appellant to the Mills in satisfaction of the claim and costs then outstanding. The mills were granted a preliminary deco sions. After the expiry of the period fixed for execution the mortgage was executed on the 23rd December, 1939. On the 25th of September, 1940, the corporation passed an order sanctioning sale of a part of the mortgaged property, 20 Round Tank Lane towards payment of the amount due and payable by the two defendants to each of them. The appellant then instituted a suit against the respondents for recovery of the sum due on that sums. The trial Court dismissed the suit as barred in view of section 82 of the Transfer of Property Act as he had not used the word "subrogation" and consequently, section 43 Of the , except where there is a contract to the contrary. Held, that the words "the con tract" can only refer to the main contract between the promisors on the one side and the promisee on the other and in the absence of a contract or con tract to the contrac tive effect the provisions of section 43, except where such there is ' contract to show the contrary, he could not be allowed to make a contract for the contrary; this contention must fail. The suit was therefore time barred by section 82 Of the Transfer Of Property Act and it was open to the court to give a plaintiff such general relief or other relief as it deems just to the same extent as if it had been asked for, provided that occasions no prejudice to the other side beyond what could be compensated for in costs.
