The prosecution alleged that the appellants in the two appeals had created a plan to carry out their nefarious designs. At the trial, 75 witnesses were examined for the prose cution and some other objectionable articles therefrom. As far as Yadav is concerned, there was direct evidence of his involvement and he had also confessed to his guilt but gave out that he had committed the ghastly murder at the behest of the appellant Tripathi. The prosecution relied upon certain confession before a Magistrate, being Exhibit 44 and the other is extra judi cial confession. Dealing with Exhibit 44, the High Court has observed that "So far as the confession before the Magis trate, Exhibit 44 is concerned the trial court has itself had itself, hesitatingly accepted the same". From the confession I find that it was in the nature of the cross examination which is not permissible under the law and has been depricated by the Supreme Court and different courts of the country. Thus, this could not be a feature to supply the link for establishing conspiracy. Prosecution also relied upon a feature like an event of 11th April, 1983 by examining P.W.4. This witness who was a convict staying in the same jail stated that his wife had an interview with him in the jail by paying bribe of Rs.2 or Rs.3 on 11.4 and 12.1983. The father of the deceased was a student of the school and was posted as Collec tor and District Magistrate of Gopalganj District in the State of Bihar on the 11th of April,1983 and he went to his court to work in the morning and after he finished his work, both these witnesses were exami ned for the prosecution. The Sessions Court convicted the appellants under section 302 read with Section 120 B I.P.C. and has sentenced them to death. The High Court dis missed the appeal filed on behalf of the State, inter alia, observing that apart from what the High COurt has observed with regard to the confession it appeared to be exculpatory in nature and therefore would not be admissible against the co accused. Allowing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1.1. The judicial confession has to be kept out of considerations. In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law. It is unfortunate that lapses have oc curred. P.S.S., appeals dis posed of. 1.2. In this type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav, being a follower, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. prosecution relied on an event which if accept ed could provide some link between the two for the commis sion of the offence. According to the prosecution Yadav was regularly visiting Sadanand at the jail. The jail records do not support such visits.

The dispute between the four appellants companies and the respondents workmen was referred for adjudication to the Industrial Tribunal. The main dispute which gave rise to the references was with regard to wages, dearness allowance and gratuity. The references included other items but it held that these were comparable concerns and in the case of the clerical and subordinate staff and directed adjustments also on the same basis. On reference two references both related to the dearness allowance for clerical and subordi nate staff, and on the other two references the main award dealt with the main dispute relating to wages and dearness allowance. The Tribunal by its order dated April 8, 1959 held that in applying the industry cum region formula which was the basis for fixing wages and of dearness allowance had not been properly applied by the Tribunal and it accordingly gave the same dearness allowance to the factory workmen as to the clerical & subordinate staff. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Tribunal has gone wrong in applying industry cum Region formula which is the basis of fixing wages, and dearness allowances and has made comparison with concerns which are not comparable; (2) in determining what should be the minimum wage for various categories of clerical and Subordinate staff prevalent in these comparable concerns so far as clerical, subord ici nated staff were concerned, it took into account certain differences between the two companies as well as their living conditions; (3) in fixing the same scale of dearness allowances, there was no such discrimination on the part of the Tribunal which should have been avoided; and (4) if the formula which lays down minimum wages for the clerical staff are fixed more or less on the higher than the lowest in other comparable concerns, then it cannot be said that the total wage packet fixed could not be justified. Held:(1) The Tribunal was right in following the trend that has begun in this region and in fixing a uniform scale of pay for subordinate staff, it had relied solely on a number of cases in which the maximum would be reached. Where there are a large number of industrial concerns of the same kind in the same region they would be proper to put greater emphasis on the industry part of that industry cum rationalisation of wages and maintenance of standard of living should be made with reference to clerical and, subordinate staff as well, for the purpose of fixing wage scales and dearness pay allowance. [374 G] (ii) In applying the industries cum region principles for fixing the wages of different categories of employees of different kinds getting same wages it would be open to the Tribunal to fix the same rates of dearness allowi cations for factory workmen also as for clerical staff; but in doing so the Tribunal must when making comparisons take into account the total price packet (i.e. basic wages fixed by it as well and then compare it with the total wages packet of comparable concerns which would stand comparison with the dearness pay packet of similar concerns and thus arrive at a just figure for basic wage. [375 D] The principles which emerged from these two decisions are that in granting awards of uniform rates of higher wages between clerical and other subordinate staff a member of 'the subordinate staff drawing the same wages would get less dearness allowance than a member belonging to clerical.

On appeal by both sides the High Court held that though the conveying brother was a co mortgagor with the plaintiffs, he had no right to sell their interest in the equity of redemption. In the appeal under article 136 of the Constitution it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where there were more occupants than one in respect of the same occupancy each has his own rights and the fact of registration of one of them as the registered occupant attracts the operation of the Code and confers certain rights or imposes certain obligations on the registered ' occupants as laid down in the Code but does not take away the rights of other occupants. Held, that under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, as it stood at all material times, such a relinquishment can be in favourof more persons than one, and it does not mean that if any of the occupants other than the registered owner desires to relinquish his occupancy, he cannot himself give a notice of relinquishment but must give it by and through the registered tenant. Lalchand Sakharam Marwadi vs Khendu Kedu Ughade, (1904) L. R 32 Ind App. No. 22 of 1945, which was filed by defendants 1 to 4 and L.P.A. No 22 of 1944, which had been dismissed by the District Court on March 15, 1909, it had not come into being during the pendency of the appeal to this Court and that consequently the decision of the Division Bench in Letters Patent Appeal No. 756 of 1942 was correct and the principal contention urged before the High court must be negatived.

The appellant company which was formed in 1965 and went into production the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the . The employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for certain benefits to workers in case of sickness, maternity and employment injury and to make provision for certain other matters in relation thereto. It was an obvious social welfare legislation in tune with the Directive Principles contained in Articles 41, 42 & 43 of the Constitution. The provisions of the Chapter, however, have ceased to have effect on and from July l 1973. That is the sequel to a notification issued under section 73 I of the Act. Chapter VA was inserted by section 20 of Act No 53 of 1951 which provided for the establishment of the Employees ' State insurance Corporation for administering tho scheme of Employees ' ' State ' Insurance in accordance with the provisions Of the Act, and other necessary provisions. The appellant company challenged its liability to pay special contribution under Chapter V I A by filing a writ petition in the High Court of Gujarat under article 226 of the constitution. The writ petition was dismissed in limine. Meanwhile Chapter V, A had ceased to be effective on and after July 1, 1973 consequent upon a notification of the Government dated July l1973. The main ground on which the appellant relies is that the contribution payable under Chapter IV A is a fee and its levy is illegal as the Act does not contemplate rendering of any service or conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for payment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on September 7, 1971. Against this decision an appeal by special leave was filed before this court. On behalf of the State it was contended that the payment of contribution directed to be made by the employer under the to or other similar similar payment or benefit under various social welfare legislations must either be styled as a tax or a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. The idea that such payment, contribution or whatever name is given to it should be so pigeon hold and fitted in stems from a misunderstanding of the scheme of our Constitution in regard to social welfare Legislation was to achieve this object; that such payments, contribution, whatever name ' is given should be such , etgeon held and fitted In stems from an understanding of award, the Tribunal upheld the levy of special contribution as a charge. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The very approach of the appellant to the problem at issue suffers from a basic defect. The scheme of socioeconomic welfare makes elaborate provisions in respect of it and leaves it to the Government concerned to decide when, how and in what manner the scheme should be introduced. [1091B C] 2.1 When extending the Act to different establishments, the relevant (1) , 6 SCR 101392 government is given the power to constitute a corporation for the administration of the Scheme of Employees Insurance. The course adopted by modern legislatures in dealing with welfare scheme has uniformly conformed to the same pattern.

The petitioners demanded regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna. Respondent No. 2 issued a notice on the peti tioners demanding regularisation of his services claiming that they were discharging the same duties as the regular workers. The management denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls continuously for several years even though there was no work for them; and that even though the petitioners are being paid their daily wages in spite of their being no work available for them, they cannot be regularised and their retention on the rolls is purely a humanitarian grounds so far. He stated that a Voluntary Retirement Scheme offering considerable amount to these daily rated workers has been framed which was Annexure R V to the counter affidavit filed along with the counter affi davit. The respondents contested the petition contending that there was, no vacancy in the establishment to absorb the petitioners and that for quite some time they have been re sailed on rolls and paid in spite thereof being no Work available for the petitioners. Disposing of the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. In view of the findings supported by evidence that there are no vacancies or work available in the establishments for absorption of the petitioners, and that, for quite few time they had been continued to be paid their monthly wages in despite of their having been no work as available for they. [621 F G] 2. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regularly workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same thing work is taken from him.

The plaintiffs are the tenants of a tea estate in Darjeeling Collectors. On their death, on September 24, 1931, the residuary property of Rs. 100/ owned by the two branches was transferred to them. The terms of the lease were re quired and finalised by the Government which by section 41 of the Indian Transfer of Property Act, 1882, became applicable to all kinds of transfers of immovable and other rights of the transferees. However, in accordance with the provisions Of 0. 10 of 0. VI of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, in respect of a portion of the property mortgaged, the plaintiffs filed a suit No: 58 of 1931 for recovery of possession of the said property on the ground that it was immoral and illegal to deprive the defendants of their right to the full 16 as share in the property. The claim based on the title was rejected by the Subordinate Judge but the High Court dismissed it on the view that the plaintiffs had failed to establish that the suit property with the consent of their co sharers was an ostensible owner. On appeal by certificate, Held, that even though a separate lease was granted in 1928 in favour of the plaintiffs only 1/2 as share was sold under the mortgage decree, that the sale deed exhibit 12(i) and 12(c) on which the claim was based were filed in the trial court without adverting to the sale, a piece of conduct certainly not consistent with the sale being real and intended to pass title; and so, the bar was not attracted. The proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial Court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale under exhibit 12 (i) were held to be real, the appellants plaintiffs would be entitled to a further 2 as. 13 gondas odd share belonging topire which they obtained under exhibit I(c).

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge, Karimnagar in what used to be the State of Hyderabad (now part of the State) under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code for the murder of his brother Baga Rao and sentenced to death. The conviction and sentence were confirmed by the High Court of Andhra Pradesh. On reference to the Sessions judge the High court held that the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) had not been complied with, and that as a necessary consequence of those omissions section the entire proceedings and the trial were vitiated. Held, that non compliance with section 173(b) could not be cured by their non compliance within the time permitted under section 537(a). Where failure to comply with the provisions was held to be cured, by sections 234 and 239, the court may reopen the proceedings by insisting upon full compliance with the provision of the Code. Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor (I.L.R. ,N. Subramania Iyer 's case ([1952] S.C.R., 806), followed. In cases exclusively triable by a court of Session it is the duty of the magistrate while holding a preliminary inquiry, to satisfy himself that the documents referred to in section 173 had been furnished to the accused and if he found that the police officer concerned had not carried out his duty in that behalf he should see to it that such is done. The failure complained of in the instant case should not have a more farreaching effect than the omission to carry out the provisions Of section 162 or Section 360 of the code. Abdul authorises the exercise of such power and since the failure to carryout the provisions conplu sions contained therein would entail loss to the prosecution by non compliance thereof under sections 537, 537 and 537(b), if no case of prejudice had been made out.

The appellant was a chemical works discharged effluent in very large quantities of calcium, sodium and other),-viation Litigants. The respondent Municipality after having obtained the approval of the Government issued a notice to the appellant under section 153 A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901 as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra and as amended by Act XI of 1955 ( hereinafter referred to as the 'Act), to show cause why it should not be directed to arrange within a period of nine months from the date of such direction for the discharge of the effluent through a covered pucca drainage and for pumping it over a distance of about 8 miles in the Ran ' area of Cutch near Kuda, as shown in the plan annexed to the notice. The appellant replied that the effluents were being discharged until 1943 through a Katcha Channel running parallel to the railway line in the direction of Halvad. In 1944, it was felt that as the water of some of the wells in the areas known as Harijanvas and Kolivas close to the vicinity of the channel might be affected another channel was constructed for discharging the effluent which was at a considerable distance away from Kolivas and Harijanvas still further away from the city which lies on the eastern side of the railway lines. The water of various wells in tile surrounding area so as to render it unfit for use and also prejudicially affecting fertility of the soil in the surrounding areas by percolation, was taken by the appellant along with other fertilisers. The Municipality on having obtained ' the approval ' of the government issued a notification under section 154 A(3) of that Act requiring the person to whom the notice is issued, should show cause in writing within a specified period why he should not arrange for the closure of the management of the factory. After considering the objections and after hearing the appellant passed an order on June 20, 1956, to the effect that the notice was one for discharging of the effluents in the manner specified in the notice and not to show or show cause against that the existence of the nuisance was a matter for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality and beyond the scope of the enquiry before him. The Special Officer declined to pass any further order on this ground but the matter was referred to the Government under section 143(3)(a) of it, and the Government referred the question whether the discharge Of the effluents from the factory of the respondent company amounted to a violation of article 19 of the Constitution and as the appellant 's engineer had been consulted in that respect. The Government held that the question was beyond the meaning of section 153A(1). It further observed that even if the person who made the requisition did not reply to the notification, he might forthwith pass such order as may be necessary for the purpose of regulating the discharge, of the sewage in the area and that dispute would be the subject of an enquiry by the Special Officer. The question was whether section 153(A) of 'the Act offended article 19(1)(C) of India inasmuch as it imposed unreasonable restrictions on the appellant from discharging its duty under section 295A of the Act, which could not be said to contravene article 19 Of the Constitution because it infringed the fundamental rights guaranteed by articles 14 and 31. Held, that the notification issued by the Government on June 30, 1956 was not a valid notification and did not infringe article 19. The order of the Special officer declining to go into the question as whether the nuisance in question existed as the person concerned had objects to it or the requisition contained therein absolutely no objection. The provisions of section 295 A(4) of, were ultra vires section 153 of the Indian Penal Code inasmuch as they imposed unreasonable restriction on the exercise of his fundamental rights under articles 14, 19 and 31 Of the Con stitution. There was nothing in that sub section to justify the issuing of a notice by the Municipality with the previous approval of Government.

The appellant was found committing an offence under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The prosecution relied on a report submitted by the Deputy Superintendent of Police; but the report stated that he had examined the material which he classified under 38 heads and described the same as unauctionable property. Allowing the appeal in part, HELD : (i) Even in such a case, the prosecution must first adduce evidence to show that there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. It is only when the burden in respect of this is discharged by the prosecution that the onus shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his possession of the same. He may for instance show that he has purchased the property in open market where goods of this kind are usually sold or that he did bought them from someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the facts in the instant case. [189 C D] (ii) The evidence in the case did not establish that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act and as such the question of punishment under section 2 did not arise. [15 F]. Moyalal Rostagir vs The State, ; , referred to. In the present case all the burden had to be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some, peculiarity of the goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Again, there was no evidence before the courts to prove that the goods belong to any particular railway administration but they were used or intended to be used for the construction or operation of a railway. [19 C D].

The appellants had lease of the demised premises for 11 months from May 1, 1964 on payment of monthly rent of Rs. 18 which expired on March 31, 1965 when the respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act but she remained in possession and enjoyment of the shop carrying on small kirana business. The respond ent landlord terminated her lease by notice under s.106 of Transfer Of Property Act, but later continued to remain in possession, and enjoyment thereof till date of her death. In the suit for ejectment filed by the appel lant the appellants contended that the lease hold right is an heritable estate and on death of the tenant in September 1966 the tenancy rights held by Smt. Anandi Bai had no heritable interest in the commercial tenancy under that Act. The Trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that Smt. Jain paid and the respondent accepted the rent after determination of the tenancy and so she was a tenant holding over. During the pendency of the appeal, the Act was amended through Rajasthan Premes (Control of Rent & Eviction) Ordinance 26 of 1975 which was replaced by Act 14 of 1976 which was re ferred by Act 49 of 1976. The definition of 'Tenant ' in section 3 sub clause(vii)(b) makes the legislative intent manifest that from the date of the Amendment Act came into force, on the death of tenant, his surviving spouse, son, daughter and other heir in accordance with personal law as applica ble to him, who had been, in the case of premises leased out for commercial or business purposes, ordinarily having been carrying on business with him/her in such premises as member of his family upto his death. The appellants contended (i) that the tenancy came to a terminus with its determination by issuance of notice under rule 106 of the Transfer of Proce dure Act; and (ii) that since the bequest was in favour of the third party, the testator thereby cannot confer rights under the provisions of the Rent Acts on the stranger who was not a member of the family. The legal represen tatives of the deceased tenant did not acquire heritable interest and therefore the tenancy right is heritable and on her death the heirs devolved on the heirs. They, inter alia, contended that they were entitled to remainin possession even after determination but since Smt. J. Jain had paid and accepted the lease after determination the lease she was not in possession over. The trial Court dismissed both the suits holding that the appellants did not carry on the business with her till date her death and further as the appellants had failed to carry out their business the tenancy suits were maintainable. On appeal, it was contended for the appellants that (i). the renewal of lease hold rights by the tenant to an estate of the former 's former 'tenant came into effect from September 16, 1966 and hence not heritable; and that the amendment Act did not have the effect of divesting their vested right in the lease holding held by the tenants. Dismissing the appeal for eviction this Court, HELD: (1) The lease hold fights devolved on Ms. Anandhi Bai as a statutory tenant. [13C] (2) If affords protection to every tenant against evic tion despite termination of tenancy except on grounds viola tively on grounds recogni tated by the Act and no order or decree for eviction shall be passed against the tenant unless any ground which entitles the landlord to get an order ordecree for possession specified in the Act is established. [14G] (3) The right to succession to an Estate of a deceased owner vests immediately on his/her than near est heirs and cannot be held in abeyance except when a nearer heir is then in the womb.

The appellant Board maintained a Contributory Provident Fund where the contribution is on the basis of basic wage, the Board and the employees contributing equally. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act. The Industrial Tribunal however held against the appellant but in appeal by the Board it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State Government is the financier of the Company which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4% per annum, and that no scheme run by the Electricity Board was running at a loss. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal did not look into the Act at all. Whether in view of the statutory obligations laid on ii the various sections just now referred to in analysing the capacity of the Boards to bear any additional burden in the matter of provident fund or other amenities the same considerations that applied in the case of private commercial concerns could be applied is a rather difficult question. In fact, the decision might very often depend on a close analysis of the financial condition of the board. [41 G H] Gramophone Co. vs Its Workmen, [1964] II L.L.J 131, referred to. (2) The position at present was not worse than what it was earlier and that there was no reason for the same.

One K had married to the appellant on May 27,1978 according to Sunni Muslim rites. After the marriage the respondent lived with her husband upto July 1978. The respondent alleged that during this period she found her husband to be physically incapable of carrying on sexual relationship and that her husband frankly told him that he was impotent. She further alleged that after the marriage, on November 17, 1978 the appellant sent a registered notice (Ext. 5) to the respondent informing her that he had no physical disability and he was prepared to keep her with him and discharge his marital obligations. The appellant replied stating that she had no mental disability and was prepared lo kept her with them and discharged his marital obligation. However, on October 28, 1978 she sent a notice (Exh. 5), to the Respondent informing her of his intention to maintain her husband with the appellant and for awarding maintenance against him. This reply was refused by the respondent on October 29, 1978. Thereafter the matter was taken up in revision before the High Court which differed from the view taken by the Magistrate and held that the husband having been found to be impotant, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with her. The High Court also held that though the father of the respondent had deposed about his mental disability within two years of marriage he was not in a position to accept the same. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that it is now well settled by a long course of decisions of various High Courts that impotency is no good ground or reason for the husband to refuse live with the wife merely because her husband was impollent; [707E] (ii) that a wife is not an active participant in the sexual life and therefore, the sexual pleasure to the wife is of no consequence and therefore cannot amount to cruelty. On behalf of respondent it was submitted: (a) that the various authorities of the High Courts seem to have overlooked the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure under which a wife could refuse to reside with her deceased husband if there was a just reason for doing so; and that, in the instant case, no legal effect to the legislative will and intent appears to have been given by the said decisions. (b) that so far as the applicability of second proviso is concerned, the same would certainly be a "just ground" within the meaning of the first proviso so as to make the refusal of the wife 's refusal to live separately from such a husband. Allowing the appeal in part and dismissing the petition in part, ^ HELD: 1 (a). The decision relied on by the High court in the judgment taking a contrary view must be held to be no longer good law and are accordingly overruled; [700F] (b). Merely because the father had deposed that he is impotable and his mental well being might be adversely affected, it would not be a fit case for granting maintenance if she refused to live there with the husband merely because she was impetent. Likewise, where a wife has a reasonable apprehension arising from the conduct of the husband that she is likely to be mentally harmed due to persistent demands of dowry from her husband 's parents or relations, such an apprehension also would be manifestly a reasonable justification for thewife 's refusing to livewith her husband. [708C D] 1 (c).

In dealing with the question whether a person is an officer of the Government it was considered necessary to give him a better meaning than what he was doing by his own engagement. In the present case the appellant was employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshop Workshops at Ajmer and was performing the duty of a metal Examiner known as Chaser in the railway Carriage Workshops. He was neither an officer nor a mere contractor bound by his engagement but not by the terms of his office or employment to pay a certain proportion to the Government. There was no delegation to him of any authority for coercion or interference nor was he an assistant appointed to help any one who was vested with such authority. The duties which he performed were contractual duties Adulterer deception in the discharge of which might subject him to punishment for cheating but not duties attached to any office conferred on him or his successorin title, failure to perform which with integrity could make him liable, as an officer to the special penalties prescribed for delinquent public servants. Held, further that though the appellant had been compulsorily convicted under section 161, Indian Penal Code, it was a public servant within the meaning of section 21(9) and therefore a public servants fell within the definition of a public Servant contained in section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act II of 1947. Ram Krishna vs Delhi State, A.I.R. 1918 Mad. 365, distinguished. Consequently one could not be convicted under s.5(1)(d) of the Indian Penal code and he was liable to be acquitted of that charge if the appellant accepted Rs. 150 from Nanak Singh as and by way of illegal gratification as an Officer to the Special penalties prescribed therefor for delinquent Public servants.

Section 73FF(1) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 deals with disqualification for membership of committee. Sub section (2) of Section 73FF provides that a member who has incurred any disqualification under sub section (1), shall cease to be a member of the Committee and his seat shall thereupon be deemed to be vacant. The appellant 's election was not called in question under the provisions of section 78(1). The Assistant Registrar of Cooperative Societies by his order dated 7.12.1987 removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors holding that he was defaulter on 31.1.1986, with effect from 31.3.1986 and he became defaulter under the provision of Section 74FF(2) as it stood before its amendment in 1986. The order of removal was passed on 28.12 .87 which was challenged by him in a writ petition in the High Court. On 30.8.89, the Cooperative Society dismissed the appellant ' 's writ Petition challenging the aforesaid order dated 30. 8.89 holding that the dues calculated on 31st January 1986 became recurring dues every following day and on 12.5.1986 when section 73FF came into force, the outstanding dues continued even on 18.8 .86 when he was elected as Director. The Writ Petition filed by him challenging the above order was dismissed by the High court on 30.9.89 by the Cooperation and textile Department. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. There is no room for holding that section 73(2)(f) of Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act 1960 came into operation. Section 78(I) deals with powers of removal of committees or member thereof provides as follows: "78(1)(1) If in the opinion of the Registrar, the committee of any society or any member of such committee makes default or is negligent in the performance of the duties imposed on it or him by this Act or the rules or the bye laws, or commits any act which is prejudicial to the interests of the society or its members, or wilfully disobeys directions issued by the State Government, or is otherwise not discharging its or his functions properly and diligently and the business of the Society has or is likely to come to a standstill, or where any member or Administrator appointed under paragraph (ii) at his discretion even before the expiry of the period sectionified in the order made under this sub section; (b) xxx xxx xxx" [683A] 2.1 The appellant was in arrear for the period 18.9 .86 to 21.10.1986 i.e. both prior and posterior to his election on 18 8.8 1986 i.f. both before and posterior amendments, i. e. both previous and posterior upto his election, and till 21.11.1986. admittedly the instalment was not paid on due date. There was of course some dispute as to the amount of interest payable and appropriation of the amount paid against interest instead of capital but all this would not exonerate the appellant, from being in default on non payment of instalment on due dates. [683E] 2:2 The expression, "makes default" or "stands disqualified" being in present the default must have been committed after the coming into force of section 73F and that his default even, if any, was prior to that date and not after that date. [684B C] 2."3 Reading section 78 of the Act, it could not be said that default could be on the due date only and thereafter no default but only liability. The moment the appellant after election continued to be in default, and, therefore, must he taken to have made default until repayment. [685D] 3.1 In Maharashtra State Board of Education vs Paritosh Sheth, ; , followed.

Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules empowered Government to reduce or withdraw a pension. Rule 189 contemplates withholding or withdrawing a pension or any part of it if the pensioner be convicted of grave misconduct while he was in service or after the completion of his service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government servant depend upon the good conduct of the Government servant. Rendering satisfactory service maintaining good conduct is a necessary condition for grant and continuation of pension. Rules 189 and 189 provided for grant of pension admissible under the rules to Government servants who is borne on its establishment. Rule 188 provides for granting pension admissible to Government Servants who is engaged on its Establishment. Rule 187 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part thereof if the pensionary pensioner be found guilty of grave mis conduct while he is in service and after the expiry of his Service. Granting pension and the continuance to the respondent depend upon good conduct maintain good conduct. Rindering satisfactory services maintaining good performance was a necessary requirement for the grant and continuance of pension The State Government accepted the findings and passed the impugned order reducing the pension by 50 per cent. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: In the instant case the purpose of enquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent 's pension. [189D] In M. Narasimhachar vs The State of Mysore, ; ; ; State of Uttar Pradesh vs Brahm Datt Sharma & Anr., [1987] 2 SCR 981 and State of U.P.

Section 3(1) of the , imposes certain restrictions on the landlord 's right to eject his tenant from the premises to which the Act applies. Section 16 provides that no order made under this Act by the State Government or the District Magistrate shall be called in question in any Court. This Court held in the case that the proceedings taken under section 3 were proceeding of a quasi judicial nature and the appropriate authorities, in exercising their powers in relation to such proceedings, must act in accordance with the principles of natural justice. In an appeal by special leave: Held: (per section K. Das Gupta and K. N. Wanchoo, jj.), that the limited jurisdiction conferred on the Commissioner under s 3(3) was exactly similar to the jurisdiction conferred upon the High Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The words "any order passed" in section 3(4) read with s 16 are clear and unambiguous and they indicate that the jurisdiction of the civil courts can be excluded by a statutory provision which is either express or which overrules such jurisdiction, has used clear and unequivocal words indicating that intention. Section 2 (5), and section 16, therefore, clearly exclude the jurisdiction Of the civil Courts to deal with applications made by landlords. When a plea seeks to prove that the impugned orders is a nullity in the true legal sense, that is a plea which does not come within the mischief of the bar created by sections 3(2) and 16. The facts are postulated by the decision of the Supreme Court in the present case. No other plea can be raised because all other pleas are barred by sections 2 (4) and 17.

The appellant, a Member of the Punjab Public Service Commission was alleged to have assaulted her. The Chief Minister of Punjab and two others who were alleged to be assaulted by some other members of the public service Commission had also filed their affidavits on behalf of these candidates in support thereof. These affidavits were taken into consideration by the Supreme Court for deciding whether Shri Gopal Krishan Saini, Member of this Public Service commission ought, on the ground of misbehaviour, to be removed from the office of the Member of respondent Commission. On reference being made to it under Article 317(1) of the Constitution, the President had referred for consideration the question "as to whether ShriGopal Krishan Khosla, Member Of the Punjab State Public Service Commis sioner, ought, in an enquiry held in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under Article 145", reported that the Chairman or such other member, as the case may be ought on any such ground to be so removed. " The appellant contended that before making this Reference, the question whether Shri HIG, Member could be removed was a matter which depended upon properly functioning of the Public Service Con stitute and therefore it should have been referred to a Larger Bench. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the President to make a reference to this Court under Article 143(1), is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some one other body or authority. That Article provides that the chairman or any other member of a Public Service commis sor can only be removed to his office on the grounds of misbehaviour and (ii) the order of removal can be passed after the Supreme court has on inquiry reported to the President that theChairman or such person ought to be removing from his office. The enquiry contemplated by the Article is into the facts themselves and facts also so as to enable this Court to pronounce upon the question: whether the allegations made against the Chairman are proved at all. The purpose of article 317(2) is to ensure independence of members of public services Commissions and to give them protection in the matter of their tenure. [666 C] 2.1 Article 317 provides that an inquiry has to be held by this Court in accordancewith the procedure laid down in that Article under Article. 145. The inquiry contemplated by article is into tho facts themselves, and facts and also so also as to assist the Supreme Courts to pronounce on the question wheth er there is a Prima facie case exists for an enquiry and report by this court. [643 F G] 1.2 It will not be conducive to justice to decide the reference on a consideration of the affidavits only. The credibility of witnesses who depose to facts is matters which bears directly on the adjudication of those facts. And the best method of testing whether a witness is a person of credit is to subject him (or her) to cross examine. [65 C] 1:3 All questions regarding admissibility and relevance of the evidence so recorded will be decided by this Constitution Bench instead of being made by a Magistrate or a Munsif.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under Section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act 4 of 1939) (for short, the 'Act '). The Subordinate Judge decreed the plaintiffs suit holding that the deity installed in the temple was a family deity of the Pani family and the endowment being of a private nature, the Act had no application and the order passed by the respondent regarding the management was set aside. The High Court reversed the decision of the subordinate Judge and held that the temple and the deity install therein being a public endowment fell within the four corners of the Act and the Respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. (a) It is well settled that under the Hindu law, a person who has no issue and who after installing the deity entrusteds the management to members of the public or strangers which is a clear proof of the intention to dedicate the temple to public and not to the members of any family. In other words, the beneficiaries in a public trust are the general public or a section of the same and not a determinate body of individuals as a result of which the remedies for enforcement of charitable trust are somewhat different from those which can be availed of by beneficiaries in the private trust. [831G H] (b) If in future there is no fit man in our family, any of the Baisnab Sampraday and any Hindu of reputation of the village and of the locality is entitled to take such action, it would be a conclusive proof to show that the endowment was of a public nature. The mere fact that members of public are allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the members or of the family had a right to worship in the idol. [862B C] (c) An idol is a juristic person capable of holding property and the property dedicated to the temple vests in the deity. If the main worshippers are the members, of the community who worship as a matter of right then the real purpose is to confer benefit on God. [861A B] Mahant Ram Saroop Dasji vs S.P. Das, J., reiterated. (d) It cannot be said that the property was of purely private nature and the intention of the founder was merely to instal a family idol in the Temple and worship the same in order to effectuate the spiritual benefit to the family of the founders and their descendants and to perpetuate the memory of the settlor. In The present case, the documents clearly established that the intention was merelyto instal a Family deity in the school. [863F] (e) It could not be said even that there was never any intention to treat the temple as a public one but the intention being, if at all, to continue it in the name of the Hindu family so long as the family continued. There is no recital in any of documents to show the existence of such a stipulation for taking offerings from the members by the public to worship, in the temples.

The appellant Bank originally agreed to finance the contracts and to advance monies to the appellant, against his bills for supplies under the contracts. For the purpose of carrying out this arrangement it executed an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946, but before that date he made out a bill on the military authorities for Rs. 49,633/8. The appellant was therefore authorised to sue for recovery and receive the monies due in connection with the contracts from November 1, 1952 to December 12, 1952 and handed over the bill to the appel lant for collection. On August 11, 1952, the appellant filed a suit against his assignee for a declaration that he was an assignee of the biL and that Takhatmal had no right to attach it. The Trial Court held in favour the appellant. The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In appeal before this Court by the plaintiff, on behalf of the appeLlant it was contended: (1) that there must be an agreement between the lender and the borrower that the debt owing to the lender would be paid out of a specific fund coming to the debtor 's account; (2) that the document was brought into existence in connection With a proposed transaction of financing of Malayalam Chettiar 's contracts, and that the documents were brought into operation in connection therewith with a proposed transaction of financing an agreement of financing Malhotra 's contract. HELD: On July 19, 1948, he made up for consideration the question whether a document amounts to an equitable assignment or not is primarily one of construction but would be covered by the terms of the power of Attorney. [517 F] Palmer vs Carey approved. (2)(a) It gives the payee no interest in the fund. An assignment creates an interest in 'the fund and is not revocable. Read in the light of the powers of attorney the endorsement on the bill dated July 19 created an interest by Malhotra to pay the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bills and amounted to an discretionary assignmen of the fund by way of security. [525 G] (b) The power of counterrogation creates an 'interest in the Fund and is neither revocable nor revocable, and so read it is not valid. [415 D E] Palmmer vs carey, I.L.R. , relied on. (c) A pay order is revocable mandate. It gives a payee no 'interest" in the funds.

The Income tax Officer assessed the amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. That order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner but on further appeal to the Tribunal, the High Court held that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ' it was his salary as defined in section 17 of the Income tax Act, 1961 and that since the said receipt was not assessed as his salary he was not liable to pay tax. In appeal by certificate to this Court, HELD : The meaning of section 17(3)(ii) is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to call into aid any rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High court. [445 E] In view of section 16 (1), all receipts of profits in lieu of pay have to be considered as salary. But then, the question is what is meant by "profits in lieu ' of salary". [446 F G] Case law referred to. [442 G] Commissioner of Income tax, Assam and Nagaland vs A. C. Ramachandran, , distinguished. [441 B] The word "salary" in section17 has nothing to do either with deductions or with exemptions. It is merely a provision defining the expression 'salary". Therefore there is never need to send into aid the rules of interpretation which was sought for done by this Court.

The Bihar Legislature imposed a total ban on the slaughter of all categories of animals of bovine cattle which includes buffaloes (male or female adult or calves) and which are useful as milch or breeding or draught animals. By an earlier decision, Parliament passed the Bihar Legislature imposing a total prohibition against the slaughter Of " cows " which was then defined as including a female calf of a cow, bull bullock, buffalo or sheifer and a new schedule specifying only (1) cows, (2) male and female buffaloes and (3) buffalo calves for 2,000 heads of cattle. The Bihar Legislature passed the Uttar Pradesh Act in so far as it prohibited "the slaughter of " cows ". By section 4(a), "future of bo vine cattle" was imposed on vehicles belonging to the species of boVine cattle but were not saved by section 4 Of the Act. Section 5 provided that no person could slaughter a bull, bullock or buffalo unless he had obtained in respect of such other animal a certificate signed by him and prescribed as many of them as are in employment for the purposes of food. Though the Act was repealed by the Uttar Pending Act (U. P. Act XXVI Of 1951) which came into force on November 1, 1950, it continued to operate since the Uttar Act ceased to have effect on November 2, 1950. Section 6(a) provided that where a person had died before the commencement of this Act he did not cease to be useful and was declared by the State Government to be his successor in office. The provisions of section 6(b) were, therefore, ultra vires because it imposed a ban on slaughter of buffaloes without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness. Section 7 provided that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any usage to the contrary no person who might not be able to carry on his occupation or business shall slaughter a cow. On September 2, 1951, the Uttar Pra desh Act (1 of 1951) was passed which imposed a large ban on trade and business of cattle in the State of Bihar. The petitioners contended before this Court that the impugned Acts infringed their fundamental rights under article 19(1)(g) and were violative of articles 14 and 19(6), respectively, as they prohibited the Mussalmans from performing the religious practice of the community to sacrifice the cow on the occasion of Bakr Id. HELD: (i) The impugned Act offends against article 14 on the ground that it fails within articles 84 and 90 of the Constitution. [680 G] (ii) There was also no proper remedy for the petitioners in an appropriate case to challenge the vires of sections 5 and 7 of the Uttar U. P Act. This Court has emphasised that a total or partial ban on a slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of buffaloes, male and females is not reasonable. The restrictions imposed by section 6 (a) are justified in so Insofar as it prohibits the slaughter either of cows or animals above a specified age or not suffering from some natural deformity should be allowed to he slaughtered [690 H] (iii) The restrictions placed by section 3 of the Act in respect 'future. of bo Vine cattle (cattle and buffalo) and 'foor pan ' are reasonable but the impugned legislation, in so long as they were milchor or breeding bulls or working bullocks (c cattle) is not valid.

The essential content of the definition of an employee is employment in the Office, Mains Department, eta; ,of the Company either at Nagpur or at Wardha or Wardha and not an essential characteristic of an 'employee ' as defined for the purpose of the Standing Proceedings. Standing Order No. 18 which requires a ticket or card or token. 2(a) itself authorises the issue of ticket to other employees under standing order No.

The appellant company was an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by a Government Company. In 1961, the company went into production in 1964 65 on the basis of a scheme known as "Emergency Industrial Policy". The company had to be treated as an establishment separate from Hindustan Steel Ltd., an establishment which had been in existence for a long period and had been even earning profits so that exemption could not be granted to this Company in respect of payment of bonus under section 16 of the Act. This dispute between the work men and the company was referred to the Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal. The Tribunal held that alloy steel Project could not he treated as a separate establishment because under the proviso to section 3, the Alloy Steel Project could be treated to be an establishment separately from Hindustan, Steel Ltd. but the proviso thereto did not apply in such a case, and directed payment of wages at the minimum rate of 4 per cent of wages prescribed by the Act, and also for payment of interest at 6% on the amount paid up equity share capital as at the commencement of the accounting year. On appeal to this Court it was contended: (i) that even the establishment employing less than 20 persons would be a part of the parent establishment consisting of the factory; and (ii) that the proviso of section 3 should not apply. HELD : (i)(a). Section 16(2) of the makes it clear that the provisions of sub section (1) are to apply even to new departments, undertakings or branches set up by existing establishments. Consequently, even if alloy Steel Projects is treated as separate establishments and available surplus is calculated separately for each unit, there will be no deduction at 8.5 per cent thereof of the paid up share equity sharecapital as envisaged by section 6(d) ,and the Third Schedule of the Bonus Act. [633C E] (b).

Section 3 of the Cess Act provides for levy of cess on water consumed by persons carrying on certain industry and by the local authorities with a view to augment the resources of the Central Board and the State Boards constituted for the prevention and control of water pollution. The Cess Act was enacted by Parliament under Article 252 of the Constitution with a avowed object to control the pollution of rivers and streams which has assumed considerable importance and urgency in recent years as a result of increasing industrialisation and urban isation. The Act has been enacted by the Parliament under article 252 with a purpose to control pollution of water and to ensure that the domestic and industrial affluence are not allowed to be discharged into water coars without adequate treatment. This Act is now in force in almost all states. The effect of the Act is to control water pollution and to maintain the living environment and improve health of citizens. There are also certain provisions relating to constitution of joint Boards the details of which need not detain us. The Central Government and State Governments under Article 253 of the Constitu tion has framed a scheme whereunder the cess Act was levied on the person carrying on industries specified in Sch I, and they read as follows: SCHEDULE I (See Section 2(1)) 1. Mining industry. Ore processing industry. Petroleum Industry. Petro Chemical Industry. Oil Mill Co. and Industries. 67, The State of Andhra Pradesh vide its notification dated April 24, 1977 exempted "minerals". No cess was levied from the sugar manufacturers on the ground that this industry falls under Item 15 of Schedule I to the . The Cess Scheme is not an enactment to regulate and control pollution but a fiscal measure to raise revenue for augmenting the resources. The levy and collection of cess provided under the Cess act is on water eclipse since it is based generally on how the plant or plant part is used rather than on what it This Court in State of West Bengal & Ors. vs Washi Ahmed etc. ; , with reference to the meaning of the word 'vegetable ' in Item (6) of Schedule 1 to the Cess Rules came up for consideration in Member Secre tary, Andhra Pradesh State Board for Prevention and Control of Water Pollution vs Andhra Pradesh Rayons Ltd. & Ors.,[1962] Supp. SCR 724 and Chairman and Committee for Advancement of Mining and Industrial Exams Ltd. vs The State and others, [1963] Supp; 3 S.C.R. 99 held that sugar manufacturing industry would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products industry". On the other hand, the Andhra Pradesh High Court held that Sugar manufacturing industries would fall within Entry I of Schedule, and by virtue of its decision in Chairman 's case it was held that the the sugar manufacturing units would come under Entry 15. On the question whether the industries manufacturing sugar are covered by Entry 15 that is "process ing of vegetable product industry". Dismissing Civil Appeals Nos. 6 of 1986 & 91 of 1989, filed by the State of Bihar and others. Allowing Civil Appeal No. 814 of 1990, this Court, HELD: 1. The word '60 'vetree ' has been defined in several ways. In the World Book it is defined as follows that "The usual sense. means the word vegetable is applied to those plants whose leaves, stalks, roots or tubers are used for food, such as lettuce,paragus, cabbage, beet and turnip. It also includes several plants whose fruits are the edible portions, as peas, beans, melons and tomatoes.

The respondent, an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant, his tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on the business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises. It was claimed before the respondent that the practice of the profession of an Advocate was not business within the meaning of section 10(3) (a) (iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of his tenant on the grounds of his requirement unless it was for the purpose of carrying on a business. The respondent 's case was contested but before the High Court in revision it was contended that there was a clear distinction between 'business ' and 'profession ' and that as the practice was to be given a narrow meaning, the expression business ' must be gleaned from the context in which it is used. It would not be right to ascribe to the word 'business" occurring in section 10 (3)(a)(iii). Dr. Chitaley, senior counsel for the appellant argued that there were a clear differentiation between the 'business and ' profession ' and so the practice as laid down by this Court should be beneficient to the tenant; but that would be the result if the expression "business ' was given a wide meaning so as to include any profession. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court rightly held that in the context of Madhya Pradesh Act, the word business ' has to be construed in the background of the statute in which the term has been understood in the several statutes does not necessarily throw any light on the manner in which a term should be understood generally and that sense in which 'the term has since been understood. [14B] 1.2 The expression 'business " as defined by sections 2(a) and 2(b)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 is used in a wide sense so as not to include the practice in the instant case. Neither the meaning nor the definition of the term in one statute affords a guide to the construction of the same term in another statute and the sense inwhich the word has been defined in the various statutes does nnot necessarily throw light on tho manner in Which the term should he understood generally. [15D E] 1:3 The expression business is used not in a narrow sense so that it is confined to commercial activity. It is a word of large and wide import capable of a variety of meanings. It has been only possible for a variety o meanings. A broad sense may be taken to mean everything that occupies the time attention and labour of men for the purposes of livlihood or profit '. [16E] 1 :4 The meaning of the word must be given an narrow meaning so broadly as to exclude any profession.[15D] In the instant ease, it is a case of no help to the appellant.

The respondent deposited an amount of Rs. 4,00,000 with M/s India Supplies which the appellant was the partners on 30th December 1942 and the amount as on 30 12 1942 stood with interest at 7/9 per cent per month from 1st January 1943. The respondent accepted the said proposal and thereafter a letter dated 29 27 1948 was written by Ram Ratan Gupta to the respondent recording the agreement that "a sum of Rs 4, 00000 should be debited to India Supplies as deposit at the usual rate of interest as agreed upon". The appellant on 30 6 1943 wrote a letter to Ram Ratanwala stating that "the sum of RS. 4 lakhs was credited to India1962 and a sum of money Rs. 1,00200 was withdrawn by him from the respondent as a banker and along with the interest from time to time the amount of RS 4,000 should he debited to the India Supplies. Thereafter, on 30 7 1943, the appellant wrote another letter to the appellant stating that the debt would be paid on demand. The appellant replied that "as soon as the money was realised by him there was an arbitration award. The arbitrator gave his award in favour of the respondent. Ram Ratan Lohia vs Muhammad Seth Chand, A.I.R. 1948 P.C. 518, holding that Article 60 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 was the relevant article and decreed the suit in favour to the defendant. At the trial the issues were first whether the respondent deposited the money with the appellant. The additional issues were: (1) Whether the suit was barred by time; (2) whether it was a case of loan or deposit ; and (3) whether Article 60 was the only relevant article because if was a claim of money deposited under an agreement that it was payable on demand, the limitation would commence from the date of demand and the suit is filed within three years from the demand. Held, that for a part of the amount, there must be an unqualified demand for the whole sum before the limitation can star in case of demand for return of the money deposited. The court has to satisfy itself as to how the parties treated and understood their financial dealings. If the facts of each case are such that there is unqualified demand, then the denying the claim would arise; but where there are common partners in a firm, all these factors must be present together to consider whether the transaction is clothed with the character of a deposit of money. The circumstances that the amount was deposited with the respondent cannot always be expected in regard to use and by foreign language by merchants and traders in their short memorandum. The nature of the deposit is an inherent. Grindlays. 596 The same may not always be possible to arrange presence of the writer of the entry. Though,Acquisition of money would have sufficed the needs of the appellant, who were then unable to pay the dues of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills that the parties resorted to the mode of having the use of money by way of deposit; it is in evidence that the reference to the page of the panna under that entry was written later inasmuch as the page 580 of the Panna was put on when the pancham book was written.

The petitioner, who was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue, dated February 28, 1986 made in exercise of powers vested under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. It was contended that the period of parole had expired on February 20, 1987, and since the detenu was already in custody he was taken into custody only upto February 22, 1987 and that the order of detention was liable to be quashed. Dismissing the writ petition this Court HELD: 1. The fact remains that only one point was argued. [848C] 2.1 The averments in paragraph 2 of the present Writ Petition accepts that position. It is therefore follows that Mr. Jethmalani made submissions confined to one contention which had not been raised in the earlier Writ Petition but arose out of the proceedings in court therein relating to the effect of release on parole. The order of preventive detention is dated September 28, 1987. [ 848C E] 1049 1.2 If on these facts the order would become vitiated. However, this contention is rejected, it will be open to Mr. Councils to make full submission on all as pect arising in the writ peti tion. That having not been done, it was improper on the part of Mr. Chatterjee, that he would have proceeded to argue the other points. [862D G] 2:2 The order dated September 27, 1987 indicates that the facts as stated therein are without foundation against the Bench hearing the matter, and he was not aware of the fact that he had confined his arguments to one point settled the writ Petition as senior counsel with the allegations quoted above in paragraph 3 of the Writ Petition. [850A] 3:3 In view of the positive case of the respondents that there was no summons and the detenu had been orally directed to attend the office by the authorities concerned, the Court should have condoned that aspect. The Court also indicated that it was not a matter of controversy that the petitioner had confined their arguments to a one point since he had earlier stated that his counsel had a strong, almost unanswerable case on merits but he was very keen to have the question of exclusion of the parole period decided since it arose squarely in this case. This Court therein pointed out that it is not a matters of no consequence as to whether giving up the other pleas raised in writ peti tions amounted to breach of professional duty on thepart of Mr, Jethmalani.
