In the assessment year 1945 46, there were six cash credits aggregating to Rs. 59,026 in the name of the assessee 's wife. Before the Income tax Officer, the assessee did not make a return of his income but only made a " voluntary return". The Income tax officer included this sum as his assessable income and assessed him on it for the assessment years 1945 46. 59026 could not and should not have been included in his income that the amended section 34 had no retrospective effect, that the assessment completed on February 26, 1951 was invalid inasmuch as it was completed four years after that date, (the end of the relevant assessment year) was completed eight years after which the end of that year; and (b) the benefit of extended period of limitation for assessment available under the first proviso to sub section (3) of section 34 was not available in this case. The assessee submitted a voluntary " return on January 5, 1950 showing a total net income of Rs. 1,935 which showed him a total loss of Rs, 1,936 in the previous year (assessment year 194546), and adding the same footnote to the return to the following effect: " My wife has sold her old ornaments and deposited the sum of Rs 59,036 on the firm of Assar Syndicate in which I am a partner." The Income Tax Officer included this amount as income and added the same or footnote. In appeal by the assessee under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, he held that the return was not valid in law. The Tribunal also rejected his contention that since there had been no omission or failure on the part of an assessee to make a "ossession ' showing a non taxable income, it could not possibly be 'treated ' as a return under section 24(1)(a) Of the Act and that section 34 of the Act did not apply. Held: (i) The notice issued under section 22(1), issued by the Income Tax officer on February 27, 1950, after the assessee had filed his voluntary " returns on January May 5,1950, was valid in all respects and must be quashed inasmuch as the notice issued to him under sections 22(4) and 23(2) of that Act could not be treated as invalid merely because it did not comply with a notice under section 34(1). (ii) The view of the Calcutta High Court is correct. The question whether the return in answer to a notice issued on February 18, 1950 after the assesses had filed a voluntary ' return on the last day showing income less than the taxable limit could not have any bearing on the interpretation of that provision. A return which showed no assessable income could not ordinarily be treated " as a 'assessed income ' under cl. (c) of sub section 1 of section 28 and was therefore not hit by the provisions of section 24. Under cl. 2(a), only those persons were required to make an "ossess ' showing an 'Income below the taxable minimum was filed. The notice under s, 22(2), did not require any return showing a assessable income less the taxable amount.

Under Clause 3 of the Nationalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Scheme, 1970, one Director from among the employ ees of the nationalised banks who are not workmen is to be appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India on the Board of each Nationalised Bank. The word 'superintendent ' has been defined to mean a person who had put in 5 years service either as an employee or a non worker. Clause 3(b) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in clause (3), the Central Govern ment may, after consul tation with the Nationalisation Bank make a scheme for carrying out the provisions of this Act, and that before so read, the said clause does not justify or support the impugned circu lar. The respondent Bank in Civil Appeal No. 854 of 1989 filed Writ Petitions in the High Court contending inter alia that the circular is ultra vires the Act and the Scheme inasmuch as it cuts at the root root of the representative form of selection for appointment to the Board as contemplated by the statute. The writ petitions were contested on behalf of the Bank and it was contended that (1) there is no justification whatsoever to issue any such circular for the very object of the Act is to encourage democratic selec tion of the Directors who will truly represent the interests of the various categories of persons mentioned in the Act; and (2) there was no justification whatever whatsoever to issued any such notification for the quite object of this act is to promote orderly growth of a 'management culture '. Dismissing all the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The object of clause 3 is to nationalise the banks in order to, as stated in the preamble to the Act, "control the heights of the economy and to meet progressively, and serve better, the needs of development of the nation in conformi ty with the national policy and objectives". The very purpose of the legislation is to render the largest good to the real number of people of this country 'sovereign, socialist, secular democratic republic. [859F] 2.1 In the case of non workmen employees, on the other hand, election is indeed the most logical, the most domini ty, and certainly the most equitable form of representation. They are well identified, well organised, well organized and interested associates and participants in the banking industry. They were as much a part of the bank as the management is. There can be no legitimate management culture foreign to their vital interest. There could be no valid management policy contrary to their genuine needs. The Act does not contemplate a manage ment unmindful of the true and legitimate interest of the employees. In a nationalised bank, everyone is as much an employee as he is an employer.

The assessee imposed penalties in respect of the assessment years 1954 55, 1960 61 and 1961 62. The proceedings were held by the Income tax authorities under section 132 read with section 274(2) of the Act. The assessee preferred appeals to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal declined to stay holding that it had no power to grant such a prayer. The question for determination in this appeal was whether an interim order of stay could be passed although section 64(2)(a), requiring that where an assessee has presented an appeal under section 246, the Income Tax Officer may in his discretion and subject to such conditions as he may think fit, treat the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal. ^ Held: (i) The power conferred by section 254(1) upon the Appellate Assistant Commissioner with widest possible amplitude must carry with them by necessary implication all powers and duties incidental to make the exercise of those powers, fully effective. (ii) Where the Income. tax Officer or any of his superior departmental officers can be moved for granting stay in the recovery of penalty or tax due from an assessee as a matter of course the revenue will be put to great loss because of the inordinate delay in disposal of appeals by the Appellate Tribunals. In the present case, when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction, it impliedly grants the power of doing all such acts, or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. The power under section 255(1), therefore, is not likely to be exercised in a routine manner or as a matters of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue.

The respondent, a constable in U. P., was reverted to his substantive post of head constable and posted as station Officer at Sidholi. On September 16, 1952, he was placed under suspension, but on August 18, 1953, he filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court at Allahabad, praying for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the preliminary enquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the respondent in regard whereof the magisterial inquiry was held at an earlier stage, and therefore it fell within the express terms of para 489(2). Held, that the departmental enquiry was validly held when the respondent was officer incharge of the Police Station, within his jurisdiction, and he was not subject to any inquiry under the Criminal Procedure Code. In other circum stances, the departmental trial was in respect Of seven charges which were the subject matter of the departmental investigation. The enquiry ended in the dismissal of the first respondent, but before the expiry of his leave the respondent had been reverted to the substantive post and transferred to Sitapur. There was no magisterial enquiry in respect thereof, if substantially, the subjectmatter of the mag ministerial inquiry and the departmental retrial were the same. In this case, the enquiry ended subsequent to the completion of magisterial Inquiry and therefore the departmental proceedings were validly held. Held further that the fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries did not affect the question, if orally referred, would not affect its validity. C.A. 119 of 1959.

The appellants were promoted to supertime grade II on February 8, 1971 by the Union of India. On account of various imponderables the service could not be constituted and 1963 Rules were amended by Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966 which contained identical provisions in regard to promotion from non gazetted posts in Supertime Grade I and non gazetted post in super time grade II and sub rule 2 thereof provided for absorption of departmental candidates holding posts in categories `A ' and `B ' under 1963 Rules in posts in supertime Grade 1 and `E ' to those absorbed either in the Specialists ' grade or General Duty Officers, as the case may be. The appellant contended that these 28 posts were meant only for promoting category 'C ' clinical Specialists to super time Grade II and that when a post was created in a certain grade, category or cadre, it was to be filled in by promotion from amongst those newly formed specialists ' Grade posts in the speciality in which the need had been felt from amongst these in the specialists, namely, sub inspector of the department, that post could only have been filled in from amongst them who might be promoted from 'General Duty Officers Grade I because General Duty Officer officers grade I were also promotable to super lime grade II. The respondent State Government preferred a writ petition in the High Court challenging the promotion of the said four respondents, contending: (1) that as these 28 vacancies were in Specialists Grade and the strength of which Specialists were created was reduced by 28, whenever any post out of these 28 plots added to superTime grade II was required to be inspired in, it could only be filled by promotion and not in any other manner and particularly not by transfer; (2) that the 19 unspecified specialists" posts were intended only for promotion category `C ' technicalists to Supertime grade I. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant was fully qualified for being promoted to the supertime scale allotted to him under rule 8(3). He must have been considered eligible for promotion to super Time grade II because he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists ` Grade officers formed on September 9, 1966. [51 B] 1.2 The appellant would be the Head of the Department and would continue to be in super usual grade II from which date he claimed as being eligible for the post. No one junior to him in his speciality could claim promotion from the very date on which he refused to accept promotion to a post for which he was not qualified. [52 C] 2.1 It is crystal clear that when an unspecified Specialists "post is converted into a specified post and assigned to a speciality it can be filled In either by promotion or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota system of rule,. But once there is a post in a supertime grades II which is to be filling in subsequent to the initial constitution of the Service, rule 8 (3) will be attracted in all its rigour. On a true interpretation of the 1966 Rules in general and rule 8 in particular it could not he gain that whenever an uns specified Specialists" post is converted from a specified category, it can only be made in either by Promotion or by promotion. If, however, there was some substance, though there is none, in the contention on behalf of the appellant that whenever unspecifiedSpecialists 'post is conversion into a specific grade post and assign to a 296 it can alter only so many posts as may seem suitable for promotion. The word "appointment" in the context of the 1967 Rules are not relevant considerations.

The land reform laws were enacted to bring about an agrarian re ordering so pivotal to the progress of our rural economy. Haryana, happily a granary of our country, is one of the States where land reform law are likely to generate great changes by banishing big concentration of Natur 's bounty in a fewbroken feudal hands creating an enthusiastic sense of distributive justice and exploiting the productive potential of land by the possessive passion of the landless many. So strategic island reform that special constitutional concern has been shown for this programme. Naturally the State enacted The Act whereby ceiling on land ownership was set; surplus lands were taken over for settling ejected tenants and others, peasant proprietorship created. The scheme of the Act with which we are concerned is fairly simple and somewhat scientific, although its language, what with frequent amendments dovetailed from time to time, has made for ambiguity, obscurity, marginal inconsistency and a rich crop of litigation. Indeed, the conflict of opinion at the High Court level and the bone of contention before this court arise from this drafting deficiency Legal Preface: (1) A thumb nail sketch of the 's Act is a prefatory necessity; its basic goals are to cut down large holdings and distribute lands to various landless people according to a design and to foster, according to legislative policy, an agrarian community of peasants proprietors. De hoarding and defeating hide outs are essential to make the twin objects successful and so sections 10A and 19B among others, have been written into the Act. To explore the import and ambit of these two provisions particularly the former with a view to see whether it strikes at a gift made by the respondent in favour of his sons whereby he sought to stow away some of his lands, shed some of their excess lands and look slim on as a small holder before the law Language permiting, the Court as interpretedor must fulfil not frustrate the legislative mission. 123 of 1969: One Sampuran Singh who owned 450 bighas and 9 biswas of land acting with foresight gifted half of it to his mother in 1951, perhaps with a premonition of coming restrictions by way of ceiling on owner ship. So much so, on the date when the Act came into force he was the owner of about 178 bighas which, admittedly fell safely short of the permissible permissible area as set out in section 2(5a) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953. The cumulative result of the shedding operations was to shrink the size of his holding to well within the permissible area. The Collector, however investigat ed into the matter and declared an area of 117 bighas as surplus in his hands. He reached this conclusion by ignoring the tell tale gift of February 1, 1959 in favour to the son and the three possessory mortgages executed in June 1958. The status of 'small land owner ' thus being forfeited, the threat lo the surplus lands revived but was sought lo be warded off by the petitioner moving an unsuccessful appeal Lo the Commissioner and a further fruitless revision to the Financial Commissioner. There was disagreement between the two learned Judges on the Bench and the third learned Judge decided in favour C.A. 123/1969 holding that section 19B read with section 10A did not affect the petitioner 's transfers. The High Court while upholding the contention of the petitioner substantially concurred in their reasonings but the scope of the interpretative exercise is very limited, and it can only be that although in the hands of the propositus, it is surplus land, if among the heirs it is not, then their transfers will not be affected by the interdict of section 10 A(a) the sins of the father shall not set the teeth of the children on edge.

The question whether an impartible estate devolves on a person who is not loyal or does not manage the property or does improve his cultivation or who is guilty of bad behaviour and bad administration, was referred for decision to the Supreme Court by the appellants. The question that arose for consideration in these appeals was: (i) Whether the suit was barred by section 14(1)(a) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951? (ii) Whether on the death of a Zamindar the estates should devolve upon his eldest son and in the absence of a legitimate or an adopted son it devolves upon the nearest male relative; (iii) whether the decree was competent to be set aside because as no suit was filed by the plaintiffs for setting aside that decision, the order of the Collector became final and conclusive between the parties because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two months from the date thereof, and consequently the plaintiff 's suit with regard to Malguzari lands was not barred by the decision of the Compensation Officer. ^ HELD : (1) The High Court erred in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awardable to the plaintiffs as they did not apply the correct principle of law but applied the wrong principle to them. [319 D G] (2)(a). The right to determine inheritance is a statutory one and constitutes an integral part thereof. If it is for a few days, the Deputy Commissioner will manage the Zamindari on behalf of the Zamindar and if the order is permanent, the Zamindar shall so say he be deemed to have died and the heir will get the right. But if the nearest in the line of succession is not selected the estate must be given to the nearest heir who has the prescribed qualifications and is a successor to the Zamindar. [333 A, F] (b) The right of inheritance vests in the Governor but the power is exercisable in accordance with and not in violation of the custom of the family.

Section 12(3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, provides that no suit for recovery of possession shall be instituted by a landlord against the tenant on the ground of non payment of the standard rent or permitted increases due to him as it thinks fit. The respondent landlord terminated the tenancy inter alia, on the grounds (1) that the appellants were in arrears of rent for more than six months; (2) that they had not paid rent and arrears of rents from 1 September 1964 and 11 February 1967, which were accepted by the respondent landlord after serving a notice on them under section 12(2); and (3) that their tender were made within one month of service of the notice terminating the tenancy. The trial court held that the tenants were in default. On appeal the Appellate Court confirmed this decision. In an application under article 227 of the Constitution, the Bombay High Court held that when the respondent paid all arrears and costs of the suit on 23 December 1964 it could not be said that the tenant did not comply with the provisions of section 12 (3). Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: The view taken by the Bombay two High Courts is correct. The Bombay High Courts are in error because they ignore the limitation of time within which a dispute is to be raised as to standard rent. [632 C] Ambalal vs Badaldas ; followed. In Ambaladal 's case the notice terminated the contractual tenancy of the appellants inter alia on the allegation that the respondent was in arrears for more then six months and since there was admittedly no dispute regarding standard rent and permitted increases at the date of service, it could be said to have been raised at any time prior to the expiration of one month from the date when service of notice under section twelve (3)(a) would be excluded. [643 E] Ambaral ' 's Case, followed. Vora Abbasbhai 's decision; Ambalalal, vs Badaladas Nagindas took the view that in order to avoid the operation of section 15(1), the dispute must be in existence latest within one year after service of that notice and was not enough to raise a dispute for the first time in the written statement. [537 F] Amalal '

The respondent company was incorporated in what is then British India having a capital of Rs. 3,600,000 divided into 360 shares of Rs 1 each, the Aluminium Limited (a company incorporated in Canada) held 359,790 shares in the chargeable accounting periods ending on December 31, 1940 and December 31,, 1941, respectively., December 31., 1942, and December31, 1943 and December 30, 1943, only 210 shares and in the said chargeable accounting period ended on December 1, 1941. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondent company, the aluminium Ltd appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the Respondent Company. Two of these Directors simultaneously retired and only one, namely, Mr. L. G. Bash and continued to be a director of the Company nominated by the Aluminium Ltd. Mr. jeopardy had not been revoked as far as the respondent Company was concerned, nor had it any controlling interest therein, and as such could control the affairs of the company and that in computing the standard profits the statutory percentage should be taken at 10 per cent. per annum and not at 8% per annum. This contention was rejected by the Excess Profits Tax Officer on appeal by the respondent with the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The respondent company appealed to the Incometax Appellate Tribunal which reversed the decision of the appellate Assistant Commissioner observing that in view of the powers conferred by article 90, it could control its affairs and that the directors of a Company may well be regarded as having "a controlling interest" in the company when they hold and are entering into the share register as holders of the majority of shares which under the articles Of association of companies carry the right to vote. Held, further that though Mr.L. G Tripura had not held the majority in the respondent 's company and although he might be bound to cast the votes according to the directions of his principals, the appellant could not apply either of its tests mentioned above, nor was it necessary that in order to have "a Controlling interest" the person or persons who hold the majority shares must have a beneficial interest in the shares held by them. The Bombay High Court in New Shorrock Spinning and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay, , relied on.

The respondent was an Accountant, Grade II. The promotional post was to the cadre of I Class clerk, in the Electricity Department of the former State of Hyd erabad. On 1st October 1957, the Mysore State Electricity Board was constituted under the Indian Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. An option was given to the respond ent to continue in the Government service or to opt for the Board. On 2nd November, 1972, the respondent opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect from that date. In 1960 the Mysore Electricity Board constituted an Recruitment and Promotion of Employees of the Board Regulation, 1960. The Regulations were subsequently amended on 16th December 1966. The amended Rules prescribed the passing of the S.A.S. examination for promotion to Accounts Superin tendents. On 30th December, 1966, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their having passed the S .A.T. Examination while promotion was denied to the Respondent as he had not passed the examina tion. In a writ petition filed by the respondanti nent, the Single Judge who heard the petition dismissed it and the respondent preferred an appeal before a Bench of the Karnataka High Court which dismissed it on merits. Hence this appeal by special leave against that order. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Resolution dated 19th May, 1969 as exempting the allottees from passing the Departmental Examination I and Kannada language test is only as regards services where the rules do not specifically require the passing ing of S. A.S., examination for promo tion to the Cadre of Accounts Superintendents and does not apply in the instant case as the regulations framed by the Board under section 79(c) specifi cally prescribe the passing or the Departmental Examinations and Kannadada language tests as a consequence of the judgment of the High Court of Mysore and the Supreme Court. [512G] 2. The resolution dated 5th January, 1970 cannot be understood as altering the position existing 'as before". This reasoning is erroneous for, as pointed out by the earlier Resolution was not intended to cover the case of allottees and merely because the allottees were excluded from the operation of the resolution the inference that the allottees are exempt ed from passing of S.,A. Examination was not insisted prior to that Resolution in the case. [511F] 3. The passing of a Resolution by the board cannot have the effect of modifying a Regulation which was passed by the Company in pursuance of certain proceedings of the Govern ment referred to in the Resolution itself.

% The petitioner 's son Suman Behera was taken into police custody in connection with the investigation of an offence of theft and detained at the Police Outpost. At about 2 p.m., the next day on 2.12.1987, the petitioner came to know that the dead body of her son was found on the railway track near a bridge at some distance from the Jaraikela railway station. There were multiple injuries on the body of Suman Behrahera when it was found and obviously his death was unnatural, caused by those injuries. The allegation made is that it was a case of custodial death since Suman Behara died as a result of various injuries inflicted to him while he was in police custody. The trial court held that it is a case which can be determined on the evidence led by parties and the District Judge has submitted his report dated 4.9.1991 containing his finding based on that evidence that evidence had been adduced during the inquiry did not support the defence of respondents; there is no reason to reject the finding of the District Court that Suman Beetahera died in police detention as a consequence of injuries inflicted upon him while the petitioner was in Police custody at the police Outpost Jeraiauni; and that it would be appropriate to spell out clearly the principle on which the liability of the State arises in such cases for payment of compensation and the distinction between this liability and the liability in private law for payment Of compensation in an action on tort. It would, however, be appropriate if the Court issues a suitable direction to the District judge Sundergarh in Orissa to hold an inquiry into the matter and submit a report. Accordingly, evidence was led by the parties and on the basis of the inquiry report dated April 4,1991 containing its finding based upon that evidence, and on hearing the arguments advanced by both sides, the District Judges came to the conclusion that it has been a case for compensation to Suman Be outlined in their defence and to contend that the responsibility for the safety of SumanBehera came to an end the moment Suman Behrihera escaped from police custody resulting in his death. The State of Orissa & its police officers including Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police and Constable No.127 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the findings of District Judge. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence adduced during inquiry does not support his defence and there isno reason to discard the finding that it had been caused to the deceased by lathi blows; consequently, the death had occurred in the manner suggested by the police in a train accident and it was not caused by the Police while the deceased was in their custody. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle on Which the court 's power under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution is exercised to award monetary compensation for contravention of fundamental rights are equally well settled. [591C] 2.1 The High Courts have not only the power but also an obligation to grant relief in exercise of its jurisdiction under Articles32 and 226, which itself is a fundamental right imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental rights under Article 21 of the constitution. [595G] 2:2 It is a sound policy to punish the wrongdoer and it is in that spirit that the Courts have molded the relief by granting "compensation".

Rule 549(4) of the Manual for the Superintendence and Management of Jails, provides that every prisoner under a sentence of death shall be allowed such interviews and other communications with his relatives, friends and legal advisers as the Superintendent thinks reasonable. The petitioner who was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of the sentence were rejected by the President recently on February 1, 1989. Consequently, the petitions challenging the validity of Rule 549(2) of Chapter XIV A B 'D ' of the Criminal Procedure Code were heard together by a Full Bench in regard to the constitutionality of Rule 551(4). In that petition it was contended for the petitioner inter alia that if read as an attenuation clause it is clear that the two prisoners are ready and willing to be interviewed, the Court would like to observe that the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by Article 19(1)(a) is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the press to have an unrestricted access to means of information. Allowing the Writ Petition in part and directing the Superintendent of Jail to allow the petitioner to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga, this Court, HELD: (i) The constitutional right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right asserted by him is not a right to be ascertained. [1186 D] (ii) It does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press, such for example, as there is under section 161(2), Criminal Procedure code. [ 1187 A B] (iii) The petitioner has been asked for permission to interview the prisoners right since the President has rejected the petitions preferred by the prisoners for commutation and then pass an order directing that the petitioner should be allowed to interview them. While he was on this aspect of the matter, it is not possible to say that the three petitioners are ready or willing to appear at the time of execution of the death sentence. [1108 B C] (iv) The petitioners have been asking for permission in the writ petitions challenging their validity. [111 A B C].

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd. On January 19, 1950, the Bank applied for the appointment of a Receiver. Under the terms of the bond the appellant rendered itself liable 'in respect of any loss or damage occasioned by any act or default of the Receiver in relation to his duties as such Receiver as aforesaid. The respondent moved an application asking for damages from the receiver on the ground that the fire had occurred due to his negligence and therefore the court directed the Receiver to furnish the requisite security within the time allowed to him. On the District judge, the appellant transferred the mortgage suit to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Agartala. The transferee court was created under the order of 1950 which came into force on December 31, 1950. The district judge transferred the mortgaged suit to it and the court of the Subordinate Judge transferred the suit to a court of subordinate Judge for execution. On February 26, 1950 the tea garden was damaged by fire which destroyed over 3,000 tea saplings. On October 4, 1961 the respondent moved another application asking that the Receiver be asked to furnish security. On August 26, the District Judge transferred his mortgage suit out to the Subordinate judge, West Tripura, for recovery of damages for the loss caused to the Tea garden by fire. The transferor court granted the respondent 's claim on May 31, 1956 but it allowed the respondent to carry away the amount within two months failing which the amount should be recovered from the security of Rs. 50,000. Civil Miscellaneous First Appeal No. 22 of 1956 filed against the order was dismissed for default by the Judicial Commissioner. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The Subordinate Judge of Agartala may not be the successor in office of the District Judges because "successor" in office would mean successor of the district judge in the post or office of District Judge.

Under section 2(h) of the U.P. Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Order, 1959 a contract of sale was a 'sale ' within the meaning of the . The State Government was, however, not competent to legislate for levy of tax only on transactions which were "sales" within the expression 'sale" in section 2 (h)of the Utter Pradesh Sugar Procurement (Levy) Order. 1959, by virtue of Entry 48 List II of the Government of India Act, 1935, a scheme was devised for equitable distribution of sugar and as such was subject to certain restrictions contained in clause 3 thereof. The power to tax purchases of sugarcane under cls. (e), (fh) and (j) was confined to transactions which occurred "s sales" within that expression. Sub section (3) provided that a contract where the seller agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price paid or promised shall be delivered by the licensed dealer to the Controller or to such other person as may be authorised by the Controller to take delivery on his behalf. Clause 3 of the order enabled the licensed holder to sell to the State Government 50% of the wheat held in stock by him on the date of commencement of the Order from the date "controlled prices". The appellants challenged this levy. Their contention was that they were compelled by law to buy cane from the sugarcane growers, and since purchases made by them were not under agreements, the price paid for sugarcane could not be taxed under a statute enacted in exercise of the powers conferred on them by cl. 10B. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The High Court erred in holding that there was no sale of the wagons and no income tax was payable. [682 F] (1) A contract of "sale of goods" between persons competent to contract for a sale price paid ' or promised was a transaction in which an obligation to supply goods is imposed, and which does not involve an obligation not to enter into a contract, cannot be called a "sale", even if the person supplying goods is declared entitled to the value of goods, which is determined or determinable in the manner prescribed. Assuming that between the licensed dealers and the Controller there may be some arrangements about the place and manner of delivery of wheat, and the payment of price at the controlled rate, and this was not an offer by the tax payer to the Government, the distributor in the factory zone was bound to accept it, and its agreement resulted therefrom in a contract between the parties. [683 G] (2) The expression "sale" is defined in section 3(h), as meaning any transfer of property in Goods for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration, but not including a mortgage, hypothecation, charge or pledge. (3 ) Section 4 provides that a liability to obtain possession shall be paid by the dealer to such person as arrears of land revenue. The Order is therefore not an "sale ' under the U .P. Sales Tax Act, 1948. [684 B] The mere fact that the stock of wheat was purchased in accordance with cl. 3 of order and not pursuant to the directions issued under cl. 5 did not amount to an offer.

The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was due for release from prison on June 23, 1986. On that day he was ob tained in connection with some other case. He stood acquitted on May 26, 1986 on the ground that though acquitted, he was not straightaway released from prison. The grounds were not clear to him from the record. Presumably he was required in connection w.e.f. August 7,1986 when the order of detention dated June 23. 1986 was revoked and a fresh order of deten tion was made on the same facts on the earlier date. In the meantime, the order for his detention was passed under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985, which provided that in every case where a detention order has been made under the Act, the State Government shall within three weeks from the date of detention of a person under the order place before the Advisory Board the grounds on which the order hasbeen made, the representation, if any, made by the detenu and the report, ifany, of the authorised offi cer. What is important for the purpose of this case is that there has been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by article 22(4) and therefore, the appellant is entitled to be released on July 14, 1986 as no reference had been made to the Advisory Boards within the period contem plated by section 11 of the Act. The period of three weeks stipulated by proviso to Section 11 expired on July 19, 1986 after the detention which commenced on the making of the order was revoked, and a further fresh order is made on August 17, 1986, which commenced the making on the order dated June 3, 1986 had been challenged by filing a writ petition in the High Court. Consequent upon the revocation of that order that writ petition was dismissed as having become infructuous and another Writ Petition, out of which the present appeal arises against the said order of his detention under Section 12 of the passed by the Advisory board, the request for release on July 15, 1986 at his own request. The appellant moved this Court by special leave for relief. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: It becomes imperative to read down section 15 of the Jammu & Kashmir Prevention of anti Social Activities act, 1985 which provides for the making Of successive orders of detention so as to bring it in conformity with Article 22( 4) of the Constitution ineffective. If there is to be a collision between article 22 (4) of Constitution and Section 15 of Act, sec. 15 has to yield. And such a casual and indifferent approach betrays a disregard for the rights of citizens and this has to be deprecated. [197E F] Shibapada Mukher jee vs State of West Bengal, , referred to.

The petitioner and the respondent were established Vaidyas in Rajkot. They came from a well to do family. The petitioner is advanced in age and both the father and the son have been fighting between themselves since more than a decade. The High Court found that the respondent had referred their disputes to one Kantibhai Vaidya, who had intervened between them with the good intention to bring their disputes back to an end. He made an award under section 17 of the (hereinafter called 'the Act '). In the award it was stated by the arbitrator that he had called both the son at his residence on 18th January, 1977 and that he should abide by the award dated 20th January 1977 and the said interpretation must be left to the arbitrator himself. It appears that the award was endorsed and signed by both the parties, in writing and signed as well as their respective Advocates. The agreement was in the form of a letter addressed to the Arbitrator wherein it was mentioned that both of them had appointed him as an Arbitrator to resolve the disputes between them and that it was signed by all the parties therein. In the arbitrator 's award it is stated by him that he has called both both the brothers, at his office on 18rd January,1977. He had discussed the matter with both the petitioner and respondent who have referred their dispute to one of the named arbitrator and he had told them that all the disputes should abide By such interpretation, he made the award on 18.1.1977. Below the award, both the terms of the award were also signed by the parties as well. In appeal before this Court it was contended for the petitioner that the previous proceedings were without jurisdiction. On behalf of the respondent it was submitted that the proceedings were not without jurisdiction and that the arbitrator had jurisdiction to decide the question which was before them (namely, whether the suit was barred as res judicata) and they did decide it. Dismissing the application, ^ HELD: 1. There is no such express or implied prohibition nor any inability of a Judge concerned. In this case, there was no such expressed or implied Prohibition nor any decision of the Judge concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award the arbitrator could be said to be a proper arbitration agreement in terms of section 2(a) of the Act. [538F G] 2. In view of the matter, it is clear that the conduct of the parties that there Was an arbitration clause and by signing the award paper it could be inferred to be an act of a proper contract agreement in respect of the subject matter of the suit or over the parties to it. [540A B] 3. The conduct of parties that it took was done twice, firstly by signing an endorsement below the award and secondly by entering into an agreement in the shape of a ' letter dated 14th August, 1978 (Exhibit 40). In this view of all these factors, the respondent was not entitled to challenge the award. [541D] 4. The trial Judge had made a decree in terms thereof. The copy of the agreement was also signed and signed, by both parties as also their respective advocates. The first appellate court dismissed the revision application filed against the judgment and order passed by the Civil Judge raising practically all the dispute which had been raised by the petitioner in this civil revision application. During the course of the execution proceedings, the petitioner preferred a civil revision applications against the said order. During course of Section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code, the peti tioner preferred a Civil Revision Application with leave to appeal against the judgement and decree passed by it raising practically All the disputes which had taken place by him in this Civil revision application which was rejected summarily. The main objection to the award is that there is no written agreement signed by two parties on 14th and 15th August 1978 ( exhibit 40). [541F G; 538A] 5.

The respondent, the assignee of a mortgage debt from the appellant 's son under an agreement was appointed receiver of that estate in which the properties were mortgaged. On August 10, 1908, the said receiver with the permission mortgaged certain properties to the said firm as security for the due repayment of the loan advanced by that firm. The appellant applied for and on October 30, 1935 a petition (exhibit 2) was filed stating that the order was substantially and correctly entered in column 20 of exhibit F which is a certified copy of extract from the Register of applications for executions of decrees relating to execution proceedings of Case Nos. 78 of 1922 and that after coming into force of the said Act, the attachment was cancelled and the decree in question was recorded as adjusted for the sale. In execution of this final decree the mortgaged properties were sold at a Court auction on January 30, 1937, and were purchased by the appellant for Rs. 59,000. This sale was confirmed by the court dated June 30, 1931. The respondent filed execution proceedings No. 79 of 1936 for enforcing the mortgage of which was dismissed. Thereafter the appellant filed an application in the executing Court stating as follows: "The judgment debtor having made special requests to the decree holder for an amicable settlement of the aforesaid execution case, the decree holders have agreed to the same." The trial court held that both the original and a certified Copy of the order passed on July 31, 1928 amounted to adjustment under section 36(1) (a), (b) and (c) of s.36, but not detailed in this petition of June 2, 1939, as they had not considered in this case the copy of the orders made on that date by the executing court on the application for execution of decrees pertaining to execution proceeding No. 81 of 1936 relating to Execution proceedings was not forthcoming. The trial Court ordered attachment of the properties and directed the payment of Rs. 60,000 to the respondent. Held, (i) A decree passed in a suit to which this Act applies does not mean any order of dismissal for non prosecution ' though it is said that the execution pro ceeding in execution has already been entered.

One Venkatacharyulu, the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. She executed two registered deeds purporting to be sale deeds dated April 15, 1946, (Exts. A 1 and A 2) for the purchase of certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1947 after the execution of exhibit A 1, the appellant transferred his property to the appellant certain properties allotted to the Joint family; but after the partition of her deceased husband, the widow and sons instituted O.S. No. 12 of 1954 and O. S. No 62/54 against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April '15, 1946 were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes, and were void. The trial court rejected the contention of the appellant and decreed O.A. No, 63/54 and also decreed O .S. Nos. 63/55, the decree for possession in respect of the lands covered by exhibit A I on the ground that they were made by Venkatacadharappa in favour of the joint Hindu family and the subsequent severance of joint status between the widow of the deceased and his sons, was not hit by section 6 (h) of the . In appeals to this Court it was contended inter alia that the transfers were by way of gifts and not in consideration of the past cohabitation, and that the mere agreement for transfer was without consideration. Allowing the appeal. ^ HELD: Under the Madras school of Mitakshara law by which Venkatachallulu was governed he had no power to make a gift of his undivided interest in the coparcenary properties to his concubine. The gifts were invalid as not validated by the disruption of the Joint Family. After the disruption, Venkatacheharyulu was free to make gift of her own divided interest in Ratu Musalman vs Ranchhod Zipru Bhate. The transfers were without consideration and were by virtue of the fact that they had been motivated by a desire to compensate the concubines for her past services. In lieu of her services, he promised to give his services only. The past cohabitations were the motive and not the consideration for the transfer under exhibit A1 and A2.

Section 29(2)(a) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 which provides that an appeal to a High Court except in the cases provided for by article 151 and article 153 includes all suits, appeals or application by any special or local law. The first limb of sub section (2) of section 29 is concerned only with proceedings of this kind. The procedure applicable in an appeal against an order made by a civil court under section 476 of the Code of Civil Procedure is that prescribed by the Code Of Civil Procedure whereas the period of limitation is 90 days from the date of the decree or Order appealed from, and article 151 referred to in article 156 provides for an appeal filed against a judgment, decree or order of any High Court of Judicature at Fort William Madras. In other words, if the special or Local law prescribed a period of Limitation different from that prescribed therefor by the first schedule to the Limitation Act within which the appeal should be preferred is excluded. The fact that article 156(2) (a) says that "appeal under this Chapter shall be preferred within a period 30 days from such date of order of the Tribunal under section 98 or section 99". The High Court was in error in interpreting the expression "appeal" occurring in sub section 2 of section 15 of the Limitation Acts. Section 29(1A) provides for appeals described in s.29 of the , with the result that, the provisions of section 12 of the Act shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special or other local law." The expression " appeal" in article 157 of Schedule 11 to the Indian Registration Act, does not take in the present case a period different from the period prescribed therefor. The distinction between cases falling under section 29(7) and those falling under subs.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, had questioned the validity of the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magis trate declaring Plot Nos. 702 and 703 which was within its jurisdiction for stopping their buses in accord ance with the order passed by him. The District Magistrate held that Section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magistrate 'to fix the places for the bus stand/halting place ' and directed that such permission be given under section 76 of that Act. The High Court, however, dismissed the Writ Petition filed by the appellant in this Court under Article 226 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal to this court, ^ HELD: 1. Section 68, which is in Chapter IV dealing with 'control of traffic ' confers the power on the State Government to make rules regarding the maintenance and management of parking places and stands and the fees if any, which may be charged for their use. The first question which arises for consideration is whether the area in which bus operators were asked to stop their buses was a bus stand or a halting place. [714A B] 2. A similar question arose for consideration in Municipal Board, Pushkar vs State Transport Authority, Rajasthan and Ors., , [1963] Supp.2 S.C.R. 373; T.P. Ibrahim vs Regional Transport Authority Mahara vedhi Sahiti Multipurpose Transport Co op. Society Ltd & Anr., ; , decided on 7, referred to.

The respondent was the cleaner of a truck, which was loaded with 75 bags of paddy. The consignee of the paddy was Messrs Devi Dayal Brij Lal of Delhi. It is alleged that Qimat Rai also gave a letter assuring him that it was an authority for transporting the paddy. But this was not a letter of authority, and consequently there was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export. Held, that upon the facts found by the lower courts no offence had been committed by the appellants, though the conviction was set aside on appeal. The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence. On the other hand an attempt to commit an offence is a direct movement towards the commission after preparations are made. In order that a person may be convicted of an attemptto commit an 'a crime he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit 'the offence, and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal effort. The sufficiency of the actor is a question of law which has led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commissionof a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt 'to commit it, Held further, that in order that the appellants should not have been convicted under section 7 of the , for these reasons the conviction were set aside. Though the view taken by the trial courts was correct, the High Court was right in setting aside the conviction and sentence of the appellant under sections 7 and 8 of the Act.

A dispute arose between the Sassoons in respect of certain payments made to the Sassoon and Company, Chidambaram under the Agreement entered into by the Sas impossibleons. A question was referred for consideration to the High Court who held that the managing Agency commission was earned in the hands of the person who carried on the business of the Managing Agency and not in the hand of the company and that therefore so far as the Sascoons were concerned, the Managing agency commission should be apportioned between them and their transferees. In appeals before this Court by certificates it was contended for the transferees that even though under the terms of the agreements relating to the transfer they were paid by the Companies the whole of the managing agency commission for the calendar year 1943 they had merely earned the commission or remuneration for the period of actual services rendered by them to the Company and they were not liable to tax, and that as such no part of the consideration paid was payable to them under theferent deeds of assignment and transfer did not include any income which they had earned or had accrued to them. HELD: (i) On a fair reading of the entire clause 10 of the Agreement it could be held that what was assigned was an income bearing asset, viz., the Managing Agent which was the source of income and which entitled the respective assignees to receive all the remuneration for them payable under the managing Agents Agreement subsequent to the respective dates of assignment. The mere ownership of Managing Agency cannot as a matter of law be treated as the source Of ' income, as explained above, any term in the Managing Agencies Agreement between the principal and the agent entitling only the assignee to receive the year 's remuneration and negativing to the assignor any direct recourse to his quondam principal for his share of the income. [371 G E] (ii) It was not correct to approach the consideration of this case as though the decision in Inder Kumar Das vs State of Bihar, ; , relied on by learned counsel for the assessee Sassoon General Mills Ltd., has been relied on, but since it turns directly upon the question whether any income had accrued or to the S.T.O. it is not correct, to approach that Court as though, the decision therein turns directly on the question, whether any Income could accrue to the assessee on the dates of the respective transfers of the Directors to the transferees.

The appellant was a resident of Lucknow in the District of Gonda. He had two sons, Badri and Kirpa Shanker, who lost his wife years ago. This conduct was found to have been corroborated by the evidence on record. The High Court convicted the appellant under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to death. On appeal the Division Bench confirmed both the conviction and sentence. Hence this appeal. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) A confessional soliloquy is a direct piece of evidence. It may be an expression of conflict of emotion; a conscious effort to stifle the pricked conscience; an argument to find excuse or justification for his act; or a penitent or remorseful acts of exaggeration of his part in the crime. The tone may be soft and low, the words may be confused and they may be capable of conflicting interpretations depending on witnesses, whether they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant imaginative or prosaic, as the case may be. [90H; 91A B] (2) A confession is a statement made by an accused admitting his guilt. What does the expression "statement" means? The dictionary meaning of the word "statement", is "the act of stating reciting or presenting verbally or on paper". The term "statement ' in section 157 meant only "something that is stated" and the element of communication was not necessary before "s something that is mentioned. [91H; 92A] (3) A statement, whether communicated or not admitting guilt is a confession of guilt, but there is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an evidence and the weight to be attached to it. A confessional loves is a part of the term that it shall be communicated to another. The dictionary meanings of the expression do not warrant any such extension. nor the reason of the rule underlying the doctrine of admission or confession demands it. Admissions and confessions are exceptions to the hearsay rule. [92G H] Dhupantanju Narayanappa vs R. , applied.

The appellant, a Divisional Manager of the Corporation, was suspended from August 9,1973 pending investigation into embezzlement. Explanation was called for on October 16, 1973 in response thereto the appellant submitted his reply on December 7, 1974. While dropping the proceedings, the appellant was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent. The appellant challenged it in a writ petition in Delhi High Court which dismissed the same. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended that Rule 5 of the Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Ltd. Service Rules (for short "the Rules") as unconstitutional and void offending Article 14 of the Constitution of India and therefore violative of Article 14; that Rule 7 of the Act is ultra vires of Article 19(1)(f) of the constitution; that the order terminating the services was illegal because it imposed a stigma on the appellant; that since the action was initiated against the appellant for the charges of embezzlement etc. which are misconduct, it would be violative of article 14. On behalf of the respondents, it has been submitted that Rule 9 is ultra rites and void as offending Article 19 (1)(g) of Constitution; that rule is ultra legis Diction of Article 21; that unlike Rule 9 in D.T.C. 's case the Rule provides guidelines. The Board of Directors have to take a decision, whether the need to continue the employee 's service subsist which would be based on the relevant material; and indisputably, there is a presumption in favour of constitutionality of a legislation or statutory rule unless ex facie it offends the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III of the Con stitution. If the provisions of law or the Rule are construed in such a manner as would make it consistent with the constitution and another interpretation would render the provision or the rule unconstitutional, the court would lean in favour favour of the former construction. Accordingly, this appeal is allowed but without cost. The Court intervention application filed by Shri S.S. Onkarmal Harlalka is dismissed.

The appellants were licensees in respect of 70 outstill shops. The Collector of Mayurbhanj issued a notice to the successful bidder to call for tenders in accordance with that order. On February 3, 1970 the Collector invited tenders for the grant of privilege for establishing 70 outstil shops for 1970 71. Ajodhya Prasad Shah gave the highest bid for a group of seven shops. In that process Ajodhya Prashad Shah gave a higher bid and his name was entered in the prescribed register and the entry was signed by the successful bidders and the Collector. Ajisations Prasad accordingly deposited Rs. 329/ in the High Court with the allega tion that the Collector had no authority to issue the licenses. The State Government and other respondents traversed the claim in Ajodhya Pahkar 's writ petition and pleaded, inter alia, that tho bids at the auction were not satis factionary and that the State Govern ment had passed the orders for not accepting Aj fluctuation Prasad 's bid. The High Court accepted the challenge to the vires of sections 22 and 29 of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915 and held that as the petitioner was the highest bidder on February 20, 1970 and his names were entered in a register, and the entries were signed by him, the petition er was entitled to the grant Of the exclusive privilege under section 22 by virtue of s.6(a) of the Amending Ordinance irrespective of the validity of r. 103(1) of Excise Rules. The appellants appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) since the Collector alone had passed orders for the purpose of considering the bid, he was not bound by the law as the State Government had no power to direct withholding and reauc tioning of the licenses; (ii) section 29(2)(a) did not authorise the exercise of "such absolute and naked powers in determining the sum of money" as was sought to be done by the order dated August 19, 1970. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power to accept or reject a tender without assigning any reason cannot be said to be arbitrary as section 29 (2) (a) which has been amended with retrospective effect clearly provides that "the State Government may grant to any person, on such conditions and for such periods as it may think fit", the exclusive privileges ' in question" conferred power on the State Legislature to enact such a regulatory measure.

The appellant and one S were charged with having entered into criminal conspiracy with A and others for murder of S. The trial court found that there was corroboration of the evidence of a doctor of an investigation whether he was injured or not as against accused 2 and 3, convicted them under Section 302 read with section 120B I.P.C. On appeal by Special Leave, the questions that fell for consideration were (1) whether there was evidence to connect accused No. 1 with murder; (2) whether the finding of the High Court that there had been corroboration in regard to accused No 2 and Accused 3 not only with the offence of theft but also with murder and (3) whether in arriving at its opinion there was a corroboration of their direct participation in the murder and the crime as well as the common intention. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (1)(a) The evidence which took the conclusion that accused No 1 and 3 formed part of the same transaction were not sufficient for convicting them. [621 A] (b) It is well settled that an accomplice is competent to depose but in case of circumstantial evidence it means all the circumstances which are intended to be proved, namely, that it is confirmedatory evidence and it may consist of the testimony of second witness or of circumstances like the conduct of the person against whom it is required. [522 C] (c) There must be sufficient corroborative evidence in material particulars to connect the accused with the time.

The Town Planning Officer of Surat Municipality declared its intention to make a town planning scheme under s.22 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954. In consequence of this declaration the appellant claimed compensation for deprivation of his right in the land at Rs. 50 per sq. by his order made on November 4, 1971 the Town Planning Authority awarded compensation @ the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. per sq.; and the total amount payable was Rs. 3.31,455. Not satisfied with the decision of the Town planning Officer the appellant preferred an appeal before the Board of Appeal. Before the Board the appellant reduced his claim to Rs. 9.50 p. by a subsequent order dated November 4 1971. The Board of Revision held that the appeal was not maintainable as there was no determination of the compensation to be paid by the owner under section 22 (2). Thereafter the appellant challenged the order of the Board before the Gujarat High Court by way of Writ Petition which certain provisions of the Act were also challenged as unconstitutional and it was claimed 85 that the Town Plan was invalid. The High Court dismissed the writ petition agreeing with the Board 's view taken in Shantilal 's case that the decision in the appellant 's earlier case was appealable either under clause (viii) or cl. (xiii) of section 32 (1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if the land itself is injuriously affected by the making of a town development scheme, it cannot be suggested that land itself was injuriously effected; such a view is unsupportable both as a matter of language and having regard to the scheme of the Urban Land Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court ^ HELD: 1. The Town Planning officer 's decision in an appellant ' 's Case was not appealable either by cl.(viii) nor clause (xiii). So far as the final plot for a purpose of a Town planning scheme is concerned he has to find out the market value of each of the original plots at the date of declaration of intention to policy to make the scheme as provided in section 64 (1); and (xii) calculate the contribution to be levied on each plot included in the final scheme. The expression 'person interested ' as defined in section 3 of the Land Acquisition Act means all persons claiming an interest in compensation to he made on account of the acquisition of land under that Act. [88E 88C] 2. Under section 65 increment is the amount by which the total value of the plots included in final scheme shall be liable to contribute to the costs of a City planning scheme in accordance with the provisions contained in section 66; and (xiii.)ratesizing the increment to accrue in respect of each plot include in the revised final scheme prepared in accordance. [90G H] 3. The word 'person ' as used in section 23 (1) was wide enough to cover all persons who claim an interest, but no benefit can be given to the person whose land has been acquired. Thus the Act contains the necessary provisions for estimating the compensation payable to an owner of land who has not been given a reconstituted plot. [89F G] 4. The question whether the Town Development Authority is entitled to take into consideration in determining the amount of compensation is one of the duties of the town planning officer who is required to forward the final draft scheme to the State Government for sanction. [91G] 5.

One S died during the lifetime of his father. The two daughters were married and became major, Balakrishnan paid them certain monies as due to them out of the income of the properties in May 1942. Thereafter he used to pay 224 kalam of paddy and Rs. 175/in cash towards their properties after deducting the kist each year. He had therefore used to send ted possession to the two daughters in August 1950. After the death of S he left the management of his properties to his brother and provided that as soon as his minor daughters attained majority he should give to them per head one veli nanja land and one veil of punja land in vattam No. 149. The appellant, who was the third son of the testator made a will on October 4, 1927. By this will he appointed his brother an Honorary guardian of his minor sisters as well as his foster son. He left the Management with keys to his two daughters and put the properties to their mother in equal shares. When he did not accept the right of selection claimed by the daughters the appellant who was prepared for a partition of land according to quality but was not prepared to accept the rights of selection made by them. The High Court held that the English rule of benevolent construction was evolved to avoid uncertainty and make the subject of gift reducible to certainty. It further held that on the construction of the will in this case, the right to choose was in the legatees and not in the legatee as contemplated by section 89 of the Indian Succession Act. Held: (i) (a) Under the will there is no express words from which it can be inferred that the testator intended that the daughters should get the area of land devised to them taking into account the good and bad quality of the land; (b) The scope of the words in section 89 is the same, namely, the same namely, that the son shall deliver possession. As soon as the children obtain majority the guardian will deliver possession to them of the respective lands bequeathed to them. It could not therefore be inferred even if he wanted to indicate the extent of land by use of the former words the testator was giving the right for selection to the legates according to the priority of the bequests which would indicate that good and good quality land would be taken into account in computing the area to be given to them; (c) The condition regarding partition of property as laid down in section 88 is not satisfied. Where it is not possible to say on the interpretation of a will that the purchaser himself indicated the selection or appointed a third person to make the selection but still intended to make a gift which could be made certain by selection made for the legate, the English Rule of construction is attracted and there can be no question of any selection by the legatee &rose. The rule seems to be a common sense principle to give effect to the intentions of a testator which clearly show that he intended to bequeath something which could not be made definite by choice; (d) In such cases to there was no difficulty for the testator had himself made the selection and the selection must be given effect to; (e) The words in the will mean the words when they are different in the case of daughters as compared to the words used. Where the testator is not clear, even if the language is ambiguous or obscure it would appear that the intention of the executant was clearly to select the property bequeathed; but where the ambiguity is of a less degree and the intention is of the judge to gift certain property is clear, though there may be some difficulty because there is more property of that kind than actually bequeathed, then the benefit of the rule should also be granted.

This appeal is by way of a suit for joint possession of plots in dispute, being co bhumidars. The appellant 's case was that she was living with her sons at Lucknow and her husband 's cousins were looking after the lands which consisted of agricultural lands and groves and she was given her share by her cousins from time to time. It was also alleged that the respondents had committed fraud, which resulted in a partition between the parties. The plaintiff claimed that earlier she was a co sharer with the defendants but later on she came to know that her name had been deleted from the khewat and the entire property was mutated in the consolidation of holding proceedings. On behalf of defendants it was alleged that although at some time before, the lands in dispute were joint, but during the consolidation proceedings the plots in possession of the plaintiff were occupied by Adhivasi who having acquired the rights of a Sirdar under the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950, the plaintiff lost her title by operation of law. The trial court decreed the suit for possession in respect of land left by her late father. On appeal the District Judge decreed the plaintiff 's suit for partition in respect thereof. Against this decree of the District judge in respect even 1/4 share was upheld. In appeal, the High Court also held that there was nothing to show that any fraud was practised upon the consolidation authorities so as to make the order a nullity. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The possession of defendants apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees would be in law the possession of them. Apart from this the fact remains that the District Court has come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the Consolidation operation either by the defendants or by somebody else as a result of which the rights were sought to be extinguished. [878F G] (i) In view of the clear decision of this Court, referred to above, the trial court did not fully appreciate this part of the case made out by the plaintiff and the District Magistrate in clear terms accepted the same. Therefore, the finding of the High court regarding fraud having been committed in the Consolidation proceedings was not legally sound. [879B] (ii) It is well settled that mere non participation in the rent and profits of the land of a coshareer does not amount to an ouster so as would give title by adverse possession to the other co sharers in possession. Indeed even if this fact be admitted, then the legal position would be that Mohd. Basir & Anr. vs Mahendra Singh & Ors. [1982] I SCR 1086 referred to.

The petitioner in person, filed a writ petition challenging the appointment of Respondent No. 1, Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Prime Minister of India: (i) that Respondent No 1 was just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Chief Business Minister; and (ii) that he was still functioning as the Chief Minister of Haryana when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him. Disposing of the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. Although the word "or" in the context of Article 173 read with Form VII A is merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. The use of the word 'and 'in the context, therefore, does not confer on him any power of the Prime Minister along with his other submis sions, he says that he would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. [3H; 4A B] 2.1 A mere mistake or error in the descriptive part would not vitiate the oath. This Court has laid down a rule for divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. And according to it, as long as the substantial part is properly followed, a mere mistake has or error apparent in the defective part would vitiate the poll.

The appellant company stopped work, some at 4 p.m., and some at 5 p. m. The strike ended completely, but the apparent cause for the strike was that the management of the Mills had expressed its inability to comply with the request of workers to declare the forenoon of the 1st November, 1948, as a holiday for solar eclipse, and on the 3rd November, the strike ended totally. The contention of the appellant was that it was a spontaneous and lightning strike but it was not said by them that stoppage of work did not fall within the definition of "strike" given in section 2(q) of the . Held (per Fazal Ali and Bose J.) that the action of the workers on the night of 1st ' November, III 25, as well as on on the ground that they were entitled to leave for the night shift whenever a half day 's leave was granted to the day shift workers must be held to be unjustified. Once it is found that stoppage did not bring about a breakdown of work by a body of persons employed in the Mills and that they had been acting in combination and their refusal to go back to work on the grounds that they are entitled to privilege leave and there was no provision in those rules similar to the one that has been made in section 49 B or in the new rules. The effect of the notification by which the workers were permitted to remain at full rates, amounted to a strike and the workers thus lost the benefit of holidays that they would have otherwise got under the rules.
