It was not considered that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censorors and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious nor any material to quash the proceedings. [608 G] 3. The resolution of the problem raised in this case thus becomes simplified. If it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals cannot be an ' offence, section 292 I P. C., would exonerate them because the acts ceased to be a ' offence. Section 292 Cr.P.,C. is exculpatory when read with s.5A of the Act and the certificate issued thereunder. [ 516 F G; 516 A B] 4. (a) The resolution does not spell out any justification in law for public exhibiter of prosecutions for an offence under section 292 IPC, which amount to justification within the meaning of section 79 of the Penal Code. [511 C] 5. If section 79 I P.,I.P.(C.) resolves the apparent conflict between sections 292 I, 292 IP. C. and Part II of the Cr. The prohibition operates in this province. Section79 makes an offence a non offence. When it cannot be described as an offence, definitionally speaking but; a forbidden act may not spell inevitable guilt if the law itself declares that in certain special circumstances it is not to be regarded as an 'offence '. [ 515 B C] (b) The Court would assume for purposes of argument that the facts stated in the complaint prima facie attract the offence under s. 292 IPC. If and as here the Board, after examining some witnesses, took cognizance of the offence and issued notice to the respondent, it was right for the court to discharge the accused as the charge is groundless. [500 G] 6. Section 74 Cr.p.C.) vitiates the prosecution by the order.

Pursuant to a decision of this Court in Ramachandran vs Alagiriswami, [1971] 2 S.C.R. 860 this court was put up on the question whether the petitioner 's claim as the sole representative of Government in courts is not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviolability of the high public office of Government Pleader by politicking men in the Secretariat or by practitioners of favouritism dressed in 'little brief authority '. The question that fell for consideration was whether the claim as representative of the Government Pleader 's legal grievance could have been accepted. Dismissing the special leave petition, and remitting the case to the Supreme Court, ^ HELD: 1. To our system all government lawyers must not pamper and thereby inflate the system of costs. [763C D] 2. While reserving a sort of litigation policy for the States having been evolved at an All India Law Ministers ' Conference way back in 1957 and despite the recommendations of the Central Law Commission to promote settlement of disputes where Government is a party, what we find in actual practice is a proliferation of government cases in courts uninformed by any such policy. Indeed, in this country where Government litigation constitutes a sizeable bulk of the total volume, it is important that the State should be a model litigant with accent on settlement. The State must evolve a policy in regard to its law Officers which concedes to counsel freedom to recommend settlement of cases if they feel just to do so and further aims practices distributive justice which preempts the need for adjournment because of absence of counsel and, lastly, sets a limit on the total fee payable for government work executed. [764E F] 3.1 The respondents had no rights and liabilities in these matters. [776A B] 4.2 In the instant case the petitioner has presumably fallen victim to this proclivity. The time has come for the State Governments to have a second economic look not only at litigation policy but lawyer 's fees rules (like rule 115 in the Bihar instance) especially in mass litigation involving ad valorem enormity and mechanical professionalism. Even a ceiling on income from public sector sources may be a healthy contribution to toning up the moral level of the professional system. The object is to act on the advice of the District Judge regarding the choice of Government pleaders. When there were several thousand cases in the Patna courts and hundreds of cases before a plurality of tribunals, it was but right that Government did not sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number of lawyers on its behalf, for the sake of the lucrative practice of a single government Pleader. It is inconceivable how he would have discharged his duties to the court and to his client if this crowd of land acquisition cases were posted in several courts more or less at the same time. adjourn to suit advocates ' convenience becomes a bane when it is used only for augmentation of counsel 's income, resisting democratisation and distributial justice within the profession. These principles make poor appeals to, those who count, which are a pity. [ 7684C G] 5.3 The hearing of this petition would not have been futile if the duties of Government pleader were merely to conduct in courts cases to which Government are a party. [765E F G] 6.3 Each one is a Government Pleader and may depute other lawyers and exercise control over such surrogates. In this view, there is no error even in that behaviour. Not to have provided more government counsel when the volume of litigation demanded it, would have clogged the dockets in court and helped one pleader to corner all the briefs without reference to expeditious or efficient disposals.

The appellants held out of a total issue of shares of the respondent Mills which formed part of 5,000 ordinary shares in its general meeting of the shareholders. The managing agents took steps to intimate the shareholders concerned to exercise the right if they like to do so, but the mills refused to accept shares in favour of the appellants. In the assessment for the assessment year 1943 47 the Income Tax Officer held that, the release by the Mills amounted to a distribution of "dividend" and the value of this right released in favour, though taxable under section 12 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, had escaped tax. The order of the Income tax Officer reassessing the income of the seven appellants was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and by the Tribunal. At the instance of the appellant, the Commissioners of Income Tax passed the following resolution: "Resolved that the company having a holding of 5.000 ordinary share shares in the capital of the Bank of India Ltd. having now received an intimation from the said Bank that this company is entitled to get 1,66,62 shares on payment of Rs. 50 as capital and Rs.50 as premium per each share and it was considered proper to invest in the said issue of the said bank. " The Tribunal, however, reframed the question as follows: "Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the distribution of the right to apply for the shares of Bank of I India by Navjivan Mills Ltd., in favour No. 31/1955, amounted to distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the I.T. Act, in enlarging the scope of the question and in answering it in the light of its ordinary meaning. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the distribution by the appellants amounted to "docividend".

The election petitioner appellant which was defeated by the respondent, challenged the election of the returned candidate to Haryana Legislative Assembly from Jind Legislative Assembly constituency. The petition filed in the High Court under section 81 of the Representation of People Act 1951 for short) was dismissed on the ground that except Bahre son of Sher Singh, no other witness could be examined and that as soon as the evidence of the afore said witness was recorded, the Court would proceed to record the evidence on behalf of the election petitioner; and thereafter the matter will be set down for hearing oral arguments of the learned counsel of either side. The High Court held that except Hobb son of T, no another witness could he examined and also that as many other witnesses who lost the election were impleaded as parties. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf the appellant/appellant that the purpose for which the witnesses were offered was not mentioned in the list, and therefore, the election petition could not be allowed to examine more witnesses whose names had not been mentioned in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and the rules framed by the High court. Relying upon the decision of this Court in Pradeep Kumar vs Shri Rajnarain, [1980] 3 SCR 621 it was further contended that Rule 1A was subject to sub rule (3) of Rule 1 and therefore the Court must ascertain how far sub rule(3) would carve out an exception to the enabling provision contained in Rule 1 A. Allowing the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: 1.1 The obligation to supply the list as well as the gist of the evidence are to be carried out in respect of those witnesses for procuring whose attendance the party needs the assistance of the Court. When a summons is issued by the Court for procuring the presence of a witness, it has certain consequences in law. If the summons is served and the person served fails to comply with the same, certain consequences would follow in law ensue as provided in r.10 of order XVI. The consequence is that where the witness summoned either to give evidence or to produce documents fails to attend or to produces the documents in compliance with such summons, the court on being satisfied of the service as provided therein and is further satisfied that the person has without lawful excuse failed to honour the summons, he may issue a warrant, either with or without bail, for the arrest of such person and may make an order for the attachment of his property for such amount as it thinks fit. The provision of sub rule 3 of Rule I and this has been drastically amended by the Amending Act 1976 which came into force on February 1, 1977. Rule lA which is inserted in the Code provides that after a court framed issues which give notice to the parties what facts they have to prove for succeeding in the matter which notice would enable the parties to determine what evidence oral and documentary it would like to lead, the party should file a list of witnesses with the gist 'of evidence of each witness in the Court within the time prescribed by sub rule.

Appellant, a double M.A. and holding a doctorate applied in response to an advertisement that appeared in Hindi Daily Bhirgu A Chetna and Dainik Jagran, which was meant for the post of Principal, as also on the basis of a written complaint received from an employee that he held one year 's job as Principal. The Selection Committee found him guilty but recommended his dismissal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) though the appellant had been appointed as Principal in contravention of section 16F of the Intermediate Education Act, 1921, no order was passed against him and (2) since the appointment was not made without the knowledge of the order contained in the radiogram, the appointment would be valid; and (3) the Chancellor was not justified in appointing the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power to make appointments is conferred by section 16A of the Act read with Section 16F, which has been extracted hereinbefore confers power on the State Government without making any reference to the Board to make, modify or rescind any regulation as also make such other order consistent with the provisions of the, Act. [981 G] 2.1 The State Government had authority to sanction or not to sanction the regulation proposed by the Board, and in exercise of which according to the High Court, the order writer 's appointment had been withdrawn or suspended. This power of wide amplitude will comprehend the power to stop all appointments for the time being being. And the power appears to have been exercised as Government was contemplating taking away the power of private management of non government aided schools to make appointment of teachers including Principals. [942 H] 3.1 There was nothing hanky panky in his appointment. If the power was riot suspended, it would have no difficulty in upholding the appointment of the appellant and the Court was not right in upholding that the appointment had become ineffective. [943 D E] 3(a) The marginal note of section 15E read with section 16E clearly shows that on April 7, 1981, the institution had received the order that the power under section 9F of Act (ii) discharging the function which is being regulated by the regulations, confers power upon the State Govt.

The respondents manufactured tyres to whom the fabric was supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and it was manufactured on weaving looms in the same manner as in other ordinary textile". The Sales Tax officer assessed the respondents ' turnover and accepted the case of the petitioners that they were exempt from tax. The Commissioner of Commercial Tax issued a letter to the Commercial Tax Officer to levy Sales tax on the "rayon cord fabric" manufactured by the petitioner. Thereafter, notices under section 12(1) of the Act were issued for the years 1965 to 1969 with a view to reopening the assessment on the ground that the sales of these goods had wrongly escaped assessment and that they should first resort to alternative remedies provided under the Act so that the appellate authority under section 13 of the was required to go into the entire evidence and decide disputed questions of fact. Aggrieved by this order, the revenue filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the order and its final assessment dated January 21, 1972. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the notices issued under the proviso and further directed that the order passed on each occasion should be quashed. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court ^ HELD: 1(i) It is not a question which appertains to the knowledge of technical aspects of textile weaving and production to determine at what stage threads or cords forming warps and wefts really amount to a "fabric". The scope of the term "textile" given in the Oxford Dictionary, is: "A product of skilled workmanship". [503D E; 506B] (ii) If it contains 40% or more by weight of wool and less than 40% by weight or artificial silk. or (iii) if it contains no cotton and less then 50% by 1025 weight of rayon or artificial Silk. or "yarn" and if it contain cotton and more than 60% by one weight of mill or artificial Textiles. or if it contained not contain 40% and "ty percent" by weight on manu facture, the product should have found mention specifically in item 22 in the different way as the numerous varieties of cotton fabrics are mentioned in item 19. [505C D] (iii). The term "Textile" has a wide meaning. Its first meaning given in Oxford English Dictionary is: , "Aark printing, a described by the word 'unitted fabric". It must acquire a body and a texture. Presumably it is not just the skeleton of a textile. Apparently, it is more than that. But, against pushing this point of view too far it may be urged that in the technical and commercial parlance which is dealing with a "Fabric" which is also a textile, it could have found mentioning specifically in Item 22 in item 21. [500G; 506E] (iv) Merely because the tyre cord fabric might be the end product for the Delhi Cloth Mills, the crucial question is: Does this product constitute a fabric which is a textile? A textile fabric does not cover everything which could be made into a fabric.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal Washeries on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied work. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was dismissed from service. The dispute arising therefrom was referred under section 10(1)(c) of the Act to Labour Court Dhanbad for adjudication, which was registered as refer ence case No. 4 of 1988, and after issuing notice to the parties, the appellant was dismissed by the management. The writ petition filed by the appellant challenging the Government 's notification withdrawing and transferring the pending case from the Labour court, Dhanbad to Labour court Patna, was dis missed by a learned single judge of the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The Government ' has stated that the workman is having his residence at Hajipur and it would be inconvenient for him to attend the Labour Court, Dhanbad regularly at Dhanbad. However, most of the factors do not point that way. In fact he has not denied the documents annexed to the Special Leave Petition, and not seriously disputed the factum of his residence in the colony quarter at Dhanbad.[297F] 2. It is also a fundamental principle of good administration. It extends to both the fields of judicial and administrative. The administrative power in a democratic set up is not allergic to fairness in action and discretionary justice cannot degenerate into unilateral injustice. Good administration demands fair play in action. [298C D] 3. The object of taking action ' under section 33B is not a mere administrative but quasi judicial power and the appropriate Government cannot transfer a case on the basis of allegations of one party without giving reasonable opportunity to other party to represent its point of view. This was also the view recognised by the Madras High Court in Management of Sri Rani Lakshmi Ginning & Weaving Mills Ltd. vs State of Gujarat, [1985] II LLJ 122, Workmen of Punjab 296 (P) Ltd.v. Its Workmen, ; at 433 and The Commercial Taxes Officer, Salem vs Jagrnohan, ; referred to almost all the authori ties of this Court on this aspect and emphasised that the principles of natural justice are fundamental in the constiutional set up of this country. No man or no man 's right should be affected without an opportunity to ventilate his views.[298C E] 4. In the instant case, the State has withdrawn the pending reference from the labour Court, Ranchi and transferred it to another Labour court at the distant District of Patna, on the representation of the workman, without getting it veri fied from the management [298H; 299A B] 5.

The appellant was the manager of a Hotel Imperial, New Delhi. The dispute between the management and its workmen in October 1955. was referred to an Industrial Tribunal on October 12, 1955 by the Chief Commissioner of Delhi. During the pendency of this reference the management of the hotel decided to dismiss a large number of workmen on October 7, 1955. That is how this dispute which would have been otherwise decided long ago is still in its initial stage. The main contention on behalf of the Hotel was that the reference was incompetent inasmuch as the union could not be made a party to the reference under the . , (2) the union had no jurisdiction to make a reference under section 10(1) or to specify them in the order. Held, further, that the dispute which was referred for adjudication was between the employer and its employees and it went to this length that the hotel decide to dismiss some of workmen an industrial dispute within the meaning of the , as used in the Act and that therefore no obligation could be held to lie on the Government to ascertain particulars of the disputes before making a reference. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy, [1953] S.C R 334, State Of Madras vs M. C. Sarthy, ; , followed. State Of Orissa vs C . P.Sarathy, ; and State of Mysore vs C.,P. Sarathi, [1955] 7 S. C R. 338, referred to. State 's contention that the word "as represented by the Hotel Workers Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk Delhi " in the context of the words " as represented by" in section 10 which the dispute was of a general nature relating to the terms of employment or conditions of labour of a body of workmen, to mention the names of particular workmen who might have been responsible for the dispute. Held not applicable and the order of reference made under section 30 of the Act could not make the reference incompetent merely because it did not specify the disputes or the parties between whom the dispute arose. The fact that more than three years had passed since the reference is made, was in these terms: Held further, also that the attack on the ground of vagueness also fails. There is no force in the argument that the award is bad simply because in the workman 's order of references the words were added for the sake of convenience as to where the notice to the workmen should be sent would not make it incompetent inasmuch that it does not specify how many of the 480 workmen of thirty different categories are involved in the dispute; it is clear from the part of the order "as shown by the word used as a word employed" in the section.

This view was affirmed by the Appellate Tribunal. Hence this appeal under section 130 E of the . Allowing the Appeal, HELD: 1. The Notification provides that the articles specified in column (2) of the Table and failing under Heading No, 84.09 are exempt from payment. [228E] 2. When an internal combustion pists engine in imported a knocked down condition. Finally it is difficult to uphold the contention that they are part of the internal combustion engine pistan engines falling under heading No.8406. The appellants and their counsel were the contesting parties in Civil Appeal Nos. 650, 894 and 894, who filed a suit against the respondents for declaration that they were entitled to be in enjoyment of the Dargah and grant ed rights and management to the Dargah as well as the offerings in the Dargah, and also for setting aside the judgment and decree of the Trial Court except some modifications in the relief as mentioned below. The plaintiffs flied a written statement taking plea that he was not interested in claiming his right. The respondents filed a written state ment denying their right to establish their claim. The Trial Court decreed the suit. Against the Judgment of the First Appellate Court, the appellants defendants filed cross objection in respect of a particular portion of the decree. The High Court allowed the second appeal and while setting aside that judgment and decrees of the Courts below dismissed the suit, filed by the appellants plaintiffs, dismissed the cross objections filed by them. The appellants in this appeal contended that: (1) a scheme was also drawn for collecting and receiving the offerings, gifts and other emoluments of the said Dargah as hodial collection and offerings; (2) Fathima Bee had never enjoyed the right to the Hundial Collection of the Wakf and even if she had got any right, the same should be lost as she did not claim any right till her death. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Where one co heir pleads adverse possession against another co heir then it is not enough to show that one out of them is in sole posses sion and enjoyment of their profits of the properties. The possession of one cov er heir is considered in law, as possession of all the co heirs. [594F] 2. There was no question of any ob tention of any expressed denial of Fathita Bee 's title in that litigation. It appears that the defendants were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under the Muslim Law were not entitled to any share in the management or offerings of the impairment or the plaintiffs. [525A B] 3.1 A perusal of the plaint shows that neither in the written statement nor in reply to the notice of the plain tiffs any stand was taken that the right of Fafima Bee or plaintiffs was specifically denied on any particular occu sion so as to put them on notice that from that date the possession of the defendants would be adverse to the inter est or rights of the plaintiffs of Fahima Bee. [500E] 3(a) Unless it is shown that one Out of the cir dents was in sole possession and enjoyment, of the profits of their properties, the posses tion cannot render his possession adverseo ly adverse to them to the other co heir not in possesion merely by any secret hostile animus on his own part in derogation of the other party 's rights. [401C] 4(b) The plaintiffs were carrying out a mistaken impressions all along they that females u/ss the Muslim law were not enti tled to any right or management of the offerings. The defendants are totally mistaken in taking the ground that there was no clear indication of ouster in the facts of the instant case. [625E F] P.W. 1 himself and drew the conclusion that after the decree in C.S. 116 of 1909 and another ground taken is that neither Fathna Bee nor the plaintiffs had at any time received a share in that suit nor any such question was raised or decided that females were not disentitled to any particular share in management or offering offerings in offerings of Dargah.

The question before the authority under section 15(1) of the , as to whether a house rent allowance claimed by the employee came within the purview of the definition of "wages" contained in the Act. Held, that where an employee is stationed at one 173 1352 of specified places and has not been offered Government quarters for his accommodation he ceases to be so entitled to the house rent and that allowance thus ceased to be payable under the terms of the contract of employment including regular attendance, good work or conduct and his other behaviour in terms of section 7(2)(b) and section 11 of the Act, because it was no more payable under a terms of a contract between the employer and the employee contemplates that an employee posted at one of those places would cease to be entitled to such house rent allowances. Shorn of all verbiage and "wages ' are remuneration payable by an employer to his employees for services rendered according to the terms Of the contract between them. The amount claimed on behalf of the 1st respondent was not admissible to all the employees of a particular class, as it was the value of any house accommodation referred to in the definition, that as soon as he is offered Government quarter for his own accommodation he ceased to he so entitled, whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him. The rule, therefore, did not create an indefeasible right in the employee at all places wherever he may be posted and in all circumstances irrespective of whether or not he has been offered government quarters.

The detenu was one Indru 's Ramchand Bharvani and while in Writ Petition 435/80, the detenu was carrying on business in diamonds and precious stones in partnership under the style of "M/s Gems Impex Corporation". 35, New Marine Lines Bombay, since 1971. On November 16, 1979, the Customs Officers raided the residential premises of the son Indru"s father Ram Chand Bharvani; while he was in the course of the raid, seized diamonds worth about Rs. 55 lakhs and also some jewellery and Rs. 1,40,000 in Indian currency and two gold sovereign coins and on the following day, the customs officers raided the residence of the ' son Indu 's firm and in the presence of the detenu; seized diamond bars and pearls worth about RS. 55 lacs and were arrested and interrogated. During interrogation, the detenus claimed that the gems and other articles seized were not smuggled goods but were local materials, locally acquired. They also gave the names of four persons from whom these gems had been acquired. Both the father and the son were arrested on November 23, 1979 and interrogated during interrogation, and they denied before the Customs officers that they sold the diamonds in question or gave them on 'jhangad ' basis was communicated to the detenu. The detenu also stated that they should be furnished with the safeguards relied upon by the detaining authority in the grounds of detention. The Detaining Authority, however, calledously and deliberately refused to supply the copies and conveyed rejection of this request by a letter dated February 14, 1980 which the detenu did not give them on "jhan Principle basis". The detenu challenged the detention mainly on these grounds: (1) That the detaining Authority never applied its mind to the earlier statements of four witnesses from whom they claimed to have acquired the g Receipts in question and in which they had on the basis of documentary evidence supported the contention of the detenus; (2) that the said statements were orally inconsistent with each other, and (3) that there was denial of opportunity to the detenus for making a effective representation. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1(a) The right to be afforded a fair and full opportunity of making an effective representation against his detention is one of the grounds on which the order has been made; and (b) That in addition to the supply of the ground of detention, all the basic material relied upon or referred to in those "grounds" must be supplied with reasonable expedition to enable him to make a full and effective representation at the earliest. Of course what is "reasonable expedition" is a question of fact depending on the circumstances of the particular case. [351B] Khudiram Das vs The State of West Bengal & Ors., ; , followed. (b). Under these circumstances, furnishing of copies of statements and documents relied upon in the 'grounds ' served on the detenu must have been communicated to him. On account of this chill indifference and arbitrary refusal, the detenue could get the same only on March 27, 1980 i.e., after more than one month. [353C] Khvatudiram Dass vs The Union of India & Ors, ; , referred to. (c) The supply of copies at that stage would be detrimental to the investigation in progress from prosecution point of view and might even endanger the life of such witnesses who have either deposed against the detenus or provided clues. [352G] Khushiram Das V. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. ; , applied.

Section 419 of the Code provides for an appeal in a case of acquittal. The appellant, who was tried jointly tried along with two other accused for the offence of having committed certain offences by way of dacoity and dacoity and were acquitted along with one other person without going into the merits. On the view that the Full Bench decision holding a joint appeal to be maintainable in law was not binding on it. On appeals by several persons convicted at one trial: the High Court held that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Bombay High 's Code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 is against the maintainability of a joint proceeding by the State against the other accuses; that an appeal to the High court by several accused persons convicted for offences under sections 258, 410 and 423 I.P.C., was not maintainable under Cr. The appellant, a firm registered under the Madras Income Tax Act (1922), was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1939 40. The Income tax Officer accepted the fact of partition amongst the members of the family and rejected the contention that the family was not liable under the 1918 Act and that the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act except for the income received from the house properties in Malaya. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that in the case of business carried on in foreign territory the business as such was not assessed under section 3 of the 1918Act but only receipt of the income in British India is assessed and it cannot therefore be held that the foreign business of the assessee could not be considered to have been charged under the provisions of the 1919 Act. The High Court after a reference, answered both the questions in favour of the Department under the following two questions: "1. Whether the appellant was entitled tO claim either to the parts of the relief contemplated under section 26(3). and (2)Whether the applicant is also entitled to reliefs under section 24 (3). HELD: The assessee was therefore entitled to both parts of relief contemplated by section 25 (3) in respect of interest on securities as well. [908 G] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section VR.M Palaniappa Chettiar and Others, ; , Secretary of State for India vs Chugandas & Co., ; Commissioner of I.T. Madras vs Ch.ugandas and Company, , referred to.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department on September 6, 1965 for the construction of the Capital Project,stuffshinagar. Large quantities of bricks were manufactured and supplied under the contract. The assessee made an application under Section 52 of the Bombay Sales lax Act, 1959 on November 19, 1967 to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax to determine the question whether the said supplies were sales or works contract. By its order dated November 19 , 1967, the Deputy Commis sioner allowed the respondent 's appeal holding that the transaction was a works contract and as such the supply of bricks by the assessee to the Public E spondent in terms of their running Bill No. XI dated 28th October 1967 was a sale or a works Contract. The High Court answered the question in favour of the asses seeant holding that as per the ratio laid down in Chandra Bhan Gosain vs State of orissa and others, this Court held that the transactions envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department were sales; that the con tract was for sale of bricks. The appellant contended that the contracts were permissive Clauses and are substantially the same. On behalf of the Revenue it was contended that this Court in Chandrajudicial Bhan Gosai 's case held that since the term "sale of bricks " used in a different Statute and it would be difficult to hold in the light of the special features and characteristics of the contract with which we are concerned, that the decision would completely govern the facts of the case. HELD: The transaction in this case is a contract of sale and not a works contracts. [162 E] In Chandra Bhan Bas Gosain`s case, it was held that by itself, is not decisive, there is no standard formula by which one can distinguish a contract for Sale from contract for work and labour. The question will depend upon the intention of the parties executing the contract or as one for sale. [163 A C] Chandra Bhan Ch Gosain & Ors., ; applied. Chandra Bhan Sardar Gosain 's Case, , followed. In Chandra Kumar Bhan Gosavi vs The State of Orissa & Ors. , this Court observed that since in Chandra Nath Gosain "s case this Court would completely regulate the facts and circumstances of this case, this has taken place in this ease.

The petitioner challenged the Proclamation of Emergency issued under clause (1) of Article 352 of the Constitution before the Connission of India on the ground that it had ceased to be in operation on 4th February, 1972 because the resolutions passed by both Houses of Parliament approving those Proclamations of Emergency as required by clause (2) of article 352 were neither published nor published in the official Gazette. On an earlier occasion the Commission passed a resolution that it was necessary for him to publish the Proclamation containing proceedings of the two Houses of the Parliament, and also to make a full report of the proceedings of such meetings and shall, as soon as practicable, publish it in such form and manner as the Chairman may from time to time direct. The petitioner contended that though the said Proclimations had been validly issued they were not published in their official Gazette and therefore there was no notice or order by the President for revoking the Proclamation. Allowing the writ petition ^ HELD: 1. (1)(a) There is no rule which requires that the resolutions should be published in in the Official Gazette. [436C] (b) The fact that the two Proclhamations had approved by both the Houses of parliament as set out earlier in the course of this judgment is not disputed by the petitioner. In so far as the Acts and resolutions passed at the Houses or Houses of States of Parliament are concerned, the very process of passing the law or the resolutions in the Houses, of the Legislatures and the time when the resolutions were duly adopted amounts to proof of the said resolutions. [441D G] (c) The production of the Lok Sabha Debates and of the Rajya Sabha containing the proceedings relating to the period between the time, when the resolution were passed in each of the Both Houses of them Parliament and the State Legislatures gives them ample publicity. If the two proclamings ceased or cease to operate before the expiration of those period of one year, they would continue to operate as a dissolution of the House. [442G H] (d) The two Pro clamations have been duly published in various newspapers, Radio and television are also the other modern means which give publicity to all Acts and Resolutions of Parliament and Legislatures of the States. In this connection it is necessary to examine the distinction between the two parts of Article 11 and Article 253 and corresponding provisions of law made under Article 121 of the Code of Civil Procedure with respect to matters enumerated in that Article. [444A C] (e) The framing of an opinion by Parliament in consultation with the President, may be an essential element of parliamentary consensus. There is a difference between two parts one of these Articles and the other of the provisions of the Act. Article 11 deals with the procedure for disposal of certain matters enumerated under that Article, but there is no prohibition that the resolution passed by resolutions cannot be revised or cancelled unless it has been approved by resolutions of both Houses. [443C] 2. The two clauses of article 11 make it clear that Parliament has power to pass a law directing that a grave emergency exists whereby the security of India and of any part thereof, with respect, to any matter not enumerated in any of the lists in the Seventh Schedule to it, shall cease to function at the expiration Of 6 months unless before the expiry of that period it has become approved by Resolutions of both the Legislatures. [414F] 3.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The original mandapam was thereafter improved upon by and some additional structures e.g., shops and other constructions already existing or else, and consequently, the suit filed by him under section 84(2) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1950, was decreed in favour of the appellant holding that the premises constituted a temple within the meaning of the said Act. The High Court dismissed his petition on the following grounds: (a) that the subject matter of dispute was, the private property of the family capable of alienation for public religious worship; and (b) that cl. (b), of article 133 could not apply as the judgment and decree passed by it did not involve directly or indirectly a claim or question res pecting property of value of Rs. 20,000/ or more and (c) that in execution of the decree in suit No. 650 of 1882 passed against the said Kuppaiyan the property was sold by public auction and purchased by Thoguluva Thirumalayyan, and therefore the property belonged to and was an alienable private property. On appeal the High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court but held that the property in question constituted a ' temple and set aside the decision of the authorities. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that cl.(b) could not have application as the decree passed against it did did not involved directly or directly or substantiallyate any claim or questions res pectsing property or question for determining whether the property is private or a public temple ' and that the High court was wrong in proceeding on the aforesaid assumption. HELD: 1(a) The said premises constituted temple within meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951. Accordingly, the finding of the Revenue authorities that the disputed property constituted temple and that it was alienable property and therefore capable of a valid transfer is erroneous. [157C D] (b). Even if the property be a private or public temple, it was incapable of valuation. The second contention made by the respondents in their written statement was that the properties belonged to the Thogalakshmi family and he was in management thereof for and on behalf thereof. [158C E] (c). Assuming that the possession of the premises was a private temple and the allegation of the plaintiff that it is a private property capable of transfer was 'false and misleading, the High ' Court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to the respondents the property had been inalienable and was a public Temple.

The respondents claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements, and claimed that a cash rate should be paid to them in the alternative. The appellant justified the action on the ground that the practice of employing retired persons was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations. Held, that the fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appellant can have no material bearing in dealing with the point; in the very nature of things, the said re employed person are bound to support the appellant. Chandi Charan Banerjee vs The State of Assam ( ; , referred to. On a proper construction of the relevant provisions of the Factories Act, the re employ ers are bound by the practice and the practice was being followed in many cases and that posed a serious problem to the respondents. Chandii Charan Banerjee, (1962) 2 S.C.R. 699, applied. Chand Rani Charan Banerjee & Ors. vs State of West Bengal, ; , distinguished. The fact that a re employ person has made an application supporting the practices adopted by him cannot have no bearing in deciding the point raised by the respondents for the first time in the present proceedings, and he is not bound to abide by them. Chanda Charan Banerjee 's case as it was presented before the Court by the State Government had refused to make a reference on the grounds that only 4 cases of re employment had been brought to its notice, and so, the problem did not call for any consideration at that stage. Chandia Charan Banerjee and Ors.

The appellant, who was an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund, applied for and obtained an order for attachment of the money lying in the executing Court against him. The Union of India again applied for removal of attachment on the ground that the money represented provident fund money which by section 3 Of the , was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the amount in the hands of the Reserve Bank had ceased to be provident fund. The emoluments remained at the disposal of the Railway Administration as provident fund moneys, it was exempt from attachment. In order to carry out that obligation the Accounts Officer of the railway made out two cheques in the name of Browne and sent them to the Reserve bank for conversion of the amount into sterling. The Reserve Bank was the agent of the Railways for conversion and transmission of the amounts to the Browne, the Reserve Trust Bank of India was the only authority which could permit such conversion in view of the 31 currency restrictions imposed by the Government of India. Held further, that it was not necessary for the Union of india to maintain an application for removal or removal of a attachment. But the Union Of India was not a trustee for the subscriber of the moneys. When the amount lying with the Reserve Banks as the agent for the conversion and transfer of the proceeds to his credit in British India, attracted attracted the provisions of section 50 of the Indian Contract Act.

The appellant was employed as mechanic in a workshop. The workshop was run by a branch manufacturing enterprise, issuing notices ending the employment and offering one month 's pay as authorised by the relevant Standing orders. He filed a statement before the Labour Court that although he was efficient, appreciated and awarded merit increments, the management was antagonized by his active part in the formation of an Employees ' Union particularly because oral warnings by Regional Manager against his Unionist 's union activities were not attracted. The employer thus took the Court into confidence to explain why the employee was discharged. He was consequentially shifted to the post of clerk handling posting of bins and collection of payments but the workman although denied direct access to correspondence in the Receipt and Dispatch Section, made attempt to elicit information from the section with a view to pass it on to outsiders '. The upshot of these activities of which the management is alerted was that the action being a simple termination without a sting process and consequence of a disciplinary action were not curable. A notice for the termination of his services with immediate effect, did leaking out office secrets within the meaning of section 24(2) of the Act and thus liable to be discredited. The Management contested the case on the ground that the proposed action being punitive termination without any stigma attached to it was more 'to create a ground for the workman 's claim and had been leveled as a matter of habit and routine. The management also took the court into confidence in explain why an employee, although he did vaguely refer to the termination with immediate effects. It was found that this action really amounted to punishment for misconduct and therefore the services were liable to have been terminated without any parti tion attached to them. While on all hands it was agreed that the employee 's denial of leakingout office secretts was an after thought pleaded only in the rejoinder and therefore liable to he discredited, the Management denied and the reference to trade union activities by the worker was more to create a defence for the workmen ' claim and bad been leveled. The company urged that the warning by the Regional Manager was denied and that the reference was more "to create an ground for workman ' his claim and has been levelled as a matters of habit, routine and so, if the termination were victimisation, unfair labour practice or misconduct it was foul play to avoid a fair enquiry and fall back upon power to terminate simpliciter there. The trial court also held that on the materials placed, the action could be called colourable. In appeal, the Labour Appellate Court reversed this finding and held that even in a case like the present, the requirement of bona fides was essential and if the retu nity were victimisation an automatic termination with a month ' 's salary extra. The High Court further held that if such a finding is based on no evidence, or is the result of unfair labour practices or misconduct, it would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1. In a reasonable case of a confidential or responsible post being misused or a sensitive or strategic position being abused, it may be a high risk to keep the employee, once suspicion has started and a disciplinary en quiry cannot be forced on the master. There such a termination simpliciter may be bow fide not colourable, nor loss of confidence may be evidentiary of good faith of the employer. Some testimony of unseemly attempts by the workman to get at secrets outside his orbit, some indication of the source of suspicion, some proof of the sensitive or cultural role of the employee should and would have been forthcoming had the case being bona fide. [495E G] 1:2. It is clear that loss of faith is often a subjective feeling or individual reaction to an objective set facts and motivations.

The said defendants who were their wives filed a suit against the appellants for declaration that a deed of gift was void and inoperative beyond the lifetime of the donee and was not binding on them and could not operate beyond the life of the donor. These suits were dismissed by the trial court. In appeal to the High Court it was contended, inter alia, (1) that a final settlement of the terms of marriage was made at Deoghar, and (2) that the gift was accepted by Nand Lal on behalf of his minor daughter in law and valid in Hindu Law; any such lapse of time as occurred in the execution and registration of the deed of gifts was immaterial, if the deed was in fulfilment of the moral obligation flowing from the ante nuptial agreement; and (3) that there was no reliable evidence that Sumitra Devi had made a "sankalpa" of the gift of the four houses in question after the Sampradan ceremony on the occasion of the marriage and that such a gift was again confirmed at the Gowna ceremony. Held, also that the finding of the courts below that there were no compelling reasons for the High court to differ from the appreciation of the oral evidence by the first appellate court was erroneous in law because the evidence of Sumitra Devi which related to the promise made regarding the gift, was not supported by reliable evidence and the concurrent finding of fact of the Courts below was that the gifts were made at the time of the infem ber ceremony; (2 ) the presumption of truth lies on the party who claims the correctness of either of the witnesses or of any other way whatsoever and must be raised in each case. Section 123 does not deal with nor does it affect the power of a Hindu widow to make an alienation of a reasonable portion of her husband 's estate in favour of the daughter as marriage dowry; (3 ) There is no doubt that by reason of the use of the expression " whether acquired before or after the commencement of the said Act" the section is retrospective in effect. The Explanation to the section shows that property includes both moveable and immoveable property acquired by a female Hindu at a partition or by gift from any person, whether a relative or not. The expression "property" includes immovable property acquired under a will or any other instrument or under an award of a civil court or under a decree or order of a Civil Court. Section 13 does not in terms extend to movable and immovable properties acquired by the female Hindu by inheritance or devise, or at a division, or in lieu of maintenance or arrears of maintenance. It is open to a widow to execute an effective gift in favour Of her daughter subsequent to the marriage if the conditions laid down therein are fulfilled. Case law discussed. Per Sarkar J: (i) The findings of the first Appellate Court were correct and must fail. Per Hidayatullah, J., dissenting): (1 ) While construing a document for the purpose of making the gift or cash, it is open for courts to adopt a different approach. If the words used in section 123(1) are read together these provisions are clear and unambiguous and there can be no doubt about the legal effect of those words in section123(1). The Legislature has not placed any reliance on the circumstance which could have been relied upon by the High Courts in determining whether a particular gift is reasonable or not will have to be judged according to the state of the family at the relevant time. Churaman Sahu vs Go pi Sahu, I.L.R. , Churammal Charyulu vs Narasimha Charyayya, and R.M.D. Chamarbuddudraiah Chettiar vs Narayanaiah, Mad. [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R., referred to.

Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The corrupt practices indulged in by Tej Singh had been clearly proved. [419A B] In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of section Tej singh will be deemed to have been cast in his favour cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result of the election.[419D H] In the instant case, there was nothing to show that Tej Singh was guilty of any corrupt practice. [416B C] The appellant has not disputed that the payment of vouchers .(Ex P 5) and P 6 were made by him and the vouchers were appended by him along with the return of expenses incurred during his election campaign which was verified by him to be a true and correct statement. In these circumstances, it is clear that the appellant had proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Sing Singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing of posters by Tej. Singh has been clearly admitted by him as indicated above. It would have doubtsless materially changed the result or would have bound it to be altered and the result would have been materially altered. [420B D] In these circum stances, therefore, the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing by the posters. Tej Singh further admitted in his affidavit that Bhum Raj was incharge of his election office at Moga and that he had also admitted that Bhumi Raj as well as Avtar Singh were not collected With the printing Of the posters at the instance of Tej Singh, on a perusal of the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by the parties, it clearly established beyond doubt that the allegation of corrupt practices indulging in by the appellant has been made as clear above. No interference is called for from the High Court.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal and threatened the writ petitioners to withdraw the writ petition and pursuant thereto, eleven officers withdrew from the petition. It was alleged that after having failed to threaten and demoralise the appellant through indirect means the respondent, the Superintendent of Police pressurised and threatened him to withdraw a writ petition, and pursuant to that, eleven persons withdrew from one Writ Petition. The appellant filed an application for contempt against the Respondent alleging that the Respondent had illegally withdrawn from the writ Petitioner and that after that he was transferred from the Forest Expert Special Project Cell on July 26, 1983 through the Acting Chief Conservator of Forests and criminally intimidated him to withdrawal the writ Petition. Thereafter, the Appellant filed an affidavit denying all the allegations made against him by the appellant. The learned Single Judge took the view that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the Court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In that view of the matter, the learned Judge dismissed the application and discharged the rule nisi. It is apparent from the facts stated above that the allegations contained by the Appellant, if proved would consitute a criminal contempt. It therefore, follows that the allegation made by the Respondent, if established would consid erute a Criminal Contempt, which would consi derute the criminal contempt, it would be quite clear that there was no right of appeal under section 19(1) of the Act to punish for contempt, and section 19 (1) provides as follows: "19. (1). An appeal shall lie as of right from any order or decision of a High Court passed in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punishfor contempt. If no punishment is imposed by the High Court, it is difficult to say that the High court has exercised its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution.

A notice as contemplated by section III (g) of the , was necessary before it could be terminated. The respondent contended that there was no forfeiture. He referred to the fact that the tenant had failed to obey the provisions of section 111(b) and that, in any event, he should have sent a notice as required by the amended section. Held, that where the language used is not mandatory it must be given effect to. An omission to give a notice does not amount to failure to comply with an express provision or a statutory provision which is intended for the benefit of one party and is not intended merely to defeat the other in any way prejudicial to the interest of another.[1025 C D] In the present case it was no doubt true that the appellant had complied with the provisions. The general case on which reliance was placed was not applicable in second appeal as there was a forfeiture of the lease by denial of the landlord 's title a notice in writing determining it lease within the meaning of section III(g) but by analogy to what is required to be done in order to determine a freehold lease which, by the terms of it, was to be void on the non performance of covenants it appeared that to put an end to this licence, the grantor should have given notice of his intention so to do. It is not safe, I think, to say, that when the Act was so express to provide a wide discretion, meaning no doubt, to prevent one man from forfeiting what in fair dealing belongs to some one else by taking advantage of a breach from which he is not punctuated and irreparably damaged, it is not desirable to lay down any rigid rules for guiding that discretion. F compensate for non payment of rent under section 114 of the and also because non payment was made at a time during which period the notice would be void for all purposes, or is not likely to apply where the tenant could have claimed relief against forfeiture on every occasion particularly when he was warned by the court of appeal on a previous occasion. The Court must and will always insist upon certain things when the statute does not require them and the facts of some unforeseen case may make the court wish it had kept a free hand.

Workers employed in the said quarries who were employed in a strike for 24 hours commencing from the mid night of 19th September, 1968. On 20th September and 30th Sept., 1968, at 4 P.M. when fiery speeches were made by them wherein they not only instigated the quarry workers to resort to strike but intimidated and prevented the willing workers from going to their work and threatened the supervisory staff and officers with dire consequences if they tried to work the quarries and what was more from the middle night of August, 19th Sept. and 1, 1969 forcibly and illegally occupying the area near the quarry between 4 P .M. on 19th Nov., 1968 and after breaking the deep fears and dire consequences. The preliminary Enquiry Report was forwarded to the General Manager who after considering the same and taking into account the previous service record of the respondents by his order dated 31st December, 1968 dismissed the respondents from service. That order was served on the Respondents on 30th January 1969 by which they were proceeded ex parte. On 30th Jan., 1969, a dispute having been raised with regard to their dismissal by common consent, the same was referred to an arbitration of Shri T.C. 10 A of the, the on 14th April 1969. The Arbitrator gave his Award on 9th February, 1970 whereby he came to the conclusion that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the Respondents of showing cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of their dismissal order as required by the Standing Order No. 17; he further held that though before him the management had by leading evidence proved its mis conduct by establishing the first three charges against all, the fifth charge against Emmanual and Mohd. Rauf which was found to be fully proved and the fourth charge being held not to have been proved, the punishment of dismissal in respect of Emmanicual and M.S.R. could be confirmed but set aside the dismissal in 1974 by dismissing both the writ petitions. The High Court, however took the view that though after the award had come to the con firmed award of the Arbitrator by dismissing all the Writ Petitions, the Arbitrator had jurisdiction and power to consider both the aspects and that the Arbitrator erred in law while awarding the punishment which he did so namely, that the conduct of Shri Emmanul and Mohd., Rauff was more grave than that of Rama Shankar and Barmapradhan and instead ordered their reinstatement but without back wages. Against this, the Management preferred an appeal to the Supreme Court. Meanwhile, it appears that in the award the Arbitrator gave a finding on 9.2.1970 whereby he held that the Enquiry Report which was submitted by the Company in question had been properly construed by him and the High Court affirmed the same on the ground that while fomenting the strike the conduct for Emmannaual and Rauef (fourth charge being maintained not to having been proved) the punishment imposed upon Rama Shankar & Barma Pradhan could not be interfered with because no third opportunity was afforded to the Respondent of showing a cause against his proposed punishment. The learned Single Judge of the High COurt allowed the appeal holding that since before him, the management has by leading evidences proved its misconduct by establishing tended the first 3 charges against him, its enquiry which is otherwise fair, valid and valid and was vitiated; that though the Arbitrator as well as the High court have erroneously construed the certified Standing Order NO.

Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 read as amended by Act 35 of 1969 provides that certain persons occupying lands under leases granted to competent persons to be deemed tenants notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in section 52 or any other provision of the , or any judgment decree or order of Court, shall be deemed to be a tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was in occupation of such land on the 11th day of April, 1957. The appellant and respondents surrendered lease hold rights but continued in possession to be in deemed tenants. Since the appellant had come into possession of the lands by trespass, his plea before courts below was that he was himself the owner of the area having acquired title to it by adverse posses sion. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to persons whose posses tion had a lawful origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's land of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believe to be competent to grant such leases or had come in possession with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. [114D] 2. In computing the period of occupation of a person for the purpose of clause(c), the period during which the predecessor ininterest or predecessors in interest of such person was or were in occupation shall also be taken into account.

The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. On opening them, six of them were found to contain cigarette lighters of "Imco Triplex Junior" and a bill for the consumption of electricity were also seized from the custody of the appellant together with the Godrej lock and the keys produced by the appellant. Subsequently, the seized articles were made over to the inspector of Central Excise and Customs, during the pendency of the complaint filed on 30 10 1968 under section 110 of the . The goods were confiscated. On 21 4 1968 the police officers seized the goods which contained absolutely seals of flints as also a lock and some of the six boxes were tightly packed with 1200 lighters. The appellant contended that he had been acquitted by the trying Magistrate because he had admitted the production of keys from his possession. He alleged that the portion of the room from which the goods were recovered was sublet to Dwarumal and Kishen who had kept the goods there. The trial Court accepted this contention and convicted him under section 135(1)(ii) of the Act. On appeal by Special Leave, it was contended for the appellant that since the goods in respect of which the appellant was prosecuted were not seized under the Act as provided by Section 111 of the , they could be applied when the case came up for trial before the Presidency Magistrate who actually decided them on 15 7 1969. Dismissing the appeal. HELD: 1 (a) The appellant was rightly convicted under section 138(1) (ii) only under section ' 135(i)(ii). [541 B] (b) Section 106 read with section 114 of the Evidence Act would be sufficient to enable the prosecution to ask the Court to presume that the appellant knew that the goods must have been smuggled or imported in contravention of the law.

The appellants, who were the President of an Association formed themselves into an association to collect the quota of cloth to be allotted to them and sell it on profit wholesale. The Association, at Budhar, was not a legal election within the meaning of section 4(2) Of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935 which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and further because it was not registered as a company under the Vindhya State Companies (Act, 1935). The Association functioned through a President and a pioneer worker. They kept accounts and distributed the profits. The deal of cloth and other things inter alia came to an end. On June 25, 1949, thirteen members of the Association out of the twenty five brought a suit for accounts. The association functioned by a President, and a Pioneer workers. The Federation was dissolved till February 1948. Thereafter, the cloth dealers of Budhar a town in that State formed themselves a society to collect their quota of ticket cloth to he allotted to the appellants and sell them on profit retail and retail. A suit for account lay at the instance of the plaintiffs appellants who were also members of Public Service Association was filed by one of the members of Pionet. The trial Court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed it. Held, that on the analogy of section 69(3)(a) read with section 69 (3)(b)of the Partnership Act, it should be held that the plaintiffs had a right to bring a suit to recover accounts of the Society which was dissolved in February 1948 and hence no suit for accounting lay at them. It is not open to the defendant to resist the proceedings on the ground of illegality. Held further, that the question whether any contract of partnership sought to be enforced must be decided on its own facts. The doctrine of estoppel would apply only where a party who has been engaged with another in various dealings and transactions in respect of such contracts is not illegal. Where a plaintiff comes to court on allegations which on the face of it show that the contract of Partnership on which he sues was illegal, the only course for the courts to pursue is to say that he is not entitled to any relief on the allegations made as the courts cannot adjudicate in respect thereof of contracts which the law declares to be illegal (Senaji Kapurchand vs Pannaji Devichand, A.I.R. , Vaidley vs Cooperstein, and The King Emperor vs Benanmonte, Lindley, , approved. Section 4(1) of the Vindhya Pradesh State Companies, 1935 being prohibitory in nature could not be excluded from consideration even though the bar of that provision has been raised at this late stage.

On 25.6,. 1986, the Range Officer of Forest reported a written complaint with the Judicial Magistrate at Ist Class Chaibasa alleging offences under section 51 of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972, and that the matter was under investigation by the police. The respondents moved the High Court against the order dated 13.2.1987 of the Judicial Magis trate First Class for quashing of the order taking cognizance on their complaint and summoning the accused. The High Court quashed both the proceedings against the respondents, holding: (1) that the learned Magistrate acted contrary to the provisions of section 210 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973; (2) that as an investigation by a police was in progress in relation to the same offence, the learned Magis lrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and call for a report in the matter from the police; and (3) that since the Investigating Officer had filed a final report that no offence was made out against the accused and that as investigation by Police was in connection with the same allega tions, section 210(1) of Code of criminal Procedure was attracted and that it was pending in relation, the orders under section 482 should be stayed. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 210(I) of the provides that no person shall "hunt" any wild animal Specified in Schedule T. 2 (16) in a comprehensive manner: "2(16) 'hunting with its grammatical variations and cognate expressions, includes. (a) capturing killing. poisoning. snaring and trapping of any wild animals and every attempt to do so (b) driving any wild Animalries for any of the purposes specified in sub clause (a). 51 of P.M. they along with two others; named in his complaint, fired and killed ones. There is no definition of "cusiness" under sec. 9(1), read with section 50(I ) of the Act as to "shall not be liable to be punished twice for the same offences". [465H; 466A] 2. The word "any act or omission which constitutes any offence under this Act ' in Section 56, merely imports the idea tat the same act or omissions might constitute an offence under another law and could be tried under such other law or laws also. In order that the prohibition is attracted the same acts must constitute an offi cation under more than one Act. If there two distinct and separate offences with different ingredients under two different enactments, a double punishment is not barred. [467D] 3. In view of the fact that a decision in one case that two offences are 'substantially the same may compel the same result in another case involving the same two offences where the circumstances may be such that a second prosecution should be permissible. [470G H; 466 A] 4. The expression "any acts or omission" which constitutes an offence u/s 82(a) of Cr.P.C., 1973, merely import the idea mischief tat he done with the deterioration of environment.
