The assessee company had advanced Rs. 3,21,460 to another concern, the Bombay Fine Worsted Manufacturers ' Castle Mills ". On an application under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act,1922 exemption from tax in respect of 6% of the capital employed in the undertaking 'Eldee ' as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of the Capital so employed Rs.321, 460 advanced to 'Castle ' in computing its capital so employed by it. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that there were two undertakings of the same eight partners with a share of /2/(two annas) each and that the constitution of both the undertakings being the same, the same was not a separate entity. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to it in computation of capital invested for the purpose of 429 section 15C. An application under s 66(2) for an order directing the Tribunal to state the case and refer it to the High Court was also dismissed. The appellant contended that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from the non inclusion by the Income tax Officer in the assessment of the income of 'Cultle ' and that "the factor taken into consideration by the Appellate Tribunal in coming to the conclusion, it did 'desid itself into a question liable to be referred to the Supreme Court. On behalf of the assessee it was contended that (1) since there were in these two undertakings, the entire constitution of the company being thesame eight partners, and (2) one of them with a partner carrying on business in the same concern, which had been started in the earlier years and not in the year of assessment 1951 52, the income from 'C 'astle" could not be regarded as a separate asset. HELD : The Tribunal had misdirected itself in law in arriving at its finding, and in refusing to require the Tribunalto state the matter and to refer it, the High court was in error in error.

The Minister concerned was directed to file his affidavit in regard to the allegations made in the petition. At the hearing of the appeal before this Court, the Advocate General for respondent raised preliminary objections. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that looking to the facts of the case, if the High Court came to the con cerned conclusion that the Minister was a necessary or proper party, it should not interfere in the matter. ^ HELD: The direction for impleading the Minister as a party was given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations. [97A] In the instant case, however, the order whereby the Minister concerned is directed to be impleaded as a respondent. The other part of the order which whereby the llor dant was directed would be set aside is set aside and the matter will stand disposed of accordingly. [ 97D] The parties in the circumstances shall bear their own costs. [98F] On the facts, it could not be said that the direction for the impleading of the Minister could not have been given by it. [100E] On behalf of respondent counsel to this Court it was contended that looking into the facts and circum stances of the cases, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts; and circumstances of the cir cumstances, the High Courts be directed to implead the Minister on a party which had not filed his personal affidavit in support thereof, [98A] A Ministry is essentially for the Ministerconcerned with the decision of the allegation made in a petition and has to decide in the light of the pleadings as to whether he should or should not file an affidavit. The High Court was therefore in error in directing that the Secretary be impleaded in a party.

The respondent, a tenant of the appellant, challenged before the magistrate 's jurisdiction to realise the amount by way of arrears of rent due under a lease in his favour. The Magistrate held that he had no jurisdiction to recover the arrears of rents due under the lease. On revision, the Sessions Judge affirmed the order of the magistrate and declared that the Magistrate had jurisdiction and ordered attachment of the movable property of the respondent on June 13, 1961. Against this order the appellant obtained special leave from the Court. Held, that the order passed by the High Court did not really satisfy the requirements of section 259 and consequently its opinion must be affirmed. The word 'rent ' in section 260 of the Act means what the Act or the Rules permit the Board to recover or what the rules permit the Military Estates Officer to recover. If the word ' rent ' in that section was meant by words "additioned by a Board etc" it would be rendered otiose because there is no provision whatsoever in the Act which expressly made rent claimable or recoverable by either of the two authorities specified therein, and that the section applied only to such monies as were recoverable by the authorities under the Act. Kundan vs The State of Madras, ; , Re: Hodge and perusal of section 261 of the Indian Penal Code shows that nothing in the , which expressly authorised the Board, to recover all arrears of land 'and buildings or any other money "recoverable by a board etc., was intended to be included in that expression in that s. 259. The Act did not provide for claim of rent by the Board as rent from the tenant. Though the word rent did not occur in section 259 there was no provision whatever in the latter Act which specifically authorised the board to recover arrears of money by suit under the general law of the land, and the Rules which empowered the Board could not give it a restricted meaning. An application to a magistrate was the only means open to the Board for recovery of sums covered by section 259. Section 260 does not bar the right of the Board or the Military Estate Officer under this Act to recover rent from a tenant who was liable under an express provision of the .

The appellant, a section Salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. The appellant was appointed as a section salesmen and his employ ees for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sales of the company 's product in his area. The various correspondence and other evidence produced before the Labour Court showed that the appel lant was employed to do canvassing and promote the sales. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not a "workman" and set aside the award as it held that he was not required to send reports about the publicity and advertisement of placing posters, holders, cinema slides and suggest means to canvass the sale in this area. When the appellant 's service was terminated on the ground that his service was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January 1973, they were deemed to have left the company "s service of his own account. The High Court in appeal held that termination of the appellant from serv ice was illegal. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the Labour Appellate Tribunal had given findings in favour of the appe lant on the question whether the termini sation itself was illegal and if not to what relief he was entitled to. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The finding of the Industrial Tribunal for coming to the conclusion that the termination of service of the employee by the respondent company was legal and justified and it was borne out by the document produced before it and held that there Was no question of fact or law involved in the case which was long prior to the enactment of this Act. [474D] 2. The object of this enactment and the employees covered by the enactments also go to show that persons employed for sales promotion normally would not come within the definition of workmen under the Industrial Disputes Act. The Labour Court considered the merits in detail and ultimately held that in the light of our finding the appellant could be held to be a workman employed for manual, skilled or unskilled/or clerical nature and that the provisions of the industrial Disputes Act were not ap plicable and the reference, therefore, was incompetent. [475E G] Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Company vs Burmahope Management and Staff; , ; D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others; [1973F.J. Dechane Distributor vs State 476 of Kerala and Others (1974 11 LLJ 973), referred to.

The appellant company entered into a contract of lease with the Gwalior State Government for a period of one year in Samvat 1999. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in Sampat 2005. When proceedings were initiated on 16.7.1952 to eject the Company, the Company filed suit No. 14/1960 for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The Trial Court decreed the suit but granted an injunction restraining the company from evicting the company by its order dated 1.10.1977. Hence the appeal by the State by special leave against the Order of the High Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 Section 182(2)(i) of the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1959 defines 'pakka tenant" as meaning a person holding land from the State Government under section 181 of the Code. The term `Pakhta Maurusi ' included Istmurardar tenants, Malikana Haq holder tenants, Hakkiyat Mutafarrikat Sharahyana and Sakitul Mikaqf tenants. An ordinary tenant is defined by Act No. 66 of 1950 as "a person holding a land from tho State Government or to whom a right to occupy land is granted by the state Government or the Collector and who is not entitled to hold land as a Bhumiswami shall be called a Government lessee in respect of such land". The term 'Pakhti Maur Advice ' included 1stmur Sardar tenants, 11111115 holders Hakki Mutafarhi Sharahmi & Sakit ul Mikognised tenants. It was from that judgement that the Company had brought to this Court Civil Appeal No. 299 of 1967 and that appeal was, as stated earlier unconditionally withdrawn by the company in 1971. Thereafter, the State entered into an agreement with the company to grant a fresh lease for a term of ten year in respect thereof subject to payment of enhanced rent as agreed upon between the parties. Since the Company failed to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the lease, proceedings were started by the Additional Collector and by his order dated 13.5.1977 for eviction of the company. [179E F] 1.2 Section 182 of the code is attracted. That section reads: "182. Rights and liabilities of Government lessee (1) A Government lessee may be ejected from his land by order of a Revenue Officer on one or more of the following grounds, namely: (i) that he has failed to paid the rent for a Period of three months from the date on which it became due; or (ii) that the term of his lease has expired or (iii) that, he has contravened any of the terms and conditions of grant: Provided that no order for ejectment of a Government lessees under this sub section shall be passed without giving him an opportunity of being heard in his defence". It was in terms of sub section 2(i) in respect 'of such land. The finding of the Additional Commissioner is a finding of fact based on evidence and is not liable to be questioned in these proceedings. His findings show that large amounts are due and payable by the Company as rent and that the rents have remained unpaid for a periods far in excess of three month from the dates on which they became due. In the circumstances, the Additional Collec ted Collector was well justified in having recourse to the proceeding prescribed under section 182 of that Code.

Section 1(3) of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960 provided that notwithstanding anything contained in Article 13 no law providing for the acquisition by the State of any land in an estate under the personal cultivation of the holder, compensation shall not be less than the market value thereof. The petitioners in C.A. Nos. 31 and 32 contended that when the principal Act was enacted it became law in force and the ceiling limit prescribed thereunder became effective even though Ch. IV was not extended by a notification under section 1(2). HELD: (1) By virtue of section 45 of the principal, Act "the interests of the person to whom the surplus lands relate and of all land holders mediately or immediately under whom the land were being held stand extinguished and the lands vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances. " The expression "law in force" means "in force". [595 B] (2) By section 45 the right of the land holder was, therefore, guaranteed by the second proviso only where the land is within the ceiling limits applicable to him under any law for the time being in force. An Act cannot be said to be in force unless it is brought into operation by legislative enactment or by the exercise of authority by a delegate empowered to bring it into operation. [595 D] (3) The right to compensation which is not less than in the market cent, when the land was within the limits applicable only to him at under a law for that purpose being in existence.

The appellants, who were reversioners in respect of a deed of surrender executed by a Hindu widow, to recover possession of the properties belonging to the last male owner during the life time of her husband 's estate, contended that the transfer was not for legal necessity but made by a bona fide order. Held, that under the Hindu Law no surrender could be effective if the widow had already parted with her interest in the property by a voluntary act of her own or her rights therein have been extinguished by adverse possession of a stranger. Such an alienation would not necessarily affect the right of the reversioner and do not validate a surrender as has been held by the Privy Council in Sreeramulu vs Kristamma (I.L.R. [Boys J.) in preference to a mere device to share the estate with the reversioners, and since there was no necessity for alienation the interest which she himself holds and which she can convey to others is not an indefeasible life estate but an estate liable to be defeated on the happening of certain events which in Hindu law cause extinction of the widow 's Estate. Sreemanamuluv vs R. P. Boys J. in the Allahabad case ; distinguished. As surrender by the heirs was not in praesenti, it could not prejudice the rights of the persons acquired by grant from the widow or by prescription against her prior to the date of surrender and these rights would be, in law, endure during the entire period of the surviving widow ' 's natural life. It was therefore for the reversioners also entitled to prove that it had become competent to alienate those properties and they were not bound to wait till the widow actually died. The heirs, who came on record as occupants of lands without any right, were entitled to remain in possession of their lands. But there could be no question of transfer of property after the expiry of the period of surrender. Sulaiman J. was in error in treating the gift valid for the reason that the reversioners became immediately entitled to recover the property during her lifetime on grounds of equity. In order to decide whether a surrender by a widow prior to surrendering her husbands estate could be challenged by the reversioner during the year 1950, it is necessary that such transfer should take the form of transfer, e.g., when the widow conveys the entire estate of her deceased husband. In other words no equitable considerations arise at all. Held further, that the Hindu law does not countenance the idea of a widow alienating her property without any necessity, merely as a device to vote on her behalf and it is open to one who acquired the widow interest by adverse Possession against her. The reservation of such small benefit absolutely necessary for her maintenance did not invalidate a surrender in favour of the reversioners during her life time but by reason of the opinion expressed by all the Smriti writers that the widow should live a life of moderation and cannot have any power of gift, sale or mortgage except for religious or spiritual purposes. If the effect of surrender, as explained above, was to destroy the widow whose estate could, if she suffered physical or civil death, there was a risk always attached to the transaction, and there was nothing in law which secured to him necessarily an estate for life. Such a transfer would be void if it was not supported by legal necessity, but was made for a proper or necessary purpose, and as such must affect anyone 's interest.

% On November 15, 1974 the cotton mills Company acquired 35.75 shares of Rs. 10 each from its members, including the respondent in the appeal. The Government did not send a notice to the company under section 169 calling upon it to call an extraordinary general meeting of the company and that the requisitionists were required to give an opportunity for being heard before the general meeting was held. On July 24, 1974, the State Government passed orders under sections 18AA(1)(a) and (b) read with section 190 of the Act appointing a Receiver in respect of the shares in question, attaching them and ordering that 3,50,000 shares be pledged in favour of the Government of Uttar Pradesh against a loan for the purpose of meeting the dues payable to the employees of the Cotton Mills Company. The company filed a petition under sections 397 and 398 of the Madhya Pradesh Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958 impleading five of its shareholders as respondents. In that petition it was alleged that with a view to mismanagement by the Investment Company, the Company and other Directors of the Polytex Company in which the Cotton Mill Company had acquired 10 lakhs shares of rupees, it could not meet the wage bill, the dues of the U.P. Electricity Board and several other monetary claims against it. The High Court allowed the petition holding that since a Receiver had been appointed by the Collector in respect thereof from the company, they had also been attached, the shares held by the Cotton mills Company could not be taken into consideration for determining the required qualification to issue the notice under section 170 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913 and that if those shares were omitted from consideration then the shares holding by the other requisitionists would not be sufficient to issue a notice under. 169 of the said Act. The appellants contended: (a) that the special general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton mill Company had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the ' Polytex company by reason of the appointment of a Receiver by the collector of Kanpur in respect whereof, the attachment of shares under section 149 of the Land Revenue Act, 1901, amounted to an order made by the Central Government on April 13, 1978 under Section 18 AA(1) (a), and (g) that since the stocks had been pledged in their favour by the Government, they could not therefore join the other requisitioningists in issuing the notice. (b ) that there was non compliance with the orders of the Board. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.

The petitioners were plaintiffs. They filed a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the court of Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were the owners in 194 posses sion of the suit land along with some others. The Gram Panchayat Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala District Sangrur in the State of Punjab (the Panchayat) had no sort of right in the suit property and that the suit lands had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Panchayat by the entries made in the revenue records which were not binding on the plaintiffs ' and for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering with their possession. The Panchayat filed a revision petition before the High Court against the judgment of the trial court, but the same was rejected on the ground that since the question involved in the case was simply one of title to the suit, it was not necessary to decide whether the suit Land was shamlat deh or not and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not being shamlat mallat deh. It also held that since no question involved was involved in this case, it had jurisdiction to try the suit. Aggrieved by the said finding recorded by the trial Court, the Panchayat filed revision petition in the High court of Punjab and Haryana in Civil Revision Petition No. 571 of 1986. The State has preferred this petition before this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution of India contending that since question involved therein was simply One of title, it could not be necessary to decided whether the property was shamli deh or was not shamlatted or not. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 A civil court shall have jurisdiction (a) to entertain or adjudicate upon any dispute whether any property or any right to or interest in any property is or is not shamilat deh vested or deemed to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961; or (b) to question the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner or the Collector or the Panchayat under this Act.

The appellant Board in its petition under Article 226 of the Constitution contended that the Electricity Board has power to demand additional security but the average consumption of three months should be taken as the basis for calculating the amount of such security. The High Court rejected the writ petitions on the ground that in the present case no such order was passed since the matter is stated to be pending. In the special leave petition filed by the appellants it was contended that there is nothing to indicate under the scheme of the Electricity Act or Schedule VI of the Supply Act that interest must be paid on the security deposit and the default in payment of electricity bills is of no avail because that relates to the manner of keeping accounts by the licensee not being applicable to a Board. Special leave petition was also filed against the judgment and order of the High Court. Dismissing the special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The true nature of the transaction in these cases is one of advance payment of charges for consumption of electricity estimated for a period of approximately three months. In one sense, the consumption security deposit represents only a part of the money which is payable to the Board on the bill being raised against the consumer. [278C F] 1.2 There is nothing in the scheme to indicate that interest should be paid for the securities furnished to the board. The Electricity Board 's interest requires that there should be some protection by way of security of advance deposit in respect of the consumption of this three months period. The regulation relating to non payment of interest at certain rate, in the case of Rajasthan and Orissa the Boards have clearly stipulated that no interest shall be payable on the securities supplied to the consumer upon such terms and conditions as the Board thinks fit. [279E] M/s Mills, Bharatpur vs Assistant Engineer (D) R.S.E.B., Bharatpur AIR 1965 Andhra Pradesh 58 at page 68 69; M/S Mills, Bikaner vs Assistant Engineers (D), Rajasthan & Orissa and Orissa State Boards have not clearly stipulated under the Scheme of the Act or schedule VI to the Supply Rules relating to interest paid and accrued on consumers ' security deposits. [285G H] Bangalore Woollen, Cotton and Silk Mills Ltd., 28 at page 1136; Mls. Mill, Bharatpurv Assistant Engineer, (D). R. S.E., B.S.; Bharatpur ; M/o Textiles & Silk Mills Limited., 28, at page 1237; Ml Rayon & Silk Mill Mills Ltd.

The petitioners are working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre. The recruitment to the different cadres in the Posts and Telegraphs Department is made under the Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I (Telecommunications Re search Centre of the Posts & Telegraphs) Rules, 1962 (the Recruitment Rules). The Recruitment Rules were General Central Service Class I posts and they continue to be so till today. In response to the said advertisement petitioners 2,3 and 4 applied for recruitment and they were selected for appointment to the posts of S&T.O. Grade I. At the time of filing of these writ petitions there were in all 21 officers who had been recruited at the entry level of Junior Class I post of S & T.Os grade I. They are holding the posts which are directly under the control of the P & T Board of the Ministry of Communications, Government of India. The Telecommunication research Centre is engaged in research and development work concerning the Wireless equipment for the use of the Depart ment and in advising the P&T Board on relevant technical matters relating to the introduction of new equipment and technology in the existing public communication net work. The Recruitment rules were General Service Class 1 posts and those, who are Post and Telegraph Officers Grade II (Teotcommunications) and who are directly recruited through the Union Public Service Commission by written examination followed by an interview followed by a interviews, followed by written interview followed and all along with the Writ Petitions filed by the petitioners. It was contended that the petitioners were not entitled to any Special Pay but the transferred officers from the Indian Telecommunications Taxation Centre which is directly under control of P &T Board of Respondent No. 1 Union Public Services Commission after a rigorous competition examination need to be paid Special Pay. It is further alleged that the peti tioners are not entitled ticable to any special pay but the transfer officers from their Indian TeleCommoms Service who are working in the Samarporudi Research Centre discharge same functions as the petitioners and that the transferred officials had to perform in the telecommunication Research Centres duties which are not in their general line. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The first question relating to denial of promotional opportunities to the petitioners according to the Recruitment Rules is left open to be decided by the Central Administrative Tribunal. No opinion on the said question. [1011 B] 2. It will be open to the Central Government to consider whether it was a fact that Special Pay is not given to a few graduate engineers recruited specifically for TRC when the qualifications, functions, duties and responsibilities of these officers inTRC are the same as those of the field officers transferred to TRC & what is the reason for not doing so. [ 1012 C] 3.1 The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belong are not given any Special pay in the instant grades and they are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It would also be open tnment to be agitated before the Central Industrial Tribunal. [1001 G H; 1001 B] 3:2 Since the transfer officials have to be en tered in the pre sent officers, it is not deputation allowance. It does not mean that persons who are either directly recruited and working in any branch centre are inferior to those who enter the centre by transfer. Therefore, there is no justification to deny the Special Pay at the same rates to the direct recruits working in their organisation functions which are neither in their own general line nor in a position. [ 1001 A B] 8:3 In the instant case, it was not the case of the Government that the Petitioners were not competent and were not able to discharge their duties. All the direct entrants are graduate engineers and have been working throughout in the office of P& T Directorate. They do the same job as the transferred Officials.

The appellant, who was an employee of an industry governed by the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, filed an application under section 42(4) of the Bombay, Industrial Relations act, 1946 and prayed that the orders of dismissal be set aside on that ground alone. The Labour Court after holding an enquiry took the view that the findings of the enquiry officer were perverse, held that the order of dismissal was passed by a person not authorised to exercise the power and consequently the Labour Court directed reinstatement of the third respondent with all back wages. The appellant flied an appeal before the State Industrial Court contending inter alia that the third respond ent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application tinder section 42 (4) Of the Act which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour court and prayed for setting aside the order passed by the LabourCourt. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42, including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour Appellate Court. On appeal to this Court it was contended: (1) As the scheme of Chapter VIII was that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it did not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the Industrial Tribunal; (2) The clause in the proviso to section 78(1) had an independent operation and could only be resorted to after efforts had been made to settle the dispute and no agreement had been arrived at; and (3) the order dismissing, discharge removal or suspension of an employee would come under section 78 (1). HELD: 1. Under section 42 of the Act an employee desiring a change in respect of an indus trial matter not specified in Schedule I or Schedule III has to give notice of such intention in the prescribed form to the representative of the employees. He must also send a copy of such notice at a conspicuous place of the premises where the employees affected by the change are employed. In other words effort must first be made by the employer intending to effect any change in relation of matters covered by section 42 against any order passed before it, pending its final decision and no agree ment had been reached at.

The appellant a registered society filed the suit out of which this appeal arises in the Court of the District Judge, Jaipur City. A prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by one Hari Narain Swami through another lawyer claiming to have been elected as the Secretary. The suit was later transferred to the court where it was renumbered as Suit No. 116 of 1974. After the institution of the suit, an election of the office bearers of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as Secretary. On 4.9.74 a prayer for withdrawal of the said suit was filed by Hari Narain Mahant through another counsel claiming to be elected as Administrator. When he learnt about the fate of the proceedings, an application was filed for recalling the order of withdrawal and restoring the suit to its file. The trial court after holding that the appellant was not elected as secretary had no locus standi to withdraw the suit and accepted the case of Hari Narain Lakshmi Swami by accepting the case which allowed the suit in his favour to be withdrawn. According to the case on 4.09.74, the prayer for withdraw al suit was not maintainable and the error committed by the trial court while recording the finding on merits of the case was such which the High Court ought to have rectified. In reply, it has been argued by the appellant that the trial Court had no jurisdiction to recall its order permitting the withdrawal of suit under its inherent power, if it is ultimately satisfied that Hari Narain obtained his consent and also accepted the Case which of Hari Narayan Swami. The respondent contended that the High COurt in C.W.P. No. 1406/1975 did not decide the dispute finally and left it to be settled by the civil court. A writ petition filed thereafter by Hari Narayan Mahant before the High 892 Court (registered as C.A.W No. 1506/75) was dismissed. The Trial Court after holding on the merits of t he case, held that the appel lant 's application was not justified and proceeded further to consider the question as to who was the duly elected Secretary of the society entitled to prosecute or withdraw the Suit and accepted his case of Sri Laxmandas Swami. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant (i) that the application under sec tion 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the Suit was maintainable; and (ii) t he trial court had no jurisdic tion to recall the order permitting withdrawal of that suit under his inherent power. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. A court has inherent power to correct its own proceedings when it is satisfied that in passing a particular order it was misled by one of the parties. [237B] 2. In view of the High court 's judgment that is the position, but it declind to exercise its revisional power on the assumption that it had no Jurisdiction to do so, the trial com plete Court has rightly held that it has jurisdiction to cancel the order directing withdrawal of t his suit under Its inherent power if it was ultimately satisfied (that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree on a fraudulent repre sentation made to it that the party had actually consented to it. [236C D] 3.

The appellant was charged with the offence of being in force on July 11, 1953 when the offence was alleged to have been committed by him. The trial court and the High Court concurrently held that the Ordinance promulgated under the emergency powers vested in the Governor General under section 72 of the Business Act, 1947, was in operation during the period of emergency but could continue after April 1, 1946. The appellant came to this Court with special leave. Held: (i) The Ordinance in question having been promulgated during the periods between June 27, 1940 and April 1. 1946, was perpetual in duration and continued in force until it was repealed. Consequently, in view of section 72 and section 26A of the Act as they originally stood were equated with the Acts of the Federal Legislature or the Indian Legislature, as the case may be, the period for which an Ordinance could be promulgated is separate and distinct from and must not be confused with the emergency which occasioned the pawing of the act and the clear effect of the words of the, Act on section 72 is that Ordinances promulgated under that subsection during the said period are subject to no time limit as regards their existence and validity unless imposed by the Ordinances themselves or other amending or repealing legislation, whether by Ordinance or other. In the present case, the Ordinance in dispute continued in operation even after April 1946 when the Ordinance lapsed or ceased to be in force. The law in the State of Jammu and Kashmir with regard to those High Denomination Bank Notes issued before January 13, 1946 was thus brought into line with the law as it obtained in the rest of India.

The appellants were charged with murder and to extract money from the complainant 's house. At the time of occurrence the deceased gave information that he had killed her son, daughter and sister due to injuries caused to him. The first appellant fired at the deceased on his head and the other two shot wounds as a result of which she died on the spot. On further investigation the appellants were charge sheeted under section 302 I.P.C. and convicted with imprisonment for life. The High Court affirmed the conviction of the appellants but reduced the sentence to one years rigorous imprisonment, under section 376(1) (a), (b) and (c). The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Taking the cue from the English legislation on abolition, it is the concern of the statesman and, therefore, the domain of the Legislature, and not the Judiciary. Section 302 I P.C., 1860 confers upon the court a discretion in the matter of punishment to be imposed for an offence of murder and the Court has to choose between a sentence of death and a sentence 'of imprisonment for 10 life; while under section 354(3) Cr.P., 1973, the Court is enjoined with a duty to record 'special reasons ' in case the extreme penalty is awarded [1075B G] Rajendra Prasad vs State of Bihar ; ; , followed. 2. The offence may be shocking and yet the criminal may not deserve death penalty. But the crime may be more shocking than other murders and yet, the callous criminal, e.g., a lethal economic offender, may be jeopardizing societal existence by his act of murder. [1076D] 3. When a sentence is passed it is subject to confirmation by the High Court under section 366(1), Cr. P. C. and the accused also has right of appeal to the High court under 5. It would therefore be manifest that it is neither feasible to define nor legally permissible for this Court to limit or circumscribe the connotation of the expression 'special ' reasons ' occurring in section 354 (3) of the Code so as to bring about a virtual abolition of the death sentence. [ 1074C] 4. The assessment of public opinion on this difficult an(l complex question was essentially a legislative function, not a judicial function. [1007E] 5. The deliberate extinguishment of human life by the State for an incident of murder, they reasoned on metaphysical theories of punishment, was a denial of human dignity. They concluded by stating that the death penalty was usually inflicted only on a few, i.e., the poor and down trodden who are outcastes of a society which led to the irresistible inference that the punishment was not fairly applied [1071F G] 6. The answers given in the dissenting opinion of this Court in Rajendra Prasad 's case are clear enough to point the softening of the sentence, to one of life imprisonment. [1000A B] 7.

The appellant was in service upto 30th April 1958 when he was prematurely retired. The appellant also claimed arrears of salary but a departmental enquiry had been held by him and his case was that he had made various investments in the name of various members of his family far in excess of and disproportionate to the known sources of his income. The enquiry officer held the enquiry and the punishing authority found that the charges levelled against the appellant were either "grossly negligent, careless, inefficient, or corrupt in the performance of his duties as Income tax Officer". However, he reduced this claim to Rs. 16,561.29. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner reduced the claim to that of an income tax officer but reduced the appellant 's claim to the extent of Rs.16,560. The order was confirmed in 1952 which was upheld by the High Court on 17th November 1969. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that a fresh enquiry into the same charges was not permissible under the Departmental Rules and was also barred by principles of natural justice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. All relevant facts had been examined by the officer who held the inquiry and by the punishing authorities. No mala fides against either the Inquiring Officer, Shri A. K. Bose, Deputy Director of Investigation or against him were alleged. There are, however, suggestions that Shri G. section Srivastava and Shri R. N. Srivastava, Inspecting Assistant Commissioners, were pursuing the appellant for some unknown reason which we do not find anywhere. The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact [585C E] 2. If an enquiry is held, at a particular stage, possibly to determine whether regular proceedings should be drawn up or started it does not debar a departmental trial. That was the nature of previous enquiries. It is only after the appellant had his activities had become more than notorious that further enquiry was undertaken and regular charges framed. The defence of the appellant seemed something similar to the much too common a defence of his accused in criminal trials attributing all their misfortunes to the hostility of the police. [585E F] 3. Under section 10 of the Income tax Act, 1961 a person whose income is liable to be taxed has asked the assessee and if so required he had asked for permission from the punishing Authority before it inflicted the punishment of demotion. There was no affidavit before the High court that any particular points argued before the Division Bench had not been referred to or dealt with by the Bench. The matter must have been heard and decided on merits. Since there were some arguments which could be raised, there was no declaration that the departmental proceedings were null and void. [582 B] 4. Unless such a point can be raised there could be no declaration of that the Departmental proceedings were " null and valid. There is also an application before this Court for revocation of grant of special leave to appeal by this Court on the ground that some material facts were suppressed or misrepresented for the purpose of obtaining special leave. [584G H] 5. In a case where the departmental proceeding in null and un void the plaintiff in such a suit could obtain the relief he had applied. This Court would not interfere with the finding of the departmental authorities. If there was any patent error, a writ petition lay.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State. The M.M.T.C. had entered into direct contract with their foreign buyers. The appellant 's contract was integrated into inter alia with the contract entered into by the M.S.M.,T. C. and the appellant 'successor in the State, who was the exporter and shipper of the goods, which included the import of manganese ores out of the territory of India. The invoices also showed that the export did not commence till the slip left the port. In course of export it took place but on board it passed over to the appellant that stage. Subsequently, the M/s.M,T.F., entered into a direct contract which provided for the sale and purchase of goods from the Company through the exporter. The appellants contended before the Sales Tax authorities that the contracts were different and, therefore, there should be examination of five other contracts. The High Court held that these contracts were intrinsically linked and connected and that the sales effected were held to be sales in the course of or export out of territory of U.P., and that there was no privity of contract between the manganese merchants and the foreign buyers from the S.T.,C. and that, therefore there should he examination of the five other contract. The writ petitions filed by the appellants challenging the assumption made by the High Court to the effect that all contracts between the appellants and the MM.S,T., C & F were similar, while the Writ Petitions were pending in this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i) that the M,M.E.C., could not be the last purchaser of goods within the meaning of section 5 of the Sales tax Act because property in the goods passed from the appellants to the M M.T.; and (ii) that there were six contracts and it had been the case of the appel lants that the contract was different, and therefore there must be examination for five other Contracts, and that though the M &M. T.C did not agree to sell the goods to their foreign buyer they could not claim that the said contract was in the nature of a contract between them and the appellants; (iii) that it was inconsistent with the contracts entered into with the foreign buyer on F.O.B. basis, the High COurt held that there existed a bond between the M and the entered into independent contracts with their Foreign buyers on F F.o.B basis.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973 on a monthly salary of the month from August 8, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974 with effect from 19th October 1974 with further effect from May 19, 1974. Consequent upon this termination, an industrial dispute was raised and the Delhi Administration referred the following dispute to the Labour Court, Delhi for adjudication: "Whether the termination of services of Shri Mohan Lal is illegal and/or unjustified and if so, to what relief is he entitled and what directions are necessary in this respect?" The respondent management at one stage failed to participate in the proceedings. The reference was heard ex parte and the Labour court made an award on 2nd May, 1977 directing reinstatement of the appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs 520 per day from the date of termination till reinstatement. However, the respondent moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate In the proceedings which motion was granted. The respondent contended that the appellant was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of the initial period, his service was terminated by an order dated 12st October, '74 as he was not found suitable for the post to which he was appointed. The Labour Court held that the termination was neither illegal nor improper nor unjustified and the claim of the respondent was negatived. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the Appeal and setting aside of the Award of the Labour Tribunal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In industrial employment or for that matter in any service, sickness, authorised leave an accident, a strike which is not illegal, a lockout and cessation of work not due to any fault on the part of the workman. The excepted or excluded cases are where termination is by way of punishment inflicted by way disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workmen, retirement of a workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf, and termination of the service of aworkman on the ground of continued ill health. The excluded cases were where termination was by way Of punishment inflicted for by way off disciplinary action.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. On February 5, 1955, the appellant was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour and an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the Settlement Officer with which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed. The appellant filed his explanation to the charge sheet. An Enquiry Officer submitted his report. Thereafter, the settlement officer submitted his final report to the Deputy Commis sioner stating that the chage relating to recklessly gratification from a person and had demanded illegal gratification from one Ude Singh. Thereafter the Deputy Commi ctroller of Settlement passed an order dismissing the appellant from service on March 17, 1965. The High Court held that the appellant had not discharged his duties as he was occupying and by the impugned order the appellant could not be dismissed or removed from service but his employment being terminated because no penalty was imposed upon him, the order was invalid. Held further that the order passed by the Deputy Commission ernment in the enquiry will not fall within the principle of Ram Narayan Das 's case (1958) S.C.R. 828 and the appellant cannot be dismissed nor removed from serv ice until he had been given reasonable opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. State of Orissa vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, ; , referred to. The order passed under the provisions of the Act was therefore not invalid. In the present case the enquiry made by the Settlement Offi cer was made with the object of ascertaining whether disciplinary action should be taken against the appellant for his alleged misdemeanor and, therefore, there was no stigma affecting the future career of the public servant by the order terminating his employment for unsatisfactory work and conduct.

% The appellant was promoted to the post of Professor in the colleges. On June 1, 1969, he was assessed by the Commission for selection and appointed a Selection Committee consisting of 21 selected candidates. It was stated on behalf of the respondent that its recommendations were made on the basis of the marks obtained by the respondent, which were called "Jammu and Kashmir Professors of Colleges (Selection) Rules, 1969". The State Government considered the recommendation and sent its recommendation to the Commission, but the Commission did not give any reasons. In a writ petition filed under article 32 of the Constitution it was alleged that the Commission was consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and that as this requirement had been duly complied with, the High Court erred in taking a contrary view. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, HELD: 1. The State Govern ment at first framed rules on November 15, 1968 for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the Colleges. By Notification No. SRO 161 dated March 25, 1969 those rules were replaced by the rules made by the Governor specifically for the appointment of Professors which were sent to the Commis sioner and that they were interviewed and examined by the Selection Committee which was "formed" by the Con stitution. The Commission set out the reasons for its decision and finally made its recommendation on merits. The Selection Committee was therefore consulted on the suitability of candidates for promotion as Professors and the second requirement of sub section (2) of section 133 was also complied with. [872 H; 873 A B] 2. Although it has been urged in the written arguments of the appellant that section 133(2)(b) of the Constitu tion requires that the Commit tee shall be consulted on all matters mentioned in the rules to be strictly followed in dealing with them, this question was not so.

The petitioner was a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly. The Speaker who was appointed to the Committee of Privileges by the House of Commons on May 30, 1957, suspended the Secretary for being present at the meeting and gave an opportunity to the petitioner to show cause why appropriate action should not be taken against him for breach of privilege, whereupon he filed a petition before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the proceedings on the ground that such proceedings were illegal as the Chief Minister of the State Dr. section K Sinha himself had been the Chairman of the Committee and was therefore illegal and invalid. On merits his case was that the House is not a public office nor does it deal with State Government, and although article 194(3) forbids the publication of an incorrect report of the debate or proceedings on a true and faithful report of proceedings That Article provi sions (1), (2) and (3) of article 194 covers both Houses of Parliament and Parliament. Held: (i) The law made by the Legislature in respect of the powers, privileges and immunities enjoyed by a House of the Legislature of a State and of the members and committees thereof can be made by Parliament under Entry 74 in List I to the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, unless it is saved by any law prescribing reasonable restrictions within the ambit of article 19(2). The right conferred on the Legislature under Article 19(1) (a) is preserved notwithstanding the provisions of either of these Articles. (ii)The Legislature has not broken any of the rules of the Assembly relating to the committee of Privileges, and even if it did, by reason of Article 212(1), Parliament made a law under entry 74 in list I to 855 the Seventh schedule defining the powers privileges, privileges or immunities enjoyed for that State, the validity whereof was not questioned at all. (iii) article 194 is not made subject to Article 19 of the Constitu tion and, therefore, if the House Of Commons of the Parliament of the United Kingdom had the power or privilege to prevent the publication thereof, it had also a similar privilege or power and it could exercise it notwithstanding the fact that it infringes the fundamental right of a citizen. The Act prohibited the publication by which the rights, privileges, immunities and immunities of a House or Houses were preserved under Article 194(2) of the constitution, as it stood before its amendment in 1955, and the House was not providing for any such provisions. (iv)The expression 'the privilege ' is included in r. 216 of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly case, [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 809, followed. The object of the Act was to prevent certain persons from publishing proceedings of the legislature or at any rate such portions of it as were ordered to be expunged by the Speaker, and therefore, it could not be said that the power, privileges which is enjoyed by the Houses of Commons of England and its members and Committees in present case had been infringed. (v)The provisions of cls.(1),(2)(3) and r. 215 of the Rules framed under the Act on June 27, 1958, made it abundantly clear that the action taken by the Committee was not illegal merely because a mere publication of the newspaper was published in its entirety " " but a failure to do so would have deprived the citizen of his fundamental rights which are guaranteed by the Constitution. The procedure prescribed by rr. 215 and 213 thereof is a summary one and does not offend article 19 (1) of , as it may be, the impugned Act has contravened the provisions Of articles 19(i)(a), 19(3). % The Government of Orissa took over the management of the College on and from March 9, 1971. The college was taken over by the Government in pursuance of a unanimous resolution of the managing committee of February 18, 1970, and the transfer to the Govern ment was of all the assets of the college but without any liability. The management continued to be liable for the outstanding liabilities, if any, of the Colleges for which Government was not liable. The College after taking over the Management as a Government College, continued to function further in accordance with the transfer of the institution. On 9th March 1971, a formal agreement was executed between the managing Committee and the Governor of the State. In terms of the contract it was provided that the decision to follow i ts principles shall be forwarded by the P.S.C. for determination of their suitability for appointment as Readers shall also be simultaneously referred to the P,S. C e lice for determining their suitability to hold posts in Class I or II as the case may be. The services of those who were not found suitable by the Commission shall be finally absorbed in the respective Trade of the O.E.S., (Orissa Education Service) for which they are found suitable. It was stated in that circular that the "Government had been pleased to order that follow ing principles shall hence forward be followed in the ap pointment Readers, namely, (a) no officer who has not at least 8 years of teaching experience as a Lecturer would be eligible for consideration; and (b) that the post of Reader shall initially be filled up by promotion subject to satisfactory performance and conduct of the officer as a lecturer". On 7th September 1971, the Government issued a Circular extending the period of six months and lateron it was stated that "the State Govern ment shall offer ad hoc appointment to all staff inposition on the date of take over. " In pursuance of the unanimous resolution dated 9th February 1970, the Director of Public Instructions sent on April 20, 1971 to each of the Respondents appointments letters whereby they were appointed as Lecturers in Class II temporarily on ad hoc basis for a period of 6 months with effect from the forenoon of March 9 1971 or till the appointment is made in consultation with the Orissa Public Service Commission. whichever was earlier. The Respondent No. 1 thereupon filed a writ petition before the High Court (Respond ents) claiming equal opportunity under Article 16 of the Constitution in tho matter of ap pointments and also for appointments as Readers, contending that although they had all the requisite qualifications for the appointment as Reader and they were all holding the posts of Reader before the take over, they were drawing a salary less than Rs.600/ on the dates of taking over. their names were not referred to it in the Government College. The appellants made applications to the State Transport Authority for grant of temporary permits to ply their vehicles on the route. The U.P. State Road Transport Corporation (Corporation for short) also made an application for grant or renew any permit during the period intervening between the date of publication of the scheme and the date fixed of publication thereof. The appellants applied for a temporary permit for the period ending between the dates of publication, which was rejected on the ground that once a scheme has been published in view of the provision contained in section 68C of Chapter IV A the Corporation alone could to the exclusion of others, as it was not entitled to obtain a temporary permits. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court of Allahabad did not meet with success. In these appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) there were 4 vacancies for which 4 temporary permits could be issued by the State Road Corporation and (2) the strength of vehicles on route in question was raised from 13 to 20, and hence the applications were rejected on that ground alone. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. Section 68 F(1 C) lays down a situation where application for a permanent permit is not made under section 68 F (1 A) by the Corporation. And there is felt need for providing transport service on the routes in question. [851 E; 984 B] 2. The Corporation has published a scheme in respect of the route in dispute, and even when a scheme is published it is open to the concerned State Transport authority or the Regional Transport Authority as the case may be to fix or increase the number of vehicles that may operate on the one route. But the power to increase strength of fleet operating on the Road is conferred and has to be exercised in public interest meaning transport facility to travelling public. [90 E] 3. The overall consideration namely the service should be available for the benefit of travelling public should never be overlooked for a moment. Reverting to the facts of this case if the approach of the High court is accepted it would lead to a startling result. Assuming there were 10 vacancies for temporary permits and the Corporation was able to provide only one vehicle and therefore applied for only one permit, according to the state Transport Appellate Authority as well as the High Courts that no temporary permit could be granted to any one else. Obviously section 68 E(1) does not admit of such a construction. The case of the appellant is that there were 7 vacancies for a period which 4. temporary permits can be issued because the scheme has since been published. Therefore, therefore, there was 9 vacancies for the remaining seven vacancies.

Where a Hindu governed by the customary law of the Punjab succeeds to his maternal grandfather 's estate, is the property in his hands ancestral property qua his own sons: Held. (i) The principle of stare decisis did not apply because the Privy Council decision in Narotam Chand 's case was of laying down an inflexible rule of law which had become settled by a series of decisions generally is binding on the Courts and should be followed in similar cases. It would be difficult to say that these observations were obiter dicta of the Privy council, correctly decided by this Court as early as 1895 and 1895. (ii) The doctrine of stare overruling was not so imperative or inflexible as to preclude a departure therefrom in any case, but its application must be determined in each case by the discretion of the court, and previous decisions should not be followed to the extent that error may be perpetuated and grievous wrong may result. (iii) Where there is no doubt that under the Hindu law the property inherited by a person from his maternal grand father is not ancestral property but is ordinarily inalienable (especially amongst Jats residing in the Central Districts of Punjab, except for necessity or with the consent of male descendants or, in the case of a sonless proprietor, of his male collaterals. The question which arose was whether the appellant 's property was ancestral property or not. Held, further that, under the law the suit filed by the appellant could not be held to be ancestral property because the doctrine of imparti decisis did apply because an alienation is not binding on a plaintiff according to custom. The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge on charges under section 449 and section 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came there and while one of them caused a shout at the same time catching hold of Wing ofour. The other three appellants attacked Haji Efbrar ALI with knife. When Abdul MEs injunction to save him from further injury was raised by them, they were found sitting on the side of his cot and leaving the dagger with their hands. After their crossing the door of the house they opened the house with a dagger while the other three were holding him down. The five appellants attacked the deceased pursuant to the common intention of killing him, and that in furtherance of that common intention they inflicted an injury on the neck of one of his sons as a result of which he died. Both the appellants were convicted under section 302/34 Indian Penal Cfinder.I./O/F] The High Court upheld their convictions but granted certificates of fitness to appeal by this Court, under article 134 (1) (c) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court on the question whether there can be no conviction under section 450 unless murder has actually been committed. Held: Section 448 of the I.P.C. does not make any offence punishable by the said section. The words "in order to" have been used in section 34 of the and section 457 of the Penal Code have reference only to the act in order to a 'deJudicial 's commission '. An act can be said to be committed "in a different manner as if it were done by him alone.

The respondent had been in possession of certain lands in village Kingarian, which was acquired for the Kangra Valley Railway and a sum of Rs. 1,539 7 0 was awarded to him as the daughter of Gurdial. On an objection by the appellant that it was not a collateral of Gurdial at all, the Subordinate Judge held that the lands in suit being in possession quite one degree excludes the daughter from succession to the self acquired property of her father and consequently the suit for declaration of title thereto was maintainable but the High Court in revision found that the evidence as to the succession to property of Harnam Singh was of no assistance to the appellant. In appeal by special leave, Held, that on production by the respondent of the Riwaj i am of proceedings of the Revenue Authorities the burden shifted to the respondent and it was enough for the court to say that irrespective of whether the properties in dispute were ancestral or self acquired the collaterals in that case could not succeed. The appellant has failed to discharge the onus that was initially on him by producing in evidence the Rwiwaji am which is a reliable and trustworthy document, but the respondent has failed not cited a single instance of a daughter having excluded the collateral from succession. The trial court therefore rightly decreed the suit in respect only of the lands. Fundamental Rule 54 of the Indian Succession Act enjoins that the daughters are excluded by the widow and male kindred up to certain specified degrees. There was no inconsistency between this rule and the general custom applicable to them. The power which the Court can exercise under section 53 of the Evidence Act is akin to section 53, Evidence Act, 1872, as it then stood in the case of Mohammed Khalil vs Mohammad Bakhsh (1905) L.R. 44 I.A. 89, referred to.

The appellant, a Managing Director of the Companies registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was acting as Managing Agents of several companies registered under a . The company applied to the Collector of Calcutta for adjudication of duty payable on power of attorney marked as Exhibit A in the proceedings which he proposed to execute. By that power he empowered Messrs George Varghese Chisholm Fairbairn and John James Brims Sutherland jointly and severally to act for him in his individual capacity and also as executor, administrator, trustee, managing agent, liquidator and all other capacities. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) of the Act to the High Court of Calcutta stating his own opinion that the stamp duty was payable on the power "foras many respective capacities as the principal executes the power". The reference was heard by a Bench consisting of the Chief Justice Das, Das, J. who differed in their opinion and held that the different capacities of the executant did not constitute distinct matters for purposes of section 5 Of the Act, and therefore the proper duty payable thereon was Rs. 10 under article 48(d) of Schedule 1 A of the Calcutta Stamp Act as amended by section 13 of Bengal Act III of 1922. The question in this appeal was whether the instrument in question consisted distinct matters or not and must be stamped in accordance with section 5. Held, that the agreement in question did not comprise distinct matters and the suit was rightly dismissed by the High Courts. It was equally well settled that when two persons join in executing a power of Attorney in respect of all the matters in which he could act, it should be held to comprise distinct matter. But where several donors having separate interests execute a single power of agency with reference to their respective properties as, for example, when A constitutes X as attorney for management of his estate Black acre and B constitutes the same person as agent for the management of the estate White acre then the instrument must be held second in each case by the parties themselves. Held further, that in construing the section in the light of that scheme the expression "distinct matter" must in the setting be construed as distinct categories. In order to find out whether a power is incidental or ancillary there should be several steps and one step would be necessary to examine the nature and extent and the extent of the authority conferred thereby. The fact however, that it does not detract from the position that he is entitled to deal with those properties and exercise all the powers in relation thereto though with the limitations imposed upon them by reason of the capacities which he enjoys.

% The Karnataka Electricity Supply Corporation was constituted by the State Government with effect from 1.1.1968, under the provisions of the Karnataka Power Corpora tion Act, 1963, subject to the control and supervision of the Bangalore Division Bench of the High Court in the Writ Petition filed by the respondent. In exercise of its powers conferred under Section 16 of the Act, the Karnataka Electricity Distribution Corporation invited tenders from registered contractors of appropriate class. Paragraph I of the notifi cation listed three "Minimum qualifying requirements" viz., that the intending tenderers should have executed civil and architectural works including insulation in a power plant/industrial complex, preferably in power plant; (2) should have an annual turnover of atleast 1 crore for each of the preceding 3 years; (3) should had an annual turn over of almost Rs.1 crores for each subsequent year, and (4) should be having an annual taxable turnover of least Rs. 2 crores for every of the previous three years. C.C.; and this was much more than three conditions set out in para I of N.I.T., had no application since they were not fully satisfied with the prequalifying condi tion. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition as being violative of the equality clause contained in Article 14 of the Constitution as also principles of natural justice, on the ground that there was nothing unfair or arbitrary about the award of the contract tO the M.B.C and had no just or reasonable relation to the object of inviting tenders namely, to award the contract to a sufficiently experienced person who would be able to run efficiently a find class restaurant at the Airport. The Division Bench also held that the contract was void as being discriminato ry since it excluded other persons similarly situate from tendering for the contract and it was plainly arbitrary and without reason on that basis, though there was no acceptable tender from a person who satis fied the condition of eligibility, the 1st respondent could have rejected the tenders. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (i) Central Government had in view of section 16(1)(a) of the and (ii) the experience laid down under the Act is not mandatory; (ii). Allowing the appeal, this Court, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court has not found any mala fide or unfairness about the com pensation of the contracts with the appellant in accepting the tender of the 4th respondents even though they did not satisfy the pre qualification requirements set out by para l. There was a discussion as to what extent this lacuna made the conditions in para l was for the K.P.C; and that it is obvious that both having regard to the constitutional mandate of Article 14 as also the judicially evolved rule of administrative law, the High Courts were not entitled to act arbitrarily in accepting a tender of M.D. in the absence of any clear opinion as to the nature of the requirements set ing out in Para l, but was satisfied on an overall view that there would be nothing unfair and arbitrary about it. In pursuance of an oral exchange dated October, 1947, the appellant. who was a displaced person from Lahore had taken possession of the Danepur Road House in Pakistan, after the transfer to her of the property in his favour on October 10, 1947. In pursuance of that exchange in Pakistan Malik Bahadur had taken over the said agricultural lands and was put in possession by him exclusively. The appellant challenged the legality or propriety of any such order of the Custodian General on the grounds (i) that under section 5 A of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947 ( East Punjab Act XIV Of 1947) as amended in 1948 and applied to the State of Delhi, such a transaction required confirmation by the Custodian; and (ii) that the application for confirmation which was made long prior to the time when the office of the custodian General was set up and he was clothed with powers under section 27 of the Central Act XXXI of 1950. Held, that in view of the provisions of section 58(3) of the , the orders confirming the exchange were subject to revisional power of the evacuee Custodian General under section 26 of the Act and as such an order passed by him was not open to appeal or revision but became final and conclusive. The extension of three years period by a general order of confirmation passed in 1952 would clearly be subject to the revisional power and jurisdiction of the appellant under section27 of the said Act. In the present case Mohammad Atti vs Irving, (1915) I.A. 176 and Harihar Prasad Singh vs State of Bihar A.I.R. 1951 Patna 153, followed.

The respondent No. 1 a locality in the city of Bombay, was studded with small hardware businesses where pipes and fittings were made and/or sold. These establishments, well over a thousand employ a considerable number of workmen in the neighbourhood of 5,000 although each unit has (barring four), less than the statutory minimum of 20 workmen. The respondent No 1 claimed bonus for the relevant four years prior to 1965 when trouble began. Though rooted in goodness and grace, the annual repetition of these payments ripened, in the consciousness of the workers into a sort of right nothing surprising, when the State Government asked for relief, it stated that a scrutiny of accounts of the firms was unnecessary since the demand is not based on profits or the financial results of the employers but is based on custom. The appellant objected to this approach and contended that what was pleaded was profit based bonus only and, therefore fell squarely within the Bonus Act. The Tribunal dismissed the claim in limine on the ground that it had not provided for those categories of bonus and confines itself to profit based Bonus, customary bonus or one which was a term of the employment itself. On appeal by Special Leave: ^ HELD: (i) There is no doubt that custom has been recognised in the past as a source of the right to bonus as the several decisions cited before the Tribunal by Shri Sanghi make out and section 17(a) of the Bonus Ordinance, 1965, in a way recognises such a root of title. Vaidialingam J. in Churakulam case (1951) S.C.R. 491 followed. (ii) The challenge to the jurisdiction of the courts below is not barred by res judicata. [609 E] (iii) What was sought was profit relying on bonus based on law and service condition not one based on profit. The problem about the policy of the Parliament that was agitated in that case turned on the availability of the as an independent method of claiming profit bonus de hors the Bonus Active Act and the Court took the view that it would be subversive of the scheme of the Act to allow an invasion from the flank in that manner. [510 F] Mill Owners ' Association vs Union of India & Ors., , referred to. (iv) What then came for examination was whether an industry carried on by a company falls within the purview of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 or not. The answer to (c) must fail because the claim that only a profit based wage has been claimed by the workers. The argument that the bonus had been paid for several years and what transpired at the conciliation stage was clear from the letter of the Commissioner of Labour who adverts to the 'usual ' custom and practice of payment of bonus. The Sabha does not mince words when, in praying for relief it states that the Tribunal "be pleased to restore the custom usage and conditions of service represented by the payment of Bonus in these firms. In their statement before the tribunal they have asserted that a bearing bonus was claimed by them was irrelevant because the demand was not based upon profit.

Under Rule 12 of the Punjab Superior Judicial Service (Second Amendment) Rules 1976, a direct recruit on a cadre post with effect from a date not earlier than the date on which he completed his probationary period. The proviso to it provided that the seniority of the members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers, shall be determined by the length of continuous service. Rule 12 provided for quota and rule 13 stipulated that the inter se seniority of members of each Service, whether directly recruited from the Punjab Civil Service (Judicial Branch) and the other between the control over district courts and subordinate courts vested in the High Court by article 235 of the Constitution as well as the power conferred upon the Governor by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitu tion. Rule 13 provided for adjustment of temporary vacancies by promotion or by direct recruitment, and Rule 14 provided that in respect of the temporary vacancies, all temporary vacancies were to be filled up by selection from amongst members of all the subordinate judiciary. Rule 15 provided for confirmation of permanent vacancies. Clause (a) of the rule making power under Article 309 made a provision for seniority on a vacancy based upon seniority, and under cl. (b) seniority was determined with reference to the dates on which the appointment is made. Rule 16 provided for recruitment and clause (c) of this rule prescribes that seniority should be determined according to the date of confirmation. Clauses (1), 8, 9 and 1039. The petitioners who were promotees appointed directly from the Bar to the Haryana Superior Judicial Services filed Writ Petitions in the Punjab High Court questioning their seniority inter alia on the ground that the ratio of 2: 1 between the promotees and direct recruits had to be maintained at all stages, that is, to say, not only at the time of appointment but at the point of time of confirmation also. The recruitment to the Superior Judicial service was governed by a rule of quota only and not also by the rule of rotation; and that even if such a substantive vacancy was available, the confirmation of a promotee in that vacancy was postponed arbitrarily and indefinitely, that promotees were treated with an unequal hand qua direct recruits: for example, a promotee despite his satisfactory performance and the availability of a substantive post in which he can be confirmed. The High Court held that the validity of rule 12 was not challenged by any of the promotees; and therefore it held that seniority of direct recruits and promotees must be fixed without applying the rule or rotation; in so far as the retrospective effect of the rules concerned, the amendment was made without consulting the High court, which struck down the rule. PG NO 623 The High con tempts to follow a uniform principle.
