The appellant, a mortgagor in possession of certain properties purchased by him through the respondent Bank, filed a suit against his son for recovery of possession of those villages. The claim was resisted on behalf of the respondent bank and it was contended that he had no power to grant the permanent lease in question to the defendants as the same was not a party to that suit. Held, that section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act has nothing to do with the mortgagor 's power to leases the mortgaged property. The object of the burial ground is to grant rights of burial and if the mortgagee takes his security with knowledge of the purposes to which the land is applied he would have certainly no defence to an action at the instance of the mortgagee. An illustration of this view is found in the ease of Moreland vs Richardson, (1878) 9 Barn & Cres. 245 (6) L.R. 76 I.A. 93, and Pope vs Briggs, , considered by the courts as justifying the applicability of the provisions of section 66 ; Held further, that it is for the lessee if be wants to resist the claim of the Bank to establish that the lease in his favour was granted the usual terms in the ordinary course of management. As long as nothing took place which impaired the value or impeded the operation of the mortgage, the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for a term. The true position has been stated in agreement by Mukherjee, in the present case that the mortgagor had no interest whatever in the property demised to him. Though section 66 has no application to leases of the mortgaged properties the decision of Jenkins C.J. in Balmukund vs Motilal, (1940) L .R. 75 I. A. 93,. disapproved.

Section 5 of the Arbitration Act provides for appointment of an arbitrator and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause 68 and issued notice to the respondent, the respondent is duty bound to appoint an arbitrator, and on its failure it is open to him to approach the Court for appropriate remedy under section 8 of the Act for appointment/performance of obligations by the parties. The respondent filed an arbitration suits in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5, 12 and 33 of the for short the Act. His claim was that while executing the work he sent the bills on July 12, 1979 but payment was not made. For the first time he sent notice on Nov. 28, 1989 to the respondents for reference to the arbitration. On receipt thereof, the petitioner filed an Arbitration suits in Calcutta High court under sections 35 and 33 for short of the Acts. The learned Single Judge cancelled the arbitration clause 68 of the contract in a matter Nos. 1326, 1364 and 1365/90 dated November 23, 1990 on November 23. 1990. On further appeals the division bench by its order dated December 18, 1992 in Appeal Nos 104/90 etc. dismissed the appeals. Thus these special leave petitions arose out of Arbitration Agreement said to be executed by the petitioner on May 27, 1978 which provided that the petitioner had to execute the work within 9 months. The petitioner contended that Clause 68 of Contract provides for arbitration of all or any of the disputes or differences enumerated therein that have arisen between the parties at the instance of either party to the contract. It would further be open to the petitioner to avail clause 68 in the contract seeking reference to arbitration and no such action was taken till November 28,89, immediately on receipt of the notice, the respondents invoked the jurisdiction of the Calcutta high Court under Sections 5 and 12(2) (b), but demand was not given. The Division Bench of the High Court allowed the appeals by holding that though the petitioner was said to have made the claim for payment for the first year in July 12 1979, he did not take any action from then. The Special Leave Petitions were filed by two other arbitrators under sections 53 and 72 of the Indian Arbitration Act against quashing the award dated November 18, 1991 passed by the learned Single judge cancelling the arbitration Clause 68. It was further contended that section 5 has no application to the facts of this case. Allowing the appeals in part, the Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations as they apply to the proceedings in court. [366G] 2.1 There is no express provision in the Contract Act which provides what may be called as pre requisite for arbitration in a suit. In a modern arbitration, the principles of equity must be applied just as they would now be applied in a court of law. The courts below have justifiably exercised their discretionary power and jurisdiction under sections 151 and 72 respectively. [367E F] 2:2 It is well settled that where on a special case for the opinion of the court under Section 7(1) (a) read with section 37, if the or the Judicature Act, 1925, section(s.94) has vested in the Court permitting a party to avail the remedy under sections '5 and 12 to rescind the arbitration agreement. [368C] 2 :3 It is not a condition precedent that there should in the first instance be an order appointing an arbitrator or umpire and then the same cannot be revoked except with the leave of the Court.

The property mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of section 2(1) and the notification issued under section 3 (1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 which included both Bakasht lands as well as other lands. The appellants filed a petition for passing a final decree on September 19, 1955. The Estate mortgaged the properties in question and claimed that they did not proceed any further in that proceeding but on the other hand filed on June 18, 1958 an execution petition to execute the mortgage decree against the appellants in respect of the same claim was dismissed. In appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the executing court. On this view it was not necessary to pursue that line of argument but tried to support his contention on the broader principles of res judicata. The real question for decision in this case was whether the dismissal of Misc. case Nos. 94 and 110 of 1959 for default of the judgment debtors could be said to be a final decision of ' the court after hearing the parties. Held, that the decision in Sidheshwar Prasad Singh vs Ram Saroop Singh must be held to be not correct. The proper way for construing section 4(d) is to find out the implication of the clause extracted above. In construing an earlier decision this Court would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions of the Act do not fall within the protection of the said Act" and again at page 578 "Having regard to the said scheme, it was difficult to confine the application of section 4 (d) only to execution proceedings in which the decree holder seeks to proceed against the estate of the debtor. In fact, an execution proceeding to recover the decretal amount from the estate which has already vested in the State would be incompetent because the said estate no longer belonged to the judgment debtor. " Thakur Krishna Prasad and Ors. vs Gauri Kumari Devi, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 564, followed.

Rules introduced by Notification No. 13016/4/86 AIS(1) dated 13.12.1986 (Published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part 1 Section 1). The Tribunal rendered its main judgment in Kurnar (O.A. No. 206/89 Alok Kumar vs Union ofIndia & Ors., and 61 others. Before this Court it was contended on behalf of the Respondents that the view taken by the Tribunal is based on a correct interpretation of Rule 4(iii) of C.P.S Rules, 1955 inasmuch as the rules are discriminatory; that the order of the Central Administrative Tribu nal has set out only the facts in the case of Alok Kumar (OAs) upholding the validity obi tence of the Second proviso to rule 4 of CSE Rules which insists that a candidate who was allocated to the I.P.,S. or to a Central Service Group 'A ' and who has been permitted to abstain from the probationary training in order to appear at the next Civil Services Main Examination cannot either join that service or the serv ice to which he has already been allocated on the basis of the previous C.SE and that therefore the reasons given by the Government to justify the introduction of the proviso have any rational nexus to the object of the scheme of recruitment to all India Services or/and whether such reasons are arbitrary, unfair and unjust; that since the Tribunal has set aside only the ted portion only the nature of the grievances in the one case of the services by a candidate within the same Group 'C ' and the question involved is as to whether the reasons indicated by the Govern ment to justify introduction of proviso have no rational nexus with the object intended to be achieved. It was also contended that the representation made by the candidates against the second part was not considered in accordance with Rule 17 of the Rules; that in any case there was no justification for introducing a new proviso which is ultra vires cl. (iii) and that the reasons attributed for such a classification on the ground of neglect of train ing, financial loss, unemployment situation, loss to service are all common to all Central Service group A ' listed in the CSCS(Main) and as such it is violative of Article 14; that under Rule 4 (iii), a candidate whose has alreadybeen allocated to a service on the results of an earlier examination will be eligible to compete for IAS, IFS, IPS or central Services Group 'B ' and considered only for those appointments. Disposing of the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The second proviso is held to be discriminatory against the candidates appointed to the C&S (Main) Examination, 1990 and as regards others who have been allocated to that service in either of the groups to which they has been allocated or appointed to one of those services in either ti th group to which the petitioners had been allocated. [97B]. 1.2 The restriction/embargo contained in Rule 17 is, if a candidate has been approved for appointment to IPS and expresses his intention to appear in the next CSE (Main), he should either join either that service/or the service to which him has already being allocated on tile basis of earlier Civil Services (Main). [97C] 1.3 The restriction or embargo is constitutionally invalid not flowing from any constitutional provision but from Part III of the Constitution. Since different rules are struck down by this Court in some Central Services Examination, the provisions of Rule 17 are equally applicable to all those candidates who have already been allocat ed to any of the First Services (Prelimi nary) Examination.

The appellant was detained under Section 3(1)(i) of the COFEPOSA Act for short) long before the Advisory Board had given its finding in rejecting the detenu 's request for assistance of a friend, namely, Mr. Sundararajan not being a friend of the detenu, and as his professional experience he liked to help the detenu. The Advisory Board after considering the facts on which the ground is raised are not in dispute. There has been no denial of this fact. The appellant was, however, not given an opportunity of appearing before the Board with the aid of a legal practitioner or a legal adviser would be in breach of Article 14. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: l(a) It is not for this Court to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the appellant on account of such denial. [792B C] (b) The refusal by the Advisory board to permit the appel lant to be assisted by his friend was bad and continued detention of the appellant became vitiated. [789D] (c) At the hearing of the representation of the appellan tant, Mr Sundararajan was allowed to be represented by counsel. In para 9 of the Special Leave Petition the appellant had alleged that on 25th November, 1986 while the detaining authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise the detenu was denied assistance of an retired Assistant Collector of central excise, and should the same had been refused. [784G] (d) The order of detention is quashed.

In 1946, the Government of India issued a notice under section 75 A (2) Of the Defence of India Act, 1939, for acquisition of movable property. The assessee challenged this notice on the ground that it was not served by the company as required by r. 75 A(1)(ii). Held, that in view of the fact that the suit was in respect of a transaction between the company and its managing agents for the purpose of requisition under section 25A of the Act, the orders of requisition were properly served on the assessee and not on the Managing Agents as required in r. 115 Of the Rules framed under the Act. Held, further, that the notice could not be said to have been served on a company or a corporation. The service of the notices of acquisition in this case was effective service on the mills as owners for the purposes of requisition. Where the name of the managing agent did not contain in so many words the entry in r 75 A shows that the service should be in accordance with r. 119 of the Companies Act and r. 120 of the Rules made thereunder would apply and the property in the goods passed to the Government was free from any mortgage, pledge, lien or other similar encumbrance and the period of requisition thereof shall end. Held further, also, that since notice of acquisition under section 24 A (1) (ii) of the Defence Of India Act was served on an individual if it was intended that such a property should be requisitioned under his own law for the specific performance of the contract and not to the assessee, the provision in r.(2) did not make the requisition invalid. Held also, further that when the service of notices under section 74 A(ii) is affected by some defect in the form or mode of service it was for the assessee to take advantage of that defect. The period of service of such an order is necessary on the person who can place the goods.

The assessee was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. Sometime in 1955 56, the assessee had been contesting the proceedings taken against it under Section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. In appeal this Court, HELD: It cannot be said that the High Court was right in holding it to be a provision and not a reserve. [113C] Metal Box Company of India Ltd. vs Their Workmen, ; , relied on. Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. Ltd. etc. vs Commissioner of Income Tax Andhra Pradesh etc. ; , referred to. The question referred to by the High court was whether in Metal Box it is a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. [ 113G] Metal box Co. of India Limited vs Their Employees, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 533; Vazir Ahmed Tobacco Co . Ltd. Kerala & Anr. , referred ted. In Metal Box, which has been followed in Vazir Diwan Sultan Tobacco co. Ltd., etc. V salient distinction between a provision providing and reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between the provision and reserve (in commercial accountancy fairly known, that whereas a provision is a charge against the profits to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P.& L. account, a reserve is in appropriation of profits, the asset or assets by which it is represented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business". Bearing in mind the aforesaid broad distinction, we will indicate how the two concepts are defined and dealt with by the " Applying the said test it must be held that the provision made by the assessee in its books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23 A) was indeed a provision. [114D E] Metal boxes which have been followed In Vazir Ahmad Tobacco Co., Ltd. & Ors. vs The Commissioner of Incometax Andhra Pradesh, etc. , Vazir Commodities Co. Pegler 's Book keeping and Accounts 15th Edn. p. 42; applied. The High Court in appreciating the questions referred to it must hold that the said clause itself is a provision or not a reserved. [ 115A] Metal Item Box, and which has, however, been followed by the Tribunal, must be read consistently with the context of the case. It must be taken as a whole and consistent with the subject matter sought to be considered.

Clause 9 of the Indian Railway Establishment Code, 1948 provided that no officer recruited directly or indirectly by any authority to represent all temporary Assistant Engineers (on a later point) in a representative capacity across which stand arrayed the Union of India and the Railway Board as respondents. All the temporary Assistant Officers were subjected to competitive written and personality tests and when selected on the basis of the results of the competitive examinations, they too were placed above those appointed on the 'Bearance ' at places). While the President was the appointing authority of the Engineers, the Railway had taken a decision that the officers so absorbed into the Indian Railways of Engineers would be given weightage in seniority 'on the basis thereof and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the income from the date of their absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and that if any given year, the candidates appointed by the Railway were placed below those appointed, on the strength of selection by the Union Public Service Commission. While the Union was the selecting authority of Engineers, there had been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority of the absorbers was to be determined with reference to the date when they filed the connected writ petitions in this Court. Dismissing the Writ Petitions, the Court, HELD: (1) The distinction between 'the two services was well marked in Katyani Dayal 's case, if not the strict principles of res judicata. The distinction and the classification of temporary Assistant officers and members of the public service of Engineers Class I fell clearly to be identified and marked. The only method of 679 of fusion was by means of a phased absorption as noticed in paragraph 9 of that Report detailed detailed. The scheme having met with approval of this Court cannot by mere passage of time be taken to have become vulnerable by subsequent exponence and dimension of Article 14 of the Constitution. [1025E F] (2) If the matter has been settled in this particular service, its unsettling by means Of a petition under Article 32 of the Constitu tion is impermissible. [1125F G] (3) As far as the determination of seniority in this case was concerned, at this juncture on the touch stone of equality would be to unsettle a settled position. That venture is neither in the interest of justice nor in the interests of service. When there has been complete absorb ment of personnel of some of the class of employees and the senior absorbers are to be counted from their date of absorption as envisaged in their appointments matters and as held by this Court with weightage of half the length of service subject to a maximum of five years, it would otherwise be imprudent now. At this juncture again on the lan stone of parity would be appropriate for the then writ petitioners to either involve all parties who could possibly have an interest or a likely affectation in the litigation, or to sue them in a separate representative capacity if not individually.

The Saurashtra State Public Safety Measures (Third Amendment) Ordinance, 1949, was enacted to provide for public safety, mainte nance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquillity in the State. By a notification under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949 the High Court, acting under article 226 of t he Constitution, held that the Ordinance read with the Second Schedule (as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra), was discriminatory as offending against the provision of article 14 of the Constitu tion. The State Government issued a notification dated 9th February, 1951, by which certain specified individual cases in which speci fied persons were involved to be tried by the Special Court under the special procedure while any person committing the same offences outside those areas would be tried in accordance with a special procedure prescribed for the purpose and section 11 lays down that "all offences under the Indian Penal Code shall be investigated, inquired into, tried, tried and otherwise dealt with according to the provisions hereinafter contained", and that all offences under sections 302, 307 and 392 read with section 34 of the Indian penal Code (as extended to the accused) shall be tried as expeditiously as possible in accordance With a special provi sions framed by the State Government, the Government was pleased to direct (i) that a Special Court shall try such offences or classes of offences or such cases or class of cases as the State Govern ment may, by general or special order in writing, direct." The notification issued by it under section 11(2) of this Ordinance was bad as it contravened article 14 Of the Constitution. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that sections 9 and 11 were discriminatory in that the offences alleged to have been committed by the appel lant within the specified areas are required to be triable by the special judge under the general procedure, while any such person committing them outside those area would be trying by ordinary courts under the normal procedure. Held, that the challenge of the classification was not confined merely to a remote area than one occupied by an earlier notification but was also liable for the same or kindred offences. The contravention of section 11 of the Ordinance in so far as it authorised the State to direct particular "cases" to be try by special judge constituted under the Act, offends against the equal protection clause of the Constitution and as such were void under article 13 of the Consti tution; that section 11 was constitutionally valid. When an Ordinance is challenged on any ground it is open to a party to contend that the impugned tax was not discriminatory in character; but it is concerned only with the grouping of "offences", "classes of offences" or "cl classes of cases" for the purposes of the particular legislation as recited in its preamble and, it would be the duty of the State government to classify offences or classifi cation or classes thereof as the Government of the United State of pradesham tory, for the State Gov ernment is in a better position to judge the needs and exigencies of the con tract. The Legislature has left it to the discretion of the Govern ment which can classify offences and cases in any way they like without regard to any objective and as Such the statute is open tO the challenge to making arbitrary discrimination on grounds similar to those urged on behalf (1) that sections 3 and 11 are invalid, because, section II of the Saurashtra Ordinance provides for special procedure not to be adopted by a Special Judge appointed under the Ordinance, and that the State Govt.

Rule 7 of the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation Rules, 1950 provides that 'retrenchment ' means termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever. For this provision, it was provided that such termination can be extended, and further provided that in cases of transfer of undertaking or closure of undertaking as if the workmen had been retrenched. The employer terminated the employment on the ground of unsatisfactory service. Thereupon an industrial dispute was raised questioning the legality of their termination and the State Government referred the dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication under section 10 of the . The Labour Court held, overruling the stand of the employer that section 25F of the had no application to the effect that the discharge was invalid, and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that(i) there was an 'ret retrenchment ' within the meaning of section 2(oo) and those orders were bad for non compliance with the provisions of section 25 F; (ii) such termination of service was not due to discharge of surplus labour force and, therefore, did not amount to retrenchment. It is the stand on behalf respondent Corporation that the consensus of judicial opinion in later decisions was against the appellant 's stand and, consequently, did no amount to retrenched; The question of the correct interpretation of the definition of the expression "retrenchment" and posed the following question: "The question however, before this Court is whether the discharge of the employees from service amounted to retrenchment?" It is an admitted position that the employees were probationers at the time of discharge. There was no dispute that as a condition precedent to discharge the requirements of section 26F had not been complied with. If the discharge from service had been grounded upon unsatisfactory service during the period of probation, it has been argued that such terminated service was " retrenchment". The High Court negatived this contention and upheld the award of the Labour Tribunal which set aside those orders and gave appropriate relief to the workman as understood in section 2 (oo). In this appeal by Special Leave there is one set of costs.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposes of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration and on 1.4.1952 the assessee applied for registration as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941 in respect of the unconnected or unclaimed goods, and was accordingly registered. It submitted returns of sales effected by it of unclaimed goods year after year and paid sales tax pursu ant to the assessments made by the Sales Tax Department. However, in assessment proceedings for the four quarters ending March 1959 the assessee application applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of the registration of the assessee as a "dealer" under the Act. The Commercial Tax officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal of unclaimed Goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the asses see 's activities, and that therefore a sale of goods took place. The Revision application filed by the Appel lateer was rejected on the finding that the sales effected were sales under the Railways Act and the assessee was a " dealer". Hence these appeals. Allowing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1. In the case of the assesses South Eastern Eastern Railway, what were sold were unclaimed goods. The Railway was a carrier of the goods and if at the stage of delivery goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose them of. There can be no doubt that the activity of so disposing of the Goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of goods. It seems to South Eastern Rail Railway wasa smanee for the purposes of the Bengal Financial (Sales tax) Act 1941. [781B C] 2.1 The activity of disposing of goods was adjuctive to a principal activity for the purpose of the Indian Railways (Sales ' Tax) act, 1941. In other case, the assessee Eastern Railway disposed of scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423.

The appellant was appointed Principal Officer of a company to purchase and sell securities, in respect of the shares purchased by it from other companies. The Central Government issued an Order called the " managed bank ". Subsequentiy of this order was a charge sheet against the appellant with respect to certain offences including that for failure to deliver the deposit amount of the purchase price and delivery of securities to the company for being made over to the Union Agencies, before the expiry of sixty days from the date of receipt by him. The appellant contended before the High Court that the Managing Director of a Company was not authorised to purchase or sell securities on behalf of the company unless he was authorised in writing by the Chairman. Held, that the essential ingredient of section 409 is that there must be something done with the intention of doing an act and the mere failure to do so would not make any the offence of the accused charged. In the present case, though it may be shown that either Gurha had supplied the office with the fictitious cash statement or was not a case of the securities missing but a case Of the Insurance Company not getting those securities at all, it can be said that he mentioned Bhagwati Trading Company as a party to the conspiracy. The charge under section 409 I.P.C. is one of substance and it cannot be said in the circumstances of the present ease that the company was acting to help the diversion of funds of the Insurance company to the Companies. In view of the popularity in which money had been paid to the companies through Bhagwati Trading Companies with the Bank at Bombay, the appellants could not have been convicted under section 120 read with section 409 Indian Penal Code for having, therefore, committed an offence punishable under section 408 I. P.C., and it was not necessary that the shares should be sent for to the head office in December, 1955. Held further, that in view of section 4(2) Of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, the appellant could not be convicted under s.120 read with s.409 I.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat Service of the State. By an order dated August 19, 1966 the Government appointed the officers of the secretariat and Kutch States to be posted in the Secretariat of the new State of Gujarat under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act 37 of 1956. The officers of a secretariat were later posted in different districts in Saurashtra and Kutch. Under the two orders dated August 18, 1966, the Government had been empowered to appoint promotions from among Senior Assistants, as provided by r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules which was con tended to be "illegal" or void and of no effect". On September 7, 1966 a new Commission was constituted under section 115 of the , framed by it in exercise of its powers under article 309 of the Constitution on the division and integration of the services in the new States. Under section 81(1) relating to service other than All India Services were made and by section 82 of the Act the Government was authorised to establish one or more Advisory Committees to "advise" the State Government on the Division and integration between the officers who were allotted to another State could not be varied to his disadvantage except with the previous approval of the Central Government. The two orders were issued from time to time fixing their scales of pay and seniority. In exercise of the powers under Article 309 of its Constitution, the Govt. sanctioned certain rules called "The Allocated Government Servants ' (Absorption, Seniority, Pay & Allowances) Rules, 1957" which governed the servants who were allotment to the State of Bombay on reorganisa tion. The appellants were allotted permanent posts by the State in connection with the affairs of the erstwhile State of Saurashtra and the Gujarat Secretariat Service. By virtue of section 8 of the States Reorganization Act 37 the new Province of Bombay was not carved out of the territory of the former State of Gujrat, and under section 80(1)(c) a guarantee was given to every allotted public servant that his conditions of service shall not be changed except with previous approval. The posts in which they were posted were transferred by the Government to the Secretariat and on terms not derogation invade the statutory right vested in the personnel of the latter Saurashtra and Saurashtra States which they acquired under the , to hold posts in them in the merged State of Andhra Pradesh, were allotted. By section 83 power was given conferred upon the Central government to give directions to the States. Those provisions were obviously inconsistent with the provisions of sections 115, 116 & 117 of the ' the Act. Section 86 provided for the continuance of officers in the same posts. One of the conditions of the service applicable immediately before November 1, 1956 was that the State cannot vary the conditions Of service applicable again before November l6 1956 unless previous approval was obtained thereto. The Government on August 19 1966 issued a notification to the following effect: "The question of regularising the appointment to various posts in Secretariat Department on and after 1st May 1960 of the drafted persons was under consideration of the Government for some time. Government is now pleased to direct, in consultation with the Gujarat Public Service Commission, that the persons shown in the accompanying statement should be treated to have been regularly appointed in the posts shown against their names in column 4 of the statement. As regards fixation of their pay and senior appointments orders having already been issued in the Government Resolution General Administration Department No. SCT 1161 KH, dated 14th March 1964, they were allotted at later date. The respondents who were appointed from the districts challenged the validity of the order of the Govt., but the High Court dismissed the petition.

By a second proviso to section 5(1) of the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948, it was provided that such tax shall not be levied on the purchase or sale of declared goods at more than one stage and shall be refunded by the dealer to persons from whom it is collected if the goods are sold in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The second proviso thereto provided that the tax payable under that law in respect of any sale or purchase of such goods inside the State shall not exceed 2% of the sale or Purchase price thereof, and such tax should not be leviable at more then one stage. On December 15, 1969 the Punjab Legislature passed Haryana General Sales tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967. The petitioners were dealers of ginned cotton for manufacturing yarn and selling the said cotton also to registered dealers both inside and outside the State. The system of assessment was challenged on the ground that there was a possibility of tax being levied at more late one stage, the provisions of the second proviso notwithstanding. The Punjab High Court upheld the validity of the Haryana General sales Tax (Amendment & Validation) Ordinance. 1967 which by sections 15 and 16(1)(a)(vi) were in conflict with section 15 of the Central Act. Dismissing the petitions ^ HELD: 1(i). The definition of "dealer" in section 2(d) and in the proviso to that section clearly show that the taxable turnover should be determined on the turnover of a dealer, is to levy the tax on the first purchaser.[549 F G] (ii) Section 3(a)(II) and section 3(2)(a) define "dealer". The definition shows that the two conditions must be satisfied. Firstly that the person who buys cotton is liable to pay sales tax should therefore be liable to purchase tax, secondly, that that he is liable under section 5 (2) (a), and that he cannot claim the benefit of section 11AA and ask refund of the same at a later stage; and thirdly that he can claim exemption under section 12 of the Act. [549 F H] 2(i)(ii). The tax is at the same rate and therefore the tax cannot be said to be higher in the case of imported goods. Therefore, on a proper construction of section 3 (a) of Act, it has been made mandatory that the amount paid by him in respect thereof shall be deducted from his taxable turnover for determining the taxable turn over. [550 B C] 4(i) The two conditions are: (i) that the goods must be sold by the last dealer liable to tax and (ii).

The plaintiffs sued for enforcement of a mortgage against the present respondent, who was an original plaintiff in a suit. They contended that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment of the amount directed to be paid by them. Held, per KANIA C.J., PATANJALI SASTRI, MUKHERJEA J. Under section 14 of the Madras Agriculturists ' Relief Act a mortgage decree is one and unsolicable exceptions to this rule are admitted in special circum stances where the integrity of the mortgage has been disrupted at the instance of the mortgagee himself; e.g., when there is severance of the interests of the mort gliest with the consent of the par ties incorporated in the terms, he could not make a new decree for the parties. Rainier vs Srinivasiah (I.L.R. , Ramana Sundari Koer & Others vs Mallikarjunathu (A.I.R , Narayanaswami Pillai vs Seetharam (A I.R., 1950 Mad. 38) and Satyavathi Amma vs Subramanyi nal (A .I. R. , distinguished. Although the Privy Council has taken a view in all these cases that principle is right or wrong, it has in no applica tion to a case like the present, to express any opinion as to the correctness or otherwise of these deci sions. The general law undoubtedly is that a mortgage decrees is one & indivisible and exception to this Rule are admitted In special circumstances where the sanctity of the main propensities of a mort gagor decree has been completely disrupted in view of the provisions of the Act, the Court would be entitled lo have his debts scaled down under the Agriculturists ' relief Act, but there were purchasers of the mortgaged property who were not agriculturists and the question arose whether a purchaser could get the benefit of the debt scaled up in favour of the original debtors.

Under section 13 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act (Bombay Act No. LX of 1947), if a tenant of any premises is determined for any reason, any subtenant to whom the premises or any part thereof have been lawfully sublet before the coming into operation of this Act shall subject to the provisions of this section be deemed to become the tenant of the landlord on the same terms and conditions as he would have held from the tenant if the tenancy had continued. " The City Civil Court was called upon to decide whether the suit filed by the appellants could be entertained by that court, having regard to the provi sions of sections 28 and 29A of the Act, he had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but did not record any decision on the merits of the appellants ' case. On a proper interpretation of the provisions Of section 28 and section 29A, the High Court was of the opinion that the City Civil court had no jurisdiction to try the suit in view of section 29 A(2) of the , as it purported to bar a party to a suit, proceeding or appeal mentioned therein, in which a question of title entirely arose out of the pro visions of section 28, and that no other Court could deal with it. Held, further, that in a suit under section 28 of the City Small Causes Act, on the termination of the tenancy of the first plaintiff there was only one relating to possession of premises to which the provisions con tained in that section applied and in that suit claims and questions arising out Of the Act or any of its provisions had to be dealt with. The suit did not cease to be a suit between a landlord and a tenant merely because the defendants denied the claim of the plaintiffs. The plaintiff 's case fell under section 29(A) of Bombay Rents., Hotel and ing House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, which contemplates filing of any suit relating to the possession of any such premises to Which any of the provision of Part 11 of the said Act apply between a landlords and a par tendant. The contention that the suit was one which arose out Of an .from the , and therefore was not one in respect of possession arising under the provisions o the Act must be negatived. Section 28 of Bombay Rent Act, 1946, does not in terms cover a case where in a case in a such suit another party seeks to establish his title to the premises, is that a title which section 29 provides for a defendant to establish in a Civil Court other than the specified in section 28 is not a suit binding on him and against the tenant. Such a claim was one relating only to possession and does not arise out of it and cannot be determined by the City civil court. In the present case, as the tenancy was terminated by the landlord and the latter had been continuing his sub tenants he could resist eviction only if he established his right to continue in possession under the pro ceedings of section 14 of the Rent Act. Held further, also that it is settled law that a contract of sale between a tenant and a subtenant cannot be said to have any effect on the happening of a transaction of sale and not on the expiry of the period fixed for execution of the decree. In a suit by a landlord against a tenant the jurisdiction to adjudicate upon such a question is exclusively vested in the courts specified in that Section and no other.

The respondent was a private limited company carrying on business under the name and style of Oriental Metal Pressing Works. On May 26, 1955, when he transferred his business to the respondent by an agreement made between him and the appellant, a private company as he was appointed the managing director. This resolution was challenged in a suit filed in the City Civil Court for certain reliefs and for various other reliefs which were inter alia incidental thereto: (1) appointment of the appellant Govind as the Managing Director was void; (2) appointment by a directors of another person as the managing directors was not hit by section 312, inasmuch as the Act was passed after consultation with the company, that the view taken by them in a proceeding under section 312 of the in terms of section 312 had been accepted to be correct and that section 302 of the Indian Penal Code could not be said to have intended that the word "assignment" in the section included "appointment", and so, such an appointment would also be void under the section. Held, that on a plain reading of sections 255 and 317 of the , it was clear that it was not intended that a managing director could appoint his successor after another person was appointed as his successor; but such a power did not offend section 312. Consequently, in view of the fact that the power to appoint alternate directors was given by the articles, such, such appointment would be "assign". The word "appointment" in section 312 meant "appointment ' and meant a "appointment".

The appellant partnership firm carry on business in the name and style of M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart. On the ground that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the shop let out to the appellants M/S. Adija Chetty Street, G.T. Madras. The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellant tenant on the ground inter alia that they were unlawful sub tenants; that the appel lants having unlawfully and having unlawfully after obtaining the previous consent of respondent sublet ted the shop, let out by them to M/ s. Adarseshwar Glass Handicrafts Mart and were liable to be evicted forwil ful subletting under section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and 419 Rent Control) Act, 1960, that they had unlawfully sublet the said shop to M. Adlery Ammal Road, GT. in the eviction petition on the grounds inter alia: that they have unlawfully sublet t ed the same shop to the respondent; that they are liable to evict forwil gess under the provision of section 10 (2)(i) of Act; that it is only by virtue of the provisions of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. It was also urged that the application against the partnership firm was not maintainable because there was no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that the appellant had sublet t he shop to another partner; that there is no evidence to show that M/D firm M. The Appellate Authority dismissed the said appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appe lants. In the appeal by special leave it was contended: (i) that the Code in Civil Procedure was not applicable to proceedings under the Rent Act either and hence, the ratio laid down in Chhotelal Pyarelal, the partnership Firm and others vs Shikharchand, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 435; (ii) that as the provisions o f order 30, Code of C.P.C., 1908, were directly applicable to the proceedings before the Rent lordi ty, it was only by way of virtue of section 5 of the Act that a Firm can sue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 It is not open to Mr. Nayar, to raise this contention at this stage at all; (iii) in the instant case, there is evidence to establish that M /s. A.T., who carried on business at the said premises and that firm was carried on, business in t he said premises even for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the business there. Moreover, although a notice was given by the respondent to the appe llant and M//s Adihij Glass Mart to produce their income tax returns, assessment orders as well as account books and ledgers for the relevant period, these were not produced. [420G; 420A] 1.2 In the instant ease, the partners of the firm are before the Court though in a wrong name. No such objection has been raised at all till the stage of special Leave and it is surely not open for the appellants to raise such an objection at a late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. This contention must be negatived. [ 420B] Chhotelhal Pyarelal 's case, relied upon by Mr. Coffee, J.I.T (in C.R.) No. 156/79 dated 5th February, 1981, followed. In Chhotelalsal Pyare Lal 's ease, relied on by Mr, Nayar, the objection to the main tainability of the petition was raised at the earliest stage and was wrongly repelled by the Trial Court.

A cf. the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Act, 1971 was passed by the Andhra Nadu Legislature in exercise of its power conferred under section 3 of the , with a view to imposing ceiling on urban immovable property and acquisition of such property in excess of the ceiling area and all matters connected therewith or ancillary thereto should be regulated in the State. Chapter IV which deals with "vacant land" provides for the imposition of a ceiling on vacant land. The explanation to section 2(f) defines " Vacant land", by providing that any land situated within the limits of an urban agglomeration and referred to as such in the master plan, shall not be deemed to be used mainly for the purpose of agriculture, if such land is not entered in the revenue or land records before the appointed day as for the purposes of agriculture; " The appellants contended that the Andhra Act was ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competence of the Andhra pradesh Legislature. In support of their contentions relied on the decisions of this Court in Union of India vs V. It Iswarapani Dei & Anr., ; , the High Court referred to the provisions of the Act, which took a contrary view by taking into consideration. On behalf of the appellants in CA Nos 14 to 23 they contended that: (1) the Andhra has no legislative competence to enact the Central Act, (2) it is an expensive concept and any area with an existing or future population of more than one lakh could be notified as an urban 1965 agglomeration under section 2 (n)(A)(ii); (3) it fails to give due effect to the definition of family unit in section 3(f), and the provisions Of section 4 did not contravene article 14; and (4) it was violative of Article 31A. They further contended that on a proper construction of the relevant provisions of Andhra Pradesh Act, a divided minor son was not liable to be included in the "family unit", as defined in section 2ndn)(a)(ii). The High Court held that the definition was violative by the fundamental right of equality and therefore the law must be struck down. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 There is no doubt that so far as these urban agglomerations are concerned, it was not within the legislative competency of the said State Legislature to provide for imposition of ceiling on land situate within those urban aggl sects. It is only in respect of land remaining with a person whether an individual or a family unit holds land in excess or in any area included within the local limits of a municipality (by whatever name called), a notified area committee, a town committee, city and town committee a small town Committee, a cantonment board or a panchayat but does not include any such land which is mainly used for the pur pose of agriculture. Therefore, it could not be said that the whole of the State of Andhra was ultra competence of Andhra pra Pradesh Legislature in so far so as land situate in the other areas of the two States is concerned. [1155G] 1.2 The Andhra Pradesh Urban (Ceiling and Regulation) Act was enacted with a avowed object to Providing the equitable distribution of land in urban agglemy manner, etc., for preventing concentration of urban land in the hands of a few persons and speculation and profiteering therein and with a profit motive to promote such an equitable distribution amongst various categories. The Andhra Act had been passed by Parliament alone which was competent to legislate with respect to ceiling on surplus land situate at these urbanisable agglomerilities referred to in section 1(2) of that Act and its scope would be restricted to the class of land situated in all the other States of Andhra State of Kerala. [1106G; 1069C] 1:3 The definition of "family" in Section 2(g) is materially in the same terms as the definition to (1)(A) in the Andhra Andhra Pradesh, Act.

The appellant company was declared a public utility service under the . It was alleged by the workmen that on account of an illegal and unconstitutional strike which took place on several previous dates, the management had no option but to declare a lock out of certain Works except some special shifts. On September 17, 1953, another notice was issued by the Company lifting the lock out with effect from December 1, 1953. The company replied that unless they voluntarily recorded their willingness to do normal work, they would be considered as no longer employed by it from 2 p.m. on April 10, 1953 and that if there were no improvement in the attitude of the workers, they should also be taken back in employment. The workmen 's conduct was not satisfactory but the appellant company accepted some of the demands. The question for consideration was whether the discharge and/or suspension of these workmen was justified if not to what relief those men were entitled. Held: (i) Even assuming that the notices bore the construction which is put on them, the workmen did not join on or before Saturday, September 19, 1953; they reported for duty on October 1, 1952, but failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence and was not justified in refusing leave. If a large number of workmen are arrested by the authorities in charge of law and order by reason of their questionable activities in connection with a labour dispute, as in this case, the work of the company will be paralysed if the Company is forced to give leave to all them for a " more more or less indefinite period. (ii) The workmen were entitled "to be taken under the existing Standing Orders of the Company from October 2, 1953 to October 2 and that "the management had reasons to believe that many workers are desirous of resuming work" etc; but on the contrary, the workman was denied permission. (iii) The Tribunal should not have interfered with the decision of the management unless it found that the decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. 53 R. C. 51, followed.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Rajasthan Universities Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for appointment) Act 1974 held interviews on 20th June, 1989 and selected Dr. Nathawat for the Post of Professor In Bot any. On the vacancies caused within the cadre during six months of approval of the Syndicate as also within a period of 6 months from the date of approval by the Syndicate, the candidates found suitable and placed in the reserve list be appointed in the order of priority given by the Selection Committee. The syndi cate approved the select list and appointed Dr. V.Nathawat on the said post. Dr. Urea Kant was appointed as Professor in the Department of BotAny. Dr Shiv Sharma, Dr. Sudhakar Mishra and Shri Uma Kant as Professor w.e.f. 30th September, 1989. Dr Sheo Kant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of Dr. Shiv Sharma on the ground that the Selection Commit tee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a selected person joins the post then selection made by it was exhausted and the person named in the reserved list could not be appointed against a future vacancy. The learned Single Judge held that the constitution of the Selection Board was valid but as regards the appointment from the reserve and not on the appointment, of Dr, Ureaitta from the Reserve List it was held that once selected person joining the post, the reserve lists stood exhausted and that the person mentioned in the Reserve list could cannot be appointed to a future vacancies. The Division Bench upheld the order. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the respondents that the reserve List is always prepared to meet the continu gency of anticipated or future vacancies caused on account of resignation, retirement or promotion. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of preparing a reserve list would be defeated if the view taken by the High Courts is accepted that once such a person selected by the selection committee has joined that post then select ment made by the Committee is exhausted and in the present case Dr. Uma Kant was recommended by the Super intendent Committee constituted for the selection of a teacher in the University. Thus no fault can be found that the incumbent recommended in the reserves list by the Respond ent or the Selection Authority had approved and recommended the name of the appellant Dr. Sheo Kant as valid on the post held by Dr.V.Nantwat. [421B D] 1.2 The expression 'appointment ' in sub section (1) of Section 3 shall mean appointed initially. Then, sub sec.(1) Of Sec. 5 provides that for every selection of ana teacher or of an officer in a University, a Committee would be constituted of the persons mentioned therein. The High Court was wrong in taking the view that a regular vacancy of Professor having arisen on the retirement of Dr Dr. G.S.Nakathawat when Dr. S.Natwat retired on 30th Septem ber, 1989, a fresh Selection Committee should have been constituted and no appointment on such post could have been made from the reserved List prepared by the Con stitution of the University as per Section 5(1).

The petitioners are owners of plots of land on which the development plan was prepared and published under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954. The draft of a section of the development Plan for Greater Bombay was published in January 1964 by the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay which contained sections 3 to 17 relating to development plans generally. Section 4 provided that at least once in every ten years from the date on which a declaration of intention to prepare a development plan would be given, every local authority shall carry out a survey of the area within its jurisdiction and submit the same to the State Government for sanction. Under section 10(1) the State Govt was given the power to sanction extension or revocation of commencement certificate in respect of any land which is in the course of the compa ny of development plan, subject to certain conditions. The petitioners filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of sections 9, 10 and 11 (3) and their action was challenged on the ground that the provisions were ultra vires the Constitution of India and that they had applied through their architect who had written a letter to the Municipal commissioner for permission for construction of two factory buildings and lavatory blocks in contravention of section 9 of the Bombay City Town Planning act, 1954 which deprived them of their right under article 19(1)(f) and (g). The High Court held that the residents of the City of Greater Bombay had made applications through their engineers on January 2, 1962 for permission to change the existing user of their lands by putting them to industrial use and had written letters to the municipal Commissioner. On appeal by special leave: HELD : The objections raised as to the invalidity of sections 8, 10, 11, 11 12 and 13 (3), were not tenable at all and that no one could be heard to say that the local authority after making up its mind to acquire land for a public purpose must do so within a short period of time as possible. It would not be reasonable to place such a restriction on the power of the local authori ty which is out to create better living conditions for millions of people in a vast area. They could only do this by proceeding with their scheme gradually, by improving portions of the areas at a time, obtaining money from persons whose lands had been improved and augmenting the same with their own resources so as to be able to take up the improvement work with regard to another area marked out for development. The preparation of the final development plan and the final Development Plan was not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the Local authority. After a development scheme was prepared, the question was a simple one like whether the commencement certificate could be given without doing any violation to the development scheme. After the approval of the State improvement plan, the matter was examined by the Town Planning Officer and the report submitted by the Development Committee which was approved by him, who after considering the proposals made in the tentative development plan had to guide itself. The Authority must therefore look into all material available to it including the tentative plans and the preliminary development plan which then made up its minds as to whether a commencement certificate should be granted or not. If the provisions of the Act are borne in mind, and the rules framed thereunder complied with, as appears to have been done in these cases, there was little or no scope for the local authorities acting arbitrarily under section 13 of the impugned Act.

The petitioners, who were five writ petitions under article 32 of the Constitution and three appeals against the Judgments of the High Courts of Gujarat and Delhi, under article 226 of the constitution, challenged the validity of the award on the ground that (a) India claims that there is no territorial dispute as there is a well established boundary running roughly along the northern edge of the Rann of Kutch as shown in the pre partition maps which needs to be demarcated on the grounds; (b) the Gujarat West Pradesh Regulation of Trade, 1948, which was subsequently amended by Act 40 of 1961, provides that "the general and abstract doctrine laid down by the High Court at Bombay that it is beyond the powers of British Crown without the consent of Parliament to make a cession of territory within the jurisdiction of any of the British Courts in India, in time of peace, to a foreign power; and (c) the award merely fixes or demarcates the boundary between the State of Gujarat in India and West Pakistan regarding which there were disputes and much friction, and by the Award no cession of Indian territory was contemplated. HELD: (1) The claim made by the claimants that in imple menting the award of the International Tribunal, an attempt is made to cede any part of the territory of India which formed part of their duties, is not supported by survey maps, correspondence between the officials of Kutch State and the British Administration, assertions made in the Annual Administration Reports for 75 years before 1947 Statistical Allocations relating to British India, Bombay Administration Reports Gazetteers, Memorandum on Indian States and a number of official publications, and the claim made from time to time by the British authorities which were not accepted. [301 A C] (2) There is no evidence that it was part of Great Rann between the two. The border between the other States is 'Indian territory ' and deprivation of the rights of the citizens under article 19(1)(d), and (e). [305 B E] State of Bombay vs Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh ([1954] S.C.R. 1069 overruled.

The appellants, a company registered under the Companies Act 1913 and have their factories at Pimpri and Chinchvad in the District of Pune (Maharashtra) got their factories from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or Alandi or places enroute to TELCO Factory at Pimprecha or Chinchwad. The appellants let out transport facilities to the employees from Pimpri Railway Crossing and onwards either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey. In addition, they were charged at the rate of Rs. 5 per month on account of inclusive fares in respect of the stage carriage or stage carriages held by them but not levied any charge on those employees who were in supervisory grades. In the course of arguments, it was pointed out that when the company was prepared to grant free transport facilities for the supervisory staff there was no reason why the same amenities should not be extended to the other employees and Mr. Nariman, learned counsel for the appellants frankly conceded that in future no charges would be realised from its employees. In view of what we have already said it is not necessary for this Court to go into such meticulous details, because the legal position appears to be clear enough. As counsel for respondent has already undertaken not to charge any amount from the employees for providing transport facilities, the point has now become more or less academic and to the appellants provided free transport as in the case of supervisory staff. One point has been raised by the learned counsel that even if a nominal charge is realised from the employee that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act, and therefore, it cannot be said that the transport vehicles provided to the workmen by the appellants could be a public services vehicle in any sense of the term.

The appellants, a firm carrying on business in the country ofky and a cinema licence in the locality, filed a petition under Article 226 questioning the validity of an order dated 27th December 1977 passed by the State Government of Madhya Pradesh granting a "no objection certificate for a period of six months". This license was granted earlier upto 30th June 1976 and there was no further renewal up to 30th September 1976. The First Respondent made an application on 5th December 1975 for grant of a licence for a temporary cinema, and the District Magistrate having jurisdiction issued a no objection certificate vide his order dated 10th February 1976 for a Period of six month. This application was turned down by the Distt. Magistrate as well as by the District Magis trate on the ground that Paras Talkies with permanent cinema licence which was closed, had now been functioning in the area and, therefore, a renewal of the licence for temporary "a temporary cinema in the same locality would not be proper". Respondent 3 carried the matter in appeal to the State Govt. which by its order dated 26th December 1978 granted a no certificate for the period of 6 months. The order of the District Officer was challenged by the appellants in a writ petition before the High Court, which dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that if before the grant of licence to the third respond ent the appellants filed their objections which were taken into consideration by the Dist. Magistrate, they should have been heard and the decision arrived at by the Sate Government appeal at their back was violative of principles of natural justice and the order granting the no objection Certificate is violative of the principles of Natural Justice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants did not file any objection at that stage "no Objection" certificate was granted to the second respondent. Thereafter when an application for no objection certificates for a renewed cinema licence had passed muster long before on 10th Febru ary 1976 and appellants had not raised any objection to the grant, it is possible that the "No objection ' certificate would have been refused", and in that event the applicant would not have applied for a cinema license. On that short ground the appeal must fail. [ 801 G; 801 A B] 2.1 The facts of this case show that there are various stages through which an application was for a quasi permanent cinema license, and as a first step selection of a site where the cinema house is to be located, the Selection of the site and its clearance by the licensing authority by the issuance of a no ' objection certificate was an important step to be taken in the direction of finally constructing a cinema house and obtaining a licence. When any person desiresto erect a cinema meaning thereby a place where an exhibition by means of cinematograph is to he given, he must apply for a no objections certificate in respect of the sites where the Cinema house isto be constructed. When such an application is received it is tobe advertised in the manner prescribed inviting the public to file objections.

The plaintiff had agreed to assign the mining lease, that they were ready and willing to perform their contract, and that they reserved their right to file a suit for specific performance. The defendant filed his written statement in that suit on November 5, 1957 he wrote a letter to the plaintiffs that the earlier letter was not necessary because he did not receive an answer within a certain time but stated therein that it had been communicated to him before November 6, 1957 when the plaintiff did not accept the offer either orally or by any letter sent to the defendant. On November 1, 1957, the appellant wrote the following letter to plaintiffs: "Subject to your agreement dated 3rd August, 1957 I hereby agree, to assign to you the said mining lease subject to your paving me one lakh and eighty thousand rupees at your option to be decided by you within three months from this date. This document though couched as an agreement was in point of law an offer only. As a matter of fact on September 2, 1957 the plaintiff had not agreed to purchase the mining leases. Till both parties were bound there could be no con cluded contract. The promise to keep the offer open for three months was not supported by any consideration. The respondent filed his suit (O.S. No. 46) against the defendant claiming a declaration that they are entitled to remain in possession of the mining area, and claimed specific performance of the contract. His defence was that the contract was concluded on September 3, 1957 and that it was concluded only after November 6. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court allowed the appeal preferred by the appellant. HELD: (i) There was no concluded contract between the parties, and in O.S., No. 47 of 1957 was not a suit to take shares. [583F G] (ii) The plaintiff had failed to establish the new case, because the plaintiffs were not an acceptance of the offer, not was it intended to be an acceptance. It is not usual to accept a business offer by a plaint; nor is it usual to communicate an acceptance by serving a copy of the plaint through the medium of Court. [585 F] In re: Pellatt 's Case (4) this Court rejected Bloxam 's case turned on its own special facts. Blox Wam could be regarded as having dispensed with the necessity of the communication of the acceptance, and so it was not proper to express any opinion on this question.

The appellants were office bearers of M/s. S.K. Sugar Ltd., Ltd., (Lauriya). A complaint was registered against them under sub rule 3 of rule 3, read with section 7 of the Sugarcane (Control) Order 1955. The appellants pleaded that pursuant to the directions given by the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1950 and the Act they had failed to pay the sellers the price of the sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The complaint was being investigated. The charge sheet alleged inter alia that on various grounds investigation the complaint was investigated. All the three contentions raised were covered by section 3(1) read with s.7 of the (to be read along with section 9 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (i) that sub rule (3) of rule 2 should not have been validly issued under section 3 of the . (ii) that the said section could not he used for controlling the payment of price of food crops; it can only deal with foodstuffs and food crops are outside its scope. This contention was repelled by the High Court holding that there was no merit in this contention; (iii) that section 3 cannot be validly made for controlling payment of the price but could only deal in topics which are outside the purview of the 'Act. HELD: (a) Section 2(a) of the is a specific mandate. If the Bihar Act provides anything to the contrary the same must be held to have been altered in view of article 372 of the Constitution which provides that all laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed by a competent legislature or other competent authority. [674 B C] (b) The effect of section 11 as stated above is to bring under control the cultivation and sale of foods. It is not disputed that the Parliament had declared by law that it was expedient in public interest that it should exercise control over foodstuffs. That being so it was well within the competence of Parliament to enact the Act and hence the power conferred on the Government could not be challenged as invalid. [676 E F] (c) No court has yet taken cognizance of the case.

Section 8A of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957 provides that a cash refund will be allowed on all sales tax paid by a new industry on raw materials purchased by it for the first 5 years from the date the Industry goes into production, eligibility to the concessions being determined on the basis of a certificate to be issued by the Department of Industries and Commerce. The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An order dated 11th August 1975 was issued which recited that after the order dated 12th January 1977 was issued, the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not prescribed any ceiling limit or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted: The said order dated December 12th July 1969 inter alia provided as under: "Consequently, the Governor of Mysore is pleased to sanction the following incentives and concessions to the entrepreneurs for starting new industries in the Mysore State: (1) Sales Tax A cash refund should be allowed only on all Sales tax paid on raw material purchased by them for the previous 5 years. (2) The concession of refund will he limited to 10 per cent of the cost of fixed assets per year, thus not exceeding the total of 50% over a period of five years for which the concession is available." A Division Bench of the High Court held that it would not be proper to hold the Government to the promises or the assurances it had given under the said order and that it was not necessary to hold that the Government had no authority to provide for the grant of refunds. In appeal by special leave before this Court, on behalf of the appellants the State contended that: (i) the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Govern ment of Karnataka that the concessions granted under the order of 30th June 1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same; (ii) the Government was having, therefore, failed to establish the requisite ground or basis of which it might be allowed to go back on its promise. 949 Allowing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 In order to test the validity of the order on 30th July, 1969 one has to see the substance of the concession granted under tho order and not merely certain words used out of context. Although the benefit regarding sales tax granted to the new industries is by way of refunds, although in a more limited manner and that is not even the case of the appellant.

The prosecution alleged that on the day of occurrence, there was a long standing enmity between the parties and they had cordial relations. During the last 30 years, there had been murders and rioting between the two factions. The deceased was suffering from severe injuries on his left legis ly. He had come on parole. On the day, of occurrence at about 7.00 A.M., when he was passing near the field of A 1, the nephew of PW 3 was attacked by the accused party. There were as many as 18 injuries on the person of the deceased. Seven of those were deep penetrating wounds, 8 lacerated wounds and remaining were contusions. The injuries sustained fracture on the right perietal bone result ing in the opening of the skull. On hearing the body of the victim, PW 1 who was passing on the field at about 6.00 a.m., when the deceased was passing behind the field went into the Tobacco garden of A I.I.R. he tried for the offences under sections 147, 148 and 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. on the allegations that they caused the death of Madda Laksha mandas by which they caused his instantaneous death. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A 6 under Sections 148 and 149 I P.C., and acquitted them. Aggrieved by the same, two appeals were filed before this Court by the appellants contending that after the acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below, the conviction of the appel lants under Section 148 and on applying 149 I 5I.P .C. cannot be sustained. It was contended that the appellants being three in number there was no question of their forming an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 I. P. C., and that they formed an unlawful fir dating along some unidentified persons. The counsel for the appellants submitted that after acquittal, they could not have formed an incid eration within the definition of Section 142 I. i.P., Cr. Pc. On behalf of the respondents it was contended by them that after tho acquittal of accused persons in the courts, their conviction under section 148 and of applying 149I. P C. cannot he sustained. Allowing the appeals on the limited ques tion of applicability of Section 149 I 49 I. HELD: 1. There is force in the contention of the learned counsel for appellants that after an acquittal of 4 accused persons, by the trial court, the appe lants could not had formed an assembly within tho meaning of section 141 I .P. The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam which he had purchased in 1958 1958 for the price of Rs. 16,500. On 25th December 1965 the assessee sold the house for the same price at which it was purchased and no capital gains accrued or arose to him as an result of the transfer. The Income Tax officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Income tax Act seeking reopening the assessment of the assessee for the year 1966 67 and requiring the assessee to submit a return of income within thirty days of the service of the notice. 48,500 to tax because there was admittedly no under statement A of consideration in respect of the transferred of the house and it was not possible to say that the transfer was effected by the assessee with the object of avoidance or reduction of his liability under section 45. The assess ment for the assessment year 1966 68 also failed before issuing a notice in terms of section 148(2) of the Act seeking to reopen the assessment. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, agreed substantially with the view taken by him and held that in order to bring a case within section 52 sub section (2), it was necessary that there should be under statement of consideration for the transfer and once it was found that the fair market value of the property as on the date of the transaction exceeded the full value of consideration declared by the assesee in respect thereof, section 52(2). The Tribunal took a different view; views taken by the Tribunal in the case of Vishwanath Iyer J.B. Dadachanji and Vishwanath Iyer JJ. were not confined to the facts of this appeal except as stated above, on a plain natural interpretation of section 52 of the , sub section 2 thereof, the only condition for attracting the applicability of that provision is that the provisional market value should be determined in accordance with the provisions of section 34(2)(b). The Revenue sought to bring in a case under sub section(2), which must show not only that the consideration received by the assesses was more than what was declared or disclosed by him, but also that the considerations had been under stated and the assessee has actually received more than the sum of Rs, 16500 shown by him. The two circulars of the Central Board of Direct Taxes refer to above must therefore be held to be binding on the Revenue in the administration or implementation of which sub section only provides for determining the consideration actually received by, the assessee is more than whatever is declared or declared by him; and since in such cases it was very difficult, if not impossible to determine and prove the exact quantum of the suppressed consideration, sub section 1(2)" has no application in case of an honest and bonafide transaction where the consideration in question.
