The appellant was dismissed from serv ice on 13.1.1966 by the Collector of Madhya Pradesh on a plea of limita tion. The order of dismissal was communicated to him on 19.9.1960 and filed his suit on 30.9 1969 asking for declar ment that the order of dismiss al was inoperative and he continued to be in service. This suit was dismissed in the courts below on acceptance of the defence plea that it had not been filed within three years from the date when cause of action first arose, as required under Article 58 of the First Schedule of the . When this appeal came up for hearing before a Division Bench, reliance was placed on the decision of this Court in Sita Ram Goel vs The Municipal Board, Kanpur & Ors., ; in support of its view being C.I.T.v. and the other three Judges Bench decision in Pierce Leslie & Co. Ltd. vs Violet Ouchterlony Wapshare & Ors. , held that Article 113 of the is a general one and would apply to suits to which no other Article in the schedule applies, and the appeal must be dismissed. In the special leave petition it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Article 114 of the Limitation Act deals with suits to Which no other article in the Schedule applies, which includes suits outside the purview of the shall continue to be gov erned by Article 58. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. If the original order of punishment is taken as the date on when cause e tence first accrues for purposes of Article 58, of the great hardship is bound to result. On one side, the claim would not be maintainable if laid before exhaustion of the remedies; on the other, if the departmental remedy though availed was not finalised within the period of limitation, the cause of actions would no more be justiciable having become barred by limitation.closed from the purview Of the shall remain suspended by Article i657. [54C] 2. As far as Government serv ants are concerned, Article 58 may not be invocable in view of the special limitation.

The appellant was the owner of certain properties. He had alienated several properties to his father. His case was that the alienations affected by his father as well as the sales held in execution proceedings against his father were not binding on him and so his share in the properties covered by the said alienations was not affected by them. The trial court rejected the appellant 's contention that certain alienations did not bind him, upheld all the alienations as well made a preliminary decree for partition passed in his favour. On appeal, the High Court held that the Appellate decree which set aside the findings of the trial court on two grounds was in law a decree of affirmance and that the decision of the High Courts below was correct. It further held that even if the variation is made in favour of the intending appellant it was not a case of affirmation but variation, and this position was not likely to affect that position. Held, that in determining the question as to whether the Appellate Decree passed by the High court affirmed the decision on two contentions, the trial Court must be considered as a whole under article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution the word "decision" meant the decision which conclusively determines the rights of parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in suit and it is also true that a party aggrieved by a decree may appeal only against a part of it and is not bound to file an appeal against the whole of the decree; but, when, however, a variation is effected in regard to the order as to costs such a variation would not confer a right of appeal as regards matters unconnected with the matter in respect of which there has been a variation. The principle of affirmment postulates either affirmance or variation by the appeal Court as an act of adjudication and that necessarily means the decision. A party aggrieved against a decree can prefer an appeal only, against a portion of it, but not against a other part of the order or final order of one judge of a High Court. Held further, that the question whether the appellate decree passed by a High court affirmance in favour is one of affirmence or not must be answered on the basis of the surrounding circumstances and that could only be decided in appeal. Where there is a variation made in the award in regard of the award it would amount to a decree a judgment of affirmoration, whether the variation as to cost is made or not. The result can be no different from the one in appeal between the parties under article 134(1) (a). Even if the Appellate Court makes a variation in regard, the decision in appeal could be in favour 'of the intending appel lant and not against him. Section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not confer such a right on the aggrieved party and it would be inappropriate to adopt a technical or pedantic approach in interpreting the material words used in the relevant clause which would lead to anomalous results. The application of the test of the value of the subject matter has to be determined by reference to the subject matters which is actually and for the first date of the suit.

The High Court, in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with section 115 CPC, had exclusive jurisdiction under sections 115 and 115 to the District Court specified therein. Section 115 provided that any amendment made or provision inserted in the Code Of Civil Procedure by a State Legislature before the 1st February, 1978 would stand repealed except insofar as such amendment or provision was consistent with the Code as amended by the said Amendment Act. The High Court had exclusive jurisdic tion under section 107 of the Act to remove, in order to prevent miscarriage of justice, any jurisdictional error committed by a subordinate court in those cases where the error could not be corrected by resort to its appellate jurisdiction. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court possesses revisional jurisdiction over more than Rs. 20,000/ and above, and even in the alternative the revisional jurisdiction under section 5(c) of the U.P. Civil Laws (Amendment) Act, 1972 vested exclusive jurisdiction to the High Courts under section 151 Civil Procedure Code in other cases. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: The High court was not vested with revisional jurisdiction within section 115 Code of Criminal Procedure over a revisional order made by the District Judge under that section. [40D] Har Parasad Singh & others vs Ram Swarup & Others and M/s Jupiter Fund (Pvt.) Ltd.

The respondents challenged the validity of a notification issued by the State Government under section 52 (1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 for the acquisition of certain lands belonging to them required by the Urban Improvement Trust , Jaipur for a public purpose namely, for implementation of a development scheme namely, Civil Lines Extension Scheme. The Special Officer adjourned the case from time to time and issued several notices to the respondents for personal hearing under section 51 (2) or his jurisdiction to proceed with the inquiry under section52 (3). The respondents went before the Special Officer who adjourned the matter from time and issue several notices thereafter to the appellants for personal hearings under section 53 (1). Neither did they raise any objection as to the power and authority of the State Govt. to acquire the notified land under section 49 (1), nor did the respondents place any material before the special officer to show that they really needed the notified 'land for the purpose of expansion of their business activities to the State of Rajasthan. The State Government in its Special Leave Petition stated that the remaining land was required by them for construction of a Three Star Hotel, which was necessary for implementation and/or expansion of the development scheme of the Trust. The Improvement Trust accordingly issued a notice under section 50(2) requiring the respondents to surrender or deliver possession of the lands acquired immediately or upon their failure to do so to take immediate steps to secure such possession under sub section (6).

The appellant, a cooperative society, was in the occupation of one of its offices. Later, the building in question was put to rest by it on rent at Rs. 250 for a period of ten years from 6 4 1977 to 7 7 7 1 1976. Both parties filed an eviction suit against them. The respondent terminated the tenancy of the appellant and terminated the lease hold charges. The appellant challenged the notice terminating his tenancy and obtained an order of eviction. The lower appellate court dismissed the suit, but on appeal the High Court confirmed the finding that the building was exempt from the operation of the new Rent Act on two grounds: (i) The building in suit was constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to section 2(2), which contemplates that where a building has been constructed substantially of funds by way of loan or advance from the State Government, or Life Insurance Corporation of India or a bank or a Co operative society and the period of repayment of such loan or advances exceeds ten years, then the reference in this sub section to a period Of ten years shall be deemed to be a reference to a duration of ten year or the period ending with the date of actual repayment of each loan or the time ending withthe date of the actual repayment, (ii) In case of building subject to assessment, that date on which the first assessment thereof came into effect. (iii) Where the said dates are different, the earliest of the said years, and in the absence of any such report, record or assessment the date onwhich it is actually occupied for the first time. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the new Act did not apply to the building. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court rightly decided the case on 23rd February 1982.

The Government of Bihar appointed an arbitrator to refer the dispute to arbitration. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948 and sent a copy thereof to the parties. On February 25, 1948, the Secretary to the Government informed Col. Smith that the draft agreement had been slightly modified in consultation with the Government Pleader and he also wrote to the Executive Engineer that certain formal corrections should be made in the agreement. The respondents thereupon filed an application before the Court under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree for accounts and consequential reliefs. During the pendency of the arbitration proceedings, the arbitrator on February 6, 1948 passed a decree in terms of the award except as to a part which he held to be in excess of the claim. The appellant contended that as the copy of the contract had been sent to the respondents by his Secretary to execute the agreement the order was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of the bills and that further the essential feature,of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private Tribunal and it could not therefore be brought within item 2 and that accordingly it fell within item 12. Held, that the award in question was not a mere original instrument but a copy of it. It is open to him to raise a new contention if he raises a new plea which has already been raised by him and the Court cannot go outside the scope of the contest. The law is no doubt well settled that the copy must be certified and the document in Court be attested and signed and all have its effect on altering the true character of the instrument. There can be no doubt that it is the original and not a copy or of the Award. What the arbitrator did was to prepare the award, in triplicate, sign all of them and send one each to the party and the third to the Court. This would be an original instrument, and the words "certified copy" appearing thereon were a mis description and cannot have the effect of altering the correct character of a document.

On various dates in the year 1980 some complaints were received in the Department against the respondent pertaining to purchase of sign boards which were required by the department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the aforesaid orders. In the year1980 some complaints relating to the purchase of signing boards were received, in the department against the Respondent pertaining to the purchases of the sign boards. vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau to enquire into the complaints and ultimately a First Information Report was lodged on August 27, 1985 against the re spondent under sub sections (1) and (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. In response to the complaint received from the respondent for getting the First information report quashed, the Respondent retired from service with effect from October 31, 1982. On September 30, 1983, the respondent moved a petition in the High Court for quashing of the prosecution against him on the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of signed boards in 1979 was in the teeth of Rule 2.2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules by the Governor, it could not be filed and it was only when the challenge to the First Information report was repelled by the High court that a challan was filed on August 28, 1985 in the event that the said Rule placed an embargo on initiating judicial proceedings for prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years of the cause of action or the event referred to in the said rule and the High Courts committed an error of law in taking the view. The High Court, relying on an earlier decision of this Court in Des Raj Singhal vs State of Punjab quashed the First Report by its order dated February 12, 1986. Mangal Singh Minhas also appealed against the said order. Allowing the appeal by Special Leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1.1 An assurance to an employee that he shall not be prosecuted after his retire ment, even though guilty of committing a grave misconduc or negligence during the period of his service, after the lapse of a particular time which has been fixed in the instant case as four years would fall within the purview of "conditions of service" as contemplated by Article 309. Making a provision that a Government servant, even if he is guilty of grave misconduct or negligence which constitutes an offence punishable either under the Penal Code or Prevention of corruption Act or an analogous law should be granted immunity from such prosecution after the expire of a specific time so as to provide incentive for efficient work would not only be against public policy but would also be counter productive. By that time period prescribed, if any, for launching prosecution may have expired and in that event on account of such period having expired the government servant concerned would succeed in avoiding prosecution even though there may be sufficient evidence of an offence having been committed by him. Such a situation can be created by framing a rule under Article 309 laying down an embargo to the prosecution as a condition of service. [918G H, 919A C] 1.2 There is no doubt with regard to the interpretation of the said r. 2.1 that on the plain language of article 309, the proposition that any rule framed under this Article has to be confined to recruitment and conditions of service of persons mentioned therein admits of no doubt. The question which, therefore, presents itself for answer is whether the said rules should be interpreted as laying down a absolute or general embargo on prosecution of government servant if the conditions stated therein are satisfied. [936B C] 2.3. It is true that the object of framing the aforesaid rule was not to grant immunity from prosecution to a Government Servant, but it was made for to provide an exception to the power of the government in the matter of withholding or withdrawing etc. of pension of a retired government servant contained in clause (b) of Rule (2). [936D; 919G] 2:4.

The respondent Company was incorporated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. Its business was to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". For the years ending March 31, 1947, March 31. 1948 and March 31st 1949 the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs. 38,750/ : Held, that the Explanation to section 23 A is in reality a clause which defines what a company is, in which the public are substantially interested: (1) where shares of the Company carrying not less than twenty five per cent of the voting power are held by persons other than the controlling group. HELD: The Explanation raises a conclusive presumption in those cases where shares not entitled to a fixed dividend carrying not more than twenty one per cent or more of the ordinary shares. In assessing whether shares carrying not exceeding twenty five percent of the shares are vested in persons other, than the control group, the shares yielding a fixed rate of dividend have to be excluded. The presumption under the Explanation is sought primarily against the accumulation of undistributed dividends to avoid payment of non corporate rates of super tax. But the shareholders who are entitled to shares outside the controlling com mencement group would be regarded as a member of the public for the purposes of the third proviso and the Explanation thereto has no operation. [75 G H] (2) The Explanation to sub section (1 of section 23A does not apply because no presumption on the facts found could arise thereunder.

The first appellant 's selling procedure was that of the goods specified in the " ready sale note" and "such other person who is not a principal or an agent of the buyer. The appellant obtained delivery of the bales from Dharsi Moolji on account of the 13 bales, less Dwarkadas Khetan & Company. By despatching the goods to Dharsi nilas Daga, he was asked to do so by the appellant. He was later charged with offences under sections 7 and 9 Of the Essential Supplies Act (No. XXIV of 1946) on two counts. The first appellant denied all the allegations but claimed that the evidence adduced against him showed that the false delivery order was made because of these facts. His plea was accepted by the Presidency Magistrate who tried the case and also the High Court on appeal confirmed his conviction in respect of the first count. Held, further, that the charge relating to the 6 bales being a similar one, the fact that the goods did reach the reliaholder in the end, or rather his proper agent, and it was not necessary to do more than outline them here, was not a case which called for the severe strictures which were to be found in the trial court 's judgment. Dwarkadash Khetan could not be described as "important" because the goods arrived at Dharsi and not cast their identity on the account of their actual possession. The goods did not reach the borrower in possession but only a mere physical delivery. It was a printed form. In any case, where the person lives abroad over a period of years and leaves his house and furniture in charge of an agent who has the keys of the house and immedi ate access to and physical control over the furniture, it would be difficult to say that the agent was not in physical possession. Held further, also, that having regard to the nature of the case, the High. Court had rightly convicted the appellant under sections 3(4) and 9 of the Act on two grounds, namely that they were taken into consideration together in a particular case and that the finding of fact recorded by it was perverse. The charge relating lo the 6 goods was a similar offence and not one which called as for the the severe mandatory strictures issued by section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act and would be liable to be set aside, and, on the basis of this evidence, both the trial Judge as also the appellate court had rightly found them guilty. Dwarakkadas Daga vs Emperor (A.I.R. (1947) Lah. 1), relied on.

The respondent was a Senior lecturer at the appellant college. He was then a resident of a college affiliated to the Gujarat University. In April 1964 the Physics practical examination for the first year B.Sc. was to be held by the Gujarat university. One of the centres was Surendranagar, that he had accepted gratification of Rs. 500/ as other than legal remuneration for showing favour to a candidate Jayendra Jayantilal Shah by giving him more marks than him deserved in the Physics gener examination. It was alleged that in April 1964 he had obtained that amount through Thakkar, and according to him he had been charged with commission of offences under section 161 Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) read with section 114 of the Indian Penal code. The Special Judge who tried both these persons found them guilty and imposed a sentence of 2 years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine on both the convicted persons. On appeal, by the accused the High Court held that even though an Examiner was a public servant he could not be regarded as holding any office when he was appointed for the purpose of examining certain answer books even though that may fall within the meaning of ninth clause before the amendment of section 21. Hence these appeals by certificate on the questions : (i) whether the respondent was guilty of an offence under section 5 (1) (d) of the Corruption Act or not; and (ii) whether he was a Public servant at all. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The word "otherwise" has wide connotation and if no limitation is placed on it, the words "corrupt", "illegal" and 'otherwise" mentioned in the clause become surplusage for on that construction every abuse of position is gathered by the clause. So some limitation will have to be put on that word and that limitation is that it takes colour from the preceding words along with which it appears in the cl. that is to say something savouring of dishonest act on his part, [327 E] 2. The use of the word "or otherwise" makes it clear that a public official has by such means obtained any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage he will be guilty of the offence. But the abuse of the position as a public Servant would be essential whether the means are corrupt or illegal or they were of the nature covered by the word 'otherwise". [328 F G] 3. The words "legislative" and "otherwise ' mentioned in section 161(1) ', therefore, qualify the word as an "otherwise" or also the words to be found in it. It would, therefore be reasonable to put on clause (d). a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. According to the, the use of a term "or any other person by abusing his position as public servant", is essential. The illegality resulting in abuse of a position as any public servant would be of substantial import and would not constitute an offence. [329 G H; 319 A] 4. It cannot be said that the word has wide amplitude and if it can be held to be an expression "otherwise".

The petitioners had put in more than 360 days of service. Though counsel for the petitioners had pointed out that the Administration was requiring continuous service for purpose of eligibility, learned Additional Solicitor General on instructions obtained from the Railway officers present in Court during arguments has clarified that continuity is not insisted upon and though there is break in such continuity, the previous service is also taken into account. After referring to para 2511 of the Indian Railway Establishment Manual (as also the different orders and directions issued by the Administration it was contended for the Administration that out of forty four petitioners in this group of writ petitions had undergone medical examination and were granted temporary status as Khallasi and then promotion to skilled category after conducting the trade test is admissible. The Senior Signal & Telecom Engineer stated before the Court that they are project employees and do not belong to the open line. According to him employees in the open Line acquire temporary status on completion of 120 days of continuous employment previously. The respondents contended that out the forty four writ petitioners in each of these three cases had undergone Medical Examination and were conferred temporary status, as Khalasi; that the Railway Administration was demanding regular pension i.e. wages for the period of their temporary service; that terminal benefit of pension is not admissible to casual labour acquiring temporary status; that some employees of both categories stand at par; that they did not belong either to the said open line or in the Open Line; that no pensionary benefits were admissible even to temporary railway servants and, therefore, that retiral advantage was not available to casual workers acquiring temporary disability. The respondent contended that the petitioners were project employees since they had put more than 240 days of work. Disposing of the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1. When a temporary status is acquired, casual labourers of both kinds stand at ad par and willing project casual labour are combined for the purpose of screening and forming of panel on the basis of seniority depending upon the days of Work put in. In view of the submission, learned Advocate General has clarified the position that continuity in service is not insisting upon and although there is breaks in such long continuity the previous services are also taken in account. The Railway Establishment manual has made provisions for their protection but implementation is not P effective. Several instructions issued by Railway Board and the Northern Railway Headquarters were placed before us to show that the administration is anxious to take appropriate steps to remove difficulties faced by casual labour but there is perhaps slackness in enforcing them. [144B C] 1.2. The contention of the petitioners that the allegation of discrimination does not exist cannot be sustained. Disputes arising out of termination of employment and inter se seniority came before this Court in the Writ Petition No. 147 of 1983 (Inderpal Yadav & Ors vs Union of India). This Court changed the existing practice for reckoning seniority and directed that seniority of project casual labourers should be combined and prepared departmentwise and category wise and in terms of the directions of this Court, steps have been taken. It has been further contended that by the time these writ petitions were filed, the Railway Board 's order of 1st of June, 1984 had not been given but with those directions now holding the field, the ambit of grievances has been very much reduced. [145D] 2.1 The respondents shall have a direction to consider the claims of each of the Petitioners promptly and make appropriate orders for their regularisation. For over ten years, litigations of this type have been coming to the Court. About three years back, this court directed a scheme for absorption in Yadav 's case which has been framed and is operative. Casual labour seems to be the requirement of the Railway administration and cannot be avoided. The Writ Petitions are disposed of with the directions indicated above without any order for costs.

The Forward Markets Commission is an association which has been recognised by the Central Government under a. 6 of the Forward Markets Regulation Act, 1952. Under the bye laws it had to be deemed to be closed out at such rates as may be fixed by the Forward Market Commis sioner and the provisions of sections 12 and 13 of the Act were intended to achieve the object of the legislation in view of its objects. There were negotiations between the members of a public which was that though they agreed to be free, the Government might not have delegated their powers under section 12 of the . The question for consideration as to whether the new bye law was ultra vires the Constitution; Held, that the notification dated January 24, 1956 issued by the Board was illegal and so the appellants would be entitled to issue a writ of mandamus restraining the respondents from enforcing the bye law. There was no force in the contention that unless retrospective operation was given to the provisions Of section 12, the objects of the Legislation would be defeated or the purposes for which the power was conferred could not be fulfilled. The notification dated 1st January, 1956 by the Reserve Bank was illegal as it did not purport to confer any such powers on the Central Govern ment by necessary implication. The word "prescribed" in that section means any prescribed percentage of marks obtained at the qualifying examination or the aggregate marks obtained in accordance with the requirements of the provisions. The words "pertain in a bye law" were used to indicate that the restrictions imposed were only on the exercise of the power conferred under the Act and not on the commission by the Government thereunder. That was clearly an indication that the power could be exercised not by the Directors or by any other person after consultation with them. The relevant provision was that such a power could have been delegated to a meeting which might, in the opinion of the Board, be necessary for the purposes of carrying out the objects. This contention had no force inasmuch as the notification was not given retrospective effect by reason of the fact that the authority vested with the powers as required by section 12(1) of the , and (2) there was nothing in the Act which prohibited such delegation by the regulations.

Rs 28, 125/ for subsequent years. In respect of subsequent references, the High Court by its judgment dated July 25, 1969 held that the entire amount for each year was income in the hands of the assessee, but it only a portion of it being dividend within the Taines of section2(6 A) of Income tax 'Act, 1922 which was statutorily payable on compensation is income and not capital gain. Allowing the appeal on the questions : 1.1. If the expression "other sources" is not part of accumulated profits and if dividend be distributed to the shareholders out of those capital gains, to ' the extent of the distribution out of such capital gains to the dividend must be deemed exempt from liability to tax under section 12 as dividend income liable to tax, the same is exempted from tax under Section 12 as dividends liable to incometax. In that case, no such question was referred. On behalf of Income Tax it was urged that distribution by the assessee company in the composite hands of a shareholder held by him for grant of long term leases after 31 st March 1948, which was not in the discharge of his statutory obligations under section 16(2) of 'the Act, and that the interest which is statutorily payable was on compensation. 1.4.1948, but interest which was legally payable on the compensation is, income and was not capital gains: 1.5. The expression "plantation" is defined in section 2 (6A). It could not be said that the receipt from the capital gains was still income liable ' to tax from "other source", along with the provision of section 12 of the Indian Income Tax Act, for no such issue was referred to. 1:2. In support of this contention, it was submitted that if dividend is distributed to shareholders of the company out of these capital gains by the company, a receipt of compensation for land compulsorily acquired which forms part of the fixed assets of a Company is of a capital nature. Senairam Doongarmall vs Commissioner of Income [ Assam and Jammu Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Patiala, (2) The assumption made that the whole amount of compensation was deemed to be capital gain cannot therefore be sustained. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1:1. Even with the consent of the parties, the order is subject to another infirmity. [35B] 2:2 In appeals Nos.

A forest produce was seized under Section 51(1) of the Kerala Forest Act, 1961. The magistrate issued process to the respondent for removal of Sandal wood oil and also by confiscation of sandlewood oil found in transit or in possession of the manufacturers, but no order was passed thereon. The Panchayat Officer, Forest Range Officer, quashed the complaint holding that Sandal Wood Oil is not a wood oil as defined under Section 2(f) (1) and therefore, it is not forest produce. On appeal by Special Leave to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant/petitioner that inclusive definition of forest produce must receive extended meaning; it must also be construed in the context in which it is used and the purpose the Act seeks to serve and the family to whichkshaw wool oil belongs being an essential oil would include wood oil; that the word 'wood oil ' means wood oil oleo resin from Dipterocarpus alatus (family Dipteracure) by industrial process, and therefore the court was right in taking the view that inclusive definitions of forest Produce must receive a extended meaning and it must be construed liberally, that if given acceptance would lead to manifest frustration of the purpose of the Act. It was also contended that inclusive list of wood oil must receive liberal construction, drawing the context of which the words are used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. The Court examined the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Forest Produce Markets Act, 1971 and the Rules made thereunder and held that the Legislature in defining the word "forest produce" should be interpreted according to the intent expressed in the Acts themselves. It is settled law that the expression 'materially altered the accommodation or is likely substantially to diminish its value ' in the construction to a shop. The restricted meaning canvassed by the counsel would defeat the purpose and the literal interpretation would defeat tho object. The legislature did not intend to restrict the word wood oil nor does it find any compelling circumstances in the Act to olive restricted meaning that only oil derived from Diperocar Autat (family life Dipteroocarpuceae) a tree of India and other regions of Southern Asia. Khori in his 'Materia Medica of 504 India and theirrapeutics ' and Pharmac Grievtimatehia Indica by Willim Dymock defined wood oil in the same strain. All these technical literatures were concerned in finding out physio chemical properties contained in wood oil, and the source from which they are drawn for use in industrial purposes. The literal interpretation given therein if given accepted would lead lo manifest frustration or of the purposance of the object of the legislation giver" would defeat its purpose and defeat the object and the guidance conferred on it by the legislature and invest it with a meaning which will harmonise the law with the prevailing concepts and values and make it an effective instrument for delivering justice.

There were two brothers who along with Mt. Rameshwari and a daughter who were tried by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 read with section 34, I.P.C., but acquitted. The High Court accepted the testimony of one eye witness Hazari P. W 3 and two witnesses before whom Shivlal was alleged to have made two dying declarations. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Court erred in accepting the testimony in support of the correctness of the two dying declaration of the nature referred to in the statement of Hazari. The second point on which the judgment of the High court is assailed is the lack of compelling reasons for setting aside the conviction if the statement Of Hazari the sole eye witness is disregarded as it must be disregarded in this case; because ordinarily a dying declaration is by itself insufficient for sustaining a conviction on a charge of murder. Held, further, that notwithstanding the infirmities which the testimony was put to medical witnesses, it would not detract materially from his reliability that it would be dangerous to accept his testimony as being of any great value which is still more diminished by the finding as to the innocence of Mt. Peja vs The State of Madhya Pradesh ; , relied on. Narainilal vs The King, Aher Raja Khima vs The Sate of Sikkim, A.I.R. 1949 Bom. 162 and Kiniram P. C. 289 approved. It is not proper to contradict the statement in the statements of Hazari made before the trial court and he should have been asked to mention it. But it cannot be said that the opinions of these authors were given in regard to circumstances exactly similar to those which arose in the case now before this Court nor was this a satisfactory way of disposing of the evidence of an expert unless, the passages which are sought to discredit his opinion are put to him.

The appellant company was an All India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar there were disputes between the management of the appellant company 's factory and its workmen employed in the factory at Jamshedpur and their workmen represented by their union that an industrial dispute exists or is apprehended between the Government Company 's workers and their employees represented by the Indoxco Labour Union. The said dispute was referred for adjudication to the Tribunal who after observing that the appellant Company 'show cause notice was given to the company as to why it should not be granted special leave to attend the law courts for matters connected with the workmen and the management, to attend a meeting of its executive authority, gave its award. The Tribunal found that the constitution of the said IndoxCo Labour Union came to be amended from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company and its Indox Company does not materially affect the position that the dispute raised by the union is in respect of the employees of the company wherever they may be stationed. The appellant company challenged this award on the ground that it is inconsistent with section 18 of the Act, because, the Central Government had amended its constitution on January 6 1963 and, therefore, as the Tribunal had also made a clear distinction between the employer 's constitution and the reference made by the Government to it for adjudication no matter other than those set out in the agreement was referred to the tribunal. The High Court allowed the petition holding that since the said award was made before October 1963, i. e., after October 1963 the company 'his wage scales were satisfactory compared the rates of overtime paid by other industrial concerns in Jamshedpur and awarded 1/4 times the ordinary wages for overtime work exceeding 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours per week. Hence this appeal by special leave. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant company that the Tribunal was in error in making its award operative not only to the said workmen at its Jamshedpur factory but also to workmen at their other establishments and that in doing so it acted beyond jurisdiction. On behalf of its respondents it was urged that (1) the appellant 's establishment was duly amended on January 3, 1963 as claimed by the Union and held by the Tribunal; (2) that the company did not produce any evidence to show that the amendments purported to have been carried out by the said resolution dated January 6. 1963 were sent to the Registrar as provided in the aforesaid provisions and therefore, the/ndian Oxygen Workers ' Union represented the workmen of the Company ' 's mill at Jamshedpur; (3) that since it was made expressly clear that the disputes referred to them were those set forth in the Agreement and the statement and no other dispu sions would be held outside the hours of work; (4) that, therefore the appellant did not know before hand on how many occasions the executive committee meetings of the union and other meetings would be hold when the company would be obliged to give special leave with pay to the union 's representatives. HELD: (1 ) The company was in fact increasing the hours and thereby altering its conditions of service. If after taking into consideration the facts of the comparatively higher scale of wages prevailing in the appellant, the Tribunal fixed the rate for overtime worked at 1/2 times the normal rate of wages, it is impossible to say that the tribunal erred in doing (1).

Section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, provides that where a person who was at the commencement of the Act carrying on any business profession or vocation on which tax was at any time charged under the provisions of the said Act is succeeded in such capacity by another person, the change not being merely a change "in the constitution of a partnership", no tax shall be payable by the first mentioned person in respect of the income, profits and gains of the previous years. Where any such claim is made, an assessment shall be made on the basis of the Income, profits, and gains Of the previous year exceeding the amount payable on the date of dissolution from April 1, 1939. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm was dissolved in March 1943, before the Incometax tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 had come into force and that it succeeded to the business on April 1. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3) or (4) Of section 25 of the 1922 Act. The Appellate Tribunal agreed with the view of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, but the High Court held that succession to the family firm Messrs. Hakam Mal Tani Mal was taken place on April I, 1939, and that firm alone was entitled to relief under section 25(1)(3) of that Act in relation to the assessment in question under the Indian Incometax Act, 1918. On appeal by certificate it was contended for the appellant: (i) The deed of partnership which was executed on June 29, 1939 was a different document embodying the terms of the document and reciting the dissolution of the earlier partnership was executed by both partners of the firm Gajjan Mal, who entered into an agreement to carry on the business in the name of R. B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala son of Lala Gopi Mal Tiani Mal (an assessee) that the accounts were settled upto March 31, 1939 and upto March31, 1939; and (ii) that all the partners had become separate would imply that the firms of Messrs Hakammal TaniMal continued till the midnight of March 31. 1939, after the dissolution came into force. HELD: The agreement which is being reduced to writing and the terms thereof reads : "We we agree that your act is an ambiguous recital : it may mean that the dissolution had taken place at any point of time immediately on the expiration of March. 1939 i.e., the business has continued for the whole or a part of the day on April Ist, 1939 i,.e., that the business had continued for its whole or part of a day on the April 1st of , 1939, or it may be ' mean that from the end of March31st of 1939, there had been separation. When a deed recites that a transaction is effective from a particular date it has to be determined in the context in which that expression occurs, whether the date mentioned has to he excluded or to be included. [647G H] In the present case the agreement recited that all partners had became separate would indicate that the partnership of Messrs. R.B. Jawadha Mal was settled on March 31 1939 and till March 31 , 1939. It is then recited in the instrument that all those partners had been become separate, would imply, that the agreement took place on 4th April 1941 i. e., the partnership business had continue for the entire or a whole part of it day on a day that is about to say, whether it had to be deter mined in the light in which the expression occurs.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the (briefly the Act) for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimandhar. Some of the respondents preferred appeals against the said order to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and obtained stay of the order till he produced the relevant documents and the permit was issued on the same day. Against the order of the State Road Transport AppellateTribunal granting the permit to the appellant the respondent filed appeals before the Collector and obtained a stay of that order, The appeal of the respondent was dismissed by the State ' Transport Appellate tribunal which held that the Secretary to the Regional transport Authority had no jurisdiction to issue the permit under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of the permit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The rules prescribed the procedure for appeal to the various authorities appeal are a creature of the statute. There is no dispute that section 64 of the Act is the only section creating rights of appeal against the grant or other matters with which we are not concerned here. [641 C] 2. The appeals before, the State transport Appellate Tribunal are, therefore, not competent under section 64 to entertain the appeals and to interfere with the order granting the permits which had already been affirmed in appeal by the respondent State Transport appellate tribunal and further in second appeal by Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal.

The appellant was the sitting member of Parliament. Among the rival candidates there were seven rival candidates. One Prakash Vir Shastri secured 1,49,943 votes while the appellant secured 1.000,01875 votes in an election meeting held at Hapur on 7 February 1967. The appellant challenged the election on grounds of corrupt practices as mentioned in sub sections (2), (3A) and (4 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. At the hearing of the appeal, the appellant appeared in person after counsel on his behalf had obtained leave of this court to withdraw and to allow the appellant to appear in person. The oral evidence on behalf of the appellant was that the meeting which was held at the Hospital was not held. The news item was referred to by Mahesh Chandra Agarwal, P.W. 12, P,P.W, 19, P W 26 and a report of 9 February 1967 wherein it was stated that a big meeting was held in support of respondent Prakash Vir Pal Shastri. The newspaper report contained a statement of the correspondent from Hapur bearing the date 7 February, 1967 stating that a large crowd meeting was on 7 2 1967 at Hapur Town Hall Maidan and others members of the Congress Party and that the party was raising slogans that they were championing the cause of Harijans and Muslim youths from Aligarh University. The respondent contended that the speech which was said to be an attack of respondent Dev Raj Shastri in answer to the petition did not state any material about the alleged incident. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that no meeting was hold at Hapur City on 7 6 February,1967 and there was no attack on the office of the Republican Party. With regard to the meeting at the Town Hail Maiden at Hapur he relied on the oral evidence of PWs 11, P 36, 12 and 13 who also stated that the appellant 's witnesses belonged to particular castes and sects. The criticism on behalf the appellant with regard to Hapur meeting was that respondent Prakashvir Shastri had attacked the office by beat of drums which were the election symbol of Prakash Vir Gandhi and he therefore published false statements in relation to personal character and conduct of the candidate and secondly, the statement complained of must be one which is reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospects of the election of the person. Under the provisions contained in sub section (3 A) of the said Act the promotion of, or attempt to promote feelings of enmity or hatred between different classes of citizens of India on grounds Of religion, face, caste, community, or language was the mischief which is sought to be avoided by making the same a corrupt practice. The sub section further says that such promotion or attempt would be for the furtherance of the ' election of candidate or prejudicially affecting the election or of any candidate. Annexure KK was not proved and therefore it cannot be said to constitute any communal propaganda within the meaning of subsection (3).

A decree holder auction purchaser in execution of a final decree for mortgage himself purchase the disputed property in the auction sale held on July 14, 1978 at a sum of Rs.30,000 on the basis of which the appeal was filed is not competent in view of clause (3) of Article 133 of the Constitution. It was contended that as the application was filed more than one year after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the . The learned District Judge took a contrary view that after the insertion of Explanation II to section 47 by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1974, Article 136 prescribing a period of limitation of 12 years for execution of the decree and not article 134 of Limitation would apply. It rejected the contention that after amendment of Section 47 of Code of C.P.C., an application under Order XXI Rule 95 will be governed by Article 136 of the and that as held by the learned Single Judge of the High Court, Article 137 stands impliedly repealed by section 47 read with Article 136. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The period of time limitation prescribed by Articles 136 and 134 has been reduced to a considerable extent, but that also cannot be taken into consideration for the purpose of interpretation of the provisions of the Limitation Act. [365G] 2.1 It may be that before the amendment of section 47 of C P.C. an auction purchaser can file a suit for recovery of posses sion of the property within 12 years from the date on which the sale becomes absolute as prescribed by Article 180 of that Act, but in view thereof, no application for delivery of possession of the im pugned property of the auction purchaser will be maintainable under section 115 of the Code.

The appellant filed an election petition claiming a declaration that the appellant 's election was void on the ground that the election of the appellant to Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattancherry Constituency No. 73 was declared void on his ground that he had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Representation of People Act, 1951. The first respondent alleged various corrupt practices on his part and in support of the petition that the offending poster containing a news item in daily "Malayala Manorama" dated May 22, 1983 were marked as exhibit P 1 and two photographs of the wall poster were marked: as exhibit p1 and two photograph of the earth poster were exhibited on the walls of the Triloki. The High Court negatived all the said charges except those two, viz., (i) printing and publication on March 22, 1987 a day prior to the election; (ii) publishing and publication of a wall= both maligning the personal character and conduct of the first respondent. The pamphlet containing the reprint of the daily " MalayalaManorama", which meant that everybody knew the hands behind the murder was clearly calculated to create an impression in the mind of the elec torate that it was the first Respondent who was the murder er; (iii) publication of the entire poster with the consent and connivance of the appel lant and his election agent and was distributed by them among the electors knowing the advertise ment to be false and calculated to affect the prospectus of his election. On an appeal, the High Court held that both these acts amounted to corrupt practices which were committed within the term of Section 100(1)(a) of 'the People Act and were sufficient to void the election. The question is whether it was necessary for the election petitioner to state in the petition the extrinsic facts to spell out the innuendo meaning of the words complained of. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1: 1. From a reading of exhibit P1 it is clear that the publication was intended to create a false impression among the elector ate that he was a murderer, and did so. [778D] 2:1.

The appellant No. 5 who proposed to construct a five star hotel on a tract of land valued at 44,820.49 square yards at Bandra, Bombay in the 1966 sanctioned Development Plan of Greater Bombay, respondent No.5 submitted an plan to the Municipal Corporation of GreaterBombay for the construction of a five Star Hotel. The Commissioner of the Municipal Corporatio n, however, rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said land under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the respondent No 5 preferred an appeal to the Government under section 47 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act 1966. The appellants contended that the whole of the land should be kept reserved for a green belt or recreation ground in the interest of general public; that the entire land should he kept reserved exclusively for a park and recreational ground in view of sections 46 and 31(6) of the Act and having regard to the position that in the sanctioned plan of 1966, the said lands was included in the residential zone and no proposal to exclude it therefrom in the draft revised development plan had been published, the Municipal Commissioner was not justified in rejecting the application for approval of the Plan submitted by the respondent Coon lated No. 2. The Respondent No.2 set aside the rejection order of the Department on the ground that the property was proposed lo be reserved for public purpose or for recreational ground; that it had overlooked the provisions of section 46 and also the provision of section 20, of the Urban Land Ceiling Act. The High Court held that even the proposed revision could be taken into account as one of the relevant factors.

The Industrial Court dismissed the complaints of the appellant union questioning the correctness of the decision of the Industrial Court. The Union thereupon filed two special civil applications in Bombay High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution questioning the legality of the correctness dismissal of the decisions of the industrial court. The High Court dismissed both the petitions and dismissing the complaint. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD:1. When it is claimed that the employer has resorted to closure of industrial activity, the industrial Court in order to determine whether the employer was guilty of unfair labour practice must ascertain on evidence produced before it whether the closure was a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or whether it was bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employer. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employers at the time of closure but is not decisive of the matter. [68A] 2. When in this case, the issue was whether the contended that the industrial undertakings of the employees had never been closed or at any rate had resumed working In full and that the old workmen were not being re employed they would be re inducted in service and that as resumption of production is gradually expanding, the old workman will be re induction in service. There may be close closure for any of these reasons although these reasons are not exhaustive but are merely illustrative. To say that the closure must always be permanent and irrevocable is to ignore the causes which may have necessitated closure. change of circumstances may encourage an employer to revive the industrial activity which was really intended to be closed, [68B E] 3. Keeping in view all the relevant circumstances at the stage of closure decide and determine whether there was a closure or not.

The appellant company, which was incorporated on July 29, 1924 by way of investment, inter alia, took over the assets of the Tata Engineering Co. Ltd., and took over all its shares of the value of Rs. 1,33,930. In 1930, reconstruction scheme of the Appollo Mills Ltd. 48 took place under which debentures held by the company in the Sassoon Group of Mills were redeemed and the proceeds were reinvested in the new issue of shares made by the appellant Company during the year ending 30th June, 1940, shares of Loyal Mills sold to the members of the staff and shares of that value of those shares were handed over to the creditors. The assessee company in August 1930, which, according to its petition dated July 29,, 1924, had manufactured a sum of Rs., 1,29,333 including shares, securities and immovable properties of the company during the previous year ending December 30, 1946, and claimed that it was not a 49 dealer but merely an investor. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that no question of law arose out of its order. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner also held that the investments were held by assessee company as the stock intrade of its business which it carried on during the earlier year and also in the preceding years; but after the return had been filed for the year 1943 44, the assessee Company withdrew its return and filed a revised return on March 7, 1944, contending that it could not have one status for Excess Profits Tax and another for Income taX. The Tribunal rejected the plea of the assessee company holding that in the case of the appellant company not only the Memorandum of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but the case was of the Company all along in the past was that it is a dealer in shares, security and immovable property during the assessment year in question. The High Court rejected the assessee 's contention that as no question had arisen out of the order of the Tribunal, it could be referred to the High Court under section 66(1) of the Act, but, it remanded the case to the trial court for a fresh statement on the aforesaid questions, which were referred. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The questions actually framed by this Court on the last occasion are not appropriate and (ii) the question as to what are the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investor was itself a question of fact. [52H; 53A] Inland Revenue Commissioners vs Soli lives Steam Navigation Co., Ltd., ; G. Ont. V. Sadhanant Balaji Iyer, [1939] 59 I.T.R. 73 (P) referred to.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. In 1947, a charge sheet against him was framed against him on April 2, 1953 and he was later transferred to the Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, which later became the Subordinate judge of Masilipatam. Subsequently, his period of suspension expired. When the charges were framed against the appellant at the time of enquiry, the following charges were added: " That you in or about August 1950 being at that time Additional Sub Judge, Masulkipatnam entered into a conspiracy with two other accused for obtaining a bribe from the parties to obtain a bribe on the file of your Court and to cover his defaults, he had altered the records of the court so as to be consistent with those returns. charges were further framed against you and it was stated therein that the said two accused did not intend an oral enquiry to be held or only to be heard in person. The appellant filed his written statement in answer to the charge on June 22, 1953, but the High Court dismissed his application holding that as Rule 4 of the Madras Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules 1954, came into force from October 1, 1953 it was only a Tribunal as provided in r. 4(1)(a) of those Rules that could enquire into the charges, and that the proceedings in the High court of Madras subsequent thereto were without jurisdiction and consequently void. The question for determination before this Court was whether the concluding proviso in r.(4) of the said Rules qualify both sub rules ( 1) and (2). Held, that, though Rule 4(a) is retrospective in character, the main ground of objection on which the application of the appellant was founded was no longer tenable. In view of this conclusion, it became unnecessary to consider the contention, whether by reason of the Andhra Civil Services Rules coming into operation with effect from October I, 1953 the High Courts had ceased to have jurisdiction to proceed with the matter as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution, and was, therefore, intra vires.

The respondent was a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company which had in the United Kingdom. The Imperial Bank of India Ltd. obtained probate of Gannon 's will in the Federal Kingdom and appointed the respondent James Anderson its attorney to administer the estate in British India. Anderson applied for and obtained in India on August 14, 1946 Letters of Administration "durante absentia" under section 23A of the Income tax Act, 1922 addressed to "James Anderson Administrator to the Estate of late Mr. Henry Gannon ' reciting that he had reason to believe that Anderson 's income assessable to income tax for the year ending 31st March 1949 had escaped assessment and that he proposed to re assess the escaped income and for that purpose called upon Anderson to make a return of his total income and the total world income assessable for the years ending 31 March 1949. In compliance with the requisition Anderson submitted a return, but did not include therein the dividend deemed to have been distributed under the order dated March 26, 1953. The Income tax Officer included dividends deemed to be distributed in respect of the shares held by a shareholder when before the date on which the fiction of distribution became effective viz. May 26, 1947, and December 22, 1947 of the General meetings of the Company. For the assessment years 1946 47 and 1947 48 the Income Tax Officer made an order on March 26 and June 1953 under section 24A of that Act referring to " James &erson Administrator" the Estate in question to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal but did no include therein, the dividend was deemed to he distributed as dividends amongst the shareholders as at the date, namely May 26. Held:(i) The expression "assessee" in section 2(2) of the Indian Income tax (Second Amendment) Act, 18 of 1933 includes a person by whom income tax is payable if he has not died, and if the expression "tax which would have been payable under this Act, if he had not died", was intended to impose liability for tax on income received in the year of account in the course of which the tax payer died. (ii) The provisions Of section 24B do not warrant the application of two different interpretations in the matter of extension of the legal personality of the deceased according as the income is actual or notional. The Legislature not having made any provision generally for assessment of income receivable by the estate of the late person, the expression 'any tax which would be payable by him under this act if he bad not died ' could not be deemed to had supplied the machinery for taxation of income received by a legal representative to the estate after the expiry of the year in the institution of the proceedings. Commissioner of Income Tax Bombay City II vs Shakumtala and others, [1960] 2 S C.R. 771, followed.

The appellant, the Ruler of the State of Baster, entered into an agreement with the Government of India whereby he ceded to the Government the State Government of Madhya Bharat on January 22, 1951. Under a. 3 of the Act vesting of proprietary rights in the State government takes place on certain conditions mentioned in that section, being complied with, the definition of 'proprietor ' was stated in section 2(j) and it is "in relation to merged territories, means any area other than land in possession of a raiyat which has been separately assessed to land revenue". The appellant claimed recognition for the purposes of the Constitution as Ruler by virtue of the provisions of article 366(22) of the Constitu tion, but this was denied on behalf of the respondent State. Held, that the appellant was an ex ruler and that article 366 (22) did not make him a Ruler for the purpose of the , and that the view taken in the past was correct. The word 'maufidar ' had been given in the Act to be a person who by or under the provisions contained in the wajib ul arz applicable to his village, had the right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such villages. The appellant was within the class of persons who were by name specifically included in the definition Of 'proprietor and therefore clearly within the scope of the tion of the word 'proprietor" in the ,.

Respondent was transferred to the Central Administrative Tribunal, Eastern Circle, Shillong. Disposing of the appeal, the Court, HELD: The guidelines require the two spouses to be posted at one pi" as far as practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. [403B C] [This is evident from a persual of Article 323 A of the Constitution. The constraints and norms which the High Court observes while exercising the said jurisdiction apply equally to the Tribunal created under article 323 A are applicable equally to this Tribunal created by Article 323A. The guidelines say that as far possible, husband and wife must be posted in one pi". As far as possible, the husband and husband must be postings at the same station even if their employers be different. [ 432E F] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta, [1992] 1 S.C.C., 306 rendered by a Bench of which one of us (J.S. Verma J.) was a member. In the instant case, the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order of transfer. The order of the Tribunal reads as if it were sitting in appeal over the order dated of transfer made by the Senior Administrative Officer (competent authority).

Appellants were tried for the murder of one Jawahar. Three charges were framed against them. A7 was charged under Section 302 read with Section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder. The second charge related to rioting wherein A1, A2, A4, A5 and A6 were tried under Sections 147, 148 and 149 I. P.C., respectively. They were convicted under Sections 148 and 148 I.I.P .C. and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for five years. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1to A3 but reduced the sentence in respect, holding that the commission of offence by A1 was proved beyond doubt which was altered by the High CoUrt. The case was remanded back to the Trial Court for a de novo trial. In the event of non payment of fine the appellants shall undergo rigorous imprisonment for 5 years and the amount of Rs. 21,000 per annum shall be paid to the father/mother of deceased Jawahar. Appeal disposed of in terms of the judgment in the High COUrt 's case. Allowing the appeal by special leave against the order of the High court, the Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the appellants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them came within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34, I P. C. and instead convict them under Section 325, IP. C., read with section 34, IPC. [3D E] 2.1 In the instant case the intention of A 1 was to causing grievous hurt. The appellants were convicted by the Trial Judge. There fore, they were no difficulty in giving a finding in favour of the prosecution. Even on according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit P 6) all that first accused had remarked was that the attack on him was in retaliation for the injuries Jawahar had caused on the first accused a few weeks earlier. [4E F] 2.(a) The intention was to prevent grievous hurt or as such, the offence com pleted by them comes within the purview of Section 320, IPC read with Sections 34, Indian Penal Code. [320C] (b) The identification of the assailants in the backdrop of injuries on the person of the deceased and the facts and circumstances of this case, is not too reduction. It may be a safe ground for holding that all accused persons could have intended to cause such injuries as would be sufficient. In such circumstances, the 3 offence committed in by the appel lants comes within its purview. [325G] (c) There was no doubt that the intention mind of the appe lant was to inflict grievous hurt but there was no suggestion of a specific sentence and even assuming that the accused persons were seen present on the dead body of Jawahar, it would be covered by Section 325 IPC.

The appellant Bank filed a suit in the Sub Court, Eluru for recovery of the amounts claimed by it from its partners. The respondents contested the suit by filing written statements contending that the loans were advanced by way of loan by the Bank after its nationalisation and that in addition to the hypothecation of the A and Schedule properties made in its favour to secure repayment of the aforesaid amounts of loan, the other partner, the respondent No. 3 created an equitable mortgage in favour of the Bank on December 22, 1969 in respect of D schedule properties of the plaint. The respondent firm also created another equitable mortgage on September 6, 1974 in respect/E Schedule properties of it. The appellant Bank was nationalised on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act V of 1970, and it had two partners, namely, one section Doranna Choudhury, since deceased, the father of respondent No 3 and the respondent NO. 2, Sunkavali Rajlaxmi. The case of the bank was that in derogation of the provisions of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, the appellant Bank created a equitable mortgage of an equitable mortgages in favour Of the Bank, on December 21, 1969 for Rs.18,14,817.91 being the balance (inclusive of interest) of three principal amounts of Rs.3.00 lacs due to the insurers in these two cases, namely; the respondent Nos. 4 to 12, the alienees, while denying the creation of the mortgages contended that they were bona fide purchasers for valuable consideration and that the Bank was bound by alienations and transfers made in their favour of properties alleged to be under mortgage. The bank and its partners had filed written statements denying the create of any equitable mortgage by the deceased partner and the respondents Nos.4 to 12. The trial court decreed the suit against the respondent firm but the High Court, in decreeing the suit decreed it against the appellant firm only after the scaling down of it in accordance with provisions of Madras Agriculturists ( Relief Act IV of 1938) which, after the creation and/or creating the State of Andhra Pradesh, was made applicable to that State as the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Agriculturists Relief act IV of 1937, was applicable to the said State as that State. The Bank preferred an appeal before the High COurt. contending that section 4(e) of the Act, which provides for scaling down the debt in accordance therewith has no application to this case inasmuch as the appellant bank was formed by or under and not in pursuance of the Banking companies Act, and that as such, the Bank is entitled to recover the entire amount without the same being scaled down as provided in section 13 of the said Act. On behalf of the respondent Bank it was contended that the words `special Indian law ' are placed after the words 'an Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom; that the Banking Company Act is a special law and the provisions relating to law made by an Indian Legislature, was only speaking of special Indian law enacted by the British Parliament for India. It was submitted that the expression `special Iary Indian Law ' has a clear and unambiguous meaning and there is no need for its interpretation. 971 Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of sections 4(a) to (e) are not applicable to this appellant Bank and, therefore, there is any justification for laying down that the expressions `special English law ' should be interpreted in the light of the setting of the same in the words of the provision of section 4.(e)of the Act. [963C F] 2.

Under section 3(2) of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, a Central Government is given power, if it was of opinion that it was necessary or expedient so to do for maintaining or increasing supplies of any essential commodity or for securing their equitable distribution and availability at fair prices. No doubt the object of the Act is to provide for control of the production, supply and distribution of trade and commerce in, essential commodities in the interests of general public as well as that the Central Government may pass orders under the Act if it is necessary or desirable so to exercise, for maintaining and increasing supplies thereof at fair price. No attack has been made on the vires of the order itself. Held, further, that, the impugned notification was beyond the authority conferred on the Central Govt. by section 3 of the act and cl. 5 of the Order and in any case it is bad as the Act and the Order are valid. The object of section 3 is undoubtedly to secure specified commodities at fair rates for the general public, i.e., the consumer; but it does not follow from this that this object can only be achieved if retail prices are fixed and that there is no reasonable basis for such clasification. The power of the Central Govern ment to fix prices in the interest of the general Public was control at any of the three stages mentioned above. Accordingly, the notification brought about no discrimination by the impugned Notification and not in accordance with section 3 (2) (c). Re: 2. There is discrimination between different regions and the question whether the impugned order is beyond the power conferred on Central Government under section 3 Of the Act was a matter of policy. Held further, also that in any event the impugned Order could be challenged only under article 19(1)(g) inasmuch as it imposed an unreasonable restriction on the petitioners ' right to carry on trade under article19 (1)(f).

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956 transferred the dispute to the Third Industrial Tribunal under section 10 of the , which came into force on August 28, 1956. The Company and the Union were dissatisfied with this decision of the Second Industrial Tribunal. In the second written statement filed by the Company before the Tribunal it did not say that the previous award was not terminated in accordance with law. It also stated that it was not necessary for the company to have a separate issue and the union would have been in a position to establish that notice had been served on the company as required by section 19(6) of the Act. In fact, the Tribunal gave no indication of any substantial increase in the dearness allowance on the basis of the information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal. The Tribunal went wrong in taking the rise in the cost of living index between the years 1954 and 1957 instead of taking the fluctuating rate in the index between August 30, 1951, and the date of the present reference in the year 1957. On the other hand, it fixed the basic wages and the rate of dearness allowance payable to the employees. The award was modified by the Tribunal by its orders dated September 29, 1961, and published in Calcutta Gazette on the 29th November 1957, and modified by that date. The company moved a petition under article 136 of the Constitution for questioning the correctness of the Tribunal 's decision. The High Court allowed the petition holding that there was rise in cost of live index between employers and employees and the absence of any provision in the Act by the Amending Act, was not material to make up its mind and therefore it set aside the award. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) In respect of proceedings pending in a Tribunal constituted under the , it is for this Court to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction only in cases where awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice, causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation and final decision by this Court or disclose such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit the consideration of this Court. Article 136 is couched in widest terms, it is necessary for this court to exercise his discretionary jurisdiction even in cases when awards are passed in violation Of the principles Of natural justice. The limits to the exercise of power under article 226 cannot be made to depend upon the appellant obtaining the special leave of this court, for two reasons viz: (1) at that stage the Court may not be in full possession of all material circumstances to makeup its mind; and (2) at the time of granting special leave or at the date when the appeal is disposed of. It will be seen from section 19 (6) which says that "Notwithstanding the expiry of the period of operation under sub section (3), the award shall continue to be binding on the parties until a period of two months has elapsed from the date on which notice is given by any party bound by the award to the other party or parties intimating its intention to terminate the award" cannot be held to have been pressed before such tribunal. Pritam Singh vs The State of Madras, ; and Indian Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. vs Their Workmen, , followed. (ii)In regard to matters covered by it, the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore the date Of the agreement was the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working class cost of the living index in the years 1957. The question, therefore, is what did the parties intend to agree by the aforesaid clause in the agreement. Pritam singh vs The Union Of India, ; , applied. (iii)In both cases, the Government had made the order of transfer on April 9, 1957, i.e., after section 2 of Amendment Act 18 of 1957 was deemed to have come into force.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The validity of an order under section 3(f) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1947 (the Act '), for the purpose of providing a summary remedy under the latter Act and for determining whether the scheme was consistent with the provisions of the former Act or was valid at the relevant time, was challenged on the ground that it offended his fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) and so could not be enforced. Held, that section 3 (a) and (b) clearly bring out the fact that where the legislature wanted the conti nuance of the action taken under the provisions Of the earlier Act only if the said action was consistent strictly with the relevant provisions of that latter Act, it has so provided.
