The scheme of section 103(a) & (b), clearly brings out the further facts that where a Legislature wanted the institution to be settled or modified by the court in a suit under sub section (1) or on an appeal under sub s.(2) or any scheme deemed under section 103, clause (d), to have been settled or adapted under the pro visions of that Act without examining whether all the provisions are necessarily justified by, or consistent with. the provisions, it had so provided: Held, further, that even if a citizen was deprived of his fundamental right by a valid scheme framed under section 66(3) he would not be entitled to challenge the validity of the scheme on the grounds (1), that it deprives him of his property rights as soon as the Constitution came into force and become void on the date of the enactment. R. S. Das vs The Commissioner, Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments, ; , applied.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E., School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986. Though the period of summer vacation during all these years was not approved by the educational authorities but no action was taken by the said authority. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 121982 but not later than 31st December, 1984. The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation and held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Validation Act on the following reasoning: "Admittedly, the petitioner was appointed on 12.7.82; and continued till 18.7 1986 with breaks in between and the petitioner 's appointment was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. His case, therefore, will not come within the preview of the validation Act and, therefore the question of issuing any direction to regularise his service in a substantive vacancy because of the validating Validation Act does not arise. " The appellant 's case however, was that the appel lant was entitled to be regularised as Hindi Teachers with effect effect from June 12,1982 because of his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned on by the stipulations that he shall continue until replacement by a candidates from the Select List. His Case, therefore will not coming within the purview of the Validating Act and therefore, the question was of issuing necessary directions to regularise the appellant ' s service in substantive vacancy since of the validate tedly, there is no approval by the Education authorities for the period subsequent to 1986.

The appellant being defeated by respondent No. 1, was declared elected by the Punjab Legislature on 7 6 1967, under section 100A of the Representation of People Act, 1951, on the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly. Respondent No. I challenged the election petition in an Election Petition contending that he had been disqualified to be chosen as the candidate for being chosen to a member, because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time, as much as he held an office and thus not entitled to any mileage allowance. The High Court dismissed the Election Petition on the first two questions against the appellant so that the petition had to be dismissed on this ground. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Under r. 3 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads Non Official Members ( Payment of Allowances) Rules 1965, the Chairman was entitled to draw travelling allowance and daily allowance even when travelling within the district. The second provision under rule 3 is in addition to the payment under r. 2 for a journey performed by him for his official duties outside the district, while the rules 4 to 7 govern cases where the journey is performed outside the District. [427 B] (2) Under those earlier Rules of 1961, the chairman was entitled only to Rs. 6/ per diem when a Member of the Panchayats Samiti performs a journey in connection with his official duty outside the districts. But, under these former Rules, he was entitled, according to r. 5, to any pay, salary, emoluments or allowance. [421 D E] (3) The daily allowance is invariably fixed after estimating what extra expenditure in a day in the person concerned would have to incur. A Chairman, it appears, was expected to incur more expenditure per day than a Member and that seems to be the reason why a higher rate of daily allowance was prescribed for him.[427 B C] (4) The appellant has failed to establish that the allowances payable under rules 3 to 7 of the Rules result in any pecuniary gain to a Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti and, consequently, there is no question of any disqualification arising. [ 427 E].

The appellant was a tenant of the tenanted premises. On a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem, the respondents purchased the building from the erstwhile owners in 1963 a year later they filed a suit for eviction on various grounds including the 972 ground that the appel lant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damages to it and hence the trial court decreed the suit with no findings of fact. On second appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the order of the first appellate Court on the findings that none of the construc tions formed material alteration justifying eviction under Section 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952. The High Court held that the partition wall constituted 'material alteration ' and it was a temporary wall of 6 feet height. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) A permanent construction tends to make changes in the accommodation on a permanent basis, while a temporary construction is on temporary basis which does not ordinarily affect the form or structure of the building, as it can easily be removed without causing any damage to the building. The Full Bench held that conversion of a single storeyed shop into a double storied structure by constructing a pucca super structure on the roof of the shop materially altered the accommodation. [977E] (2) The construction of tin shed could not be held to have materially altered. [978G] In the instant case, the disputed constructions which were the subject matter of the suit are 'material alterations ' and they could be removed only without causing damage to it, but they bring about substantial change in the front and structure of tho building. A permanent construc tion tends to making changes in its original form and a tin shed marked by letters CDGH on the Eastern side on the open land adjacentto the accommoda tion. The provisions of Section 3(1)(c) are cumulative in nature, each one of them are necessary to be established before a decree for eviction can be passed against the tenant.

The respondent firm filed a suit against the appellant under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent firm on 22 4 1975 against the company, and the summons was sent to the registered office of the Company in Calcutta. The respondent firm was not present at the hearing when the ex parte order was passed on 22 5 1975. According to the case of the appellant, the company came to know about the ex vide ex parte decrees dated 22 4 1974, pursuant to which summons for settlement of issues were sent to it by registered post to the Registered office of Company in Delhi and is said to have been served on one Shri Navlakha on 17 3 1975. On 29 7 1975 the appellant retired from the post of Sales Deputy General Manager, Sales Department, in Calcutta and died on 22 6 1976 while the respondent had filed a Miscellaneous case under Order IX Rule 13 C.P.C., for settingaside an exparte decree for money due to the first time when its constituted attorney was posted at Indore on 25 3 1975 under Order VI Rule 17 CPC for settlement. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to knowledge about the decree on 29 7, 1975. Hence he set aside the ex exparte decree. The High Court allowed the revision set aside its judgment of the Trial Court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The judgment of this Court setting aside the decree was correct. [1032G] 2.1 It is clear that the appellant has furnished bank guarantee for the decretal amount, and it has agreed to continue the same till the disposal of the suit. This agreement can be read in the background of the provisions contained in Order 5 Rule 17 of the C. P.C. [ 1033A B] In the instant case nothing of the kind was done by it. It was not the case, when the service summons as effected in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of the CPC is annexed to the counter affidavit filed by the respondent that the service of summons as ordered in accordance thereof will be deemed to have be duly served. No contrary finding has been recorded by the High Court, which was clearly wrong in upsetting the judgment of that trial court. There was no error of jurisdiction committed by it, and hence it is set aside.

The respondents were alleged to have been in possession of certain land in dispute. The Magistrate passed the final order declaring the appellant to be in possession on the basis of a police report. After passing an preliminary order on the 29th July, 1976 (wherein the Magistrate recorded reasons for his being satisfied that a breach of peace existed and such a finding was implicit in the final orders passed by the Magistrate so it was not necessary for him to repeat what he had stated in his final order also. The respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. for quashing the order of the Magistrate. The High Court held that as there was no clear finding by the magistrate that there was an apprehension of breach of the peace, therefore, the final final order was bad and the High court accordingly allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate for deciding it afresh in accordance with law. In appeal to this Court HELD: 1. In the instant case the Magistrate passed a final order in favour of the appellant without specifying any dispute about the existence of a dispute likely to cause breach of that peace existed even in thefinal order. Once he records his satisfaction in the preliminary order, the High 'Court was well justified in holding that the final conclusion was erroneous and cannot be allowed to stand. [95B] 2. When the parties filed their written statements they did not state that no dispute between the parties existed but whereas one party said that there were no apprehension of any breach from their side. The other side took the stand that there is an apprehension from their party, that there would be an apprehension to breach of a peace. Though this was an error of procedure, it was evident in Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal & Ors., ; , relied on. Hari Ram and Ors. v Banwari Lal and Ors., [1978] 3 S.C R. 1211, followed.

The Income tax department did not accept the correctness of the figures as shown in the accounts and that it had contrived to suppress them by resort to certain devices. It was contended, inter alia, on behalf of the appellant, that the question of benami was one of mixed law and fact, and that the observations relied on did not apply only to non residents and since there were provisions in the Indian Income tax statutes which only required the Tribunal to refer the questions to the court, the decision of this Court in Commissioner of Income tax was final even though the Court might not, on the materials, have come to the same conclusion if it had the power to substitute its own judgment. Held, that though the question as framed by the appellant in its application under section 66(1) did not specifically raise this point and was of law, no contention was advanced that sections 42(1), 42(3) and 42(4) were applicable only to residents and applied only to residents, nonresidents and consequently there could be no question for referring the question to the High Court under section 8. Commissioner of Excess Profits Pax vs section Sen (2) and Jones vs Leeming ([1855] A.C. 54), relied on. It is not necessary in cases of a mixed law that a finding on a question of fact is open to attack as erroneous, in that case the findings of the Tribunal were open to review by the court only on the ground that it was not supported by any evidence or perverse but also on the grounds that it is not a proper conclusion to come to on the facts.

The appellant was carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. For the assessment year 1948 49, the assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to the General Manager, Shri J.P. Vaish, which had been disallowed by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal on the ground that it was excessive and quite unreasonable looking to the salary paid to Shri Vaish in excess of tiffs amount Was not really paid wholly for the purpose of carrying on business. The High Court answered the question against the assessee. Hence this appeal by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that in view of section 10(2) (xv) and 10( 2)(xv), the only conclusion which was required to be considered was the amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of business, profession or vocation as required under section 10 (2)(Xv). Dismissing the appeal. HELD : The question referred by the Tribunal must be answered in the manner indicated and this appeal is accordingly allowed with costs. Appeal allowed. C.I.T. Bombay vs Walchand & Co. Private Ltd., ; , distinguished. Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. P. Ltd. vs C. I.T., U.P., 10, C.C.I Commissioner of Income Tax, U. P., U .R. vs Wal Chand & Co., Private Ltd. , and Swadesi Cotton Mills (Co.) Pvt Ltd. Ltd., vs C .I. T., Bombay vs Mar Walchand and Co. Pvt. Ltd.; , applied to the present case.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. On January 13, 1954, he submitted a written reply denying the charge and asking to be excused. On March 7, 1957, the appellant made an order terminating his services with effect from January 18, 1954. An industrial dispute raised on this question was referred along with a number of other disputes to the Industrial Tribunal, Bihar, by a notification dated April 29, 1955. The appellant filed his application to the Patna High Court on March 13 and the Tribunal rejected his prayer for his representation by a person of his own choice in place of Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union. Held: (i) The appellant was an individual workman within the meaning of section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act unless it is taken up by an union of workmen or by a considerable number of workmen. In assessing the requirements of this principle, it is necessary and proper to take note also of the fact that when an individual workmen becomes a party to a dispute under the Industrial Dispute Act he is a party not independently of the union which has espoused his cause; (ii) in view of all the circumstances, the Tribunal committed no error in refusing the appellant 's prayer for representation through representatives of his other choice in preference to Fateh Singh; the Secretary 's strike was a question of fact which could not be allowed to be raised at this stage. Held further that the Industrial Tribunals are not justified in interfering with the order of the High Court rejecting the appellant "s application for a writ: (a) The mere fact that an individual employee becomes a respondent to a re spondent to a proceeding under the industrial Disputes Act, he is not independently competent to decide or hear his claim; and (b) section 36 must be strictly complied with.

The appellants instituted a suit for ejectment of the respondents on the allegation that the respondent was the tenant in the house who had sub let the premises to defendant No. 2. The latter was impleaded as defendants but did not name the other defendants. A preliminary objection was taken by the respondents that the deceased belonged to a joint Hindu family and other members of the family were already on the record, and it was not necessary to bring on record any other person. The trial court dismissed both the applications. On appeal by defendant No 2, the District judge set aside the decree for ejectment against defendant No 1 and confirmed rest of the decree against defendant Nos. 2 and 3. In a second appeal before the High Court, the respondents contended that the appellant was not competent to continue the appeal in view of O. XLI r. 4 Of the Code, because they were his heirs and legal representatives. Held, that the High court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving appellants when the appeal by the deceased respondent had abated. Rule 33 really provides as to what the Appellate Court can find the appellant entitled to. It empowers the appellate court to pass any decree and make such further or other order in the proceedings before it and thus could have reference only to the nature of the decrees or Order in so far as it affects the rights of the appellant. The discretionary power cannot be exercised to nullify the effect of the abatement of the appeal so far, as Kedar Nath was concerned. In fact such an exercise of power will lead to the existence of two contradictory decrees between the heirs of Kedar Nath and the respondents one passed by the appellate Court and another to the contrary effect by the court below which has attained finality consequent on the abatement. This is always avoided.

The appellant tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954 evidenced by a deed dated March 1, 1962. In the eviction petition filed against him on November 14, 1967 the proviso to section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act was amended so as to include the possession of an alternative accommodation. But in the High Court the appellant tenant fell back on certain defences grounded on ss.106 and 111 of the P.P. and on the score that no notice to quit had been given nor notice of forfeiture, as prescribed by those sections. The landlord sought to break through these defences by urging that the lease has expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111 (g) and no notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 would be needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise can be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111. This plea was rejected by the Rent Controller, on appeal held that no action was taken against the appellant on the ground that no proper notice had been issued and that there was no notice of forfeiting the tenancy. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant, inter alia, that only where a lease has been duly determined giving rise to a right to present possession under the Pant Act can the landlord sue for recovery of the building; but, in the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 as amended by the Amending Act of 1929 did not apply proprio vigore to such demises and their determination could be upheld. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Before a landlord can institute proceedings for recovery the premises he has to make out his right (a) under the Transfer Act; and (b) under section III(g), not having been given to the lessee in the present case, determination of the demise under section Ill (g). [918C] 1.2 In the instant case, the provisions of the Act which are but a statutory recognition of the rules of justice, equity and good conscience also govern those transfers. If there is no specific statutory provision, the rules relating to the conditions contained in section 111 cannot be called a rule of equity.

The Governor of Assam by a notification dated April 1, 1965, passed an order under proviso (c) to clause (2) of article 311 of the Constitution. But in the said order he had stated that it was "not expedient" to give him an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him and gave a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges and where after such inquiry the third step to be adopted was that, if it was proposed to impose on him any penalty of dismissal. removal or reduction in rank was not desirable; but he had also stated that the Governor was satisfied under sub cl. (c), of the proviso to clause 2 of article 31; that in the interest of the security of the State and under the proviso, the Governor had to arrive at his satisfaction on the question of inexpediency of holding the inquiry as required by the amended article 311(2) as well as section 240(3)(c). The High Court accepted the contention of the appellant. In appeal the decision of this Court in Khem Chand vs Union of India and Ors., [1969] Vol.VI Assam Law Reports 192, followed. Khemchand vs The Union of india & Ors., , followed. These two decisions were rendered by this Court on the point whether after such enquiry as may be necessary under section 240 (3)(a) of the 1935 Act, the Government servant must be given a reasonable opportuni tion and thereafter, in the case of such misconduct or reduction, he has to be given an opportunity of showing cause against any punishment proposed tobe imposed on him. The requirement of clause "was not satisfied with this requirement of article 320(3) which lays down when the Public Service Commission shall be consulted" is that a reasonable show cause must be communicated with the authority and, under the Proviso, the President 's satisfaction need not have to be reached before an order is passed by him. In other words, in section 240 the word "shall" used in the Article, the word 'may ' means ' The State Government servant should also be given one opportunity of putting forward his defence at the enquiry and to cross examine the witnesses produced against him and by examining himself or any other witnesses in support of his defence; and finally after such inquiries, the third one step was to direct that an inquiry be held against him. This right cannot be restricted only to cases where the Governor himself passes an original order imposing the penalty of dismiss ment on a government servant, but is also subject to the express provision contained in section 308(3), which lays it when the public Service Commission should be consulted.

HELD: To constitute serious infraction and/or infringement of their fundamental rights guaranteed to them under articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution in the matter of enjoying religious faith and performance of religious rites, practices and observances on certain plots and properties situated in the said Mohalla and buildings situate in the aforesaid Mohalla of Varanasi and in particular are seeking a declaration that the members of Shia community of that Mohalla have a right to perform their religious functions and practices on the said plots and structures thereon as also an appropriate writ, direction or order in the nature of mandamus commanding respondents 1 to 4 not to prohibit or restrain the Shias of the Mohalla from performing their religious duties and practices thereon. It may be stated that this Court by its order dated December 12, 1978 not merely granted permission to the petitioners under Order I Rule 8 C.P.C. to institute the present action qua themselves as representing the Shia Community and respondents 5 and 6 on the basis of some Register of Waqfs said to have been received by it. However, the judgment in this case was pronounced allowing the Writ Petition and issuing directions to the effect that no Mohammedan would be allowed to read prayer in the mosque itself as representing Shia Muslims, Sunni communities from holding their Majlises and imposing other restrictions on the occasion of celebration of MOHAR festival at the bury site. The Court in the earlier litigation set aside the Allahabad High Court Judgment and decid ed the issue of the impugned order dated January 26, 1944 and directed that the properties and structures be so released in favour of the Shiana community. The petitioners and respondents Nos. 5 and6 filed separate affidavits in this behalf but they have not produced any evidence to support their case. On the other hand the Petitioners and respondents No. 6 and 7 denied the allegations made by them in their writ petition. Respondents Nos.

Section 74 of the Income tax Act, 1922, provided that no loss which has not been determined in pursuance of a return filed under section 139 shall be carried forward for more than eight assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed. In its return the assessee stated capital gains of Rs.3.10,200 but claimed set off of capital loss incurred by it during the assessment years 1957 58 over sale of shares to three associate concerns. It was maintained by the asses see that the loss had been sustained in the previous year rele vant to the assessment Year 1957 58 and the same should be set off against the Capital gains in the assessment order in question. The Income Tax Officer however disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that when in the assess ment year 1957 58 the loss is claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of the appeal allowed the assessee 's claim on the ground that loss had not been deter mined as required under section 24(3) of the Act to the asses sees by an order in writing. The Tribunal relying upon the decision of this Court in L.T. Ref. No. 722/71 dated 9 11 1972 held that it was a notional capital loss. On reference, the High Court agreed with the conclusion of the Tribunal and held against the Revenue. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court HELD: Section 24 of the 1922 Act which applied to the assessment year 1957. applies to a case where in law a return could not have been filed under Section 139 because in these years this section was not on the Statute Book.

The respondent, a Senior Scientific Officer was recruited to the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production ( Air), while he was working as an Assistant Director at the relevant time, the Defence Engineering Service had three units under it, namely, 1) Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). However, at that time, his services were inter changeable and inter transferable be tween them. All, the service conditions of the staff belonging to the three units including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. were the same and were regulated by the same set of rules viz., Defence Science Services Rules, namely. Defence Science Post Code, Defence Science, Engi neering & Production (Air) and Defence Science Department. In the year 1979, the respondent was recruited as a Senior Research Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Scientific Science Service, and after recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the said three units. Their 22 services were Inter changeable. All the service condition of the persons working in the three Units including scales had a common Rule which was r ate 3. Since the respondent had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for the members belonging to different units, and merely because the superannuation age of the members of the Defence Research Service was increased, it could not be held that the respondent who belonged to another unit, viz., DAQAS was entitled to the said benefit. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The appellant Union of India retired by the order dated October 24, 1985 read with Rule 12 quoted above. [85B C] 2. In spite of the decision of the Tribunal and even pending the appeal when no stay was granted, the Appellant Union of india retired the respondent at the age of 58 years. [86C D] 3. The order of the Central Administrative Tribunal is both proper and valid, and there is no substance in the present appeal. [87D E] 4. It appears that those who were already working in either of the three other units were deemed to belong to the respective newly constituted service. This being so, their service conditions will have to run parallel and no discrim ination can be made between them by an unilateral action. The classification made between the parties further has no rational basis and no nexus of such classification to the object sought to be achieved has been shown to us by Mr. Subba Rao appearing for the appellants. [88E G] 5.

The appellant challenged the election of the first respondent to the Sangli City Municipality under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965 on various grounds set forth in paragraph 3 of the petition. The first ground was that he had published all the phmphlets mentioned in the petition and distributed them amongst the voters and he had come across the first pamphlet during the process of distribution. Held: (1) Even under section 21(1) of the 1961 Act, which does not contain a similar provision it has been held by this Court that "although" the trial court should be at arms length and the court should not really enter into the dispute as a third party, but it is not to be understood that the court never has the power to summon a witness or to call for a document which would throw light upon the matter, particularly of corrupt practice. R. In this case, if the two persons had not been examined, the Judge might well have decided the issue the other way. But the Act certainly gave him the power of doing so and no exception can be taken to the course adopted by the trial judge although it must be recorded that his earlier order refusing to issue summonses to them in the first instance when asked to do so on the 21st August was hardly justifiable. R, In re P. Sahanth, , referred to. The provisions of section 21 sub section (2) of 'the Maharashtra Municipalities ' Act, 1966 are wide amplitude specially when investigation is being made into allegations about the commission of a corrupt practice and if the Court was satisfied that a corrupt practices had in fact been perpetrated and may be by one side or the other it was absolutely necessary to find out who was the author of that corrupt practice, he would have gone into the matter and found out why there were two Gazette publications and which was the publication to be taken into account for computation of the period of limitation prescribed by section 21 (1). Therefore, the order of the High Court under article 227 of the Constitution could not be interfered with. The jurisdiction under article 226 of the constitution could not have been exercised on the facts of the case by the issue of a writ of certiorari. Even if section 21 of the Act is not applicable to the case, it cannot be said that there was no evidence on which the High court 's power of superintendence is confined to seeing that the trial Court had not transgressed the limits imposed by the Act. R in re Pamlakhanahil Kunju vs State of Kerala, ; , relied on. (2)(a) The second contention was that section 21 did not prescribe any essential prelime limitation for the examination of a person as court witness as envisaged by the Code of Civil Procedure; that there could be no doubt that the appellant was guilty of trying to arouse religious sentiments of the voters of the particular ward a majority of whom were Muslims and, therefore, he had been charged.

Section 3 A of the U. P. Sales Tax (Validation) Act, 1958 as it stood on March 31, 1956 provided that the State Government may by notification in the official gazette declare that the turnover in respect of a goods or class of goods shall not be liable to tax except at such single point in the series of sales by successive dealers as the State Govt. may specify. The respondent State imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute and it became payable, but the same was struck down by this Court as unauthorised and inoperative, because (1) the Sales Tax Act made a declaration that the punctuation ordinance was ultra vires; and (2) that the tax imposed from the date when the notification was issued could not be referred to that power, that it was in exercise of the powers conferred on Government under section 3 A as it then stood prohibited the State legislature to enact the impugned act. After the amendment in section 3A of the Act by which the whole of sub section (2A) and section 4 "shall have effect on and from the first day of April, 1956". 'Me validity of the Validation Act was challenged by the respondent State under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that there was a difference between the existence of a power and its actual exercise, that while by reason of Act XXIV of 1957 a power had been conferred on government to issue a notification on March 1, 1956, the notification actually issued on that date could not he referred to a power, and that therefore the impugned tax was invalid as being ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature under the Constitution. Held, further, that in view of sections 8 A, 14 and rule 23 of the United Provinces Sales Tax Ordinance (No. LXIII Of 1948) which were inserted into the U . P. Act IX of 1956 by the U P. Legislature to validate a sale for the purpose of entry 54 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, it was not necessary that the Validation Acts should be extended to pending proceedings and except in certain cases the tax was one of sales tax which could be passed on by a State legislature within the meaning of Entry 54 in the Constitution; Held, that the validation Act is not ultra vires as being beyond the powers vested in the State Legislatures under entry 54, and the impugned section cannot be held to be one with respect to sales tax. The definition of sale in section 2(b) of the Sales ' Tax Act was a comprehensive and comprehensive definition and fell within the purview of the definition of "sale" contained in section 4A of that Act. Brijnandan Kapur vs Chief Election Commissioner, Bihar, ; , followed.

A philanderer of 22, appellant overpowered by sex stress in excess, hoisted himself into his cousin 's house next door. In broad day light overpowered the temptingly lonely prosecutrix of 20 four, Pushpa, raped her in hurried heat and made an urgent exist having fulfilled his erotic sortie. The screaming victim complained to her mother working in the field, thereafter a first information, prosecution and conviction ensued, a sentence of 4 years R.I. was imposed by the Sessions Court and the High Court affirmed it in appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: An analysis which accords with theutilpec bility to convict has been jettisoned by the courts below. [582G] Sunil Batra 's case and later that, constitutionally viewed punitive deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative apart from being deterrent. The insulated years behind the insensitive bars must possess a hospital setting if correction is a social purpose, as Gandhiji often insisted. In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restore restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. The functional failure of our pachydermic prison projects, exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, deserves judicial cognizance. [595D E] Sunil Bhagat 's Case and later followed.

The respondent, a limited company dealing in land, was requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal under section 5. Requisition of Land Acquisition Act, 1951 by a notice dated December 27, 1952 to the appellant for executing the award but the amount credited it in its suspense account on the same date. During the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the relevant accounting period being the year ended March 31, 1956, the Income Tax Officer brought to tax a sum of Rs.7,24,914 which included the difference between the sum of RS.737,190 payable to the assessee in terms of the award dated July 29, 1956 of the Arbitrator and a sum Rs.12,276 out of that amount which had already been assessed to tax. The Income Tax officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the respondent on the date of the Award and held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by it. The assessment was confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Income tax on first appeal but in second appeal by the respondent 's order dated February 22, 1964, he fixed the amount of compensation at Rs.30,10,873 on account of the permanent acquisition of the land, thus enhancing the original amount ofcompensation by RS.513,624 on which he directed that further recurring compensation at 5 per cent per annum from January 8, 1953, the date when possession of the lands was taken by the State Government for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year of assessment 1956 57 should be paid to the assesseee and the said sum should be deposited with him from the date it was requisition till the date the date for acquisition. Instead of depositing that amount the Income tax Officer took an entirely wrong view of the matter and, therefore it allowed the appeal accordingly by its order dated March 22,1964. The appeal preferred by the asses ssee to the High Court failed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The object of section 4(1)(b) is that the right to receive payment is in dispute and it is not a question of merely quantifying the amount to be received; but it must also not be forgotten that, even if a court was awarded enhanced compensation, there is a right of appeal by Government to the Commissioner or to the Supreme Court.

The respondents landlords filed a suit against the appellant tenants for eviction from their suit premises and for certain other reliefs. The appellants contended that the compromise decree was void, inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Act. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to the execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case in part. The High Court having dismissed the writ petition of the respondents, the appellants came up by way of a special leave before this Court contending that: (1) paragraph 1 of the compromise petition was an admission in respect of only the first part, namely, the positive aspect of clause(f). and not of the second part, viz. that the landlord had no other reasonably suitable nonresidential accommodation. (2) The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly was agreeing to suffer a decree for eviction because the landlord in the circumstances is entitled to have such a decree under the law; and (3) the provisions under Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The language of Section 12 of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 is somewhat different from many similar State Acts. [881E] 2. A compromise of such suit is permissible under the said provision of law. The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 23 Rule 3, when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise. , the court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction to be recorded and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit". If the agreement or a compromise for eviction of the tenants is found on the facts of a particular case, to be in violation of a specific Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act the Court would refuse to record the compromise as it will not be a lawful agreement. However, there is nothing in Section 12, in the Act which may prevent the tenant in agreeing to vacate the accommodation in future. [850F G] 3. In the instant case, on the plain reading of the provisions contained in the section as a whole and remembering the beneficial object of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act for the protection of a tenant based upon public policy, it would appear that the inhibition related to the filing of the suit only. No suit can be filed for eviction or even by agreement without anything more. The compromise decree must indicate whether on its own face or otherwise, the Court is satisfied on consideration of the terms of the said compromise and, if necessary, by considering them in the context of the pleadings and other materials, in order to avoid risk of protracted litigation expenses, it is open to them to do so. [851C D] 4. A comparison of the particu larly 's case shows that the same was legal and is within the purview of the plaint.

The proposition that in the absence of Rules or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution.
