It was a case where no separate quota for promotion to post of Assistant Engineer was kept for degree holder Junior Engineers and diploma holder Junior Engineer. The degree holders Junior Engineers had sought a relief that such a quota be kept. It is while dealing with this grievance, their do support the petitioner: " Prayer No. 4 for declaring the petitioner Graduate Engineer as a separate category amongst Junior Engineers & give them equal quota like the Diploma holder Junior Engi ners out of the 50% quota for promotions a Assistant Engineers.

The first petition was by an Advocate practising in this Court, praying for the issue of directions to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies of Judges in the Supreme Court and the several High Courts of the country and ancili cal orders of directions in regard lo the same. In response to the rule the Union Government took the stand through the Attorney General, that the petitions were not maintainable inasmuch as the petition was not maintainable and the filling up of the vacancy in the superior courts was not a justiciable matter. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the petitions are not maintainable; (ii) the writ petition is vague because (a) the petition is not maintainable because the petitioner has an additional ployee to sue '; (b) it is a matter exclusively within the domain of the constitutional scheme and concern of the concerned constitutional functionaries; (c) there is difference of opinion amongst the trict Judges in regard to appointment of a Judge in a High Court, the opinion of none of the Constitutional functionaries is entitled primacy but after considering the opinion o6I to 976 place before the learned Chief Justice for constituting a Bench of nine judges to examine the two questions; (d) if there was no response forthcoming within the time, the Union should be in a position to proceed with the recommendation of the Chief Justice of the High Court ; (e) the direction is violative of judicial independence; (f) the petitioners are seeking directions for an interim measure to fill the vacancies by making the various constitutional authori ties and the decision of this court in S.P. Gupta 's case relating to the status and importance of the system of appointment involves a process of consultation with the Chief justice, the Governor of the State, the Chief Judge of the Supreme Cou pal Court; (g) the above order is discriminatory because it does not deal with any of the matters specifically mentioned in section 15(2) of the ; (h) it provides for a time frame must be set for the response of the statu tory authority in the State and if there is no responsecome ing within the period, then the Union may lose its confidence in the matter; and (i.e.) the plea of the peti tion cannot be accepted as correct; (j) the principle of `consultation ' is to safeguard the independence of the judiciary and to ensure selection of proper persons by providing appropriate names to the Chief Judges of the Court concerned, which may have been dealt with in a pragmatic way on the basis of the existing need. It is in this context that by the Amendment Act, 1987, the contended before this Court was that the Court alone does not exist as a court nor can it be said that the executive after bestowing such consideration on the result of consultations with the judicial organ of the state, would be at liberty to take such decision as it may think fit in the case of appointments, is an over simplification of a sensitive and subtle constitutional sentence and, if allowed foul play, would he subversive of the doctrine 'of judicial independ ence.

The Respondent was a Head Cashier in the K.G. Road Branch of the Bank in Banga lore city availed of 15 days leave from April 17, 1978 to May 1, 1978 and was allowed an advance of Rs.2,500 on April 4, 1978 under LFC to be adjusted later on his submitting the LFC Bill. He submitted a bill for Rs. 2,800 on May 5, 1978 along with a stamped cash receipt purported to have been issued by M/s. Shri Manju Travels of Bangalore and claimed reimbursement for the same. The said bill was passed but subsequent investigations revealed that the firm of the respondent was a spurious one which indulged in issuing bogus travel receipts. Upon being informed about the same by the Assistant General Manager 's letter dated January 23, 1979, the Respondent was served with a charge sheet dated October 12, 1978. A reply was received from the said firm but the respondent sent a reply on August 10, 1978, followed by another departmental enquiry which revealed that he had made the claim on the basis of fake receipt; that the Firm of M/S. Shri Nagar Travels was a forgery one and indulged in passing fictitious travel receipts; that when the Respondent requested him to furnish details of the persons who traveled and the amounts received by the said firms, no reply was sent from the office but he was served only with the charge sheet wherein it was stated that though the Firm had resigned from service on January 31, 1979 he continued to function as an Enquiry Officer and concluded the enquiry against the Respondent by the end of 1979; that after his superannuation he continued in service. Not having done so he continued under the bank management. The respondent challenged the order of discharge in a Writ Petition before the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that since the said order got merged in the appellate order, the initial defect, if any, stood removed, was repelled by the learned Single Judge on the grounds that (i) such an enquiry is incompetent; and (ii) even otherwise the appellant could have appointed a non official as an an Enquiry Offi cer and, therefore his orders imposing punishment were clearly incompetent and without jurisdiction. Hence this appeal by special leave to contend that since it was not the holder of a departmental de facto office he was actually in possession of it under colour of title which indicated the acquiescence of the public in its actions and hence his actions and decisions could not be invalidated by his subsequent retirement. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 There is nothing on the record to show that any formal decision was taken by the appellant to continue the services of Shri U.B. Menon as an officer de facto and hence the order imposing punishment was clearly incompetent. The findings recorded by the Enquiry Officer cannot be sustained especially when they are performed by officers de jure. [204 H] 1.2 An officer who was due to retire within a few days only was chosen to act as an Offi cic of the bank. The de facto doctrine, as explained earlier, envisages that acts performed de facto by officers within the scope of their assumed official authority are to be regarded as binding as if they were perform ed by officers after de jure orders. This doctrine has three requisites viz., (i)(a) the possession of the office and the performance of the duties attached thereto, and (b) colour of liabil ity, that is apparent right to the office, and acquiescence in the posses sion thereof by the public. According to this doctrine the acts of officers de facto performed within the sphere of their assume official authority, in the interest of the 'public or third parties and not for their own interest are generally held valid and binding as a if they are perform ed with by officers duly authorised. There is no restriction on the powers of an execu tive officer to hold an inquiry and take disciplinary action against a delinquent employee.

The respondents are owners and in possession of certain premises. As the building was an old construction and required urgent, extensive repairs on October 16, 1965 the respondents submitted to the appellant plans for its sanction for execution of work consisting of repairs, additions as well alterations to the said building. The Commissioner of the appellant Corporation by letter dated February 4, 1966 informed the respondents that their application for execution had been refused on the grounds:that the proposal was under acquisition and also effected in the ROW and the land was residential under construction against proposal of commercial. The plot was provisionally covered by the Master Plan. On October 16 1965 the respondent submitted a representation to the Commissioner that their revised plan had not been prepared as required by bye laws and contravened section 336(2) (a). The Commissioner refused to accord sanction as asked for by them. The High Court allowed the writ petition of the respondents. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) There was no violation of any law or rules having failed and that, therefore, the order refusing sanction could not be sustained; (2) section 14 of the Development Act would be violated; (3) The Master Plan prepared by the Authority for Delhi which had statutory force, had come into operation under the Development act. HELD : Under section 11 of the Enquiry Act no development of land shall be undertaken or carried out in any area by any person or body including a department of Government, except in the manner provided therein. After coming into operation of any of the plans in a zone no person shall use or permit to be used any land or building in that zone otherwise than in conformity with such plan: Provided that it shall be lawful to continue to use upon such terms and conditions as may be prescribed by regulations made in this behalf any land, building or work in that Zone otherwise than In accordance with the procedure indicated therein. [172C E] (a) Under section 8(1) of the Act there is a duty on the Authority to prepare the Master plan simultaneously with the preparation of the Master plans, or as soon as may, be thereafter, the Authority shall proceed with the prepare the new master plan. [173G H; 174A] (b) The relevant provisions of section 8 which are mandatory under section 8, will have a vital bearing in considering the soundness of the stand taken by the appellant. It is not the scheme of the Corporation that the moment a Master Plan has come into existence and if it contains a proposal regarding the width that a road should have, all use of land adjoining that road is prohibited for an indefinite period. The reasonable interpretation to be placed on section 14 will be that if any particular and definite user of land is indicated in a Master plan, a different use of that land cannot be permitted. Similarly if a Zonal Development Plan provides for a particular use of any land and any building in the area or Zone, it cannot be put to a different uses. If neither of the plan provide for the particular use by any land nor a building in a area or zone, section 14 would have no application whatsoever. [174H; 175A B] [The Master Plan had been prepared under section 7 by the authority on September 1, 1962 and it had also come into force as contemplated by section 11. Though section 8 contemplates preparation of a Zonal development plan simultaneously along with the preparing of the master plan, or if there may be thereafter no Zonal Development plans has been prepared. That assumes considerable importance in this case because it is the Zonal Development Planning Plan under section 6(5) which will show the approximate location and extents of land use proposed in a Zone for roads; further under sub cl. (d) of section (2), no such Zonal Development plan has been framed.

The appellant No. 1, the Minister of Industries and the appellant No 2 was the Secretary to the Government of the Commerce and Industries Department of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. The Secretary to Government of India in connection with a political party called the Rajpramukh 's Legislative Assembly set up in Parliament in August 1949 and on 6th April 1949 the Minister who was outside was requested by the Governor that he should go to Rewa and see the appellant " The appellant No 1 informed the appellants about his visit to the Supreme House on 9th March, 1949 but was asked by the appellants to do so. The appellant no. 2 went to the said dressing table opened the top drawer of the dressing Table in the bedroom of the appellant no 1 and handed over them to him after being furnished with the documents which were produced before him by the prosecution witnesses including the statements made to them on their tallying of the numbers contained in the memo prepared when the raid was organised with the numbers of the currency notes actually found in the Bed room of the appellants No. I to 25. The Additional District Magistrate taking into account all these facts convicted both the appellants under sections 120 B and 161, I.P.C. and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for one year and a fine of Rs. 2,000 each with default rigorous imprisonment. On an application made by the appellant against his conviction and sentence the Judicial Commissioner affirmed the order of acquittal passed by the Special Judge but convicted both of them under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and also under section 161 of the Code. The appellants contended that (1) having regard to the fact that the appellant had applied for leave to appeal to the High Court, the Judicial Commis sion could not depose to such statement even though the same was not recorded as required by the provisions of section 164, Cr P.C., (2) that the statements were inadmissible in evidence and could not be proved orally by him; (3) that there was no corroboration of the facts given by the appel lant No. 2 with respect to the giving of the statement to the two witnesses because they were a colourable pretence to avoid the provision of section 165, Cr. P. C., and (4) that even assuming that there had been no such corroboration it was not safe to rely on the statements which were inadmissible to be proved under section 164 Cr. The Judicial Commissioner reversed the order and convicted both appellants under section I. P .C. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the statement made by a person charged with an offence charged against him must be rejected with due respect to its finding as to the truth of the allegations contained in it, but for this reason the statement was inadmissible in respec tively evidence and so could not have been proved orally. The statements made on behalf of the appella nant No 1 were admissible under section 162 Cr. A. P., and were admissible in evidence against the appellants, because they had no evidentiary value as it then stood, and the statement of the S was inadmissible; for the purposes of s. 164 Cr, it merely relied on the confession made by appellant No, I to the witnesses in respect of which the Magistrate took into account the defrauded amount of money and the payment of the sum charged or the illegal gratification to the appellant not having been made.

% The respondent was serving the State Police as a Constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971 and led to the prosecution of the plaintiff along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the respondent was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. After a long time, suits were filed by the parties, namely, whether the suit was barred by limitation and whether the order of dismissal was illegal on the ground that the plain tiff was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. Both the issues were decided by the trial court against the plaintiff and the suit decreed in favour of the respondent. The High Court dismissed the second appeal in limine. It found that only two questions were pressed by the party, namely: whether the suits was barred either expressly or impliedly on the grounds of limita tion and whether an order of dis crimination was illegal, on the aforesaid ground that, the plainti tiff had been not served as a showcause notice before passing the order. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1 :1. The question involved in this suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High Court in the manner it has been done. [720D E] 2. Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 mandatorily directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to rigorous imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed, and this mandate of law cannot be ignored on the view that in the case of another member of the Police force a mistake was committed. [297D F] 3. The power conferred on the authority by rule 16.02(2), namely, for taking decision in regard to pay and allowance for the period the plaintiff remained out of service because of his being in jail. The respondent 's case is distinguishable.

A person carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites, and also acting as agents for selling tea; in fact the bulk of its income was from selling commission on tea. The assessment year in question is 1959 60 in the relevant previous year which ended on June 30, 1958, the assessee entered into a contract with M/s. Raghunath & Sons (P) Ltd., for 500 bales and 2500 bales. On June 18,1958, the latter had contracted to purchase 1100 bales of corn sacks: the contract for B Twill and 2500 foodgrains respectively. The transactions thus resulted in a loss of Rs. 98,534 to the assessee and the assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its taxable income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions were not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh ; and D. M. Wadhwana vs Commissioner of Income tax (supra) overruled. The question was whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in holding that the transaction described above entered into by the assessee were mere sales of delivery orders or Sales of goods so as to bring them to charge under section 3 of the aforesaid Act. A question which arose for decision in this reference was: Whether on the materials of the ease there were two separate transactions of sale so that tax was payable at both the points under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939? Allowing the appeal and setting aside the order of the Income tax Authorities, HELD : The answer to the question referred to the High Court in the present case has been correctly answered. [186G] (a) For income tax purposes speculative transactions means what the definition of that expression in explanation 2 says. Whether a transaction is speculative in the general sense or under the Contract Act is not relevant for the purpose of this Explanation. The definition of "delivery" in section 2(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act 1922, includes both actual and constructive or symbolical delivery has no bearing on the definition definition of speculative transaction in the explanation. [185F] (b) Explanation 1 states that where the speculative transactions are of such a nature as to constitute a business, I ) the business shall be deemed to be distinct and separate from any other business. Explanation 2 defines a speculative transaction as a transaction in which a contract for purchase and sale of any commodity is periodically or ultimately settled otherwise than by actual delivery or transfer of the commodity or scrips. [188F G] (c) The definition does not invalidate speculative according to explanation 2 if there is no actual delivery of the goods to that expressing for purposes of income tax only. In enacting the Explanation 2, the legislature did not intend to affect any transaction of sale wherein the goods were not physically delivered by the seller to the buyer but only laid down that if there was no actual or physical delivery, the loss, if any, would be a loss in a speculative trans action which could be allowed to be set off only against a profit in a transaction of the same nature. The object of Explanation is not to invalidate the transaction which are not completed by actual deli very of the taxable goods but only to brand them as speculative transactions so as not to put them in a special category for income tax purpose. [187C E] D.M. Wadhwani and Manalal M. Verma & Co. vs Commissioner, Income tax; Calcutta (1955) I SCR 951, relied on.

The first respondent was a candidate for the general seat. He filed a petition challenging the election of the appellant to the Punjab Legislative Assembly under section 36(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Tribunal decided in his favour by majority of two to one and declared the whole election void. The main question for decision in these appeals was whether the Returning Officer was right in rejecting the first respondent 's nomination papers. Held : (i) The first respondent must be accepted that no attempt was made at the presentation stage to satisfy the Returning officer about the identity of the persons who signed the blank paper and their marks are not attested it is evident that they have not been signed " because " subscribing " imports a "signature" and as the Act sets out only kinds of "signatures" which it will recognise as II signing", for the purposes of the Act, there must be construed in the sense set out above. (ii) The second respondent must leave it as it is. (iii) When the law enjoins the observance of a particular formality it cannot be disregarded and the substance of the thing must be there. Whether this attaches exaggerated importance to the authorisation is not for us to decide; What is beyond dispute is that this is regarded as a matter of special moment and that special provision has been made to meet such cases. In the case of illiterate persons unable to write their names it is necessary to guard against misrepresentation and fraud by requiring that their signatures should be formally authenticated in a particular way. (iv) Except for this reason, the non compliance with section 33 would not vitiate the election.

The appellants, who were employees of the Company, went on an indefinite peaceful strike with effect from August 30, 1972 pursuant to the strike notice given by the company and requesting the Company for re instatement of three of the union leaders who had been dismissed. The appellants made certain demands before the Industrial Tribunal in respect of the industrial dispute concerning the re instatedment of the 16 employees including the appellants. The Tribunal refused to entertain such applications observing that since they were interested in the service of the company, their names had been struck off from the rolls of the society and had totally abandoned the Company 's service ' their names have been struckoff from the roll roll of the Society. It is Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: (1) The appellants had been continuously absent in connection with the notified strike notice issued to the company by their registered union called "the Association of Chemical Workers", and had not even otherwise terminated the service. These workers were not entitled to any compensation under standing orders but that was not what the appellants purported to do. [609C] (2) The conduct of the appellants indicating or suggesting an intention on their part to abandon service which in view of the ratio of Gopal Chandra Misra 's case, can be legitimately said to mean to detach, unfasten, undoing or untie the binding knot or link which holds one to the office and the obligations and privileges that go with it their absence from duty was purely temporary and could by no stretch of imagination therefore be construed as voluntary abandonment by them of the employer 's services. [613C D] Express Newspapers (P) Limited vs Michael Mark & Anr., ; Express Newspaper (P), Limited vs Chhetham Co., [1959] SCR 1036, followed. Express Newspaper and Scamless (P.) Ltd. vs Meherles & Anr. , applied. Express Newspapers Limited vs989 Reporter Co. Bombay, ; Express Newspapers Ltd. v Michaenkensham Co. vs Venkatiahah and Anr. [1970] 2 SCR 168, Jivarajbhai Ujam Newspapers ( P) Limited (P). Ltd.v. Micha Thael pack & Anr.[1969] 2 section CLR (SC) 1011, Express Newspaper, (Pg) Limited v Michihael mark & Anr; , Express Newspapers, (p) Limited V Express Newspaper.P) Ltd. [1957] 1 SCR 1040, Express Newspapers P. Ltd. Limited vs T.M.

The trustees of a public trust created an enquiry into the affairs of the public trust, and in order to secure repayment of Rs. 5,000 from three instalments the entire amount remaining unpaid shall become due and recoverable from the mortgagee property. The trustees did not pay the instalments due under the decree, and on failure to do so they applied under 0. 21 r. 89 Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale but the Subordinate Judge passed an order disposing of the execution application directing that Rs. 250 out of the amount deposit by the trustees be paid over to the appellant. On appeal, the District Court reversed that order holding that since the trustees had failed to comply with the requirements of r. 92, the executing court had no jurisdiction to set aside the purchase held in execution proceedings and directed that Rs, 250 out o payment be paid to the auction purchaser. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) under section 36 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act which provides that "in any suit or legal proceeding in which it appears to the court that any question affecting a public religious or charitable purpose is involved, the Court shall not proceed to determine such question until after notice has been given to the Charity Commissioner", made it obligatory upon the Court to issue notice to the public trustee and if that officer desires to be joined as a party to implied him in a proceeding to enforce a mortgage by sale of the mortgaged property, the condition requiring the judgment debtor to deposit in court for payment to the decree holder. (2) that even though there was a judgment of a Single Judge of the High Court which he is a member or of a Division Bench of that High Court, he is not bound to follow that precedent because by following the precedent the Judge would act contrary to section 165 of the Evidence Act and would also violate the oath of office taken by him when entering upon his duties as a Judge under the Constitution; and (3) that a judgment delivered by a Full Bench of the same High Court after due consideration of the points before it was liable to be regarded as irrelevant by any judges of that Court. HELD: (1)(a) The Legislature did not intend to put any restriction upon the power of the Civil Court executing a decree for recovery of money due from the trust, by sale ,of the property of the trust. [458 B] (b) When a Judge in deciding a case follows a precedent he only regards himself bound by the principle underlying the judgMent and not by the facts of that case. It is true that every Judge of a High Court before he enters upon his office takes an oath of Office that he will bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established and that he would duly and faithfully and to the best of his ability, knowledge and judgment perform the duties of office without fear or favour, affection or illwill and that therefore the decision of Bhagwati, J., in Pijare Karimbhai 's case did not Jay down the 'correct law or rule of practice, it was open to him to recommend to the Chief Justice that the question be considered by a larger Bench. Judicial decorum, propriety and discipline required that lie should not ignore it. [459 G H; 460 A B] State of Gujarat vs Gordhandas ; , followed. (c) It is hardly necessary to emphasise that consideration of judicial propriety and decorum require that if a learned single Judge hearing a matter is inclined to take the view that the earlier decisions of the high Court, whether of a Bench or of one Bench, needto be re considered, he should not embark upon that enquiry sitting as a Single judge. But when a Judge or a Division bench of a Court makes a reference on a question of law to a Full bench for decision it Is liable to he regarded as invalid by Judges of that court. [460 F G] (2)(a).

The Government of India issued instructions in 1962 to the effect that the retirement under Rule 2(2) of Pension Rules should be effected when such retire ment is necessary in public interest. The appellant by an order dated April 21, 1970 retired him from service under Rule II(1)(j) of the Pension Rules. He assailed this order before the High Court. The learned single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no in firmity in Rule 2 (2) pension Rules. The Letters Patent Appeal filed by the Union of India has been accepted and rule 2(1 ) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950 is declared invalid. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The object of Rule 2 of Pension Scheme need not be to operate in different fields but the operational effect of the two rules is that a Government servant who has attained the age of 55 years can be retired prematurely under F.R. 56(j) only on the ground of 'Public Interest ' whereas another Government Servant who is only 51 and has completed 30 years of qualifying service, can be picked up for premature retirement under the Rule. Since no safeguards are provided in the Rule, the discretion is absolute and is capable of being used arbi trarily and with an un even hand. [800D] 2. The order of retirement has to be in 'Public interest ' and as such there is no vice of arbitrariness in the Rules. There is thus no substance in the argument and we reject the same. [899E F, 800C E, 899A] Union of lndia vs R. Narasimhan, ; , referred to. 2.1 The object provi sions of Rule 2046 is to chop off the dead wood. Rule 2 gives unguided discretion to the Govt. to retire a Government Servant at any time after he has completed thirty years of ' qualifying service though he has a right to continue till the ageof superannuation which is 58 years.

The respondent firm was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable account period was 1 4 1943 to 31st March, 1944 which was the accounting period ending March 31, 1944. There were two partners of the assessee firm, namely L. Phoolchand and M/s Biharilal Balkishan each having profits in proportion of 11 annas and 5 annas respectively. The work in connection with the extraction of Katechu was carried on in Nepal by 1.4.1943 to 31.3. 1944 and was done. In the facts and circum stances of the case, the assessee was allowing a set off of the deficiency of profit relating to periods 20th October, 1940 to 31th March, 1943 failing in the financial year ending March 30, 1946 and 23rd November, 1942 to 31nd March, 1941 falling in the middle of that accounting period. In support of its claim for set off the excess profits made by it, it had produced a muster roll of accounts maintained in the books of M/S BiharilalBalkishan in the account styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". The assessee firm did not maintain any books of account and the entire record of business transaction was maintained in these books. However, the sales were effected between 26th July, 1943 to 4th April, 1944 and April 1, 1944 to 31rd March, 1945 failing in their financial year ended March 31st, 1946. Sales took place from May 30, 1941 to March 31. The assessee did not maintaining any books Of account and that the entire records of the business transaction were maintained in its books of accounts styled " Kalyanmal, Phoolchand", and the sale of Kat Copiesu was effected between April 1. The Excess Profits Tax Officer held that business carried on during October, 1941 till 30th May, 1941 was completely differ ent from the business carried out during the chargeable accounting period under consideration. He further held that there could be no profit or loss during the said chargeable accounting periods. Accordingly he held that the assessee had no profits and losses during the accounting year ending on 31st January, 1944, and as such there could not be any deficiency of profits during those two chargeable accounting Period. In appeal, it was contended for the revenue that the manufacturing operations were carried on by them during the offi cial years and as there was no sale during the financial years ending on March 31th, 1943, sales took place during that period and no part of it was sold. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May, 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University. Petitioners who had qualified in Civil engineering had to answer the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had appeared in the written test conducted by the KPSC as was intened, 8 Writ Petitions were filed by candidates holding Civil Engineering degrees. By these writ petitions, the preparation of a common rank list and also the procedure of the examination and a method of selection were challenged. It was contended in the applications that the applicants who had secured 543 marks in Civil Engineers question and answered the questions indicated in Category II on the other hand and candidates who had been qualified in Mechanical Engineering and answered questions indicated at item No. 2 in the question paper could not rationally be included in a common seniority list after the interview. It prayed in the Writ Petitions that the K PSC be directed to effect selection and prepare and publish separate rank lists of selected applicants holding Civil and Mechanical Engineering degrees, and that the Government should accept the directions given by the Single Judge and proceeded to take steps for implementation thereof. The Kerala Government and the K Pradesh Public Service Commis sion of Kerala proceeded to make the two separate seniority lists, namely, one for the Civil Bench and the other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted. As per the directions issued by the High Court in its order dated 23rd April 1980 quoted above, the Government and Public Service Devel opment in pursuance of the directions made by this Court, proceeded to prepare separate lists, which was referred to in the earlier orders in the case of the petitioners holding Civil engineering degrees. The KP SC was directed not to prepare a common list.

The plaintiff respondent No. 1 had a proprietary business along with his brothers defendant Nos. 1 and 2. Though the appellant claimed that he was a partner of a partnership firm, it was later converted into a partnership partnership firm by a regular deed. During his life time the business was under the control of Abdul Samad, but on his death the defendants nos. 1 & 2 had effectively taken charge of the business and excluded the plaintiff. The Income Tax Officer passed an order in 1981 on the basis of the false allegations made by the defendants. The plaintiff challenged the order by a civil revision application before the Calcutta High Court which was dis missed, whereupon special leave was granted. It was contended that it was manifest that relief to the tune of lacs of rupees has been claimed by the plaintiff in the suit and he said that he had laid claim to a sum of Rs.1,26,796.72 besides another sum over Rs.84,000 as his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income Tax department mentioned in paragraph 11 of the plaint. The trial court rejected the objection and allowed a larger share 'in the well established and reputed business of auctioneer known as "Russell Exchange" and its assets and goodwill as well as the amount lying in the Habib Bank, Karachi Branch solely and absolutely '. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. In a suit for accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit. [512G] 2. The Court is bound to accept that" made on behalf of the plaintiff before the Allahabad High Court in Aizaz Ahmad vs Nazirul Hasan, AIR 1935 Allahabad 849 was rejected, after observing that there was some authority for the extreme view as urged by two Calcutta decisions but later a different view was taken by the said Court as also by the Allahabad Court. In Attar Singh vs Manohar Singh, ILR (1938) Nagpur 590, the plaintiff non applicant before the High Court filed a suit praying for accounts from appellant No.1. Rejecting his claim to put any valuation under section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act and not by section 7 (iv)(C). The trial Court was justified in rejecting the objection made by him that it could be tentatively valued at Rs.50 only. [511D E] 3. Ordinarily the Court shall not examine the correctness of the valuation chosen, but the plaintiff cannot act arbitrarily in this matter. If a plaintiff chooses whimsically a ridiculous figure it is tantamount to not exercising his right in this regard.[545C] 4. The decision in Mata Ram vs Daulat, ILR ; affirmed by the High court on the ground that it is a case covered by section 6(iv) (c). of the court Fees Act should be held to be wrongly decided. [ 511D F] 5. It is true that in a suit where for accounts, the defendant is not bound to state exact amount as which would affect after taking out all the account and he need may put a final valuation upon it but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, ; , referred to.

The assesses ' claim for exemption from sales tax for certain periods in question was accepted by the High Court, and the State filed Special Leave Petitions. The assessees contended that the Assessing Authority could not travel beyond the terms of the notification to. In view of this, the assessee 's claim that they were eligible for the exemption under the 1981 notification, is not an empty formality but before granting the certificate, the Industries Department has to see whether all the requirements as con tained in the instructions are fulfilled and complied with or not; nor is it necessary for the rules of deferring the payment of tax under the rules framed for the purpose. Allowing the appeals in limine, this Court, HELD: 1. The question of grant of exemption certificate by the Industries De partment Department is not something which would bear upon its true scope and scope. It is open to the State Government particularly in view of section 22D, to frame such scheme for the pur pose as it may deem fit. The provision for exemption, however, needs to be spelt out under section 12, in a statutory notification. Secondly if, as is being urged on behalf of the State, it is clear even on the terms, of the Notification that traditional industries are excludes, it was not necessary for tile rules of deferred payment of sales tax. [622F G] 1.2 The language of para 20 and 21 of the Full Bench decision that the exemption extends only to the cases covered by the subsidy/loan schemes prevalent earlier, is clear and envisage no denial of exemption to traditional indus tries, this question does not survive.

Rule 6 of the Delhi Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1953 provided that "Rule 7 REGULARranging : Recruitment after initial recruitment shall be made by the Administrator in consultation with the High Court from amongst the members of the Union Territory of Delhi. Appointment to the service shall be on the recommendation of the High court". Rule 8 provides for recruitment to the Delhi Judicial Service as well as by promotion on the basis of selection from the membersof Delhi Judicial Services. Rule 17 provides that "the seniority of direct recruits vis a vis promotees shall be determined in the order of rotation of vacancies between the direct recruits and promotees based on the quotas of vacancies reserved for both categories by Rule 7 provided that the first available vacancy will be filled by a direct recruit and the next two vacancies by promotees and so on. In exercise of this power, the Administrator decided to fill following substantive vacancies in the service by making temporary appointments thereto from amongst members of Delhi Judicial & High Court, namely : (1) recruitment of persons to the Service shall be by the administrator in consultation of theHigh Court. (2) appointment to the Services shall be in a substantive capacity and secondly, the appointment has to be by direct recruit; and (3) appointment has also to be to the post of Additional District & Sessions Judge, that is, to a post in the Service. The Schedule to the Rules shows that the initial authorised permanent strength of Delhi Higher judicial Service was 16 out of which one was to be a District and Sessions Judge and 12 were to be Additional District and Session Judges. By clause (2), the seniority of members of other services promoted to the Punjab Judicial Service shall, therefore, be determined according to the dates on which direct recruits were appointed to their respective posts and the dates from which the promotees have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the Delhi judicial Service or in substantive vacancies to which they were appointed in a temporary capacity. The petitioners who were selected along with other candidates challenged the vires of Rule 6, which was stated to be ultra vires Article 14 of the Constitution on the ground that it had reserved one third of the substantive posts in the . Rule did not use the negative language, as the proviso in the instant case did not apply to direct recruits. It also laid down a quota of one third for 374 direct recruits ; it only enables the appointment of direct recruit to substantive vacancies so that they shall not hold more than 1/3rd of the total number of substantive posts of service in the services. Similarly, by Rule 31A, proviso was added to the rule which provided that if temporary posts in a service are created as has been done in this case by the Administration, only the quota rule contained in the proviso to Rule 7 must inevitably break down when such appointments are made. The respondents after making representations filed writ petitions before the High Courts contending that seniority between promotees and direct recruits must be determined, in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District Judges and Sessions judges and that, direct recruits who were appointed as Additional Distt. & Sessions Judges after the promotees were so appointed, could not rank higher in seniority over the promotees. The writ petitions were contested by the respondents contending that the petitioners had made representations to the High est for making representation in 1977, but this was denied. Every opportunity afforded to them of being heard was also granted and the writ petition was dismissed in limine taking the view that the provisions of Rule as well of the constitution must be given effect to. It was reiterated that the seniority between direct recruits as also promotees could not be disturbed unless Article 14 provided for a quota for direct recruits; it only enabled the appointment to substantive posts so that, they shall maintain a stop gap arrangement and thus avoid injustice. The High Courts rejected this contention on the view of the Court in Chandramouleshwar Prasad vs Patna High Court & Ors. Allowing the Writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1.1.

The Income tax Officer, Ambala supplied to a 12 Sup. C/70 11 3912 Ambala Flour Mills a return in the status of an association of persons other than the assessee after annulling the assessment in the case of Ambala Flour Mill. The Income tax officer was of the view that the business belonged to Debi Parshad and he was liable to be assessed personally in respect of the income of the Ambala Flour mills. In appeal by Debi Parl, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order holding that the partnership stood dissolved on April 29, 1948. The High Court in reference set aside an ex parte direction for assessing the income in the hands of Debi ParII after annurating the assessment of the assessee in the earlier case. In appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of Debvi Parshad that by the order of the A appellate Assistant Commissioner it was directed that he may be personally assessed by the Income tax Offi cer in respect. the income tax proceedings against Ambala Flour mill were, however, not challenged as being barred by limitation. HELD: (1) The expression 'any person ' in section 34(3)(b) includes a person who would be liable to tax for the whole or part of the profits that went into the assessment or reassessment of any person other than tho assessee after the expiry of the period of limitation specified in section34 in consequence of or to give effect to any finding or direction contained in an order. [390 C D] Commissioner off Income tax, U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate; , followed. (2) It is not necessary that all persons other who may be affected by the orders passed by the Appellate Commissioner should be impleaded as a party to the appeal or revision and no such enquiry into the power of the Appellate Asstt. Com missioner to make the direction was competent.

Section 7(iv)(a) of the Madras Court Fees Act, 1950, provides that if the taxing officer, to whom such difference is referred by the office, is of opinion that the point raised is one of general importance he can refer the said point to the final decision of the Chief Justice or such judge of the High Court as the Chief justice shall appoint either generally or specially in this behalf. The appellant 's case was that he had been adopted by Lakshmi Achi in 1922 and Lakshmi A were adopted and after his adoption he claimed to have a share in the joint family properties and in the assets of the joint Hindu family, and therefore, was the basis on which a claim for partition had to be made. The respondent pleaded that it was open to him to value his relief on the memorandum of appeal under section 7(v) of tho Act and he claimed that the proper court fee to be paid on the basis of the value of Rs. 15,00,000 as the value for the purpose of jurisdiction and it was not open to the appellant to value the relief on a memorandum of Appeal under s.7(iv). Held: (Per Imam, J., dissenting) (i) There is nothing in section 7 which confers upon the appellate court any power to examine the sufficiency or otherwise of the court fees paid not only on the Memorandum of appeal but also on the plaint in the suit which comes before it and if the court was satisfied that proper court fees have not been paid then it can pass an order requiring the party to pay so much additional fee as would have been payable if the question had been rightly decided in the first instance. (ii) A reading of section 7 along with the proviso makes clear that section 7 confers upon appellate Court authority, reference or revision jurisdiction to deal with the question of adequacy of court fees payable on the plaintiff whenever the suit in which such plaint has been filed come before it. If the scheme laid down for computation of fee payable in suits covered by the several sub sections of section7 is considered it would be clear that in respect of suits falling under section 6(iv) a departure has been made and liberty has been given to the plaintiff to value their claim for the purposes of court fee and that is natural enough. The valuation therefore made by the appellant in respect Of the value fixed for jurisdiction must not, therefore, be questioned at this stage. All that the High Courts have done was to collect under section 13 of the Act a correct balance of convenience between justice and fairness between litigants in suits falling tinder section 7 (iv)(b) of Madras and all suits falling within section 7.(iv) of that Act and not to confer jurisdiction on the appropriate court to examine upon the sufficiency of Court fee paid on such plaint whenever the case in which the plaintiff is given the option to value her claim for payment of court charges.

The New Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) sought special leave to appeal against the decision of the NDMC dated 18.2.1987, declining permission to sanction the Revised Plans for construction of "Statesman House" a high rise building on plot No. 148, Barakhamba Road New Delhi of which the first respondent was the lessee. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition and directed the NDMC to convey its formal sanction of the building plans on or before 5th day of May, 1989, and also to convey it formal sanction within 3 weeks thereafter. Aggrieved by the decision, NDMC preferred an appeal before this Court against the said order. In the meantime, the Master Plan and the relevant bye laws of the New Delhi were amended and fresh amendments were made in these Bye laws which provided for a "Refuge Area" (Rs. 15,000 sq ft.) [601G H; 602A B] The High Cou rt found that many measures had been taken by the NDMC for construction, safety and welfare of innocent persons and that there was no impediment to the sanction. However, the Court overruled the objection based on bye law 16.4.8 and directed that the exemption of the proposed construction must be limited to the buildings in each floor. The NDMC thereupon moved this Court seeking special leave against the order of the High Court dated 24.4.[601C D] Smt. Indira Nehru Gandhi vs Moonath Kumar Mukherjee; , referred to. 3.1 A reasonable construction byelaw 16.9.1, 16.3.8. and 16. 4.8 would detract from the validity of the first Respondent 's claim and establish that the clearance from the Chief Fire Officer is one of the conditions for eligibility of the plan to be considered for accord ing sanction by the Council is not in substitution of the requirement of compliance with the objec tive prescriptions of those bye laws. The primacy to the Chief fire Officer 's implicit in the approach of the Court is erroneous and virtually render the clearance of the Chief Executive Fire Officer binding on the NDMC. A reasonable conse quent construction bye laws 6.2.[602D E] 4.1 No. 23, Barkhamba road and that no departure from Bye law 16,9.8 was involved in the case of thearun bers Ltd., and its Managing Director, respondents 1 and 2 respec tively, sought to impugn the decision dated 18th February, 1987 declining sanction to accord sanction to the plan was unjusti fied; that whatever reservations it had as to the ade quacy of the fire safety measures, as envisaged in the Building design, were allayed by the Chief Landvel opment Officer 'his clearance and held that thereafter there was any impediment to tile sanction.

The joint family carried on joint family business of a grocery shop, liquor shops and a ration shop. The members of the joint Hindu Family filed a suit for partition against the plaintiff of all the joint family properties including the accounts of all businesses. During the pendency of the suit, in order to secure complete partition of all its joint family, the appellant entered into a compromise on March 7, 1946, whereby the appellant was agreed that prior to 1942 all the accounts should be taken up to March 31, 1946. The appellant did not want his brothers to interfere with the exclusive running of the liquor business after the 31st March 1946, and he filed a fresh suit for a partition against him as accounts would have been taken of all those businesses up to the date of the final decree. The trial Court held that the cause of action for the present suit was different from the cause which the appellant deliberately relinquished. His appeal to the High Court was allowed by the Courts below and he gave certain directions. After delivering themselves of some conflicting findings to which reference will in detail be made hereafter, they held that though the motor business carried on after the partition had ceased to be a joint family ', yet as it was carried on by some members of a family their position was analogous to that of a partner carrying on partnership after dissolution and applying the principle underlying section 37 of the Partnership Act he held that since the motor bus business carried out after the dissolution had ceased with a joint Hindu family business yet, as it existed prior to the commencement of the Act, he was liable to render accounts for the profits which were attributable to the employment of the assets owned by the parties jointly. The appeals before the High Courts were dismissed. While dismissing the appeal against acquittal, the High courts held that although the motor commercial business carried 'after the partition having ceased to function and applying a principle underlying s.37 it was open to all the brothers as being fair and reasonable to give undue advantage to any party over the other. The appellants contended that the case fell under: Order II of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, that the suit was barred by res judicata from resjudicata and by order II rule 2(3), of the C.P.C., but they relied on the decision in the previous Suit No. 39 of 1945, that a matter once concluded between the parties who were dealing with each other at arms length could not now be reopened. Held: (i) On a fair reading of the compromise arrived at between the two parties in the circumstances, as seen from section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act, it follows that the plaintiff is barred by the principle of res judicata for all reliefs to which he was entitled. The compromise having been found not to be vitiated by fraud and misrepresentation, mistake, mistake or misunderstanding, and the decree passed thereon has the binding force of resjudicata.

The appellant was a ployer ' within the meaning of section 2(k) of the . The definition of " factory " in cl. (m) of section 1 2 of the Act is as follows: "" " 'factory " means any premises including the precincts thereof, (i) whereon ten or more workers are working, or were working on any day of the preceding twelve months, and in any part of which a manufacturing process is being carried on, or (ii) wherein twenty or more persons are employed in any manufacturing process, 20 or more of such building as shipments, Vishwanarayan Hegde vs The State of Bombay ([1955] S.C.R. 710), Ramanatha Pillai & Co. vs The Election Commission for India ([1954] 2 S.T.R., referred to. Held, that the respondent was not satisfied with this view and in his reply dated September 13, 1952, that salt works as such do not come within the definition of the word " factory ", and it did not raise the contention that salt worked as such did not come under the definition Of the word ' workshop " in the Act. Held also, further, that even assuming that all the processes carried out in the Salt Works and described above came within the purview of the expression " manufacturing process" the conversion of sea water into salt does not amount to manufacture of salt as defined by section 2 (k) , for as there was nothing in the definition or section 2 of that Act which made it uniformly compulsory for every occupier of a factory to comply with every requirement of the said Act, the appellant ' Salt Works did come within this definition of manufacturing process and did not fall within the word" Factory " as defined under the Act and that the appellant had rightly been convicted of the offence of working the factory without obtaining a licence.

The respondent was sent on deputation to serve in the Polytechnic at Devangere and he joined duty there on December 1, 1949. The period between his reversion and reposting to the Polytechnics was treated as leave. On the re organisation of States with effect from November 1, 1956, his services were allotted to the new State of Mysore. Later, the respondent continued to make representations to the Government praying that his absorption should be related back to 1949 and he be given the benefit of revision of pay scales in the years 1957 and 1961 and weightage benefits thereunder. The Government did not accept the representation. On April 21, 1965 another batch of 108 persons were similarly promoted as Assistant Engineers with retrospective effect from 1st November 1956. In 1953, the then State of Madras set up the Department of Technical Education and the Poly endeavoured Centre at Devantangere became part of that Department. A Departmental Promotion Committee was constituted to look into the claims of the previous employees and to ascertain whether their case was recommended by the Government for promotion with effectfrom November 28, 1949 when he originally resumed duty on deputation, or whether it was found unsatisfactory or whether he was unsuitable in any way unfit for further service. The State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission who examined him, and after a review of the recommendations made by the State Public Service Commis sioner held that the temporary reversion of the respondent to his parent department was not justified. Thereupon the respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the Government to fix their seniority also on the basis that they had become Assistant Engineers from the dates on which these vacancies were put in charge of sub divisions between March 1944 and January 1946, by promoting them as Assistant Engineer. It was contended that the absorption of the employees which came on deputation from a particular date was a concession which could not be claimed as of right and consequently a writ for mandamus should not be issued. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that he had been invidiously discriminated against. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that in making the impugned order, contrary to the recommendations of the State Government, the State Govern ment had acted arbitrarily and in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution; (ii) that there was a break in the service of the Respondent in the Department and therefore there was no need to classify the post to which he was transferred under the then existing rules. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) As against this it, the High court was fully justified in granting relief, it did to the respondent. [259C D] (2) The acceptance of the respondents ' contention would have unsettled pre Constitution matters and it would have been directly productive of results going against section 115(7) of the States Reorganization Act. Moreover, it had not given any concession to a different batch of 41 Surveyors who were appointed after the petitioners ' case was identical in all respects, and six other officers similarly situated, were absorbed from the date on which they had come in deputation; even though Narayanaswamy Chetty who was admittedly junior to him, was accorded the same treatment. [260C D]. (3) acceptance of respondent ' 's contentions would have affected even if the absorption was set aside as a break for his service. Nor did it amount to reduction in rank. [261B] K. V. Rajalakshmiah Setty & Anr., vs State of M.P. and Ors., ; , followed. In the instant case, seven employees had come on deputation with other departments to the polytechnics and all of them except the respondent, were similarly situated. They were absorbed as permanently in the department of Technical education with effect 'from the dates they became. The reason why the absorption should not have been made as a measure for unfair discrimination treatment to those borne permanently.

% The petitioner, an advocate practising in this Court, complaining of malpractices indulged in by social organisations and voluntary agencies engaged in the work of offering Indian children in adoption to foreign parents. The letter referred to a press report based on "emptive investigation carried out by the staff of a reputed foreign magazine" called "The Mail" and alleged that not only Indian children of tender age are under the guise of adoption "exposed to the long horrendous journey to distant foreign countries at great risk to their lives but in cases where they survive and where these children are not put in the Shelter Relief Homes, they in course of time become beggars or prostitutes for want of proper care from their alleged foreign foster parents. " The petitioner filed a writ petition in this court contending that (i) the provisions of paragraph 17 no institution or organisation can make any arrangement for the adoption of an Indian child by Foreign parents unless such institution or Organisation is licensed as a social welfare institution and under Clause 21, it would be unlawful to make or to give to any person any payment or reward for or in consideration of the grant by that person of any consent required in connection with the adoption by a foreigner of that person; (ii) the procedure to be followed by the Court in determining whether a child should be allowed to be adopted by foreign parents and if so, the procedure for making the adoption in accordance with law of that country can be followed. The petitioner contended that (1) the social or child welfare agency sponsoring the application of the foreigner must also undertake while forwarding the application to the social welfare or child Welfare Agency in India in that it will ensure adoption of the child by the foreigner according to the law of his country within a period not exceeding two years and as soon as the adoption is effected, it will send two certified copies of the adoption order to the Social or child Advisory agency in India; (2) the right to take a child in adoption for the welfare of the children with leave to remove the child out of India and take it to his own country for the purpose of adopting it in accordancewith the law should be exercised by the foreign parents making the application or in other words, whether such adoption will provide moral and material security to the child with an opportunity to grow into the full stature of its personality in an atmosphere of love and affection; (3) the rules made by the courts are not mandatory, and (4) the manner in which applications for guardianship are processed is a matter of judicial concern. The Court issued notice to the Union of India to appear before this Court for examination of the application for adoption made on behalf of the petitioner. On receipt of the petition, this court directed that every application of a foreigner even for taking a child has been sponsored by a social or Child welfare agency recognised or licensed by the Government of India or the Government, of the State in which it is operating, or to put it differently in the language used by the Indian Council of Social Welfare in the reply filed by it in answer to the writ petition, "all private adoptions conducted by unauthorised individuals or agencies should be stopped".

The appellant, a Senior Commercial Tax officer in 1953 was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax Officer in 1954, then as a Joint Commercial Tax officers in 1962 and later as a Deputy Commercial Tax Officers in 1968. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On September 28, 1975 he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d) and his Service Book showed that he had an excellent record of service. He had earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The several promotions gained by him react his good records of service and but there was one dark spot while the 1969 entry noted that an enquiry was pending with the Vigilance and Anti Corruption Department in regard to the allegations against him. In 1969 when he was working as Commercial Tax Inspector it was noted in his Confidential file by the Deputy Commissioner. Respondent Board of Revenue (CT) was requested to frame charges separately as for a major penalty against Thiru D. Ramaswami. On 29th November, 1974 the Government accepted the views of the Full Board and dropped the charges making the following order on 11 1974: "As the preliminary enquiry disclosed a prima facie case of corruption, a detailed enquiry was taken up by the Directorate of Vigilance and anti Corruption both. The Government examined the report of the Directorate and considered that there was a primafacie case in respect of certain allegations and the charges were not substantiated, and that the charges should be dropped". The Government accepted its views and directed that all the charges framed against Thiru R. Ramaswami be dropped. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court which allowed the same holding that the charge may be dropped, but it was left to the final stage for final hearing after considering his representations regarding his superannuation by filing an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal on the basis of allegations levelled against him and sending its report thereon. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of November 29, 1974 of the Government was to grant absolution to the appellant from the repercussions of, the note of the Deputy Superintendent of Commercial Tax made in 1969. If there was any ambiguity about the effect of the government order, it was cleared by the circumstance that within a few months, on May 7, 1975, he was promoted till Deputy Commissioner in 1965 and posted as Members Sales Tax Officer, Sales Tax appellate Tribunal, a prestigious post. It has to be mentioned here that the post of a Deputy Commissioner is a Selection post. Under Rule 36(b) (i) of the Tamil Nadu General Rules for Commercial Taxes Service: "Promotions in a service or class to a selection grade shall be made on grounds of merit and ability, seniority being considered only where merit and capacity are approximately equal". So, what do we have ? There was an adverse entry in the confidential file of the appellant in 1969 which said that "He is sincere and hardworking. He 'manages his office very well. He exercises adequate control over subordinates. He maintains a cordial relationship with public. Because of his stiff attitude some of the assessees complain about him stating that he is rude in his behaviour this perhaps is due to his unbending attitude. With a little more tact he will be an asset to the Department". One curious feature of the case was that while the 1970 entry noted hat an enquiry is pending with Vigilance and Criminal Department in respect to the allegation against Thiru P. Ramaswami, the ultimate result of the enquiry which was that the allegations should be kept dropped was nowhere noted in the personal file of respondent Board of Excise & Anti Corruption. Charges were framed against the appellant by the Board of revenue. [79F G; 80A B] 2(a) The post of Deputy Commissioner to Commercial Taxes is a selection post. under Rule 36 (b) and not under Rule 2(b). What do we cannot have?

The respondents challenged the validity of the three schemes framed under Chapter IV A of the nationalising motor transport in certain areas. The High Court dismissed the petitions and held that the Regional Transport Authority which was specifically mentioned in section 68D(1) is empowered to issue the permit to the transport undertaking "notwithstanding anything contained in Chapter IV of the . Under sections 68 D and 68 D, stage carriages are intended to be nationalised and all persons affected by a scheme published under section 68 C can file objections before the State Government within 30 days after the publication of the schemes. The appellants contended that as they were not able to avail of the alternative remedy available, their appeals were rejected. Held: (i) A policy decision contemplated by section 34 of the Road Transport Corporation Act, 1950 could relate to the matter which under section 64C is left to the unfettered discretion and judgment of the Corporation where that is the State instrumentality; (ii) The Regional Transport Commitee which was not specifically mentioned as in section 1 0(1)(a) is competent to issue a permit by reason of section 68F(1); (iii) A scheme specifying the maxima and minima of the number of buses and services was in conformity with, and did not contravene Rule 4. D.; (iv) The procedure laid down in section 8 0(2) was not vitiated by any mala fides or that the decision to frame a scheme was taken as a result of the independent opinion formed by the respondents after an examination of the entire question.
