In a serious situation of this country, the poor in their contract with the legal system have always been on the wrong side of the law. It is an essential ingredient of 'reasonable, fair and just procedure for a person accused of an offence and it must be held implicit in the guarantee of Article 21. This is a constitutional right of every accused person who is unable to engage a lawyer and secure legal services on account of reasons such as poverty, indigence or incommunicado situation and the State is under a mandate to provide a lawyer to an accused person if the circumstances of the case and the 540 needs of justice so required, provided of course the accused person does not object to the provision of such lawyer. [529G H; 542A B] Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India, ; , referred to. In the instant case, the State Government was under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. It was a constitutional obligation of this Court as the guardian of the fundamental rights of the people, as a sentinel on the qui vive, to enforce the fundamental right of the accused to speedy trial by issuing the necessary directions to the State which may include taking of positive action, such as augmenting and strengthening the investigative machinery setting up new courts, building new court houses providing more staff and equipment to the courts, appointment of additional judges and other measures calculated to ensure expeditious trial. [540B E] Maneka Hussain Gandhi vsUnion of India ; , followed.

The appellant was the landlord and respondent a protected tenant. The appellant gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent on December 31, 1951 under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the tenancy having arisen when the notice was given it could not claim relief from the court. Held, further, that the amendment did not affect any vested right of the landlords till the tenancy actually stood terminated after the expiry of the notice. Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai (1933) I.L.R. LX Cal. 1037 580, approved. DurjibbhaiFakirbhaibhai vs J Jhavernabhai Bhikamalbhai (1923) I L. R. 58 Bom. 106 and Jeekha Bankrishna Chakrabarti vs Abdul Kader Chaudhuri, (1927) I I. L.R 57 All. 574, referred to. As the Legislature could not have intended that benefit of this beneficent measure should be extended to tenants in whose cases the tenancy had not yet terminated it was clear from that decision and sub section (2 A) would apply and a notice under section34(1), is merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention of the landlord to terminate the tenancy, but it is always open to the landlord not to carry out his intention. There is no force in this contention. If it look at the words of sub section 2A it provides that a tenant would be liable to ejectment on one year 's notice by the landlord. There was no provision in the Act which made notices which were in accordance with the previous law ineffective, and consequently, the provisions of the Amending Act which came into force before the tenancy stood terminated by the notice will have to be taken into consideration in determining the right of a landlord arising out of the Notice of termination, for the Amending act put certain fetters on this right of termination. Durgi Bankrishna Rao Chakrabarty vs Abdul Bader Chaudhri, (1933); I. W. R 55 All.

The petitioners were evacuees and the houses of some persons who had not been declared an evacuee and were evacued. The petitioners contended that the properties vested in the Custodian under section 8 of the , and therefore, they had no longer any claim to them. Held, that on the admitted facts, the petitioners must be deemed to have lost their rights in the houses by the action of the Custodian. They did not acquire any interest in the house and could not have vested in him. In view of section 12(2) of the Act " (1) , 702 Held further, that no property can be declared to be evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 7 of the . The acts of the custodian in so far as they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. The acts Of the Custodian in so much as they deprives the petitioners the petitioners could not be held to be illegal on the sole ground that it bad been filed beyond the time prescribed for it. H] In view Of section 12 (2) Of the Act, the persons concerned with evacuee properties can not be declared evacueies and their property would vest in the Central Government free from all encumbrances. Although the petitioners were not evacueees, they could not maintain a petition under article 32 of the Constitution for the enforcement of their rights as result of section 8 (2). The orders made by them were without jurisdiction so far that they deprived the petitioners and therefore the petitioners had no more claim to the properties. In fact the appellants had no interest in these houses.

The assessee company had two Departments (1) for spinning of yarn from raw and waste wool, and (2) for weaving of yarn on payment of 2% commission on net sales of the worsted plant. The assessee Company appointed M/s. Murlidhar Chiranjilal as the sole selling agents for the worstned yarn on receipt of 2%. Subsequently on December 15, 1953 the assessee Company entered into an agreement with Mis Saligram Premnath under which the latter were appointed as the successful selling agents on certain specified conditions, the important of which being that the agents were to finance the assessee company to the extent of Rs. 2,50,000/ and the assessee agreed to pay 6% interest on the advances to be made by the agents and further agreed to, pay 2%, commission on the net proceeds of sales of goods in India. Before expiry of this agreement another agreement was entered into between the assessee Companies with the agents on October 20, 1955 under which a separate sum of Rs,. 626,847/ were payable to the selling agents. The question for determination was whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the Tribunal rightly disallowed the assessee 's claim for deduction of the said sums in respect of the assessment years 1956 57 and 1957 58 respectively. The High Court held that the sum in question was not legal deductions as contemplated under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act but amounted to application of profits after they were earned. In appeal by special leave : HELD: (1 ) Under the agreement between the assessees company and the selling agent, sharing to the amount in dispute did not make out a case of joint venture or a division of profits. The provision regarding consent of the agents to the sales and the programme of manufacture was also pertinent in order to determine whether the transaction amount ted to a joint venture in the garb of a contract of agency was really a sort of a partnership or a joint adventure rather than a contract for the purpose of sharing or dividing the profits ascertained in a particular manner. The conduct of the agent in sharing half of the net profits did not appear to be consistent with the payments made to the agents for services rendered. [200 E F] (2)(b) In order to fall within section 10 (2), the deduction claimed must amount to an expenditure which was laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business, profession or vocation as required under section 9(2) (xv).

For the assessment year 1959 60, the assessee was assessed for the assessment years 1959 60 and thereafter the Income Tax Officer came to know that the assessee had been withdrawing moneys from the company. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal in second appeal upheld the claim of the assessee that the words "accumulated profits" in section 2(6A)(e) could not be construed as including current profits, but rejected the contention that the two sums of Rs. 11,000 and Rs. 6,900 had to be taken into account in determining the figure of the accumulated profits. In second appeal before the Appellate Tribunal, the Tribunal referred the question to the High Court: "Whether, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Appellate Tribu nal was right in answering the first question in favour of the asses see and against the Revenue?" 947 The High Court held that the expression "accgmented profits" occurring in section 6(2A)(a) could be construed to include current profits in the expression 'accumived profits ' by Explanation 2 to section 2 (22) of the Income tax Act, 1922. Hence this appeal by certificate under section 261 of the Indian Tax Act. Allowing the appeal and remitting the case to the Tribunal for deciding it afresh in accordance with law, this Court, HELD: The High court was right, in answering first question against the assessee, and against its Revenue. [948 H] The expression " Accumulated Profits" occurs in section 8 2(2)(e), which includes previous profits. The expression ' Accumulcated profits ' occurred in Section 2(7A) (c). Construing that clause in Girdhardas & Co. Ltd., vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay, ; , relied on In the instant case, both categories of cases can be envisaged. One consists of cases where the order of the Tribunal under section 254 operated entirely in favour one party, though in the course of making the order the Appellate tribunal may have negatived some points of law raised by that party. Not being a party aggrieved by the result of the appeal, it is not open to him to make a reference application filed by the other party the basis of his claim that a question of law sought by him should be referred. [850 A B] In the present case, one category consisting of cases which a non applicant can ask for the refer ment of questions of law suggested by it and the other in which it cannot. To the extent to which the Courts have omitted to consider the distinction between these two categories, they have erred.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan, and the suits out of which the present appeals arose were instituted by him to recover possession of various plots of land in the occupation of the defendants or in alternative for assessment of fair and equitable rent. It was alleged in the plaint that the suit lands were comprised in Mouza Nala forming part of permanently settled estate of Burdwan, which included in the permanently settled Estate of Burdwan. The trial court held that though the defendants and their predecessors had been in possession of the land for a long time without payment of rent, a presumption of a lost grant could be made in their favour. He accordingly dismissed the suits. The High Court also held that as the defendants had admitted that they were holding under a Lakheraj grant granted prior to 1931, they were not in continuous possession and enjoyment of the lands for over 200 years. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the suit properties formed part of the Mal or assessed lands of the estate; (ii) in view of the finding of the District Judge on the point of limitation the question of lost grant raised an issue of great importance and could not be taken into consideration. HELD : The Courts below had held that the suits were within time under article 131 of the Limitation Act, as the final settlement of records was published on 16 6 1931 by which certain kinds of property were to be dealt with; and (iii) the documents relied on by the defendants as containing assertions that they held under a grant in favour of the predecessors of the defend ant would not relate to the suit land. [1175 A B] Under section 36 of Regulation No. 8 of 1793 to hold that the assessed or Mal lands in an estate could have been held on an anterior Lakhejraj grant. It is well settled that it is beyond the powers of a manager management of a particular religious institution to grant perpetual lease binding the institution for all times to a fixed rent, unless there is a compelling necessity or benefit therefor. In the light of these principles it was not necessary for the courts below to raise it, if the facts in evidence went against it. [110 G] Attorney General vs Attorney General Vatna Chettiar, ; , referred to. Although on the facts found that no presumption of lost Grant could be raised in favour by the respondents as containing allegations that they hold under a rent free grant to the knowledge of the plaintiff prior to 1930 and that what all had been established by them was non payment of wages for a considerable period of time, that would clearly be beyond the power of a Mahant.

The appellant/plaintiff was the owner of certain agricultural land. The land was purchased by the respondent for a consideration of Rs. 42 lacs out of which Rs. 5,000 were paid as earnest money and a further amount of Rs 5,00 was paid on 22nd April 1966 when the period for performance of the contract for sale was extended by six months, which suit was dismissed by the trial Court and the plaintiff 's First Appeal No. 117/68 was dismissed but the appellant defendant claimed specific performance of a contract in respect of agricultural land, on the ground that the land was covered by the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 (Tenancy Act ' for short). The trial court held that the certificate had no evidentiary value and was not valid. On appeal the High Court affirmed the finding in favour of the appellant/ defendant holding that in view of the provisions contained in section 70(a) read with sections 85 and 85A of the Tenancy Act, the issue would have to be referred to the Mamlatdar for decision in accordance with the decision recorded by the competent authority on the relevant issues. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (1) in view Of the provisions laid down in section 85A, the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to settle, decided or deal with any question which is required to be settled, decided, or dealt with by any competent authority under the Tenancy and, therefore, civil court will have jurisdiction to decide the incidental or subsidiary issue and recorded a finding that the plaintiff was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Act; and (2) in a suit properly constituted civil suit the civil court had no jurisdiction to try the issue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The jurisdiction of Civil Court is ousted. [596C] 1st April 1957 and the person claiming to have become statutory owner by operation of law on that day should of necessity be a tenant and that this question would be within the exclusive jurisdiction of Mamlatdar under section 70 (mb) and that the District Judge was in error in dismissing the suit. [595A B] 2.(i) The scheme of sections 70 and 85 A is in pari materia with the scheme of ss.70, 85 and85A of tho Tenancy Act. Therefore, both on principle and on authority there is no escape from the conclusion that where in a civil suit properly brought before the Civil court an issue arises on rival contentions between the parties which is requiring to be decided by the revenue Court, then notwithstanding the fact that it arises in an incidental manner in a Civil suit cognizable by the Civil Judge, it would have been referred to.

The two assessee company was a heavy engineer manufacturing boilers, machinery parts, wagons etc. For the assessment years 1958 59 and 1959 60 the assessee claimed exemption of tax under section 15C of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 in respect of its profits and gains derived from its Jute Mill Division for the year 1959 60. The Income Tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner found that out of a total sale of Rs.28,23,127/ of steel castings goods worth about Rs.18,39,433/ were used in connection with the various Divisions of the Company. The income tax Officer and Appellate Assistant Commis sioner, on the facts, held that the assessee was maintaining separate books of account and that these were new undertakings. The Tribunal accepted both the claim for exemption under section15C of Income Tax 1922. According to the Tribunal the existing business of the asses see consisted of manufacturing boilers., wagons, etc. and for that purpose the assessee company wag purchasing the spare parts, forgings and castings from outside. Hence the Tribunal concluded that it could not be said that the undertakings were formed out of the existing "business" to come within the mischief of the exclusion clause in section 15 C(2)(i). The High Court held as follows: "The goods which the steel foundry division and the jute mill division began producing for the assessee were also previous ly used by the assessee in its business, but they were purchased from outside and this purchase from outside was replaced by produc tion or manufacture from within the assessee 's own business.

The Inam Commission confirmed the grants of the inams in favour of the hereditary officeholders, appointed persons to perform those services and placed the inams 'in their possession to be enjoyed by them as remuneration for the services to be rendered by them. The inam Commission confirmed grants in favour thereof, but the High Court dismissed their appeal. The respondents, who were holders of hereditary offices as remuneration from local income, contended that (1) the inam grants did not comprise the kudiwaram and melwaram rights in the land; (2) the inams were personal inams burdened with services and were not resumable under section 44 B; (3) section 44B was retrospective in operation and did not authorise resumption of the Inam on the ground of any alienation thereof made before 1934. Held, that the inam constituted both the warams, and the inamdars were regranted to the trustees of the temple appointed persons for performing those services. The inams were ' personal inams accompanied with service and under the directions of the Paisaldars or the trustees; (4) though the alienations were made before 1955, they were granted to the office holders as remuneration, for services to he rendered by the inamdar and were within the purview of section 44b(2)(i); (5) the right of resumption could not be extinguished by adverse possession. The Gokuladayam inams were granted 'to the hereditary offices, as remuneration under the staff of the Devasthanam, but that was subject to certain restrictions and safeguards. Held further, that in the present case, there was no period of limitation prescribed for the initiation of proceedings under section. 44 B(2) (a)(i).

The appellant Trust was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. By virtue of power conferred on it by section 2(c) of the Act the Municipality used to levy and collect house tax at the rate of 7% of such gross annual letting value less 10%. The respondent Municipality having refused refund the excess amount filed the suit to recover it on the ground that the excess rent was illegally recovered. The trial court decreed decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant Corporation came in appeal by special leave against the judgment and order of the High court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) Although by sec. 2 of the 1956 Act repealed the Indore city Municipal Act 1909 along with other Acts, the legislature by section 79 saved certain things done under the repealed Acts viz. rules bye laws, orders, notifications etc., made or imposed deemed to have been made, passed or imposed under the old Act but cl. (c) Of sec.2 provides expressly that when such a previous list is adopted for a particular official year it can be done subject to the procedure laid down in section 75 and 76. [129 E] (2) Under sections 75 and 77 the Municipal Corporation had to prepare a fresh assessment list every year. The legislature however has empowered by sec, 79 as other State Legislatures have similarly done in several Municipal Acts to adopt the valuation and assessment contained in the assessment list prepared in an earlier year provided, however, that it prepares a fresh list oncein every 4 years. But sub section 2 of sec. 79 provides expressly and cl.c) would not be attracted if the tax is assessed in the manner consistent with the provisions of sections 75, 76 and 79. [131 B C] (3) Although under the rules made under the 1922 Act the Corporation had imposed the tax on houses at the rates of a 7% per annum it was neither saved nor deemed to has been made under section 73(2). The saving and deeming provision in section 2 (c), there is no inconsistency between sec. 73, but that saving coupled with the fact that the assessment lists prepared for 1952 53 were adopted for the years in question made the entries in the assessments so adopted conclusive evidence of the annual letting values and the amount of tax assessed thereon and entitled the Corporation to collect the tax assessed on the gross annual assessable value less 5% statutory allowance.

The respondent Company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working its rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V Thomas at Medical. The Memorandum of Association provided that "the sale included chemicals and paper for manufacture which had not been sold in the course of ordinary trading but in a reali sation sale after the Company had been wound up . ". On May 9, 1943 the assessee company entered into an agreement with one Rao Sahib Natesa Iyer for the sale of the lands, buildings plant and machinery of its match factory for Rs. 5, 75,000. It was agreed that the price would not include manufactured goods, chemicals and other raw materials or any other asset not shown in the agreement of sale. The purchaser was allowed sixty days ' time for the payment of the balance of the price, Rs. 57,500 having been already paid at the time the agreement was "entered into". The purchaser made a default in payment, and on August 9, 1944 a fresh agreement was entered into between the parties, with which the assessee Company had agreed that it would not be included manufactured goods. The sale included Chemicals and raw materials for manufacture whereof had escaped assessment. The Income tax Officer took up the position that the match manufacturing had been stopped, and that business had been decided, and there thus only an appreciation of capital assets and not a trading profit. He also held that the sale could not be regarded as a realisation sale after it had the company wound up, but had the characteristics of a trading sale. At the request of the assesseecompany the Tribunal referred two questions to the High Court for its decision, and they were: (1) whether the transactions of sale of damaged chemicals and raw material was legally war ranted and whether there was legally a single transaction of the entire match factory inclusive of raw materials? and (2) Whether, in the circumstances of the case, the sum of Rs. 1, 15,259 and oddhas been rightly charged to income tax. The High Court on appeal held that by the sale no business was done; that the amount obtained was only by way of realisation sale and was not therefore liable to tax as a trading profits. The Department contended that the amounts of Rs 1,15,259 were properly brought to tax, and if profit resulted. Held, that where a slump price is paid and no portion is attributable to the stockiii trade it may not be possible to hold that there is a profit other than what results from the appreciation of the capital. The real thing that has to be decided here is what were the acts done in connection with this business and whether they amount to a trading which would 'cause the profits that accrued to be profits arising from a trade or business. In considering whether a particular case belongs to one category or the other it may have considered as determining what it is that his act amounts to; and the real thing has to he decided here was what were those acts done, in connection therewith. If the decision was applied to the present case, then the true answer would be the one given by the High court in the judgment under appeal.
